rationale: The framing assumptions the streaming translator rests on, read from a RAW upstream stream with no proxy and no provider stack in the way: a 200, a text/event-stream content type (the proxy answers 502 without it), the two payload types the tool arms key off — response.output_item.added and response.function_call_arguments.delta — and, the sharpest one, that no single event ever carries more than one data: line. That last is a spec-legal shape the proxy's splitter cannot handle: it feeds each data: line to the translator as a complete payload, so a multi-line event would arrive in fragments, fail to parse and be dropped in silence. Nothing else in the repo can establish any of this, because a fixture only proves the translators agree with themselves. P1.

rationale: The payoff for the whole budget-to-effort mapping, and the only end-to-end enforcement of it. Criticality is independent of that reach: configuration outlives the subscriptions it admitted, so a check made only at registration leaves an operator's containment with no effect on exactly the destinations they are trying to stop. The refusal is separated from a quarantine by asserting the quarantine count is zero and that delivery resumes immediately.

Publishing null does not throw. Measured greedy front at rank 88 with +2 spans and 2 exclusive spans. Kept high as the same non-interference promise the full-intake test makes, on the argument path rather than the capacity one - a publisher defect must not surface as an exception on the run that produced the event.

Lowered to P1 on the prefix rule: this declaration is outside the project P0 prefix, and the component already has a prefix-nominated P0 in Narrowing_the_allow_list_refuses_further_deliveries_and_leaves_a_visible_gap confirmed on its own contract. Held at P0 although outside the project P0 prefix: no declaration for this component is in the prefix, so the prefix nominated nothing here and the component would otherwise have no P0 pinning the contract named above.

Wiring approval before delivery and after it both yield the same publisher instance, a live approval preparer and exactly one remote gate. Enabling approval without delivery throws with both configuration section names in the message. Measured greedy front at rank 78 with +2 spans and 2 exclusive spans. A second call does not throw, the routes are unchanged and unique, and exactly one application part for this assembly is present. Measured greedy front at rank 93 with +2 spans and 2 exclusive spans. With only delivery enabled the bundle carries the disabled preparer, the live pipeline as its publisher and the system clock. Measured greedy front at rank 29 with +10 spans and 1 exclusive spans. Kept high because observing a run and gating it are separate opt-ins - the failure it excludes is turning on delivery and thereby blocking every tool call on a decision nobody has been asked for.

On a host that had no part for this assembly, enabling delivery publishes the two subscription routes, no authentication route, no approval route, and leaves the host's own controller published. Measured addsNothingNew over 169 spans. Kept above P2 for the last assertion - narrowing discovery means replacing MVC's default provider, which makes this method answerable for every other controller on the host.

With approval enabled the approvals route joins the subscription routes and the host's own, and no authentication route appears. Measured addsNothingNew over 195 spans. The delivery options bind the enabled flag and the allow-list, and two resolutions return the same instance. Measured addsNothingNew over 113 spans. Kept above P2 for the identity - registration, enqueue and every delivery attempt each re-check the destination, and a second binding could hold a different allow-list and admit at one moment what another refuses.

With both flags off the publisher, the pipeline, the multi-turn bundle and the approval store are all absent and no gate or hosted service is registered. Measured greedy front at rank 77 with +2 spans and 2 exclusive spans. Kept high because it is the whole opt-in claim stated as an absence over six registrations rather than one, and a background service started on a host that asked for nothing is work and exposure it never consented to.

The registry factory is untouched at construction and called exactly once when a thread owner is first resolved. Measured addsNothingNew over 10 spans. Kept above P2 because it is the other half of the deferral - a resolver that deferred and then never asked would answer no owner for everything and turn delivery off silently, which no wiring assertion would show.

With no resolver supplied, exactly one descriptor is registered and building it yields the sandbox resolver. Measured greedy front at rank 37 with +6 spans and 1 exclusive spans. Kept high because it is resolved rather than read off the descriptor - constructing the default must not reach for a sandbox registry, which on a host that has one depends on this object's own dependent.

A real host is built from configuration alone, started on a loopback port, and posted to: the subscriptions route answers a refusal rather than a not-found, the approvals route is matched, and both of this assembly's authentication routes are absent. Measured greedy front at rank 5 with +152 spans, the widest pick into the hosting extensions. Criticality is independent of that reach: a route table cannot show that a matched controller can actually be constructed, and the refusal is what proves every dependency resolved out of the real container - the failure it excludes is a published endpoint that answers a server error to an unauthenticated prober, announcing a misconfigured feature to anyone who asks. Component-scoped rather than a journey: the host is a fixture built by the test and a failure isolates to this wiring method.

The recorded handler-builder actions are replayed against a probe and the primary handler is found with automatic redirects off. Measured addsNothingNew over 114 spans. The contract this stands for is asserted end to end against a live redirecting subscriber elsewhere in this class, which proves the behaviour rather than the setting.

The pipeline, the publisher and the single hosted service are the same instance. Measured addsNothingNew over 190 spans. Kept above P2 because the hosted-service registration is what gives shutdown a live queue to drain - a second instance would drain an empty one while every event still in flight was abandoned with nothing reporting it.

On a started host with approval never enabled, the approval store is absent from the container and both subscription routes still answer a refusal rather than a server error. Measured greedy front at rank 98 with +2 spans and 2 exclusive spans. Kept high because delivery and approval are independent opt-ins and the controller takes the approval store as an optional parameter - if activation stopped honouring the default this host would answer a server error on every subscription request and no route-table assertion would notice.

With both flags off no lifecycle route is published, the host's own controller still is, and this assembly is not among the application parts. Measured addsNothingNew over 60 spans. Kept above P2 for the part assertion - a route that refuses tells a prober the feature is here while one that was never registered tells them nothing, and adding the part would publish every controller in the assembly rather than only the ones asked for.

A stranger's unregister is refused the way an id that never existed is refused, the pipeline's own abandon entry point is then called directly with the wrong owner and with an unknown id, and both deliveries still complete. Measured greedy front at rank 112 with +1 spans and 1 exclusive spans. Kept high because the controller's refusal means the pipeline's own owner check is never reached by the route above, so it is exercised directly - it is the check that has to hold if any other caller is ever wired to that entry point.
uncertainties: multi-component: exercises the registry, pipeline, approval store and controller together, so it has no single owning type

rationale: A pending approval naming the revoked subscription as its only approver settles as denied, attributed to the approver that left, for the right request, and the admission slot is freed. Measured greedy front at rank 24 with +16 spans. Kept high because unanimity makes the outcome already settled once an approver is gone, so leaving it pending blocks the gated tool call until its expiry for no possible benefit - and the wait is bounded so the regression it guards against fails rather than wedges.
uncertainties: multi-component: exercises the registry, pipeline, approval store and controller together, so it has no single owning type

rationale: With one attempt parked mid-flight and three deliveries queued behind it, revoking leaves exactly one attempt made while the un-revoked arm of the same race makes all four. Measured greedy front at rank 113 with +1 spans and 1 exclusive spans. Kept high for the control arm - without it a regression that lost the backlog for an unrelated reason would satisfy the assertion that matters - and because the backlog holds bodies serialized and signed while the subscription was still live.
uncertainties: multi-component: exercises the registry, pipeline, approval store and controller together, so it has no single owning type

rationale: With the queue empty and a worker asleep on a retry timer over an already-signed body, unregistering through the real controller leaves the retry unsent once the clock is advanced past the backoff band, and imposes no quarantine. Measured greedy front at rank 2 with +602 spans and 2 exclusive spans, the second-widest pick in this project, because it runs the registry, the pipeline, the redactor and the controller against one another. Criticality is independent of that reach: this is the case an unregister-only implementation is least likely to have considered, since nothing is enqueued for a stop-fanning-out fix to catch. The quarantine assertion is the second half - a cool-off is destination-scoped, so laundering a voluntary revocation as one would penalize every other subscription sharing that host.
uncertainties: multi-component: exercises the registry, pipeline, approval store and controller together, so it has no single owning type

rationale: Five callbacks are refused with their own distinct reasons: an ftp and a file scheme and a url carrying user info as invalid, plaintext as not-https, and an unlisted host as not-allowed. Measured greedy front at rank 32 with +9 spans and 3 exclusive spans, the widest pick into this class. Kept high because each row is a different way to turn the delivery path into an outbound request the operator never authorised, and they are distinguished by reason rather than merely by throwing.

A zero maximum is refused at construction with the offending option named. Measured greedy front at rank 57 with +3 spans and 3 exclusive spans. Kept high because the alternative is a registry that refuses every registration for capacity at runtime, which reads as a load problem rather than a configuration one.
A null owner throws on both the register and the listing entry points. Measured addsNothingNew over 79 spans. Argument guards that separate a wiring bug from a caller error.

A null callback uri is refused as invalid. Measured addsNothingNew over 99 spans. A guard on a field the type system already marks required; the difference it makes is a rejection rather than a server error.

Rotating a stranger's real subscription and rotating an id that was never minted produce the same rejection reason and the same message text, and neither message names the id. Measured addsNothingNew over 211 spans. Kept above P2 because any observable difference between the two turns the control plane into an oracle for which subscription ids exist, and message equality is asserted rather than merely the reason.

After a refusal the owner has no subscriptions. Measured addsNothingNew over 153 spans. Kept above P2 because a slot consumed by a rejected registration is a capacity exhaustion any caller can drive with malformed requests alone.

A refusal for a callback carrying a token in its query names the host and contains neither the url, the path, nor the token. Measured addsNothingNew over 117 spans. Kept above P2 because a per-subscriber token lives in exactly that query string, and a rejection message is written to logs the subscriber never sees.

A relative callback uri is refused as invalid. Measured greedy front at rank 62 with +3 spans. Kept high because a relative uri has no host to check against the allow list, so anything that resolved it later would bypass the check entirely.

A bare star, a prefixed star and a suffixed star are each refused. Measured greedy front at rank 89 with +2 spans. Kept high because a granted wildcard is a privilege escalation that grows silently as capabilities are added in later builds.

A bare star and a prefixed star event type are each refused. Measured addsNothingNew over 134 spans. The wildcard rule is pinned by its capability sibling, and an empty list already means every type, so a wildcard grants nothing new.

A well-formed but never-minted id, an empty string and whitespace each fail the lookup and are refused as not authorised by all three mutating entry points. Measured greedy front at rank 87 with +2 spans and 2 exclusive spans. Kept high because the alternative is a null dereference on the blank rows, which is a fault rather than a refusal.

A host listed in mixed case accepts a lower-case callback. Measured addsNothingNew over 189 spans. Kept above P2 as the false-rejection direction of the allow list - an ordinal comparison satisfies every rejection test in this class and turns away operators who capitalised their own configuration.

With delivery enabled and no host listed, both an https and a plaintext callback are refused as not allowed. Measured addsNothingNew over 114 spans. Kept above P2 because the failure direction it excludes is the worst one available here - an empty list read as no restriction makes the host an open outbound relay pointed wherever a caller asks.

An empty capability list registers and holds no capability. Measured addsNothingNew over 190 spans. Kept above P2 as the opposite default from its event-type sibling - read as everything, it would grant every capability to a subscriber that asked for none.

An empty event-type list registers and accepts a type it never named. Measured addsNothingNew over 190 spans. Kept above P2 because empty means everything here while empty capabilities mean nothing, and reading the two uniformly is a defect in whichever direction it is made.

A freshly minted owner key for the same app finds the subscription registered under an earlier one. Measured addsNothingNew over 198 spans. Kept above P2 because the resolver hands back a new instance per request - were the key compared by reference every caller would see an empty registry.

A request mixing a known capability with an unknown one is refused rather than filtered. Measured addsNothingNew over 146 spans. Kept above P2 because dropping it leaves the caller believing it holds a permission it never got, and building on that belief far from the registration that failed.

A request mixing a known and an unknown event type is refused. Measured addsNothingNew over 152 spans. The same refuse-rather-than-drop rule its capability sibling states, and the failure here is a subscriber that receives nothing rather than one that believes it holds a permission.

Two known capabilities and one known event type register and are readable back, and an event type that was not asked for is not accepted. Measured greedy front at rank 95 with +2 spans. Kept high as the accept direction of the whole validation family, and for the negative on the unlisted event type, which is what the fan-out filters on.

Two registrations under the same owner get different ids and different secrets. Measured addsNothingNew over 189 spans. Kept above P2 because reusing either would make one subscriber's leaked key another subscriber's working key.

A listing taken before an unregister and a register still holds the original two subscriptions, while a fresh listing reflects the change. Measured addsNothingNew over 226 spans. Kept above P2 because the fan-out iterates this list - a live view would either throw mid-broadcast or silently skip subscribers.

A listing under one owner returns only that owner's subscription. Measured addsNothingNew over 204 spans. Kept above P2 because this is the enumeration route rather than the by-id route, and it is what the delivery fan-out reads.

The grant, the subscription and its signing secret all stringify without the minted key, and the grant says it is redacted. Measured greedy front at rank 70 with +3 spans and 2 exclusive spans. Kept high because the failure is a signing key in every log line that ever interpolates one of these objects.

With the https requirement switched off, a plaintext localhost callback registers. Measured addsNothingNew over 189 spans. Kept above P2 because it is the only test proving the switch is read at all - the rejection theory beside it would pass equally if the requirement were a constant.

A third registration against a cap of two is refused for capacity. Measured addsNothingNew over 193 spans. The concurrent capacity test asserts the same limit and additionally the exact accepted and refused counts.

A registration returns an id, a sixty-four character secret, the owner and app it was made under, the injected clock's instant, and is immediately retrievable as the same object. Measured addsNothingNew over 201 spans. Kept above P2 as the non-vacuity partner of this whole class - every other test here asserts a refusal or a scoping failure - and for the secret length, which is what makes the minted key as strong as the fallback.

A stranger cannot end another owner's rotation overlap, and the original key still verifies. Measured addsNothingNew over 261 spans. Kept above P2 as the third entry point taking the same id - the one most easily forgotten because it was added with rotation rather than with the original surface.

After a rotation, revoking drops the previous key immediately while the current one keeps verifying. Measured greedy front at rank 22 with +20 spans. Kept high because revocation is the compromise response for a leaked subscriber key, and one that waited for the window to close would leave it usable for the rest of it.

A stranger's rotation is refused as not authorised and the real owner's key still verifies afterwards. Measured addsNothingNew over 239 spans. Kept above P2 because each entry point takes the same subscription id and each needs its own scoping check, and this one asserts the refused call had no effect rather than only that it threw.

Rotating one subscription leaves a second subscription's key verifying. Measured addsNothingNew over 250 spans. Kept above P2 because it is the only test proving the secrets are per subscription rather than host-wide - a shared secret would make every rotation a broadcast outage.

Rotating mints a different secret on the same subscription object, and deliveries signed under either key still verify. Measured addsNothingNew over 253 spans. Kept above P2 because signing with the old key and refusing the old one are opposite mistakes and both are caught here, and because rotation replacing the subscription rather than its key would break every reference the fan-out holds.

Sixty-four threads register against a registry capped at four; exactly four succeed with distinct ids, the other sixty are refused for capacity, and the registry holds four afterwards. Measured addsNothingNew over 210 spans, its reach already taken within this class by the rotation tests. Kept above P2 because a check-then-add loses this race silently - every thread reads the same free slot and takes it - and the assertion is on the exact count rather than on roughly the limit.

With the clock advanced by the configured overlap the old secret no longer verifies and the new one still does. Measured addsNothingNew over 253 spans. Kept above P2 because an overlap that never closed would leave every retired subscriber key valid forever, and it is the registry's own configured window that is asserted rather than a default.

A registry constructed from options with delivery disabled still registers. Measured addsNothingNew over 187 spans. A deliberate absence of a check, asserted where the host is the component that owns the switch.

A lookup under the wrong owner fails and leaves the out parameter null. Measured addsNothingNew over 198 spans. Kept above P2 for the second half - a failed lookup that still hands back the object it refused is a disclosure that a false return value does nothing to stop.

A stranger's unregister is refused and the subscription is still retrievable by its owner. Measured addsNothingNew over 211 spans. Kept above P2 as the destructive member of the same family - an unscoped unregister lets any caller delete any subscriber's delivery.

With a cap of one, unregistering allows a fresh registration. Measured addsNothingNew over 211 spans. Kept above P2 because a slot that is never returned turns the configured maximum into a lifetime quota that only a restart clears.

After an unregister the subscription is gone from the by-id lookup and the owner listing, and rotating it is refused. Measured addsNothingNew over 229 spans. Kept above P2 because removal from one index and not another leaves a subscription that still receives deliveries but can no longer be managed.

Six callbacks the registry refuses - unlisted host, plaintext, credentials in the url, relative, unparseable and absent - are each answered as a bad request carrying the registry's wording, with nothing registered. Measured addsNothingNew over 169 spans. Kept above P2 because these are the fail-closed egress rules, and the failure direction it excludes is a refusal surfacing as a server error the caller retries or, worse, as a registration.

An unknown capability and a wildcard are each refused, and nothing at all is registered. Measured addsNothingNew over 188 spans. Kept above P2 for the second assertion - registering without the refused capability would leave the caller holding a subscription it believes carries a permission it never got.

An anonymous principal is refused with a message naming authentication, never reaches owner resolution, and registers nothing. Measured addsNothingNew over 108 spans. Kept above P2 because it is the case the not-an-app refusal is distinguished from, so the message it asserts is what keeps the two apart for whoever reads them.

A disabled host answers a registration as not found, registers nothing and asks the resolver nothing. Measured addsNothingNew over 92 spans. Kept above P2 because a half-wired host that left this controller reachable must look like one with nothing to find rather than announce a feature it is not running.
A null body is refused as a bad request. Measured addsNothingNew over 98 spans. A binding guard, and the leak sweep already exercises this branch for what it may say.

A registration returns created with a subscription id, the callback it asked for, a secret, the injected clock's instant and no error. Measured addsNothingNew over 234 spans. Kept above P2 as the non-vacuity partner of this whole class - a controller that refused every registration would satisfy most of the twelve refusals beside it - and because this is the one response in which the secret is ever readable.

The resolver is asked about exactly the authenticated app id, the subscription becomes visible under that owner, and the other owner sees nothing. Measured addsNothingNew over 245 spans. Kept above P2 because the body carries no owner field by design, so the only thing that decides which tenant a callback is filed under is the identity the controller hands the resolver.

An action invoked with no request context is refused rather than throwing, and resolves nobody. Measured addsNothingNew over 93 spans. Kept above P2 because the principal is nullable and dereferencing it turns a refusal into a server error, which is a different answer to the caller and a different signal to an operator.

Kept above P2 because this is a fixed defect rather than a hypothetical - a subject claim read as an app identity let every signed-in user register a callback and collect a signing secret - and because forging both claims is what stops a half-fix passing.

A caller whose app id the resolver cannot place is refused, and the resolver was asked exactly that id. Measured addsNothingNew over 92 spans. Kept above P2 because it is the only test proving a null from the resolver is honoured rather than treated as an absence of opinion.

A principal authenticated by some scheme but naming no app is refused without reaching owner resolution. Measured greedy front at rank 85 with +2 spans. Kept high because there is no safe default to fall back to here, and resolving an owner from anything else is how a callback ends up filed under an identity that is not an app.

A registration naming neither capabilities nor event types is created with both lists empty. Measured addsNothingNew over 229 spans. An unknown event type is answered as a bad request. Measured addsNothingNew over 184 spans. The same refuse-rather-than-drop mapping its capability sibling asserts, and without that sibling's check that nothing was registered.

A never-minted id, another owner's id and a host with delivery switched off all return the same status and byte-identical bodies. Measured addsNothingNew over 268 spans. Kept above P2 because any observable difference makes the control plane an oracle for which subscription ids exist, and comparing serialised bytes rather than objects is what makes that assertion mean what it says.

Null, empty and whitespace ids are refused with the parameter named. Measured addsNothingNew over 11 spans. An argument guard whose failure is immediate.

An id registered once is accepted again six minutes into a five-minute window. Measured greedy front at rank 58 with +3 spans and 3 exclusive spans - expiry is reached by no other test in this project. Kept high because a cache that never expired would grow without bound and eventually reject legitimate reuse.

Ten ids at distinct increasing times fill a cache capped at eight; the newest is still remembered and the oldest is not. Measured addsNothingNew over 54 spans. Kept above P2 because it pins which entries the cap sheds, and shedding the newest first would leave the cache holding only deliveries too old to be replayed.

A first sighting registers and the same id thirty seconds later does not. Measured addsNothingNew over 40 spans. Kept above P2 as the cache's whole contract stated in one place, and as the non-vacuity partner of the eviction tests.

A zero and a negative cap are each refused at construction. Measured greedy front at rank 74 with +2 spans and 2 exclusive spans. Kept high for the same reason as its window sibling - a cap of zero holds nothing and accepts every replay.

A zero and a negative window are each refused at construction with the parameter named. Measured greedy front at rank 73 with +2 spans and 2 exclusive spans. Kept high because the failure it prevents is silent: a non-positive window expires every entry as it is written, so the cache accepts every replay while appearing to work.
Two different ids both register. Measured addsNothingNew over 34 spans. The half of the duplicate test that has to hold for it to mean anything, asserted there too.

Twenty ids are registered into a cache capped at four, and the most recent is still recognised as a replay. Measured greedy front at rank 23 with +16 spans. Kept high because amortised sweeping is where a cap silently turns into no cache at all - a sweep that dropped everything would leave every later delivery accepted twice.
Null, empty and whitespace delivery ids are refused with the parameter named. Measured addsNothingNew over 24 spans. An argument guard on the sending side, mirrored by the cache's own.
A body changed after signing is refused as an invalid signature. Measured addsNothingNew over 95 spans. The verifier's own tampered-body test asserts the same decision.

Two signatures of the same body get different delivery ids and both verify. Measured greedy front at rank 86 with +2 spans and 2 exclusive spans - the generated-id path is reached by no other test in this project. Kept high because a repeated id would be rejected as a replay by the receiver's cache, turning every second legitimate send into a conflict.

A delivery signed before the receiver rotates is still accepted after it. Measured addsNothingNew over 102 spans. Kept above P2 because it is the only test joining the signer, the receiver's rotated secret and the verifier, which is the exact scenario dual-key rotation exists for and the one an operator will hit during a real rotation.

Applying the headers to a request message puts the signature, timestamp and delivery id under their wire names, one value each. Measured addsNothingNew over 14 spans. Kept above P2 because these names are the contract with every receiver, and a rename round-trips perfectly between this repository's own signer and verifier while breaking every peer.

Stamping the same request twice leaves one signature value, the second. Measured addsNothingNew over 14 spans. Kept above P2 because a retry re-stamps the same message object, and two signature values is a request no receiver resolves the way the sender intended.

A request signed at one time and verified ten minutes later is refused as stale. Measured addsNothingNew over 85 spans. Kept above P2 because it pins that the timestamp comes from the sender's clock rather than the receiver's - stamped at receipt, a delayed delivery would always look fresh and the freshness window would be decorative.

Headers produced by the signer are put through the verifier and accepted, with the timestamp asserted to be Unix seconds. Measured addsNothingNew over 95 spans. Kept above P2 because the two sides are separate implementations - a signer that agreed only with itself would be worse than none - and the wire form of the timestamp is pinned to a literal here rather than round-tripped through the same formatter.

A request signed with the configured secret over the exact body, timestamp and delivery id is accepted. Measured addsNothingNew over 80 spans. Kept above P2 as the non-vacuity partner of this whole class - a verifier that rejected everything would satisfy all eleven negatives beside it and fail only this one.

A timestamp ten minutes ahead of the verifier's clock is refused. Measured greedy front at rank 60 with +3 spans and 3 exclusive spans - the forward half of the window is reached by no other test in this project. Kept high because a one-sided freshness check passes the past-direction test while leaving a signature valid arbitrarily far into the future.

A JSON content type carrying a charset parameter is accepted. Measured addsNothingNew over 80 spans. Kept above P2 as the false-rejection direction of the media-type check - an exact string comparison would satisfy every rejection test here and turn away most real senders.

Each of the three headers is omitted in turn and every case is refused as missing headers. Measured addsNothingNew over 46 spans. Kept above P2 because the rows are individually omitted rather than omitted together, so a check covering only two of the three would fail here.

A text content type, an empty one and a missing one are each refused. Measured greedy front at rank 50 with +4 spans and 2 exclusive spans. Kept high for the null and empty rows, which are the cases a hand-rolled prefix comparison throws on rather than rejects.

A captured callback resent with a fresh delivery id - the change that would dodge the replay cache - fails on the signature before the cache is consulted. Measured greedy front at rank 104 with +1 spans and 1 exclusive spans. Kept high because it is what makes the duplicate-delivery rejection meaningful; if the id were outside the signed payload an attacker would simply pick a new one.

A captured request has only its timestamp swapped to dodge the staleness check, and the signature no longer matches. Measured greedy front at rank 103 with +1 spans and 1 exclusive spans. Kept high because it is the test that proves the timestamp is inside the signed payload rather than beside it - if it were not, every stale capture could be refreshed and resent.

A timestamp ten minutes old is refused. Measured addsNothingNew over 70 spans. Kept above P2 because the freshness window is what bounds how long a captured request stays useful, and this is the direction an observer actually replays from.

A valid request whose body is swapped after signing is refused as an invalid signature. Measured greedy front at rank 84 with +2 spans and 1 exclusive spans. Kept high because this is the layer's reason to exist: the signature has to bind the exact bytes, not merely be present and well-formed.

A body twice the configured cap is refused as too large even though it is correctly signed. Measured greedy front at rank 80 with +2 spans and 2 exclusive spans. Kept high because this is the verifier's own cap, which applies to every caller of it, not only to requests that arrive through the middleware.
A provider outside the configured set is refused. Measured addsNothingNew over 47 spans. The middleware test asserts the same decision together with the status it maps to.

A timestamp that is not a number at all is refused as stale rather than throwing. Measured greedy front at rank 43 with +5 spans and 3 exclusive spans - the parse failure path is reached by no other test in this project. Kept high because the header is attacker-controlled and an escaping format exception is a denial of service rather than a rejection.

Null, empty, non-hex, odd-length and free-text signature headers each return false. Measured greedy front at rank 42 with +5 spans and 5 exclusive spans - the malformed-input path is reached by no other test in this project. Kept high because the header is attacker-controlled and a format exception escaping into the pipeline is a fault rather than a rejection.

A key this deployment never held does not verify during an overlap. Measured addsNothingNew over 51 spans. The two-key-set test already asserts that only the current and immediately previous keys verify.

A signature made with the configured secret verifies. Measured addsNothingNew over 41 spans. Kept above P2 as the non-vacuity partner of this class - a secret that matched nothing would satisfy every negative here.

A rotation with no overlap leaves no previous key and the old signature stops verifying at once. Measured addsNothingNew over 55 spans. Kept above P2 because it is the boundary of the deadline comparison - an inclusive test at the deadline would keep the old key alive here while passing the lapse test above.

With a null, empty or whitespace configured secret a key is still generated and a signature made with the well-known test secret does not verify. Measured addsNothingNew over 43 spans. Kept above P2 because this is the fail-closed branch: the alternative failure direction is a deployment that skipped its secret accepting every caller, which nothing else here would catch.

After a twenty-four-hour rotation overlap, revoking stops the previous key verifying without advancing the clock, while the current key still does. Measured addsNothingNew over 65 spans. Kept above P2 because revocation is the compromise response, and one that only took effect at the end of the window would leave a leaked key live for a day.

Revoking when no rotation has happened leaves the current key verifying. Measured greedy front at rank 79 with +2 spans and 2 exclusive spans. Kept high because the failure it excludes is a revocation that clears the only key the deployment has, which is a total outage triggered by an operator doing the safe thing.

After two rotations inside one overlap the newest and its immediate predecessor verify and the original does not. Measured addsNothingNew over 53 spans. Kept above P2 because the active set has to stay exactly two - an accumulating list would keep every key ever configured verifying, widening the window each rotation was meant to close.
A whitespace secret and a negative overlap are each refused with the parameter named. Measured addsNothingNew over 19 spans. Argument guards on an operator-driven call whose failure is immediate.

After rotating, the signature produced is the new key's while both keys verify. Measured greedy front at rank 81 with +2 spans. Kept high because signing with the old key or refusing the old one are opposite mistakes and both are caught here.

Ten minutes into a ten-minute overlap the previous key no longer verifies and the current one still does. Measured addsNothingNew over 57 spans. Kept above P2 because an overlap that never closed would leave every retired key valid forever, and the deadline is driven by a hand-advanced clock rather than a wait.

The string form omits the secret and says it is redacted. Measured addsNothingNew over 17 spans. Kept above P2 because the failure is a signing key written into every log line that ever interpolates the object, which no functional test would reveal.

Two independently generated fallback keys do not accept each other's signatures. Measured addsNothingNew over 41 spans. The generation is already shown to be unguessable by the fail-closed test beside it.

A request declaring one byte but carrying more is rejected once the read passes the cap. Measured greedy front at rank 36 with +6 spans and 6 exclusive spans - the bounded read is reached by no other test in this project. Kept high because the declared length is attacker-controlled, so a cap enforced only on the header is no cap at all.

An oversized declared length is refused without reaching the downstream term. Measured greedy front at rank 61 with +3 spans and 3 exclusive spans - the header pre-check is reached by no other test in this project. Kept high because it is the cheap half of the pair: without it every oversized body is streamed before being rejected.

A request with no delivery header is refused as a bad request. Measured greedy front at rank 65 with +3 spans and 1 exclusive spans. Kept at P2 as a status-map row; which headers are required is settled in the verifier tests. Raised to P1 by the exclusive-span floor: it is a front member outside the P0 prefix holding 1 exclusive spans, so dropping it would leave those product spans with no exerciser at any tier. The contract assessment above is unchanged.

A bare prefix, an empty provider segment and a suffixed path each pass through unverified. Measured addsNothingNew over 58 spans. The same three cases the route-predicate test asserts directly, driven here through a whole request.

A text content type is refused with an unsupported-media-type status. Measured greedy front at rank 107 with +1 spans and 1 exclusive spans. Kept at P2 as another status-map row over a decision the verifier tests already settle. Raised to P1 by the exclusive-span floor: it is a front member outside the P0 prefix holding 1 exclusive spans, so dropping it would leave those product spans with no exerciser at any tier. The contract assessment above is unchanged.
A GET on the guarded path passes through unverified. Measured addsNothingNew over 58 spans. Asserted directly by the route-predicate test.

A rejected request gets a plain-text response content type. Measured greedy front at rank 31 with +9 spans. Kept at P2 despite that reach because the only assertion is the content type - the spans are the same rejection path the status-code rows already drive.

The same correctly signed callback is delivered twice through the middleware against one shared replay cache: the first reaches the downstream term, the second is a conflict that does not. Measured greedy front at rank 4 with +166 spans and 5 exclusive spans, the widest pick in this project - route matching, the size cap, the verifier and the replay cache all run, twice. Criticality is independent of that reach: everything else in this layer rejects a forged request, and this is the one test that rejects a genuine one sent again, which is the vector a network observer actually has. Both signatures are valid, so only the cache can separate them.

A request to an unrelated path reaches the downstream term with a deliberately garbage signature. Measured greedy front at rank 44 with +5 spans. Kept high because this is the permissive direction that keeps the middleware from becoming an application-wide signature demand, and a mistake here takes down every other route in the host.

A timestamp ten minutes old is refused with the same unauthorized status as a bad signature. Measured greedy front at rank 109 with +1 spans. Kept at P2 because the staleness decision itself is pinned in the verifier tests and the indistinguishability is a deliberate non-disclosure rather than a behaviour a caller depends on.

An accepted request reaches the downstream term and the body it reads back is byte-for-byte what was sent. Measured addsNothingNew over 164 spans, its reach already taken by the replay test. Kept above P2 for the rewind: the middleware consumes the stream to compute the HMAC, so without it every downstream model bind sees an empty body - a total outage of the webhook route that no rejection test would notice.

A request whose signature does not match is refused with an unauthorized status and does not reach the downstream term. Measured addsNothingNew over 146 spans. Kept above P2 because it is the default arm of the status map and the one rejection that must never pass, and it asserts the downstream was not reached rather than only the status.

An unconfigured provider segment is refused with a not-found status and the rejection reason in the body. Measured addsNothingNew over 117 spans. One of a family of status-map rows; the decision it maps is settled in the verifier tests.
A null next-delegate and null limits are each refused with the parameter named. Measured addsNothingNew over 40 spans. Construction guards that fail loudly at startup.

Five paths and methods are put to the route predicate directly: the exact route matches, a differently cased one matches, and a GET, a bare prefix and a suffixed path do not. Measured addsNothingNew over 8 spans. Kept above P2 because it is the only place both directions of the predicate are enumerated, including the case-insensitivity that a real proxy will eventually exercise.

A capacity resolver the host registered first survives the library's registration. Measured addsNothingNew over 22 spans. The same guard the pricing registration test pins on the neighbouring line of the same method, and that one is on the measured front.

Registering the catalog yields a resolvable capacity service that answers with the configured window. Measured greedy front at rank 7 with +58 spans and 2 exclusive spans. Kept high on the coverage warrant - the registration path pulls in the whole catalog build - though its own assertions are a presence check and one window value. In the project P0 prefix and deliberately held there at P1: prefix membership nominates a candidate rather than conferring a tier, and the contract above is a component-level guarantee rather than the critical baseline a component-scoped P0 run is built from.

Five lookups - a model with no capabilities, a zero window under both its names, an unknown name and the empty string - all resolve to nothing. No spans were attributed to this test in the capture, which for a body that builds and queries a resolver is a capture gap. Kept above P2 because a utilization computed against a window of zero is not a number a caller can act on, and zero is exactly what an omitted section leaves behind.

A name two models claim with different windows resolves to nothing while each model still answers under its own id. No spans were attributed to this test in the capture. Kept above P2 because it is the capacity mirror of the pricing conflict rule and asserts both halves - the ambiguous name goes dark and the unambiguous ones do not.

A model whose maximum output is left at zero resolves with a window but an unknown output limit rather than a limit of zero. Measured greedy front at rank 43 with +1 span and 1 exclusive span. Kept above P2 because zero is what the binder leaves for an omitted value, and a caller that believed it would refuse to request any output at all.

The window and output limit answer under the catalog id, the provider's model name and an upper-case spelling of the id. Measured addsNothingNew over 87 spans. Kept above P2 because a generation is stamped with whichever name the layer that served it used, so a resolver answering only one of them reports no utilization for the others.
A catalog bound with no models at all yields a resolver that answers nothing rather than throwing at construction. Measured addsNothingNew over 24 spans. A null tolerance guard on the build path.

Every category rate, the accounting mode and the effective date survive the configuration binder and arrive on the resolved pricing. Measured addsNothingNew over 146 spans. Kept above P2 because the binder matches property names while the JSON path matches the wire names, so the round-trip test cannot cover this route - a key that binds under one and not the other is exactly the drift this catches.

When one route publishes rates and its sibling publishes none, both the shared catalog id and the unpriced route resolve to nothing while the priced route keeps its rates. No spans were attributed to this test in the capture, which for a body that builds a service provider and queries the resolver is a capture gap. Kept above P2 because absence is treated as disagreement rather than as something to fill in from the sibling, which is the case a conflict rule comparing only published rates would get wrong.

A provider bound from configuration with no pricing section at all resolves to nothing under both its names instead of throwing out of the registration lambda. Measured greedy front at rank 19 with +12 spans and 2 exclusive spans. Kept high because the configuration binder does not enforce required members the way the JSON entry points do, so this is the documented entry point where a null rate can appear, and the failure it pins took down any host that merely resolved the service.

A resolver the host registered first survives the library's own registration. Measured greedy front at rank 42 with +1 span and 1 exclusive span. Kept above P2 because the failure is silent and total - a host with an authoritative catalog would have every cost figure recomputed from the library's catalog instead, with nothing to indicate the substitution.

Registering the catalog yields a resolvable pricing service whose answers carry the library's provenance string and whose estimate for a stated token split is asserted as an exact figure. Measured addsNothingNew over 112 spans. Kept above P2 because the arithmetic assertion is the number that lands on the usage record, and it is checked here against hand-computed micro-units rather than against the resolver's own output.

A catalog id written in mixed case answers a lookup in upper case. Measured greedy front at rank 26 with +7 spans. Kept above P2 because usage records carry whatever casing the provider stamped, so a case-sensitive dictionary silently prices nothing for a whole model.

Two routes agreeing on base rates keep resolving under their shared name. Measured addsNothingNew over 27 spans. The identical-full-rates test in this file makes the same point over every category rather than the base pair.

A name two providers price differently resolves to nothing, while each provider's own unambiguous name keeps its rate. Measured greedy front at rank 29 with +6 spans and 6 exclusive spans. Kept high as the central judgement of this component - a usage record carries a model name and never the route that served it, so picking either rate produces a confident wrong number that is summed and believed downstream. The strongest promotion candidate here if the lead wants a second pricing P0.

Two routes with identical base rates but different cache read rates conflict, so the shared name goes dark while each route's own name keeps its own cache rate. No spans were attributed to this test in the capture, which for a body that plainly builds and queries a resolver is a capture gap rather than a statement about its reach. Kept above P2 because it is the case that proves the conflict comparison looks past the base rates.

Two routes differing only in accounting mode conflict and the shared name resolves to nothing. No spans were attributed to this test in the capture. Its single assertion is one field of the whole-record comparison the cache-rate variant already makes, and that one additionally checks each route still resolves on its own.

Two routes agreeing on every category rate, accounting mode and effective date still resolve under their shared name. Measured greedy front at rank 20 with +11 spans and 11 exclusive spans. Kept high because the conflict rule is a whole-record comparison - a comparison that looked only at the base rates or that compared by reference would drop most of a real catalog, where one model is listed identically under several providers.

One provider registers under both the catalog id and its own model name, with rates and provenance asserted under each. Measured addsNothingNew over 113 spans. Kept above P2 as the non-vacuity partner for the several null-returning cases in this file - a resolver that answered nothing for everything would satisfy all of them.

A sub-provider's own rates answer under its own model name while the parent provider's name keeps the parent's rates. Measured addsNothingNew over 9 spans. Kept above P2 because a request routed through the sub-provider is billed at its rates, so collapsing the two would misprice every routed request in one direction or the other.

A catalog-built resolver returns nothing for a name it does not know. Measured greedy front at rank 10 with +44 spans and 41 exclusive spans. Kept high on the coverage warrant rather than the assertion, which is a single null check - the catalog-building path it drags in is reached by no other test at this point in the greedy order. In the project P0 prefix and deliberately held there at P1: prefix membership nominates a candidate rather than conferring a tier, and the contract above is a component-level guarantee rather than the critical baseline a component-scoped P0 run is built from.

A pricing entry written before the category rates existed deserializes with its cache rates absent, no effective date, and the accounting mode defaulting to the subset reading rather than the additive one. Measured greedy front at rank 4 with +123 spans, the widest single pick in this project's pricing surface. Criticality is independent: the default it pins decides whether cached input tokens are counted once or twice, so getting it wrong does not fail - it silently changes every cost figure computed from every legacy catalog entry, and the file's own comments say a confidently wrong number is the outcome this component exists to avoid.

The category rates, accounting mode and effective date serialize under their snake case wire names and the record compares equal after a round trip. Measured addsNothingNew over 29 spans. Kept above P2 because the catalog on disk is written in those names - a renamed property would leave the key unread and the rate silently absent.

A directly constructed resolver returns rates, provenance and an exact estimate for a known model. No spans were attributed to this test in the capture. Provenance and the estimate arithmetic are both asserted again by the registration test, and the category mapping test covers the same constructor with a fuller record.

A legacy entry priced with only base rates reports partial completeness for a record carrying cache reads, and the estimate is asserted as an exact figure that excludes the unpriced reads rather than charging them at the base rate or at nothing. Measured addsNothingNew over 66 spans. Kept above P2 for the completeness signal, which is what tells a consumer the number is incomplete instead of small.

Every rate category, the null reasoning rate, the accounting mode, the effective date and both provenance fields are mapped from the config record onto the resolved pricing. Measured addsNothingNew over 55 spans. Kept above P2 because it is the field-by-field mapping check - a category dropped in the mapping would leave a rate silently unpriced everywhere else in this file.
A directly constructed resolver returns nothing for an unknown name. Measured addsNothingNew over 128 spans. A one-line restatement of the catalog-built unknown case.

A cache stamped a day in the future is refused and the service recovers to a valid one. Measured addsNothingNew over 524 spans. Statement for statement the missing-models-data test with a different bad field, and the future-timestamp rule it depends on is asserted directly by the validation test that calls the predicate.

A cache file that parses but carries no models payload is refused, and the service refetches, remaps, saves and ends holding a cache it reports as valid. Measured greedy front at rank 1 with +524 spans, the first pick in this project and the widest single block of it. Criticality is independent of that reach: the whole cold-start path runs here - load, integrity check, fetch, map, atomic save, revalidate - and the defect it alone catches end to end is a service that trusts a structurally empty cache, which returns an empty catalog and makes every downstream model resolution fail as unknown-model with no error anywhere to explain it. The validity rule itself is pinned directly by the reflection-level validation tests. what this adds is that rejection actually recovers.
A two-model cache must be read and mapped in under a hundred milliseconds. Measured addsNothingNew over 344 spans. A wall-clock budget rather than a behaviour contract.
uncertainties: A fixed hundred-millisecond ceiling with no baseline to compare against, so it is sensitive to a loaded machine, to first-call JIT of the mapping path and to cold file-system caches in a way the assertion cannot distinguish from a real regression.

rationale: Clearing removes the cache file from disk. Measured greedy front at rank 18 with +13 spans and 13 exclusive spans - the clear path is reached by no other test in this project. Kept high because an operator clearing a poisoned cache is the documented escape hatch, and a clear that silently left the file would leave them staring at the same bad models.
The cache info reports existence, a non-zero size, validity and the configured path. Measured addsNothingNew over 8 spans. An accessor over the file the test itself just wrote.

A cache file holding text that is not JSON at all is recovered from, ending with a valid cache on disk. No spans were attributed to this test in the capture, which for a body that drives the service through a full refetch is a capture gap rather than a statement about its reach. Kept above P2 because an unparseable file is a different input class from a parseable one that fails validation, and it is the only one that reaches the deserialization failure path.
uncertainties: The name promises the load returns null after deleting the file, but nothing here observes either. The assertions are about the recovery that follows, and they are the same three the two integrity tests in this file make.

rationale: A cache written an hour ago is read back and its model reaches the caller by id. Measured addsNothingNew over 373 spans. Kept above P2 as the non-vacuity partner of every invalidation test in this file - no HTTP response is staged here, so a service that discarded the valid cache and refetched would come back empty rather than with the cached id.

A refresh leaves a file on disk that deserializes into a cache reporting itself valid. Measured addsNothingNew over 29 spans. The save is exercised by every refetch test in this file, and what this adds over them is the round trip through the serializer.
uncertainties: Nothing here tests atomicity despite the name - the write is never interrupted, and no reader observes a partial file. The atomic write-then-rename path is pinned instead by the concurrent-write tests.

rationale: A large cache must pass the integrity predicate in under a hundred milliseconds. Measured addsNothingNew over 65 spans. Its behavioural assertion is the valid-cache case repeated. what it adds is a fixed wall-clock ceiling with no baseline, which a loaded machine can miss without any regression.

A cache whose models array is present but empty fails the integrity predicate. Measured greedy front at rank 34 with +3 spans and 3 exclusive spans. Kept high because an empty array is the shape a truncated or rate-limited fetch produces, and accepting it would cache a catalog with no models in it for a full validity window.

A cache stamped in the future fails the integrity predicate. Measured greedy front at rank 32 with +3 spans. Kept above P2 because a future stamp is what a clock-skewed or timezone-confused writer leaves behind, and treating it as fresh pins the service to a bad catalog until the clock catches up.

A models array whose entries carry none of the expected fields fails the integrity predicate. Measured greedy front at rank 35 with +3 spans and 3 exclusive spans. Kept high because this is the only case that reaches past the array's length into the shape of its elements, which is what catches a schema change at the source.

A cache with a null details dictionary fails the integrity predicate. Measured greedy front at rank 36 with +3 spans and 3 exclusive spans. Kept high because the details map is dereferenced during mapping, so accepting a null one turns a cache-hit into a crash on a path the caller cannot influence.

A cache with no models payload fails the integrity predicate. Measured addsNothingNew over 33 spans. The same branch the missing-models-data recovery test drives, and that one additionally proves the rejection recovers.

A well-formed cache passes the integrity predicate. Measured addsNothingNew over 65 spans. Kept above P2 as the non-vacuity partner of the five negative cases - a predicate that answered false unconditionally would satisfy every one of them and disable caching entirely.

One fully populated model maps to a config whose context limit, multimodal and function-calling capabilities, feature list, provider model name, four tags and both per-million prices are all asserted. Measured greedy front at rank 13 with +32 spans. Kept high for the pricing conversion - a fractional per-token rate becomes 15.0 and 75.0 per million, so a lost or extra factor of a thousand shows here as a wrong number rather than as an absent field.

A free and a paid endpoint become two sub-providers tagged accordingly, the free one priced at zero. Measured addsNothingNew over 283 spans. Assertion for assertion the same test as the pricing-variations case in the integration file, whose fixture additionally carries the free variant's own slug suffix.

Three endpoints for one model become three sub-providers, and sorting them by priority yields a named order. Measured greedy front at rank 45 with +1 spans and 1 exclusive spans. Kept above P2 because it is the only place the relative priorities of several sub-providers are pinned, and three distinct names is what makes an implementation that assigned every sub-provider the same priority fail rather than pass on a lucky ordering.

A quantized endpoint carries a quantization tag and a variant tag onto the sub-provider. Measured greedy front at rank 21 with +11 spans and 10 exclusive spans - the quantization and variant tagging runs only here. Kept high because those tags are what a caller selecting on precision filters by, and losing them silently widens the selection rather than failing it.

A reasoning endpoint sets the reasoning flag, the thinking capability and its type. Measured addsNothingNew over 304 spans. The mapping-test sibling asserts the same three things and additionally that a dedicated provider is appended alongside the aggregator, so this one is a strict subset of it.

A reader holding the cache file with the sharing a plain read takes is released partway through the save, and the fresh model must still reach the caller and land on disk. Measured greedy front at rank 23 with +10 spans and 10 exclusive spans - the rename retry runs only here. Kept high because the failure it catches is silent: the rename throws, a blanket catch swallows it, and the caller receives the stale model with no error. Asserting on which model comes back rather than on nothing having thrown is what makes it catch that.
uncertainties: The handle is released after a fixed 60 millisecond delay, so the test assumes the service's retry budget outlasts that and that the first rename attempt happens inside it. Its non-vacuity also depends on the platform - withholding delete access from an open reader is Windows behaviour, and on a POSIX runner the rename would succeed on the first attempt and the test would pass without the retry existing at all.

rationale: Another writer's staging file is held open under the deterministic name the save would use, and the fetched model must still reach the caller and be persisted. Measured addsNothingNew over 477 spans. Kept above P2 because it pins a defect nothing else here can see - a fixed staging name makes two processes sharing the machine-wide default cache collide, the open onto the held path fails, the blanket catch swallows it and the caller silently receives an empty model list.

Three catalog rows covering two models - one of them listed twice under different endpoints - collapse into two configs, with sub-providers named, per-million prices asserted on one of them, capabilities and features on both and the reasoning model's thinking type. No spans were attributed to this test in the capture, which for a body that invokes the mapper over a three-row payload is a capture gap rather than a statement about its reach. Kept high because the deduplication of repeated slugs into one model with several sub-providers is asserted nowhere else, and getting it wrong produces duplicate catalog entries that shadow each other at resolution time.

A free and a paid endpoint of the same model are tagged apart, the free one priced at zero on both sides and the paid one strictly above it. Measured addsNothingNew over 5 spans. Kept above P2 because the free variant here carries the suffixed variant slug the real catalog uses, so it also pins that two endpoints differing only by that suffix still fold into one model.

Of two endpoints for one model, the disabled one is dropped and only the enabled sub-provider survives. Measured greedy front at rank 38 with +3 spans. Kept high because a disabled endpoint that survived mapping would be selected and routed to, and the failure would surface as an opaque provider error rather than as a configuration problem.

rationale: Both registration overloads - the one taking a config object and the one taking an options callback - each produce a container that resolves the service. A catalog response carrying an empty data array yields an empty list rather than a failure. Measured greedy front at rank 11 with +39 spans and 4 exclusive spans. rationale: Eight rows drive the capability lookup for thinking, multimodal, function calling and streaming in both directions, each with the capability configured present and configured absent. rationale: Measured coverage puts it at the tail of the greedy order (rank 216, +1 span, 1 exclusive), a warrant too small to carry P0 on its own. An unregistered function errors without consulting any gate; a boundary that avoids asking approvers about calls that cannot run. The approval context carries tool name, tool call id, thread, run, generation ids, and the arguments JSON; an approver cannot make a policy decision on an uncorrelated request.
An approver that answers only once all three requests have arrived still completes within 30s; sequential preparation would deadlock, so this pins concurrent settlement.

Executor-level enforcement: the handler never runs and the result carries the Denied code with the tool call id, tool name, and reason. Measured coverage marks it addsNothingNew against the mixed-batch test now at P0, so it is not P0; it stays above P2 because it alone asserts the refusal payload's contents, which the mixed-batch test only checks as an IsError flag.
The first call's approval lands last yet it still executes first; concurrent approval must not leak into execution ordering that tools may depend on.

A refusal is reported through the streaming callback as a started call, an error, and an error result carrying the Denied code; a caller watching only the callback would otherwise see a call start and never finish.

Only the two approved calls execute while all three results are returned in input order; a batch that dropped or reordered a refused call would misalign results with calls. Measured coverage ranks it 9th in the greedy order with 186 new spans - the largest single contribution in the approval and executor path - so it carries both the allow and deny arms of batch dispatch in one test.
With the disabled preparer both calls run in input order with no errors; the compatibility guarantee for hosts that never configured approval.

Freeze maps null and empty to {}, hashes the same input identically, distinguishes whitespace-differing JSON, and emits 64 lowercase hex characters; this hash is what binds a decision to its arguments.
Asserts IsEnabled is false for the shared Disabled instance and for both unconfigured constructors; a small state boundary on the enablement flag.
The distinguishing positive for enforcement, plus exactly-once - a retry or duplicate dispatch would run an approved side effect twice.

The enforcement point: a blocked invocation runs the handler zero times and returns an error result carrying the Denied code, reason, and tool name. A verdict that is computed but not enforced is the failure this catches. Lowered to P1 on the prefix rule: this declaration is outside the project P0 prefix, and the component already has a prefix-nominated P0 in ExecuteAsync_WithAMixedBatch_RunsOnlyTheApprovedCallsAndKeepsInputOrder confirmed on its own contract. Exclusive spans are a floor rather than a nomination, so the reasoning above stands as the contract while the tier does not.

The caller mutates its argument buffer between approval and invocation and the handler still receives the approved bytes. Zero and negative waits throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException; a construction-time argument boundary.
The JSON and hash the approver sees equal what the handler receives and what the prepared invocation carries; the approver-visibility half of the binding.
A gate that ignores the token and allows anyway cannot resurrect an already-cancelled call; important because the approver is untrusted code.

One deny among allows blocks the call and surfaces the approver's reason. Measured coverage marks it addsNothingNew, so it is not P0; it stays above P2 because the mixed allow-then-deny case is the only place the any-deny-wins rule is asserted with an allowing gate present, which a single-gate deny cannot show.

RequireApproval with no gate yields MissingApprover rather than an approval; a misconfigured host must not silently execute unapproved tool calls. Lowered to P1 on the prefix rule: this declaration is outside the project P0 prefix, and the component already has a prefix-nominated P0 in ExecuteAsync_WithAMixedBatch_RunsOnlyTheApprovedCallsAndKeepsInputOrder confirmed on its own contract. Exclusive spans are a floor rather than a nomination, so the reasoning above stands as the contract while the tier does not.
Cancelling while an approver is pending yields Cancelled rather than an exception or an approval; the outcome a caller-abandoned call must carry.

The distinguishing positive of the gate protocol: two gates both allow, each consulted exactly once, and the call is approved. Measured coverage marks it addsNothingNew, so it is not P0; it stays above P2 because it alone proves the approve path is reachable at all - a preparer that blocked everything would satisfy every deny test while executing no tool.
A default(ToolApprovalVerdict) from a gate blocks as Denied; a struct default reaching the allow path would be an implicit approval nobody made.
Four near-miss outcome strings (casing, truncation, empty) all block, pinning exact-match comparison on the code that grants execution.
A throwing approver blocks as HookError with the exception message as the reason; important failure handling, since a crashing hook must not read as consent.
Host policy denial yields HostPolicyDenied with no gate consulted; a distinct policy layer and outcome code rather than a variation of the provider case.
An allow that lands first does not settle the decision when a later deny arrives; a first-answer-wins bug would execute a call an approver refused.
A deny settles while a second approver never answers, guarded by a 10s WaitAsync; without the short-circuit the principal call would hang on an unreachable approver.
A throwing host policy blocks as HookError and no gate is consulted; distinct from a throwing gate because it fails before any approver is asked.
Provider policy denial short-circuits with ProviderPolicyDenied and neither the host policy nor any gate is consulted; pins both the outcome code and the layer ordering.
Driven by ManualTimeProvider: not complete at 4 minutes, Timeout at 5. Pins that an unanswered approval expires instead of blocking the run forever, and that it expires no earlier than configured.

Combines a per-request deadline with MaxApprovalWait and checks the approver sees the earlier expiry. A second concurrent approval past MaxPendingApprovals blocks as Overload, and the slot is released when the first settles; the release half is what stops a permanent wedge.
An unconfigured preparer approves and passes the arguments through verbatim; without it a fail-closed change would block every tool call in hosts that never opted into approval.

The contract assessment above is unchanged.

Seven rejected prefixes covering the same character rule with a shorter length limit. Measured addsNothingNew over 3 spans. The prefix restatement of the function-name rule, whose combined form the prefixed-name theory pins.
Eight accepted prefixes. Measured addsNothingNew over 3 spans. The prefix side of the same allowlist.

Eight prefix-and-name combinations including one where both halves are individually valid but the joined name exceeds the limit, plus invalid characters on either side. Assigning null clears a previously set prefix. Measured addsNothingNew over 9 spans. The one accepted way to have no prefix, distinguished from the rejected empty string.

One valid prefix round-trips through the property. Measured addsNothingNew over 9 spans. A single case of the wider accepted-prefix theory.

A new configuration is enabled with no prefix and no function lists. Measured addsNothingNew over 5 spans. Field defaults on a freshly constructed object.

Validation accepts a configuration with no prefix. Measured greedy front at rank 218 with +1 span. The no-prefix branch of validation.

A fully populated configuration validates without throwing. Measured addsNothingNew over 15 spans. The largest covered set of the validate cases, but its only assertion is the absence of an exception.
The empty-original direction of the same override rule; a combination case rather than a distinct contract.
Merge lets the other options override all four run-identity fields; these ids drive the client merge key, so a dropped override regroups messages under a stale run.

Null fields on the other options must not erase the original run, parent, thread, and generation ids. Measured coverage marks it addsNothingNew over the 49 spans all three merge cases share, so it is not P0; it stays above P2 as the only case that detects a blanket overwrite, which silently destroys message grouping for every request that merges partial options.

A never-completing error body plus a token cancelled after 50ms surfaces OperationCanceledException within the 15s xUnit timeout; without the token flowing into the error-body read the principal call hangs forever. The re-run capture supersedes the earlier one this row was written against: it now measures addsNothingNew over 25 spans with none exclusive, so the coverage warrant that carried it to P0 no longer holds. It stays high above P2 under the overlapping-spans exception, because a hang executes exactly the same spans as a prompt cancellation and only this test's timing can tell them apart.

End-to-end through the retry helper with a real HttpClient over a fake handler: the handler is invoked exactly once and the 400 surfaces. Exercises the classification decision at the call site rather than the predicate alone.
A status-less transport exception with "timeout" in the message is retryable, pinning that substring detection still applies where no status exists.

A 400 whose message embeds "500 Internal Server Error" and "timeout" is not retryable: the status code wins over substring detection. Measured coverage marks it addsNothingNew over nine spans shared with the other classification cases, so it is not P0; it stays above P2 as the only case proving the status check precedes text matching, which a plain 401 cannot distinguish.

The distinguishing positive: a 500 is retryable regardless of message text, so a classifier returning false always cannot pass unnoticed. Measured coverage marks it addsNothingNew over the same nine spans, so it is not P0; it stays above P2 because it alone proves the retryable branch is reachable.
429 is retryable; a distinct status class from 5xx and the one that matters most for provider rate limits.
401 is not retryable; important because retrying an auth failure both wastes the call and can trip lockouts.
A body read that throws a retryable-looking exception must not escape into the outer retry catch: the original 400 status is preserved and only one attempt is made.

A cancellation raised while reading the final error body surfaces as OperationCanceledException rather than being repackaged as HttpRequestException, and the response is still disposed; repackaging would make a cancelled call look like a server failure and be retried.

After exhausting retries, all MaxRetries+1 responses are disposed; the intermediate ones are the larger connection leak and the single-attempt case cannot reach them. Measured coverage puts it at greedy rank 44 with 35 new spans and 15 spans no other test reaches - the retry-loop body itself - making it the fewest-tests choice for that code. Held at P0 although outside the project P0 prefix: no declaration for this component is in the prefix, so the prefix nominated nothing here and the component would otherwise have no P0 pinning the contract named above.
A tracking response proves the final non-retryable response is disposed before the throw; an undisposed response leaks a pooled connection on every failed call.
Delegation chain, scopes, and roles default to empty collections and the optional refs to null; a null collection here would be a NullReferenceException in every consumer that enumerates them.
An app-only principal has no effective user id, so it can never match a null-owner record; important failure handling on an authorization-adjacent value.
Agent-acting-for-app also yields null; a further kind combination on the rule the app-only case establishes.
The base attribution case: an end-user actor attributes to itself. Primary supported behaviour of the rule that decides who activity is written against.
Precedence still favours the on-behalf-of subject when both parties are end users; the case that distinguishes "prefer on-behalf-of" from "prefer the first end user found".

An app acting for a human attributes to the human, not the app. Measured coverage marks it addsNothingNew over the eleven spans every Principal case shares, so it is not P0; it stays above P2 as the only case that would catch the precedence being inverted, which writes activity against the wrong identity in every downstream record.

The provider is asserted to have received a single aggregated message built from a separate call and result pair, while the response coming back gets its ordering assigned. Measured addsNothingNew over 227 spans. Two tool calls in one provider response are split into two messages that keep their distinct call indices, both execute, and both results come back before the closing turn. Measured addsNothingNew over 363 spans. Kept above P2 for the parallel case: index collision or a dropped second call is invisible to any single-call test, and the executor returning one result for two calls would still look successful.

A whole tool-using turn end to end: the provider's aggregated tool call is split into an individual tool call message, ordering indices are assigned across the response, the generation id survives the split, the executor runs the function and stamps the result with the same generation id, and a second turn carrying the result history comes back as ordered text. Measured greedy front at rank 8 with +197 spans over a reach of 378. Criticality is independent: this is the loop the product is for, and each of the properties it asserts - ordering, generation id continuity, the split - fails silently rather than loudly, surfacing as a client that renders a turn out of order or splits it in two.
uncertainties: The type name on line 21 contains a zero width space inside the identifier. It compiles because C# ignores format characters in identifiers but a plain text search for the helper class will not find this use.

rationale: The quick start snippets run through both the extension methods and the transformer directly. Measured addsNothingNew over 164 spans. A compile-and-run guard for the published snippets rather than an assertion of behaviour.

The documented XML layout for one call is checked tag by tag with the four landmark positions ordered by index. Measured addsNothingNew over 118 spans. Despite the name nothing is compared exactly - every check is containment or relative position - and the same layout is asserted by the pipeline tests.

In the project P0 prefix and deliberately held there at P1: prefix membership nominates a candidate rather than conferring a tier, and the contract above is a component-level guarantee rather than the critical baseline a component-scoped P0 run is built from.

Prefix text, an aggregate and suffix text combine in order with the originating agent carried onto the result. Measured addsNothingNew over 151 spans. With a logger reporting itself disabled, repeated middleware invocations stay under a generous per-iteration budget and the enabled check is confirmed to run at least once per iteration.
