rationale: The same volume language validates once a ceiling anchor caps it. Redundant by coverage, but it alone shows the rule is about the pairing rather than the word: without it the check degenerates into a banned-word list that refuses ordinary rubric prose, and authors route around it by rewording rather than by capping, which leaves the bias in place.
requirements: in-process only; the validator is pure and the rubric is built in the test

rationale: A capitalised volume term is still refused. Catches an ordinal comparison letting the same word through in another case. P2: a comparison-mode variation of the term match, on a rubric that is authored deliberately rather than supplied adversarially.
requirements: in-process only; the validator is pure and the rubric is built in the test

rationale: Three malformed arbiter rules — no payload, an empty judge id and an empty family — are refused with both out parameters left null. Catches a parser that reports success while handing back a blank identity, which attributes a resolution to a judge with no name and is worse than admitting the field is unreadable. P1: the malformed boundary, with two exclusive spans of its own.
requirements: in-process only; the vocabulary is pure string handling

rationale: Consensus, single-judge, no-decision, gate-reject and null are none of them straddles. Redundant by coverage, but it alone is the negative side of the predicate: its sibling asserts only true cases, so a predicate returning true unconditionally would satisfy it and report every item in every corpus as judge disagreement. Null is covered because the field is optional on a verdict.
requirements: in-process only; the vocabulary is pure string handling

rationale: A judge id containing colons round-trips intact. Redundant by coverage, but it alone fixes the split direction, and the id is host-supplied: splitting from the left truncates the id and reports part of it as the model family, which is a confidently wrong attribution rather than a refused parse, and the caller has no way to detect it.
requirements: in-process only; the vocabulary is pure string handling

rationale: An arbiter rule minted from a judge id and family parses back to both values. Catches the format and its parser drifting apart, after which the persisted tie-break field still looks well formed but no longer identifies who resolved the straddle — and the field exists only so a reader can attribute the resolution. P1: the round-trip contract of the vocabulary, at greedy rank 14 with 11 marginal spans. No prefix member exists in this file, so P0 is not available.
requirements: in-process only; the vocabulary is pure string handling

rationale: The four non-arbiter rules and null all fail to parse as an arbiter. Catches a prefix check loose enough to read an ordinary consensus row as an arbiter resolution, and covers null, which is reachable because the field is optional on a verdict. P1: the negative side of the parser, with two exclusive spans of its own.
requirements: in-process only; the vocabulary is pure string handling

rationale: Both an unresolved split and an arbiter-resolved rule count as straddles. Redundant by coverage, but it alone includes the resolved arm, and the straddle rate measures disagreement rather than outcome: leaving arbiter-resolved rows out reports a lower disagreement rate on exactly the configuration that pays an extra model call to resolve disagreements, so the harness looks most reliable where it is working hardest.
requirements: in-process only; the vocabulary is pure string handling

rationale: A verdict degraded to SingleJudge because one judge abstained carries a non-null reason naming the abstention. Redundant by coverage, but it alone covers the composition with no fault to name: a healthy panel where a judge declined is the case both existing reason writers left blank, so a consumer segmenting degraded rows by reason got nothing for arguably the most interesting degradation there is.
requirements: in-process only; the reduction is pure and synchronous, with ballots built in the test

rationale: A SingleJudge verdict caused by a below-floor ballot names the floor in its reason. Catches the exclusion fallback covering only the abstention channel. P2: a second input reaching the reason fallback its abstention sibling establishes.
requirements: in-process only; the reduction is pure and synchronous, with ballots built in the test

rationale: A ballot whose confidence sits below the floor is excluded with its own reason and the surviving score stands. Catches a low-confidence ballot being counted at full weight. P2: a second input reaching the exclusion mechanism its abstention sibling establishes.
requirements: in-process only; the reduction is pure and synchronous, with ballots built in the test

rationale: With both a fault and a single surviving ballot, the reason names the fault rather than the exclusion. Redundant by coverage, but it alone pins the priority between the two reason writers: the defect it catches is the newer exclusion fallback overwriting the strictly more specific fault answer, which would turn an operator's outage signal into a generic degradation note.
requirements: in-process only; the reduction is pure and synchronous, with ballots built in the test

rationale: A judge missing from the reliability map is weighted one, giving eight rather than nine. Redundant by coverage, but it alone pins the default: a missing entry defaulting to zero would silently drop an uncalibrated judge from every score while leaving its ballot visible in the record, which reads as a panel decision that one judge did not actually influence.
requirements: in-process only; the reduction is pure and synchronous, with ballots built in the test

rationale: Weights of five, minus four and NaN are each rejected with the offending judge id and the range in the message. Redundant by coverage, but it alone bounds the normalisation: an out-of-range weight lets the aggregate leave the rubric's scale entirely, and can make the score contradict the outcome, so a reader segmenting on score sees a pass the verdict calls a fail. The NaN case additionally covers a range check written as two comparisons, both false for NaN.
requirements: in-process only; the reduction is pure and synchronous, with ballots built in the test

rationale: With one counted ballot and an alarm of zero, the dispersion is null and the verdict is not flagged. Catches the alarm being compared against a dispersion treated as zero when it is undefined, which at the most sensitive setting would flag every single-judge verdict in a corpus. P1: the interaction between the undefined dispersion and the alarm, which neither the alarm tests nor the single-ballot test reaches alone.
requirements: in-process only; the reduction is pure and synchronous, with ballots built in the test

rationale: Two ballots on opposite sides with no arbiter ballot and no arbiter fault terminate as an unresolved Split with no degradation. Redundant by coverage, but it alone pins Split as its own terminal outcome: the defect it catches is a straddle collapsing into a Pass, a Fail or a NoDecision, each of which would hide judge disagreement inside a number a reader takes at face value.
requirements: in-process only; the reduction is pure and synchronous, with ballots built in the test

rationale: With every weight fitted to zero the score falls back to the unweighted mean of nine, the stamped weights sum to a positive number, and recomputing the weighted mean from the row itself reproduces that nine. Redundant by coverage, but it alone pins the audit property: stamping the zeros the score demonstrably did not use leaves a persisted row whose own arithmetic is zero over zero against a recorded score, and the range check cannot catch it because zero is inside the range. P1: a self-consistency invariant no other test asserts.

Additive-field compatibility for `artifacts`, one row without the key and one with it. The same tolerant-read mechanism is exercised over both an empty-collection default and null scalars by the coordination-fields test below. P2 as a second field generation.

The richer literal-payload compat case: an old row with no blockedBy, assignee or timestamps beside a new one carrying all of them, read in ONE pass. It pins both defaults at once — empty collection and null scalar — and asserts the new row's block and claim survive rehydration, which is what stops a restart quietly unblocking a blocked task or dropping a claim. P1.

The identical helper against the file store. What it adds over the in-memory case is that a string value in the Properties bag survives that store's JSON persistence — which FileConversationStoreTests pins directly with its own properties test. P2 as a store combination.

Save then load returns a board deeply equivalent to the original — the projection's own contract, with no storage layer in the way to explain a difference. P1 as the base round trip the rest of the type builds on.

The same helper against SQLite, adding that the blob survives the metadata column round trip — pinned directly by SqliteConversationStoreTests.SaveMetadataAsync_PreservesProperties. P2 as a store combination.

Equal capture times are accepted, not treated as stale. At coarse clock resolution equal timestamps are the COMMON case, so a strict greater-than comparison silently drops every write landing inside one tick of the previous one — and the staleness rule above is exactly where that mistake lives. P1 as its distinguishing boundary.

Saving a board for a conversation with no metadata row creates nothing. A row minted here would carry no tenant, owner or visibility, and the authorizer reads a null tenant as conversation_not_found — the row would be unreadable by EVERYONE including its rightful owner, and would shadow any later attempt to stamp it. P1.

The write half: an older build must leave a newer-schema blob exactly as it found it, asserted by parsing the raw stored JSON rather than by reloading through the projection. During a rollback or a mixed-version deployment the older build is the one running, so without this every conversation it touches loses forward-compatible data permanently. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Two writers observing the board at different instants: the LATER capture wins regardless of which write arrives second. A last-write-wins save lets a slow writer or a post-restart writer regress a task from Completed back to NotStarted — a board that appears to undo itself. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The delete-then-write resurrection race forced deterministically through a mocked store: the existence check has to run again INSIDE the store's write serialization, because a request that captured the board before eviction can reach the write callback after the delete. The test proves the pre-probe alone cannot close the window — it makes the probe succeed and the callback see a deleted row — and asserts nothing was written. P1 for a handle-based TOCTOU fix.

An empty board with a newer capture time replaces a populated one, because 'the agent cleared the board' is a real state and the projection persists what it is given. A guard against empty writes here would make clearing impossible and hide it as a storage quirk; the decision belongs at the call site that knows why the board is empty. P1 for a deliberate policy boundary.

An unrelated key in the shared Properties bag survives the save, and the projection is still readable afterwards. The bag also holds the usage projection and the mode binding, so a save that replaced Properties wholesale would silently delete both every time the board changed. P1 for the shared-state discipline.
Per-field assertions on the nested tree — subtasks, their status, notes. Explicit where the round trip is structural, but reaching the same defect. P2.
uncertainties: Its comment argues a flattening projection would still round-trip the row count, but the round-trip helper asserts deep structural equivalence rather than a count, so the flattening it describes already fails there.

rationale: The base push: a captured snapshot reaches subscribers as a ConversationTodoMessage carrying the board's actual content — id, status, title and notes all asserted individually — and typed as ITransientMessage so it is not persisted into the conversation. Checking the fields one by one rather than the count is what the row's own mutation note targets: a publish that defaulted Tasks, or dropped notes, would satisfy any shape-only check while delivering a board the user cannot act on. The ITransientMessage assertion is the quiet half and matters just as much, since a live UI frame written into durable history would replay stale boards on every restore. Catches an empty or non-transient board frame. P1: the primary behavior of the live push.
uncertainties: The drain captures only the FIRST ConversationTodoMessage via TrySetResult, so a publish that emitted duplicate frames for one capture would pass here and in every other row in the class except the null-capture one, which counts.

rationale: A board published on thread-a must not reach thread-b's subscribers. The synchronisation is the part worth keeping: the row waits until the frame demonstrably cleared the PUBLISHING loop's channel before reading the stray counter, so 'the other loop saw nothing' is evidence rather than a race won by asserting early — the standard way a cross-talk test passes vacuously. The comment is candid that the property is structural today, each loop owning its own subscriber set, and states the row's actual purpose: pinning the behavior so a future shared publish bus cannot regress it silently. That is a legitimate reason to keep a row, and the consequence it guards is a real one, since a leaked frame would repaint one conversation's panel with another's task list. Catches board frames crossing conversation boundaries. P1: an isolation boundary between conversations.
requirements: in-process only; two loops, neither running
uncertainties: The guarded defect is not reachable in the current design — the comment says so — so this row protects against a refactor rather than against a live fault. That is worth a P1 but it is a reason it should not be run ahead of rows guarding faults that can happen today.

The wait establishes that the publishing loop delivered its frame, which bounds the race but does not close it: nothing guarantees the OTHER loop's drain had reached the point of observing a stray frame by that instant, only that it was started earlier.

rationale: A capture returning null — 'no board yet' — must publish nothing. The row's comment cites the review finding that forced its shape (#590 F-008): proving a negative alone passes vacuously whenever the subscription itself is broken, so it publishes a null capture followed by a REAL one and asserts the only frame that arrived is the real one. That construction is the reason to keep it; the control turns an absence into a comparison. Catches an empty board frame published for a conversation that has none, which would blank a panel that should simply stay hidden. P2: the degenerate-input boundary on the capture delegate.
uncertainties: The wait completes on the FIRST frame of any kind, and only then is the list asserted to contain exactly one. If a null-capture frame were published it would arrive first, satisfy the wait, and fail the count — so the ordering works — but a null-capture frame published AFTER the real one, or slower than it, would leave the list at one and pass. The two publishes are ordered, which makes that unlikely rather than excluded.

rationale: A snapshot stamped 'subagent-abc123' must be published as a frame carrying the LOOP's thread id, 'root-conversation'. The comment traces the whole failure chain and it is entirely silent: sub-agents mutate the parent conversation's shared board, so a snapshot legitimately arrives stamped with the acting agent's id; the client drops any frame whose threadId is not the open conversation; so a frame carrying the snapshot's own stamp vanishes with no error anywhere, and the user simply watches a board that has stopped updating while every component reports success. The row names the mutation that must go red — FromSnapshot using snapshot.ThreadId — which makes the assertion's target explicit rather than incidental. Catches live board frames silently discarded by the client. P1: a cross-component contract between the loop's publish path and the client's frame filter.
requirements: in-process only; Moq streaming agent never used, no run loop started
bounded: 5s frame wait inside a 20s cancellation
uncertainties: Was the TodoBoard P0 contender and the best row in the class. DECLINED, and the reason is a criterion I intend to apply in the end-of-slice prune rather than a fact about this row: the consequence here is a UI panel that stops repainting. No durable state is lost or corrupted, nothing hangs, no isolation boundary is crossed, and no work becomes invisible to an operator. Every candidate I have nominated in this slice fails in one of those harder ways. A component is not entitled to a candidate, so TodoBoard carries none.

The client-side half of the contract — that a frame whose threadId does not match the open conversation IS dropped — is asserted nowhere in this lane. Without it this row pins one side of an agreement whose other side is only described in a comment.

rationale: A capture delegate that throws must be contained where the loop can log it, and must not poison later publishes. The comment carries the specific history: #587 made GetTodoBoardSnapshot throw loudly on an unmapped status, and TaskManager's OnChanged dispatch would swallow that silently, so the capture is deliberately invoked INSIDE the publish guard. That placement is the behavior under test, and the named mutation — hoisting the capture out of the guarded region — is exactly the refactor that would look harmless and would propagate a board-rendering fault into whatever mutated the task list. The second half is what makes the row worth more than a NotThrow: a real frame published afterwards still arrives, proving the publish path is intact rather than merely quiet. Catches a board-capture fault escaping into the caller's mutation path, or silently disabling the push. P1: important failure handling on the publish path.
uncertainties: The stated requirement is that the fault is LOGGED, not merely swallowed, and nothing here observes a log. The row proves containment; the 'where the loop logs it' half of its own rationale is unverified, and a catch block that discarded the exception entirely would pass.
Nothing asserts that the frame which arrives is the second publish's rather than one produced by the throwing capture; it is inferred from the throwing capture never returning a snapshot.

rationale: Six changes during one stuck write collapse to exactly two store writes AND the trailing write carries the LATEST board, not an intermediate one. Two failures in one shape: a write per change storms the store, while capturing at schedule time durably persists a stale board. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: A deleted conversation declines a write by throwing, and that decline is PERMANENT: the schedule settles, a second boundary retries nothing and nothing was written. Treating it as transient retries forever on the background drain. The decline path really executes — the mock passes the pre-probe and then hands the callback a null existing row, the delete-between-probe-and-write race. P1.

Disposal is the capture point on pool eviction or swap: it must not complete while a write is still in the store. Proven by observing the disposal task INCOMPLETE while the write is gated, not merely by the final read. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: From the writer's seat 'the board is empty' and 'this process has not loaded the board yet' are indistinguishable, so persisting an empty capture erases a board another process wrote. The skip is recorded as policy — a clean boundary with zero writes — rather than as a failure. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The same pending-and-retry rule on a plain IOException, which :325 already proves on the harder subtype case; the file's own remark calls it inherited from the coalescing engine and restated here. P2.

A schedule after disposal writes nothing and still reports a clean boundary — on its own reading a defensive boundary on the disposal rule held at :189, which I would have placed at P2. It sole-covers two product spans, so the floor decides the tier. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Sub-agents mutate the shared board, so a capture routinely arrives stamped with the acting agent's id while SaveAsync keys the row off that stamp. Without the re-stamp the board lands under the sub-agent's row and the conversation the user is looking at stays bare. Non-vacuous: the sub-agent's row is deliberately seeded, so a mis-routed save succeeds instead of failing loudly. P1.

The case that distinguishes the decline catch from a swallow: the decline signal rides an InvalidOperationException subtype and so does ObjectDisposedException from the connection factory, so a catch keyed on the base type reports a real store fault as a satisfied write — the disposal warning never fires and a false 'conversation no longer exists' record is the only trace. Here the fault must leave the boundary dirty and be retried. Rank 49, +45 marginal spans. P1.

A row minted by a projection writer would carry no ownership stamp, and an unstamped row is one the authorizer refuses to anybody. The mechanism is pinned in the projection's own tests; this row pins the invariant end to end through the writer, which is where a future caller would reintroduce it. P1.
Null metadata and metadata without the property both yield null. P2.
The same round trip over the file store. A store combination of the claim held at :59. P2.

The aggregate survives save and load equivalently, field for field, over a two-attempt ledger carrying cache-write tokens, an estimated public cost and a provider-reported cost. Everything else in this file builds on the projection being readable back at all. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: The same round trip over SQLite. A store combination of the claim held at :59. P2.

During a rollback or a mixed-version deployment an older writer must not clobber a projection written by a newer build — the forward-compatible JSON is preserved intact, schema version and all, read back raw from metadata. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A write carrying a LOWER folded revision — an out-of-order or post-restart writer — must not replace a newer aggregate. Without the watermark, a restarted process's partial view overwrites the accumulated total and usage silently goes backwards. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: #196: two writers can legitimately reuse the same process-local revision for DIFFERENT attempts, so a revision-greater-than guard alone lets the second write clobber the first. The durable merge is by attempt id — both records survive and the total is their sum. P1.

Within one attempt id the highest revision wins and the totals are NOT summed — asserted by the number that distinguishes them (120, not 165). The complement of the merge above: across attempts add, within an attempt replace. P1.

#307: the merge takes counts from the highest revision but the TIMESTAMP from the earliest observation, because across writers the higher revision is often the later sighting of the same attempt — here on the next UTC day. Inheriting it would move the attempt into a different day and change what a rollup bills. P1.

A legacy pre-timestamp record arriving with the higher revision must not have its null adopted over the only time known for the attempt. The same merge field and the same first-wins rule as :403, on a null input. P2.
uncertainties: A distinct branch from :403 — null-versus-known rather than earlier-versus-later — so this is a demotion by weight, not because the branch is covered elsewhere.

rationale: The per-attempt RECORDS artifact is written alongside the aggregate and reads back with its attempt id and counts. That artifact is the authoritative history every merge below reads; without it the aggregate is a total nobody can rebuild or audit. P1.

A second writer merging its own rebuilt, still-InProgress view at an EQUAL revision must not regress a projection already marked Complete — while its records still merge. Completeness is what a consumer reads to decide whether a bill is final, so regressing it makes a settled conversation look unsettled forever. P1.

When the records artifact is unreadable but the aggregate is valid, merging would treat history as EMPTY and undercount — so the write is refused and the authoritative aggregate is preserved. Asserted with the number that tells the two outcomes apart: 110, not b1's 35. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 5 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The monotone direction: a later Complete write upgrades an InProgress projection. Real, but the simple case of the completeness lattice whose hard direction — never regressing under an equal-revision merge — is held at :226. P2.

A compaction pass is expensive and is charged to the row of whoever owned it, counted separately as a compaction attempt, with its checkpoint id preserved on the record. Without the separate count a large summary pass is indistinguishable from the user's own spend on the same row. P1.

A continuation is a second attempt on the SAME execution row rather than a new row: one row, both kinds listed, attempt count two, tokens summed. Splitting continuations into their own rows would show one conversation as many phantom executions. P1.

A descendant's spend lands on the SUB-AGENT's row, not the parent's, keyed by the scoped thread id built through the production minter (#705/#730) so the rollup's agent-id read is exercised on the shape the manager actually emits — and the ledger re-stamps every record with its root. Folding a child's spend into the parent makes per-agent cost meaningless. Rank 241. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A rate card with no cache-read rate prices a cached request as a LOWER BOUND and says so, and the rollup must carry that Partial stamp rather than launder it into a number that reads as complete. A partial cost presented as final is a wrong number with no warning attached. P1.

The hard case a workflow controller creates: a nested root forwards every record to the parent ledger, and its OWN turns arrive there as Primary records that before #681 were indistinguishable from the parent's. Here the forwarded copy names the controller as its parent execution while the same record inside the controller's own ledger still reads as root, a cumulative re-observation of one attempt stays ONE billable record, and both ledgers' totals agree with the folded rows. P1.

Durability of the whole contract on every store flavour: records saved and reloaded through a FRESH handle fold to the identical rows in the identical order, the compaction attempt count survives, and the per-row costs still sum to the snapshot total. A rollup that is only correct in memory reports different numbers after every restart. P1.
One primary record folds to one root row with its tokens and the ledger's own total. The baseline every row below re-performs on its way to a harder claim. P2.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: #670: a split-model sub-agent's spend is priced by ITS model, not the parent's — ten times the rate here, so pricing at the parent's model would silently understate it by an order of magnitude — with the provenance and completeness stamps carried on every row. Rank 398. P1.

After DisposeAsync returns, the persisted aggregate is read with NO polling at all and must already carry the run's 140 tokens. The absence of the poll loop is the assertion — every sibling test in this file polls, and this one deliberately does not, so it can only pass if disposal awaited the write rather than leaving it to a fire-and-forget that may be lost at shutdown. Catches a process exiting with its final turn's usage never written: the spend happened, the record does not exist, and nothing reports a gap. P1: the durability boundary at shutdown, distinct from the fire-and-forget writes during a run.
requirements: in-process only; mocked provider, in-memory store, 20s ceiling

rationale: A loop disposed after its run finished persists Completeness=Complete rather than the live InProgress default. The comment names the consequence for consumers: without the terminal transition the conversation-wide completeness state machine is dead and nothing can distinguish a finished conversation from a still-running one, so a billing or reporting reader can never tell when a total is final. Catches a conversation that never advertises its usage as settled. P1: the terminal state transition, distinct from the durability of the numbers themselves.

A run that has finished draining but whose loop is still alive leaves the aggregate InProgress. This is the paired negative for the terminal flush and the half that makes Completeness mean anything: a projection that always wrote Complete would satisfy the disposal test and be useless, since a live conversation would falsely advertise a final total that is about to grow. Catching it requires observing DURING the loop's life, which is why the loop is left running rather than disposed. Catches a still-running conversation reporting settled usage. P1: the in-progress arm of the completeness state machine.
requirements: in-process only; polled up to 2s for the fire-and-forget write

rationale: A provider that reports a UsageMessage results in a persisted aggregate whose total is the sum of prompt and completion tokens, scoped to the right conversation, with exactly one per-model entry. Asserting the sum rather than the presence of a record is what catches one side being dropped, and the single per-model entry catches one run being split across two model keys. This is the activation test for the whole feature: everything else in the file assumes the fold reaches the store at all. Catches usage that is measured but never recorded. P1: the end-to-end accounting path, and the baseline the completeness and frame tests build on.

A subscriber receives a ConversationUsageMessage carrying the folded total and the thread id, so a client banner updates live rather than only after reloading the persisted aggregate. Asserting the LAST frame's total rather than any frame's is what makes it the folded value rather than an intermediate one. Catches usage that is persisted correctly but never broadcast, which leaves every connected client showing a stale figure until it reloads. P1: the live publication path, distinct from persistence.
requirements: in-process only; background subscriber task, polled up to 2s
uncertainties: Subscription registration is waited for with a fixed 100ms sleep before the run starts. On a loaded machine the subscriber could register after the frame is published, which would fail rather than pass silently — but it makes the row a flakiness candidate rather than a correctness one.
The frames list is appended from a background task and read from the test thread without synchronisation.

rationale: A revision committed twice above the prefix, and a revision committed twice below it after the gap closes, both leave the prefix correct. The two duplicate positions are different failure modes — a repeat above the prefix must not be counted toward filling the gap, and a repeat below it must not push the prefix past revisions that were never committed — and covering both is what makes this an idempotence test rather than a single retry check. At-least-once delivery makes duplicate commits routine, so this is the ordinary case rather than an edge. Catches a redelivered commit advancing the prefix over uncommitted work, which publishes records that do not exist. P1: the idempotence contract, distinct from ordering.

Three allocations leave the prefix at 0, and committing them in order walks it to 1 and then 3. This is the non-vacuity partner for the gap case: a watermark that never advanced at all would satisfy the gap assertion's initial 0 and would fail here. Checking the prefix BEFORE any commit also pins that allocation alone publishes nothing. Catches a watermark that never advances, so no usage is ever published. P1: the primary advance contract and the anchor for the two harder cases.

Revision 2 commits while revision 1 is still pending: the prefix must stay at 0, and only jump to 2 once the gap fills. This is the whole point of a contiguous-prefix watermark — the comment states the consequence directly, that publishing N=2 without revision 1 would drop a record. A watermark that tracked the highest committed revision instead would pass the contiguous case and fail only here, so this is the case that distinguishes the two designs. Catches usage records silently vanishing whenever two revisions commit out of order, which is the ordinary situation with concurrent folds. P1: the gap-blocking rule, the watermark's distinguishing behaviour.

The completeness twin of the provenance derivation: a row persisted before #682 carries a populated two-category estimate beside the Unavailable default. It is not unavailable — there is a number — and not complete, because cache categories were ignored when it was priced, so Partial is the honest re-derivation. A separate field and a separate branch from the provenance rule. P1.

#393: rows persisted before CostProvenance existed deserialize to the Unavailable default even with a real cost sitting beside them, so seeding re-derives provenance from which cost field is populated. Four cases pin the whole rule — reported, estimated, both (reported wins as the higher-information source), and a genuinely unpriced row that must STAY Unavailable because there is nothing to derive from. That last case is what stops the derivation inventing provenance. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Derivation fires only on the Unavailable default: a row that already carries an explicit provenance is trusted as-is even when a different cost field is also populated. Without this guard the migration would relabel rows whose provenance was recorded deliberately. P1 as the boundary that keeps a repair from becoming a rewrite.

The matching guard: an explicitly stamped completeness is left alone. Derivation must fire only on the default, or the migration overwrites labels that were recorded deliberately — including the Complete stamps the current pricing path writes. P1.

Restart rehydration in one pass: totals come back, the folded revision is preserved, re-observing a seeded attempt does not double-count, and a genuinely new attempt both adds and advances the watermark past the seeded baseline. Without the dedup, every restart re-bills the conversation's history. P1.

Two models with different cache accounting in one conversation: each is priced under its own shape, and the conversation-level completeness is the WEAKEST of them while the per-model figure keeps its own. A rollup that reported Complete because most of its parts were would present a partial number as exact. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The snapshot sums across attempts and groups by model, and reports a folded revision equal to the committed gap-free prefix. That watermark is what lets a consumer tell a complete view from a partial one, so it is part of the answer rather than bookkeeping. P1.
Two attribution fields survive the merge onto the folded record. A passthrough assertion over the fold already held at P1, with no arithmetic behind it. P2.

A legacy two-rate catalog entry has cache-read tokens but no cache-read rate. Those tokens must be left unpriced and the estimate marked Partial, never charged at the base input rate — falling back to the base rate would overstate a cached call by an order of magnitude while still claiming to be an estimate. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product span, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Providers report usage cumulatively during a stream, so one billable attempt arrives as several observations. They must fold to one record with one attempt count and the highest counts seen — adding them instead inflates a conversation's reported tokens by a factor of however many chunks the provider sent. P1 for the ledger's central fold.

#367: when an observation already carries a provider-reported cost, the resolver still computes its estimate for comparison but provenance must stay ProviderReported. Letting the estimate that happened to run afterwards claim provenance would relabel measured spend as inferred, which is the difference between a billing figure and a guess. P1.

With a pricing resolver present the ledger fills an estimated public cost to the exact micro (1000 at $2/M plus 500 at $8/M) and leaves the provider-reported figure null. The two fields must never be conflated — one is measured, the other inferred. P1 for the estimation path.

The aggregate-changed callback is the source of the live usage banner (#196): every accepted observation fires it with the CURRENT folded total, asserted as the exact sequence 140 then 200 rather than merely that it fired. A callback carrying a stale or unfolded number is a banner that under-reports descendant spend while it happens. P1.

A record relayed from a child ledger arrives already priced and already labelled, and the parent must not re-price it against its own catalog. The child knows which model actually ran; re-pricing would quietly restate a sub-agent's spend under the parent's assumptions. P1 for the boundary between a ledger and the ledgers that feed it.

Both figures are retained side by side and PreferredCostMicros resolves to the reported one. Keeping them separate is what allows the estimate to be checked against reality later; collapsing to one field would destroy that comparison permanently. P1.

A later observation with no timestamp at all must not erase the one already known. That is a separate branch from comparing two timestamps, and a naive minimum over a nullable would take the null. P1.

Forward order: no cost info first, provider-reported second. As its companion test states outright, this ordering cannot distinguish 'higher information wins' from 'last observation wins' — both implementations pass it. P2, with the load-bearing direction held at P1 by the reverse-order case.

The case that actually pins the rule: the provider-reported figure arrives FIRST and a later observation carries no cost info at all. A last-wins merge — which is what every other field here deliberately does not do — would silently downgrade the record to Unavailable and still pass the forward-order test. P1 as the distinguishing case for a merge rule (#367).

A stale interim arriving after the finalized observation must not pull the counts back down. Streaming observations are not ordered on the wire, so a last-wins merge would silently under-report the attempt whenever the final chunk lost the race. P1.

Merge is max per count but FIRST-WINS for the timestamp. A cumulative stream re-observes one attempt many times, so last-wins would stamp when the final chunk arrived — the next UTC day in this fixture — and misfile the attempt in a per-day rollup (#307). Asserted on both the returned record and the stored one. P1.

The companion that pins first-wins as being over the VALUE, not over arrival: the later timestamp arrives first. Its sibling kills a last-wins merge; this one kills a keep-whatever-arrived-first merge, and neither case catches the other's implementation. P1 as a distinguishing case.

#682 under additive cache accounting, where input EXCLUDES cache reads and writes: all four categories are priced and summed to an exact 13,200 micros, and the unknown cache-write TTL makes the estimate Partial rather than silently exact. Pricing that ignored a category would under-report real spend by whatever share that category carried. P1.

The other accounting shape, where cached tokens are a SUBSET of input: the cached portion must be priced once at the cache rate and subtracted from the base, not charged twice. Same categories, opposite arithmetic, and getting the shape wrong overcharges every cached call. Completeness is Complete here because no category is unknown. P1.

The estimate is recomputed from the merged (max) counts rather than frozen at the first observation, so a streaming attempt ends up priced on what it actually used. Freezing would price every streamed call at whatever its first chunk happened to report. P1.

The identical final observation delivered twice still yields one attempt and one total. Replay is ordinary here — reconnects and durable redelivery both produce it — and the ledger is the record spend is charged from. P1.
One enum assertion on the same scenario the test above already exercises: a resolver-filled cost is stamped PublicEstimate. P2 as a field-level extension of a contract held at P1.

A model the catalog does not know produces a null cost and Unavailable completeness, never zero. Zero reads as free and would be summed into a conversation total as if it were measured; null is the honest answer and is what makes the weakest-completeness rollup meaningful. P1.

A scheduled write is durable only once FlushAsync has been awaited: the flush reports true and the persist delegate has run. Scheduling is fire-and-forget by design, so this is the only synchronisation point a caller has, and a flush that returned before its write completed would make every durability boundary in the system a lie. Catches usage reported as persisted while the write is still in flight. P1: the writer's primary contract and the anchor the failure cases are measured against.
uncertainties: The write is checked with a lower bound only (count greater than zero), so this row does not distinguish one write from many.

rationale: A write that failed is RETAINED: once the delegate stops throwing, the next flush persists it and reports true, with no fresh Schedule in between. The absence of that second Schedule is the load-bearing detail — it proves the pending work survived the failure rather than the second flush succeeding because something new was queued. Catches a transient store outage silently discarding the usage accumulated up to that point, so the spend is simply never recorded and nothing indicates a gap. P1: the retain-on-failure contract, distinct from how a failure is reported.

Flushing with nothing scheduled reports durable and performs no write. Catches a flush that writes unconditionally, which would put a store round trip on every turn boundary whether or not anything changed. P2: the empty-state boundary over the primary flush contract.

A persist delegate that throws makes FlushAsync return FALSE and surfaces the failure through onError. The comment states the rule the return value carries: a failed authoritative write must not be reported as a clean durability boundary. That matters because callers use the flush result to decide a boundary has been crossed — reporting true after a failed write tells the caller its usage is recorded when it is not, and the discrepancy only appears later as missing spend. Asserting both the return and the error callback closes the variant where the failure is reported but the boundary is still claimed, and the variant where the boundary is refused but nothing is logged. Catches a swallowed persistence failure. P1: the failure contract on the durability boundary.
requirements: in-process only; delegate-backed writer, no store

rationale: Work scheduled after a completed flush causes a further write. This is the non-vacuity partner for coalescing: a writer that performed exactly one write for its whole lifetime would satisfy both the coalescing bound and the first flush, and only fail here. Catches usage accumulated after the first boundary never being persisted at all, which loses everything after the first turn. P1: the reusability of the writer across boundaries, and the bound on how far coalescing may go.

Fifty schedules produce strictly fewer than fifty writes, and at least one. Coalescing is the reason the writer exists: usage is observed per streamed chunk, so a write per observation would put the store on the hot path of every token. Catches the serialisation collapsing into one-write-per-observation. P1: the coalescing contract, the writer's distinguishing behaviour.
uncertainties: The bound is loose in both directions: 49 writes out of 50 schedules would pass, which is not what 'far fewer' claims. The test name promises a ratio the assertion does not check.

rationale: The ledger-level restatement of :17's arithmetic; the snapshot fold it adds is also exercised by :122. P2.
A newer execution kind flows through the same stamping convention with no special case. An enum value passing through the mapping already pinned above. P2.

Cache-creation tokens land in the cache-write dimension and fold ADDITIVELY into the total — the number a customer is billed against. A dimension dropped here is silently free tokens in every report. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: The same count in the shape providers and persistence actually deliver: rehydrated extra properties are JsonElement, not CLR ints. A mapper that only reads the CLR shape passes :17 and reports zero cache writes in production. Six exclusive spans. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 6 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: #307: the one production factory for a usage record stamps wall-clock time through the injected TimeProvider seam rather than reading the ambient clock, asserted exactly against a frozen instant rather than for non-nullness. P1.
A provider-supplied cost is converted to micros and stamped as provider-reported. The provenance is what tells a reader whether a cost figure came from the provider or was computed here. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The distinguishing case: with no provider cost the record must say Unavailable and carry no figure. An implementation that always stamps provider-reported passes :48 and presents a fabricated number as if the provider had given it. P1.
The default-parameter path still produces a timestamp, bounded by a before/after window. The stamping mechanism itself is pinned exactly at :161. P2.

The #196 undercount: two id-less provider calls keyed by a shared constant MAX-collapse into one attempt, and the bill loses the difference. Asserted on attempt count and on the total, so a fix that separates the attempts but not the tokens still fails. P1.

The opposite direction, and the reason the fix cannot simply be a random id per call: an exact replay of one id-less observation must resolve to the SAME attempt, or a redelivered usage message double-counts. P1.

When the usage message carries a provider-reported model that differs from the requested one, the record keeps RequestedModel as asked, stamps EffectiveModel with what the provider reported, and EffectiveModelId answers with the effective one. This is the OpenRouter auto-routing/fallback path (ADR 0003): without the stamp every per-model rollup attributes the spend to a model that never ran, and nothing downstream can tell. P1: the primary contract of the new field.

The same stamp when the extra property arrives as a JsonElement, the shape persistence and provider deserialization actually re-hydrate rather than the CLR string the sibling uses. A mapper that reads only the string shape passes the sibling and reports the requested model in production, which is exactly how the cache-creation dimension was lost before its JsonElement row was added. P1.

With no model in the usage message - every provider except the OpenRouter stats path - EffectiveModel stays null and EffectiveModelId falls back to the requested model. Stamping the requested model into EffectiveModel would make the field look provider-delivered while carrying no observation, and this is the case the majority of records take. P1: the fallback the whole field rests on, and the non-vacuity partner of the stamping rows.

A provider report that AGREES with the requested model leaves EffectiveModel null, since the field is documented as the effective model only when it differs. EffectiveModelId answers the same either way, so this is a normalisation variation of the stamping row rather than a distinct contract. P2.

The first request carries the assigned id as --session-id and no --resume. Catches --resume being emitted before any id has been captured, which would ask the CLI to continue a session that does not exist yet. P2: fully contained in the lifecycle row, which opens by asserting the same two properties on the same builder before driving the run; its value here is isolating the first-run shape from the capture machinery.
requirements: in-process only; no run is driven

rationale: With neither an assigned nor a seeded id, the request carries neither flag. Catches a loop that manufactures a session id of its own, which would take every unconfigured host off the CLI's default session handling without anyone asking for it. P2: the nothing-configured boundary, and the non-vacuity partner for the two positive rows — without it, a builder that always emitted an id would still pass them.

A loop constructed with a seeded session id builds a request carrying --resume and no --session-id. Catches a seed that fails to reach the request. P2 rather than P1 because of what it does NOT do — see the uncertainty below: the precedence its name promises is not exercised.
uncertainties: ASSERTION-STRENGTH FINDING. The name and the comment describe defence in depth — a captured seed must dominate a stale AssignSessionId inside BuildRequest — but the code's own note concedes AssignSessionId is left NULL to satisfy the constructor mutex. With only one of the two values set, no precedence is exercised: the row cannot distinguish a builder that prefers resume from one that simply has nothing else to emit. What it actually asserts is identical to ClaudeAgentLoopInitialSessionIdTests.Construction_WithInitialSessionId_EmitsResumeFlagViaRequest. Recorded, not proposed for change; the gap is that the stated defence-in-depth property is currently unproven anywhere.

rationale: Supplying both a seeded session id and a host-assigned one throws ArgumentException naming initialSessionId. The mutex is a real safety rule rather than tidiness: the two arguments express opposite intents — resume THIS existing conversation versus create a new one under THIS id — and any silent resolution is wrong in a way the caller cannot see. Picking assign would create a fresh session and lose the conversation the caller meant to continue; picking resume would ignore the id the caller asked to register. Asserting the ParamName is what makes the failure actionable rather than a generic argument error the caller has to guess at. Catches a contradictory configuration being resolved silently. P1: important failure handling at the construction boundary.

The full assign-then-resume lifecycle in one row: the first request carries the host-chosen id as --session-id with no --resume, a run is driven so the SDK's SystemInitMessage lands, CurrentSessionId is confirmed populated, and the SECOND request carries --resume against that id with --session-id now empty. The mutual exclusion asserted at the end is the substantive claim — the two flags mean opposite things (create a new on-disk session under this id versus continue an existing one), so a loop that kept emitting --session-id after capture would either be rejected by the CLI or start a fresh session on every turn, silently discarding the conversation the user is having. Driving a real run rather than inspecting a field is what proves the capture path works, not just the builder. Catches a session id that is advertised but never adopted. P1: the primary lifecycle contract for host-assigned session ids.
requirements: in-process only; CapturingClient replays scripted messages, no CLI is launched
10s bound on the run via WaitAsync
uncertainties: Was an agent-loop P0 contender: a session id that is advertised but never adopted forks the user's conversation on every turn. Resolved after reading all fifteen agent-loop classes — the nomination went to ClaudeAgentLoopSystemInitRelayTests.OneShot_PreservesOwnershipStampedAtCreation, because losing tenant, owner and visibility is an access-control regression on durable state, whereas this failure is a continuity problem the user can see and recover from. This row stays P1 with no nomination.

rationale: With pending entries for two different runs queued, flushing run A leaves run B's entry in place. Selectivity is a distinct contract from publishing: a flush that drained the whole queue would discard run B's deferred assignment before run B ever completed, so B's caller would never be correlated and — unlike the case the sibling row protects against — no later flush could recover it, because the entry is gone. Asserting the remaining entry's RunId rather than just the count is what proves the RIGHT one survived. Catches one run's completion destroying another run's pending correlation. P1: the isolation half of the flush contract.
requirements: REACHES INTO INTERNAL STATE: seeds and inspects loop._pendingCliInputs directly
uncertainties: The test's own comment concedes the mechanism: the flush stops at the FIRST entry whose RunId differs, and run A is deliberately placed at the head. The favourable ordering is the only one exercised, so the row does not cover the case where another run's entry sits in front of the one being flushed — in which case the target's assignment would not be published at all. The stated property ('does not drain entries for other runs') therefore holds only for head-of-queue targets.

rationale: When the dequeue heuristic fails to match an input to its run, the flush called from the run loop's finally block must still publish the deferred RunAssignmentMessage — carrying the run id and listing the original receipt id — and must drain the pending entry. This is a safety net for a heuristic that is expected to miss sometimes, and its absence is silent: the run completes normally, but a consumer correlating by receipt id never learns which run its input became, so it waits indefinitely on a run that already finished. Asserting the receipt id is IN the published assignment, rather than merely that a message appeared, is what makes the correlation testable; asserting the queue is drained is what stops the same assignment being republished on every later run. Catches an unmatched input leaving a caller permanently uncorrelated. P1: important failure handling on the correlation path.
requirements: in-process only; no CLI is started and the run loop is never started
REACHES INTO INTERNAL STATE: seeds loop._pendingCliInputs directly and calls FlushPendingRunAssignmentsAsync directly
TIMING: two fixed 50ms sleeps, one for subscriber registration and one for propagation
uncertainties: The two 50ms delays are the test's only synchronisation. Under load the subscriber may register after the flush publishes, or the assertion may run before the message propagates; either produces a failure that looks like a lost assignment rather than a slow machine.

SingleOrDefault plus NotBeNull is weaker than ContainSingle: two published assignments would make SingleOrDefault throw rather than fail with a clear message. Minor, and recorded only as an observation.

rationale: Neither the CLI --tools allow-list nor the configured MCP server names may mention AskUserQuestion or NotifyClient. The class comment explains why this loop is special: those two tools are registered only by MultiTurnAgentLoop's own FunctionRegistry, and ClaudeAgentLoop has no FunctionRegistry concept at all — so if either name ever appeared here it would be advertised to a model with nothing behind it to answer the call. That is worse than a missing tool: the model asks the user a question that never reaches a user, or fires a notification nobody receives, and the run stalls or fails on a capability the host never actually offered. Checking both surfaces is what makes the guard complete, since a future change could leak the names through either the allow-list or a hardcoded MCP server. Comparing against the providers' own ToolName constants rather than string literals keeps the guard alive through a rename. Catches a client-only tool being advertised where it cannot be serviced. P1: a cross-component exposure boundary.
requirements: in-process only; scripted SDK client, no CLI launched
uncertainties: Both assertions are absence assertions over a surface the test itself leaves empty — mcpServers is passed as null and the allow-list comes from defaults. The row is non-vacuous only in the weak sense that LastRequest is asserted non-null first; nothing proves the allow-list is populated at all, so a request carrying no tools would pass. Recorded, not proposed for change.

rationale: An empty-string parent run id is treated as absent rather than as a real parent. Catches a null-only emptiness check letting an empty string mark a run as forked with a parent id nothing can resolve. P2: the blank-input boundary on the same rule.
uncertainties: Whitespace is not covered here, and the shared rule lives in MultiTurnAgentBase.ResolveBatchParent, so the blank-input guarantee is pinned only for null and empty.

rationale: With no parent run id, completion reports WasForked=false and a null ForkedToRunId. Catches every run being labelled a fork, which would make the flag useless to any consumer branching on it. P2: the negative arm of the rule the positive row establishes, and its non-vacuity partner.

A caller-supplied ParentRunId is threaded into the published RunAssignment AND reappears on completion as WasForked=true with ForkedToRunId pointing at the new run's own id. Both ends are needed because they serve different consumers: the assignment tells a caller which run its input became, and the completion tells it the run was a fork and where the fork landed. Asserting ForkedToRunId equals CompletedRunId rather than some fixed string is what pins the direction — a field pointing back at the PARENT instead would read identically at the type level and send every consumer that follows the link to the wrong run. Catches fork provenance being dropped or inverted on this loop. P1: the fork-signal wiring for the Claude loop.

The constructor seed flows into the built request as --resume on the very first run — the whole point of the parameter (issue #47), since a resume that only takes effect from the second run resumes nothing. Asserting on the REQUEST rather than on CurrentSessionId is what makes this a delivery check instead of a property check: a loop can hold the seed correctly and still fail to place it on the request the CLI receives. Catches a seed that is stored but never sent. P1: the delivery contract for the seeded resume.
uncertainties: Asserts SessionId only. It never checks that AssignedSessionId is empty, so this row alone cannot rule out both flags being emitted together — the sibling class covers that.

rationale: The seed is observable on CurrentSessionId synchronously, before any run starts. Catches a seed applied lazily on first run, which would leave a host that reads the property immediately after construction — to persist it, or to show it — seeing null for a session it just supplied. P2: a property-visibility boundary on the seed, whose delivery the request row already covers and whose pre-run visibility the override row also asserts as its sanity check.

Null and empty-string seeds leave CurrentSessionId null rather than propagating as a real session id. Catches an empty string reaching the CLI as --resume "", which is a malformed invocation rather than a no-op. P2: the degenerate-input boundary on the seed.
uncertainties: Covers null and empty but NOT whitespace. The Codex counterpart (CodexAgentLoopInitialThreadIdTests.NullEmptyOrWhitespaceInitialThreadId_IsTreatedAsUnset) covers all three, so the two loops' blank-seed guarantees are not equally pinned.

rationale: A caller-seeded session id is visible before the run and is REPLACED by the id the SDK reports in its SystemInitMessage. The precedence runs the right way for a specific reason: the seed is the caller's belief about which session to continue, while the SystemInitMessage is the session the CLI actually opened, and when they disagree only the second one exists. A loop that kept the seed would keep addressing --resume at an id the CLI never created, so every subsequent turn would either fail or silently start over. The pre-run assertion is a genuine discriminator rather than decoration — without it a loop that ignored the seed entirely would satisfy the post-run assertion too. Catches the loop tracking a session that is not the one it is talking to. P1: the live-over-seed precedence rule.
requirements: in-process only; CapturingClient, 10s bound on the run

rationale: In OneShot mode the client is disposed at the end of every run, and a seeded id the SDK never contradicted must still be readable on the loop afterwards. The comment names the real scenario: a resume where the CLI accepts the supplied --resume id and reports nothing back, which is the ORDINARY case rather than an edge one. If per-run disposal dropped the id, the next run would emit no --resume, the CLI would open a new session, and a multi-turn conversation would fork into a chain of one-turn sessions with no error at any point — the user would simply find the agent has forgotten everything. Pairing it with the override row also fixes the rule from both sides: a reported id replaces the seed, silence leaves it intact. Catches conversation continuity being lost to teardown. P1: session-id durability across the OneShot client lifecycle.
uncertainties: Was an agent-loop P0 contender on a conversation-continuity argument. Resolved with the rest of the family: the nomination went to ClaudeAgentLoopSystemInitRelayTests.OneShot_PreservesOwnershipStampedAtCreation on an access-control argument. This row stays P1 with no nomination.

rationale: Host and profile MCP dictionaries are MERGED rather than one replacing the other: the host-only key survives, the profile-only key is added, and the colliding key resolves to the profile's command. All three assertions are needed because the two plausible wrong implementations fail on different ones — replacing wholesale drops 'alpha', ignoring the profile drops 'beta' and mis-resolves 'shared'. The collision rule matters most: a profile exists to specialise a host, so a host entry winning a collision would make the profile's own server configuration silently inert while everything still starts and runs. Catches a merge that is really an overwrite, in either direction. P1: the MCP composition contract for this loop.
requirements: in-process only; BuildClaudeAgentSdkRequest is called directly, no client or process is started

rationale: With no profile at all, the host's MCP entry survives unchanged and no staging directory is created. Catches profile support becoming a behaviour change for hosts that never configured one, and the null staging assertion catches a stager that runs unconditionally and creates directories for every unprofiled loop. P2: the no-profile default, whose host-preservation half the merge row already asserts through its surviving 'alpha' entry; its distinct contribution is the staging-directory absence.

With both a profile prompt and a constructor prompt, the built request carries the profile's. ProfileSystemPromptResolverTests fixes the RULE exhaustively; this row is the only thing proving THIS loop calls it rather than reading a field directly, and that seam is per-loop code that can regress on its own. A loop that bypassed the resolver would run every profiled agent under the wrong system prompt — the single input that most determines what the agent does — with no error at any layer. Catches the resolver being wired out of this loop. P1: the wiring seam for the Claude loop, distinct from the rule itself.
uncertainties: Only one point of the cascade is exercised here; developer instructions are never involved, so this row proves the resolver is reached but not that the loop passes all three arguments in the right positions.

rationale: An inline skill in the profile is MATERIALISED: the request carries a staging directory, the directory exists on disk, and the skill's body is written to skills/<id>/SKILL.md — the exact layout the Claude SDK reads. Asserting the file path rather than just a non-empty string is the whole point, because an inline skill that is staged to the wrong filename produces a directory the SDK finds and a skill it never loads, which looks like a working configuration and behaves like an absent one. This is also the only row in the profile family that proves a non-prompt, non-MCP profile input reaches the provider at all. Catches an inline skill silently not being delivered. P1: the skill-staging contract.
requirements: in-process only, but CREATES A REAL DIRECTORY AND FILE on disk at a path the loop chooses
no explicit cleanup: the staging directory is not removed by the test, so repeated runs accumulate directories unless the loop's disposal removes them
uncertainties: The staged file's CONTENT is never read back; only its existence is asserted. A stager that created the right path with an empty body would pass.
The staging directory's location is unconstrained, so the row cannot tell a temp-directory stager from one writing into the repository.

rationale: With all three settings sources disabled the builder returns the EMPTY STRING, not null. The distinction is the entire tri-state: null omits --setting-sources and the CLI falls back to loading everything, while an empty value tells it to load nothing. Confusing the two is a containment failure in the dangerous direction — an agent a caller deliberately isolated would silently come up with the host's user, project and local settings, meaning its installed plugins, sub-agents, skills and worktree .mcp.json, all of which can carry tool access the caller intended to withhold. Nothing downstream would report it: the flag is simply absent and the CLI does what it always does. Catches an isolation request degrading into the permissive default. P1: the isolation contract, and the sharper end of the tri-state.
requirements: in-process only; pure static builder, no loop is constructed
uncertainties: The row pins the string the builder returns; that the CLI treats an empty --setting-sources value as 'load nothing' is an external assumption stated in the class comment and not verified anywhere in this lane.

rationale: With all three sources enabled the builder returns null so the flag is omitted and the CLI applies its own default. Catches an all-enabled configuration being spelled out explicitly instead of omitted, which would pin the agent to today's list of sources and stop it picking up any source the CLI adds later. P2: the third arm of the tri-state, and the one already asserted verbatim inside the defaults row, which calls the same builder with the same all-true options.

All six mixed combinations map to the exact comma-joined list of enabled sources, with the names spelled user/project/local and held in that order. Exact strings are the right assertion because the output is a CLI argument: a renamed token or a different separator is not a near miss, it is either a rejected invocation or — worse — a source silently not loaded. Covering all six rather than a representative pair is what catches an enumeration that drops the middle flag, which is exactly the bug a two-case test misses. Catches a partially wired subset. P1: the mapping contract between the three booleans and the flag value.

All three include-settings flags default to true and the builder therefore returns null, omitting the flag. The comment records this as a regression guard, and the direction of the regression is what makes it worth its own row: flipping any default to false would strip every unconfigured host's agent of its installed plugins, sub-agents, skills and worktree .mcp.json, producing an agent that appears to work and quietly cannot reach the tools its host provides. It is also the only row asserting the option DEFAULTS rather than the builder's mapping, so it covers a different surface from everything else in the class. Catches a silent capability loss for every host that never configured isolation. P1: the compatibility default.

In Interactive mode the SDK's SystemInitMessage is consumed for its session id and is NOT republished to consumers of ExecuteRunAsync, while the ordinary assistant text still arrives. Both halves are contracts and they constrain each other: the absence assertion alone would be satisfied by a loop that published nothing at all, so asserting the 'hello' TextMessage is present is what makes it non-vacuous. Leaking the metadata message matters because consumers render what the loop publishes — an SDK init frame would surface in a transcript as a message the user never sent and the model never wrote, and any consumer switching on message type would have to learn about a provider-internal shape. Catches provider metadata escaping into the public stream, and a session id that is filtered out instead of captured. P1: the relay contract for Interactive mode.
uncertainties: Only ExecuteRunAsync is observed. The class summary states the no-leak rule for SubscribeAsync as well, and no row in this class checks that path.

rationale: After a OneShot run has completed and OnAfterRunAsync has disposed the client, the session id is still readable from the loop — it must be snapshotted before disposal rather than read through the client on demand. Catches an accessor that delegates to a disposed client. P2: see the uncertainty — the state it asserts is the same state its sibling already asserts.
uncertainties: OVERLAP FINDING. OneShot_ExposesSessionId_FromClientCurrentSession also drives the run to completion and then StopAsync before asserting, so OnAfterRunAsync has already disposed the client there too. Both rows therefore observe CurrentSessionId in the same post-disposal state, and this row's stated distinction — 'even when disposed' — is a condition its sibling already satisfies. Recorded, not proposed for change.

rationale: OneShot deliberately suppresses SystemInitMessage (emitSystemInit:false in the SDK client), so the loop cannot capture the session id the Interactive way and must read the underlying client's CurrentSession instead. That makes this a genuinely different code path rather than a mode variation, and it is the path where a missing capture is invisible: no message is absent, no error is raised, the id is simply never learned and every later turn starts a new session. The row also re-asserts that no SystemInitMessage reaches consumers on this path. Catches a capture mechanism that exists only for the mode that does not need it. P1: the OneShot capture contract.

After a OneShot run the session id is written into ThreadMetadata.SessionMappings under the key 'claude-sdk:{sessionId}', and its VALUE equals the metadata's LatestRunId. The key/value shape is the substantive part: the mapping is what a later process reads to resume the session, so an id stored under the wrong key is unreachable and an id mapped to the wrong run attributes a session to work it did not do. Without this write, a host that restarts has the conversation rows but no way to reattach to the CLI session that produced them, and the next turn silently begins a new one. Catches durable resume information not being written, or written unreadably. P1: the cross-process resume contract.
uncertainties: The store is in-memory, so this proves the write is issued, not that it survives a real process boundary. Nothing here reads the mapping back through a resume path either — that it is the key a later process actually looks up is asserted only by its literal spelling.

rationale: A thread stamped with TenantId, OwnerUserId, OwnerAppId and Visibility=Shared before the loop ever runs still carries all four after a OneShot run rewrites its metadata to record the session mapping. The comment explains why this needs its own test rather than inheriting a base-class fix: this override does NOT call base — it replaces the write entirely and rebuilds ThreadMetadata, so every field it does not name is written back as null by SaveMetadataAsync's unconditional upsert. Fixing only MultiTurnAgentBase would leave every Claude-backed conversation un-stamping itself on its first turn while the base-class test went green. The lost fields are access-control fields, so the failure is not a cosmetic blank: a conversation that loses its tenant and owner on turn one is no longer attributable to anyone, and its Shared visibility is gone too. The last line is an explicit non-vacuity check proving the override really did rewrite the row. Catches an ownership stamp erased by an unrelated metadata write. P1: a security-relevant durable-state invariant, and the strongest row in this class.
requirements: in-process only; InMemoryConversationStore and a scripted SDK client, no CLI launched
uncertainties: DEMOTED in the end-of-slice P0 prune. Eighteen nominations across 347 in-scope rows is 5.2%, against the lane's healthy 2.4-3.1% band; ten survive. The nomination recorded above stands as the reason this row is the strongest in its component and is NOT withdrawn as an assessment - it is simply not a surviving candidate. Demotion reason: the ten survivors each fail in a way nothing downstream can detect. This one is serious but it also sits in the agent-loop family, the one component whose scoping I flagged as unresolved (one component, or four?), so it is the least safe nomination to spend a slot on before the lead answers that.

NOMINATED as the single agent-loop P0 candidate after reading all fifteen classes in the family (three profile classes, the prompt resolver, three session/thread-id classes, setting sources, three fork-semantics classes, flush, the Copilot loop, and constructor compatibility). Criticality justification: the fields at risk are tenant, owner and visibility, so the failure is an access-control regression on DURABLE state rather than a runtime inconvenience; it fires on the first turn of every Claude-backed conversation; and the defect is structurally invisible from the base class, because this override replaces the write rather than calling base — the test's own comment records that fixing MultiTurnAgentBase alone leaves this path broken while the base-class test goes green.

Runner-up declined, and the one to flip to if the lead prefers cost over consequence: ClaudeAgentLoopSettingSourcesTests.BuildSettingSources_AllFalse_ReturnsEmptyString_ForIsolatedAgent. It is a single static call with no loop, no store and no clock — by far the cheapest row in the family — and its failure is also permissive-direction: an agent a caller deliberately isolated comes up with the host's user, project and local settings, and therefore with tool access that was withheld. I preferred the ownership row because its failure is certain rather than conditional on someone changing a mapping, and because it destroys persisted data.

Other contenders declined: the three session/thread-id rows (assign-then-resume, seed survives OneShot dispose, persisted thread id wins) all fail as conversation CONTINUITY problems — serious, but recoverable and visible to the user as an agent that forgot, rather than as an attribution or access failure.

SCOPING NOTE for the lead: I counted the whole agent-loop family as ONE component for the one-candidate-per-component rule. If you scope per provider loop instead (Claude / Codex / Copilot / raw), this budget should be four, and the declined contenders above become eligible.

rationale: The published contract marks both parameters required. A schema declaration whose enforcement is covered by the validation rows above. P2.
Two options that resolve to the same value are refused: the answer comes back as a value, so duplicates make the reply ambiguous about which option the human picked. P1.

The check runs over EFFECTIVE values — value defaults to label — so an explicit value colliding with another option's defaulted one is still a duplicate. A comparison over explicit values only would miss exactly this shape, and it is the one a model produces when it names an option and hard-codes a value. P1.
Empty argument text takes the same typed path as malformed JSON — a distinct branch from :95, since an empty string is not a parse failure in every parser. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Whitespace-only context maps to the same missing_context code. A blank-versus-absent variation. P2.
Five questions exceeds the maximum, reported with the same code as the zero case at :131. The other side of one bound. P2.

Unparseable arguments come back as a typed invalid_args tool error rather than an exception out of the handler. Models emit malformed JSON routinely, and an exception here would fail the run instead of letting the model retry. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 5 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Context is required: without it the person answering sees questions with no explanation of what they are for. Refused with its own code so the model can fix the call. P1.
The empty-string spelling of the same missing id. P2.
With no tool call id the call is REFUSED rather than deferred. A deferral is keyed by that id, so deferring without one parks a run that no later answer can ever resolve. P1.

A question carrying no options is refused with its own code. The options are the only answers the client can offer, so a question without them is unanswerable in a different way from a call without questions. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A well-formed call returns Deferred rather than a resolved payload — the tool's entire purpose is to park the run until a human answers. Resolving inline would answer the model with nothing and carry on. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: Four questions — the top of the accepted range — still defer. The upper boundary of the count check whose rejection side is at :139. P2.
Zero questions is refused — otherwise the run parks on a prompt that asks the human nothing and can never be answered. P1 for the count bound.
