An empty argument string is classified missing_message rather than invalid_args, pinning which side of the parse/validate boundary the empty case falls on — the distinction that matters is that it does not throw before either code is reached. Catches an empty string reaching the parser and faulting. P2: an input-shape boundary over the two error classes already pinned.
uncertainties: Does not assert that nothing was delivered, unlike the sibling error cases.

rationale: A whitespace-only message is rejected as missing_message with nothing delivered, pinning that validation trims rather than merely null-checking. Catches a blank notification bubble reaching the user. P2: a value variation on the missing-message case, reaching the same code by a different input.

Unparseable argument text returns an error coded invalid_args and delivers nothing. The distinct code is the point: the model needs to tell 'your JSON was broken' from 'your JSON was fine but empty', because the two have different corrections. Catches a JsonException escaping the handler and failing the turn on a malformed tool call, which is a thing models emit routinely. P1: the parse-failure boundary, a distinct failure class from a valid document with missing fields.

Arguments with a label but no message return a RESOLVED result flagged as an error with the code missing_message, and nothing is delivered. Returning Resolved-with-error rather than throwing is the substantive contract: a thrown handler would break the turn instead of handing the model a correctable error it can retry from. The paired empty-delivery assertion is what stops a half-formed notification reaching the client. Catches a validation failure that either kills the run or emits a blank notification. P1: the model-facing error contract, distinct from the happy path.

A real MultiTurnAgentLoop is driven through a mid-run NotifyClient call followed by the model's final answer, and RunStarted must fire exactly ONCE across the whole exchange, with a single RunCompleted and exactly two provider calls. Counting the lifecycle event rather than inspecting the delegate is what makes it decisive: a tool that delivered correctly but did so by opening a run of its own would satisfy every provider-level test in this file and only be caught here. The paired callCount of 2 rules out the opposite failure, a loop that never reached the follow-up turn. Catches a client notification that re-enters the loop: an extra run per notification, each re-sending the whole history to the provider, and a recursive tool that can notify from inside its own notification. Nominated P0: 'resolve inline, never spawn a run' is the criticality argument for this tool, and this is the only row that can observe it. Confirmation held pending the facts join.
requirements: in-process only; mocked streaming agent, real loop and registry, recording publisher
uncertainties: DEMOTED in the end-of-slice P0 prune. Eighteen nominations across 347 in-scope rows is 5.2%, against the lane's healthy 2.4-3.1% band; ten survive. The nomination recorded above stands as the reason this row is the strongest in its component and is NOT withdrawn as an assessment - it is simply not a surviving candidate. Demotion reason: an extra run is visible in the conversation as an extra turn, so the failure is self-reporting.

rationale: A well-formed call returns Resolved rather than Deferred, is not an error, and delivers exactly one notification carrying the kind, detail, label, source tool name and the originating tool call id. ContainSingle rather than a non-empty check is the load-bearing part, since an at-least-once delivery would double every notification the user sees. Carrying the source tool call id is what lets a client correlate the notification back to the call that raised it rather than showing an orphan. Catches a notification tool that parks the call as deferred, which would leave the turn waiting on a resolution that never arrives. P1: the tool's primary behaviour and the shape every error case is measured against.
requirements: in-process only; delegate-backed provider, no loop

rationale: A message with no label still delivers, with the label explicitly null rather than an empty string or a substituted default. Catches label being treated as required, which would reject the common unlabelled notification outright. P2: an optional-field variation on the happy path.

With an empty store, the seeded thread id survives RecoverAsync and is what the client is started with, so the first app-server call is a thread/resume against the supplied id. This is the feature's reason to exist (issue #55): a host restarting cold has the thread id but no local metadata, and without the seed it would silently open a new thread and lose the conversation. Running RecoverAsync first is the part that matters — a recovery pass that unconditionally wrote its own null over the seed would satisfy any construction-time check and fail here. Catches a seed erased by a recovery that found nothing. P1: the seed-survives-recovery contract.

With BOTH a persisted codex_thread_id in the store and an InitialThreadId option set, RecoverAsync must overwrite the seed and the client must be started against the PERSISTED id. The class documents the rule and the reason: InitialThreadId only fills the void, so a cold-restart caller can supply a fallback without trampling real saved state. The inverted implementation is quietly destructive — the seed is a static configuration value, so every conversation on that host would resume the same wrong Codex thread, mixing one user's history into another's while every call succeeds. Seeding the store BEFORE construction and driving a real run through RecoverAsync is what makes this the actual recovery path rather than a builder check. Catches configuration overriding persisted conversation identity. P1: the documented precedence, and the strongest row in this class.
requirements: in-process only; InMemoryConversationStore and FakeCodexClient, no bridge process
uncertainties: Was an agent-loop P0 contender: a static option trampling persisted thread identity resumes the wrong conversation on every host that sets it. Resolved with the rest of the family — the nomination went to ClaudeAgentLoopSystemInitRelayTests.OneShot_PreservesOwnershipStampedAtCreation. This one loses on conditionality: it bites only on hosts that set InitialThreadId AND have persisted state, whereas the ownership defect fires on the first turn of every Claude-backed conversation. This row stays P1 with no nomination.

Only the store-populated direction is timed against RecoverAsync. Whether a LIVE thread id captured mid-run also dominates the seed — the other half of the class summary's 'live or persisted' claim — is not covered by any row here.

rationale: With no seed and no persisted metadata the client is started with a NULL thread id, so the first call goes through thread/start rather than thread/resume. Catches a loop that manufactures an id and asks the app server to resume a thread that was never created. P2: the nothing-configured boundary, and the non-vacuity partner for the two positive rows — without it, a loop that always passed some id would pass both.

Null, empty and WHITESPACE seeds all resolve to a null thread id rather than propagating. The whitespace case is the one worth having: a blank-but-present configuration value is what a half-filled config file or an unexpanded environment variable produces, and an emptiness check that only tests for the empty string would send '   ' as a real thread id. Catches a blank configuration value becoming a resume target. P2: the degenerate-input boundary on the seed, with three variations of the same rule.

With no profile, the constructor prompt beats the host's developer instructions. Catches profile support inverting the pre-existing precedence for hosts that never adopted profiles. P2: a second point on the cascade the resolver test already covers exhaustively, reached through the wiring seam the first precedence row establishes for this loop.

Host and profile MCP dictionaries merge on the way to the bridge init options: the host-only key survives, the profile-only key is added, and the colliding key resolves to the profile's command. This loop's merge is extra work rather than a dictionary union — the host side is CodexMcpServerConfig and the profile side is the runtime's McpServerConfig, so the two shapes must be converted as well as merged, and a conversion that quietly drops the command would still produce a populated dictionary. Asserting the Command on all three keys is what catches that. Reaching the assertion through a full turn (RunOneTurnAsync into a recording client) also proves the merge happens on the real start path rather than in a builder nothing calls. Catches a merge that overwrites in either direction, and a cross-shape conversion that loses fields. P1: the MCP composition contract for this loop.
requirements: in-process only; RecordingCodexClient substituted via clientFactory, no bridge process is started
uncertainties: Only Command is compared on each entry; args and the rest of the converted config are never checked, so a conversion that preserved the command and dropped the arguments would pass.

rationale: A profile prompt beats a constructor prompt on this loop. Catches an inverted precedence between the top two tiers. P2: a third point on the same cascade, on the same loop and the same seam already proven by the developer-instructions row.

A profile prompt supplied alongside host developer instructions is what reaches the client as DeveloperInstructions after a real turn. ProfileSystemPromptResolverTests fixes the cascade as a rule; this row is the only thing proving the Codex loop applies it on its start path, and that seam is per-loop code. It also pins the DESTINATION field, which is loop-specific: this provider carries the system prompt in DeveloperInstructions rather than a dedicated field, so a loop that resolved correctly and assigned to the wrong property would pass a resolver test and still run every profiled agent under the host's prompt. Catches the resolver being wired out, or its result landing nowhere. P1: the wiring seam for the Codex loop.

Unsupported profile inputs let the turn complete normally and leave the MCP dictionary EMPTY rather than inventing entries for them. The MCP assertion is the substantive half — a degrade path that tried to express skills or sub-agents as MCP servers would start the bridge with servers that do not exist. Catches unsupported inputs leaking into a neighbouring field. P2: the degrade-gracefully boundary alongside the warning row, which covers the same scenario's disclosure half.

A profile carrying skills this provider cannot honour logs codex.profile.unsupported EXACTLY once across two turns. Both halves are contracts. The warning must exist at all: silently ignoring skills and sub-agents leaves an operator believing a capability is active when nothing is wired, and the agent's behaviour is then inexplicable from the configuration alone. The count must be one: a per-turn warning on a long conversation buries every other diagnostic, which is how a real signal stops being read. Asserting the count rather than mere presence is what pins the dedup, and running two turns is what makes the count meaningful. Catches an unsupported profile input dropped in silence, and a warning that becomes per-turn noise. P1: the unsupported-input disclosure contract.
uncertainties: The loop's RunAsync task is started with a discard (`_ = loop.RunAsync(...)`) and never awaited or faulted-checked, here and in every row of this class. If that background task threw, the test would not see it; the assertion would simply be made against whatever the logger captured.

rationale: Regression guard for #246 with a real consequence: the client-only AskUserQuestion/NotifyClient tools are registered by MultiTurnAgentLoop's constructor, and copying those AddProvider calls into this CLI-backed loop would advertise a question flow with nowhere to route an answer back to. Proven non-vacuously — the ordinary registered tool must still bridge through. 51 exclusive spans, but not an inP0Prefix member, so the floor applies rather than P0. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 51 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Synthetic chunking is switched ON and an 8-char chunk size configured, yet a completion-only turn still emits no TextUpdateMessage. This is the configuration under which a naive implementation WOULD manufacture updates, so it is the distinguishing case rather than a variation of :277 — manufactured updates plus the final message render the answer twice. P1.
uncertainties: Two exclusive spans.

rationale: Incremental item.updated events become TextUpdateMessages IN ORDER ('Hel', 'lo', ' world') and the completion becomes one final TextMessage — the streaming contract the client's renderer consumes. Out-of-order or duplicated updates render as scrambled or doubled text. P1.
uncertainties: Three exclusive spans; its value is the ordering assertion rather than its span count.

rationale: The slashed app-server protocol — thread/started, agentMessage deltas, reasoning summary deltas, item/completed and thread/tokenUsage/updated — mapped to updates, final messages and a UsageMessage carrying cached and reasoning token detail. A second wire dialect through the same bridge; 66 exclusive spans, so the P1 floor applies and P0 stays with the default-protocol row. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 66 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The legacy dotted event stream mapped whole — thread start, an MCP tool call and its result, reasoning, the agent message and turn completion — plus ExecutionTarget.ProviderServer on the call and MessageOrderIdx on every content-bearing message. The baseline shape of everything the Codex bridge emits. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 17 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: P0. CodexAgentLoop is the entire seam between an external CLI provider's event stream and the message model the client renders; nothing downstream can repair a mapping that never happened. This row drives that seam end to end on its DEFAULT configuration and is the greedy prefix's first pick on the component (rank 16, 82 exclusive spans, 1018 covered): a provider-side web search must surface as a real ToolCallMessage/ToolCallResultMessage pair carrying ExecutionTarget.ProviderServer, the query in the args and a success result — and NOT as the prose reasoning line the legacy path produced. A regression turns provider-executed work into untraceable narration in the transcript.
uncertainties: Ranked 16 in the greedy prefix with 82 exclusive spans and 1018 cumulative — the single widest reach into the Codex bridge in the whole lane.
The one P0 on this component: :506 drives the same mapper over the slashed app-server protocol, so a second P0 here would stack on one code path.

rationale: After the run the metadata carries LatestRunId, a cleared CurrentRunId and the provider's own codex_thread_id in the property bag — the handle a later turn needs to resume the SAME upstream Codex thread. Losing it silently starts a fresh provider-side conversation with no history. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 13 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Prompt routing: the system prompt goes to the CLI's developerInstructions and the run input stays exactly the user's text. The only row asserting this split, and a regression prepends the entire system prompt to every user turn — billed, echoed and visible. P1.
uncertainties: Zero exclusive spans and no greedy rank — it shares its whole execution path with the mapping rows; only its assertion target is unique.

rationale: The other half of the exposure flag, and the case that distinguishes the two implementations: with exposure OFF the same webSearch item must produce NO tool messages and exactly the legacy 'Web search completed: ...' reasoning line. A mapper that ignores the flag passes :134 and silently breaks every caller still on the old shape. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 7 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Past the size threshold the prompt moves out of developerInstructions into a generated file, which exists during the run and is DELETED when the loop is disposed. Both halves matter: an oversized inline prompt is what the file mode exists to avoid, and an undeleted file leaks prompt text onto disk after the conversation ends. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 17 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The Codex loop threads a caller-supplied ParentRunId into its RunAssignment and reports WasForked=true with ForkedToRunId equal to the completed run's own id. As with Copilot, the shared rule is centralised but this loop's own run-start and run-complete sites are not, and this is the only row covering them. Driving the assertion through a scripted thread.started / item.completed / turn.completed sequence rather than a builder is what proves the fields are populated on the real completion path. Catches fork provenance dropped on the Codex loop specifically. P1: the fork-signal wiring for this loop.
requirements: in-process only; MinimalCodexClient replays scripted events
uncertainties: Neither row in this class bounds its ExecuteRunAsync enumeration. A loop that never completed the run would hang the test rather than fail it, unlike the Claude fork class which wraps the drain in WaitAsync(10s).

rationale: An unparented Codex run reports WasForked=false and a null ForkedToRunId. Catches every run being labelled a fork on this loop, which would make the flag meaningless to consumers branching on it. P2: the negative arm of the rule the Codex positive row establishes, and the only non-vacuity partner in this class.

The Copilot loop threads a caller-supplied ParentRunId into its RunAssignment and reports WasForked=true with ForkedToRunId equal to the completed run's own id. The class summary explains the shape of this coverage: the rule itself lives in MultiTurnAgentBase.ResolveBatchParent, so one happy path per loop is enough — but each loop still has its own run-start and run-complete call sites, and this row is the only thing proving Copilot's are connected. A loop that never populated the fields would still complete every run normally, so the failure surfaces only as consumers losing fork provenance for one provider while it keeps working for the others. Catches fork provenance dropped on the Copilot loop specifically. P1: the fork-signal wiring for this loop.
requirements: in-process only; MinimalCopilotClient replays scripted ACP events, no bridge process
uncertainties: The Copilot loop has no negative counterpart in this class — nothing asserts an unparented Copilot run reports WasForked=false. Without it, a Copilot loop that marked every run as forked would pass the only Copilot row here.

rationale: Thirty-two parallel Release calls on a single lease return true exactly once, and the limiter's in-use count lands at 2 rather than dropping below the two permits still legitimately held. Both assertions are needed: the counted successes prove the compare-and-set, and the in-use figure proves no phantom permit was minted. This is the property the file's own remarks single out — the paths that release a lease (normal completion, error, stop, dispose, an abandoned restart) overlap in practice, so a double release is the expected shape of the bug, and it hands back a permit that was never taken, letting the collaboration exceed the one bound that per-manager gates cannot enforce. Nominated P0: exactly-once release is the component's essential contract and this is the case that proves it under the concurrency it will actually meet. Confirmation held pending the facts join.
requirements: in-process only; Parallel.For over one lease

rationale: Capacity 0 and -1 throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException. Catches a limiter constructed with a capacity that can never admit anyone, which would present as a collaboration that silently refuses every agent rather than as a configuration error. P2: a construction guard, not a behaviour of the budget itself.

A first Release returns true and drops in-use to 0, a second returns false, and a following Dispose leaves in-use at 0. The sequential statement of exactly-once release, including that Dispose after an explicit Release is also inert — which is the ordinary teardown shape where both run. Catches a second release creating a permit. P1: the same contract as the concurrent case in its sequential form; it names the Dispose-after-Release overlap the concurrent test does not exercise.

At capacity 1 a second agent is refused, the first lease is disposed, and the second acquisition then succeeds carrying its own agent id. The refusal before the dispose is what makes the success afterwards meaningful rather than incidental. Catches a permit that is accounted as returned but never actually reissued, which would ratchet the collaboration down to zero capacity over time as agents completed. P1: the reuse contract, distinct from the release accounting.

Two permits at capacity 2, then a third acquisition returns null rather than waiting, with in-use 2 and available 0. Returning null rather than blocking is a deliberate design choice the comment justifies: a blocking acquire combined with the required root-lease-before-manager-gate ordering would be a deadlock waiting to be found. Catches the refusal becoming a wait, which would hang the whole collaboration at its capacity edge instead of declining one agent. P1: the sequential baseline of the budget, distinct from the concurrency guarantees.

A whitespace-only agent id throws ArgumentException rather than taking a permit. Catches a lease held under a blank identity, which cannot be attributed to any agent and so cannot be reconciled when the collaboration audits who holds what. P2: an argument guard on the entry point, a variation over the acquisition contract.

Sixty-four parallel acquisitions against a capacity of 8 hand out exactly 8 leases and leave in-use at 8; releasing them all in parallel returns to 0. Eight times oversubscribed is enough contention to expose a read-then-increment gap. Catches a limiter that admits more agents than the root budget allows, which is the bound protecting the machine from an unbounded subagent fan-out. P1: the acquisition side of the concurrency contract, distinct from the release side.

Eight sender threads admit questions to an agent while a ninth retires it, barrier-aligned and repeated 150 times; every admitted message must end up closed and no open inbound may remain. The remarks name the window exactly: RetireAgent runs its ONE-TIME abandon sweep without taking the bundle's delivery gate, so a sender can read the target as live, the entire sweep can run finding nothing, and only then does the admission land — leaving a reply-expecting message Accepted forever, because the sweep that would have closed it will never run again. The construction is what makes the invariant checkable: nothing in the test answers, delivers or fails anything, and the delivery callback mirrors the messenger's own finally block by freeing the inbox slot WITHOUT touching the ledger, so the sweep is provably the only thing that can close a row. Catches a sender waiting forever on a retired agent. P1: the admission-versus-retirement race on the inbound side.
requirements: in-process only; 9 long-running threads, 3000 admissions each, 150 repeats — expensive by design
uncertainties: The assertion loop only inspects ids that were ADMITTED. If the race caused every admission to be refused, the loop would be empty and only the open-messages assertion would remain — which an empty ledger also satisfies. The test does not assert that anything was admitted at all.

rationale: The same barrier-aligned race with the retiring agent as the SENDER rather than the target, checked against open OUTBOUND. Retirement has to close a departing agent's obligations in both directions, and the two are separate sweeps over separate indexes — a fix applied to the inbound path alone would pass the sibling test and leave the outbound one open, which is precisely the shape a partial fix takes. Catches a retired agent's own unanswered questions surviving its departure, so the ledger holds obligations for an agent that no longer exists. P1: the outbound arm of the retirement race, a distinct index from the inbound one.
requirements: in-process only; same race harness and cost as the inbound case
uncertainties: Shares the admitted-set weakness of its sibling: an attempt in which nothing was admitted would assert nothing beyond an empty outbound list.

rationale: Blank-identity validation at construction. P2.

The look-up-then-apply-policy ordering: sibling reads are refused under the restricted default and allowed under Open, while ANCESTRY is allowed under either — so the ordinary parent-reads-child case never requires widening the mode. Three claims that together fix what the mode does and does not control. P1.
Name resolution on the read path, plus the UnknownTarget reason. A combination of the resolve rule and the access evaluation, each held at P1 above. P2.

Retiring and abandoning are ONE operation because either alone is wrong: the message addressed to the departing agent is abandoned with the target-left reason, releasing its sender, while the directory entry survives as not-live so the agent stays describable. P1.

The other half of leaving: questions the departing agent ASKED are abandoned too, with their own sender-left reason, the recipient's open inbound goes empty, and a later reply to that correlation is refused as abandoned. Left open, another agent spends a real wait interrupt writing an answer for an asker that is gone. P1.
Retiring an unknown agent closes nothing and does not throw. Absent-input boundary. P2.

The per-target delivery chain, proven by holding the first delivery open while the second is admitted: nothing is handed over until the gate releases, and then in admission order. Without the chain the second overtakes the first and the target sees a reply before the message it replies to. P1.

A faulting delivery does not poison the chain behind it: the next delivery still runs, and the faulted send still reports admission success because a delivery records its own outcome in the ledger. One bad hand-off silently cancelling every later message to that agent is the failure this prevents. P1.

Correlation end to end, and crucially WHEN the question closes: admission only marks the answer Accepted, and the question becomes Answered on delivery. Closing at admission would tell the asker it had been answered before the answer reached it, and a delivery that then failed could never be retried. P1.

A sibling addresses a sibling. Neither agent's own manager knows the other exists, so this only works because the directory is owned by the root — the whole reason it is not per-manager. P1 for the reachability topology.

The sender-side half of the same rule, with its own InvalidSender code: a retired agent cannot send either. A stale handle still sending is ordinary after a retirement races a turn, and admitting it would create correspondence owned by nobody. P1.

The composition this file exists for: an agent that resolves but has DEPARTED is refused before anything is queued, and the sender still learns who it was and that it finished. A departed agent that swallowed the message would leave the sender waiting on a reply that can never come; an anonymous refusal would make 'finished' indistinguishable from 'never existed'. P1.

An unresolvable name is refused with the directory's own NotFound code, no target, and NOTHING queued. The empty ledger is the load-bearing half: a refusal that still admitted the message would leave a message addressed to nobody. P1.
The second source of refusal — a full inbox — surfaced through the same result shape as the directory's. One code path, two sources, and the caller does not have to know which said no. P1.

The resolve-then-admit ordering in its ordinary form: a model addresses an agent by NAME, the send succeeds, and the caller gets back the resolved stable identity plus an open inbound entry. The name is what the model has; the resolved id is what everything downstream correlates on. P1.

Only the STEER is refused for a completed agent; a question to the same agent still succeeds because a question restarts it. Both halves in one body, so a blanket refusal — the obvious over-correction — fails. P1 for a per-message-type rule.

A queued agent resolves and has an inbox but no turn to inject into. Admitting would tell the sender 'accepted' and then have the target's owner refuse the hand-off where the sender never sees it — admission and delivery disagreeing. The test also drives the recovery: once the target reports running the same send succeeds, so the refusal is transient and correctly coded. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The five-status terminality table over eleven product spans. P2.

A row written before a restart describes an agent that is no longer running, so rehydration forces IsLive false. Carrying a persisted true through is exactly how a caller ends up addressing a dead endpoint. P1.

The persisted row's wire shape: the kind is written as a NAME rather than an ordinal, so inserting an enum member cannot silently change what an old row means, plus the schema version and a full round trip back to the entry. P1.

Ancestry accumulates root-first across two levels, which is the ordering transcript access and listings read. Reversed or truncated ancestry misplaces an agent in the tree that authorization and display both walk. P1.

The distinction the whole file defends: structural depth counts EVERY node so orchestration stays visible, while a workflow controller costs nothing against the delegation budget. Collapsing the two axes either makes orchestration invisible or makes it unaffordable. P1.
Empty and whitespace agent ids are rejected. Argument validation. P2.
Oversized role text is rejected AND is not echoed into the exception message — role is collaboration-visible content, so a validation failure must not be the route by which it reaches a log. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The composed form: routing work through a controller must not consume a delegation level an ordinary spawn would have had. The single-hop table above cannot show that the free hop stays free once chained. P1.
The root's construction defaults — seventeen product spans, and every child row below starts from a root. P2.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: Null and whitespace role or description are invalid — the check spawn admission calls before a child exists. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The bound counts scalar values, not UTF-16 code units: an astral character is two code units and one thing a human reads, so code-unit counting silently halves the usable budget for non-Latin text. Asserted at the limit and one past it. P1.

A sub-agent entry with no ExecutionId serialises without an execution_id key and rehydrates with ExecutionId null. The field exists for the controller, whose spend is filed under a thread its id does not encode; writing null for every sub-agent would make each persisted row say no-execution about an agent that has one. P2: the absence side of the persisted execution_id field.

Half the racers admit new agents while the other half rewrite the root's status, so the compare-and-swap that replaces an entry runs against live insertions; a retained mark is then applied on top. Every field of the root entry must still describe the same agent — id, collaboration, kind, status and liveness together — which is what a torn write would break by rewriting one field onto a stale copy of the rest. The non-empty observed bag proves at least one update actually ran rather than all of them losing their CAS, so the field assertions are not describing an untouched entry. Catches a status rewrite silently discarding the fields it did not set. P1: entry-level write atomicity, distinct from the dictionary-level invariants.

Sixteen racers released from a barrier offer the SAME identifier under different names; exactly one succeeds, every loser reports DuplicateAgentId with a null entry, and the directory holds two agents. The class remarks justify the method rather than the count: the race is aligned with a Barrier rather than paced with sleeps, so contention comes from a rendezvous that either happens or blocks instead of a timing guess that passes on a fast machine, and the whole thing repeats eight times so a scheduler that serialises one attempt still gets many chances to interleave. Asserting the losers carry no entry closes the half-success where a caller is told no but handed a live handle. Catches a retry storm or double-spawn admitting one agent twice. P1: the exactly-once admission invariant.
requirements: in-process only; 16 long-running threads on a Barrier, 8 repeats
uncertainties: The Directory has no P0 candidate in this slice. Its five invariants here are consistency-at-quiescence properties of comparable weight, and singling one out as the component baseline would be arbitrary rather than argued, so none is nominated. Raised for the lead rather than resolved silently.

rationale: After the same contested-identifier race, EVERY loser's name resolves to NotFound and only the winner's name resolves — to the one admitted agent. The comment names the half-state precisely: identity and name bindings live in separate dictionaries and nothing spans them atomically, so the failure that matters is a name bound to an agent that was never admitted, which a later sender would resolve and then address an agent the directory does not have. Checking all sixteen names rather than a sample is what makes the absence complete. Catches a refused registration leaving an addressable ghost. P1: the write-atomicity consequence on the refusal path, distinct from the admission count.

Sixteen distinct agents register simultaneously and all succeed; at quiescence each is reachable three ways — by id, by its given name, and through its inbox — with unique ids across the snapshot. Checking all three lookups is the point, because registration writes identity and the name binding separately: a lost binding would leave an agent that the roster lists but nobody can address by the name it was given, which looks like a working system until a message is sent. Catches a partially-registered agent under load. P1: the positive completeness invariant, and the non-vacuity partner for the refusal cases — a directory that admitted nothing would satisfy their absence assertions.

Sixteen DISTINCT agents concurrently claim one shared name: all are admitted, exactly one keeps the unsuffixed name, no two granted names coincide, every granted name resolves, and each agent stays reachable by its canonical identifier. Claim-and-bind is a single TryAdd precisely so this race cannot end with two agents believing they own one name; a check-then-bind would let several racers read the name as free and the directory would then route one agent's messages to another. Replaces the contested-name latch row, which pinned the policy this branch removed. P1: the ambiguity-free grant under contention, distinct from duplicate-identifier refusal because here every registration legitimately succeeds.

Sixteen registrations of ONE agent under one name race: exactly one is admitted, every loser reports DuplicateAgentId, the plain name resolves to that agent, and the suffixed name no loser could have minted does not resolve. Duplicate-id validation checks then acts, so several registrations of the same agent can all reach the name grant; suffixing there would mint an alias pointing at the agent that already answers to the plain name, and releasing the name on the losing path would strip the winner of it. Catches a stray alias or a winner left nameless. P1: the write-atomicity consequence of suffixing on the refusal path.

The total-agent permit is taken from a collaboration-wide pool BEFORE any per-manager gate, so a second branch of the hierarchy sees a cap its own gate could never have known about. A per-manager-only cap lets N branches each run the maximum. P1.
The inbox accessor: capacity from options, a distinct instance per agent, null for an unknown id. Accessor plumbing on top of the registration already covered. P2.

One agent's NAME is another agent's identifier, and identity wins. Without that ordering a name chosen to impersonate an agent would silently receive the messages meant for it — the exact hazard this directory's remarks are built around. P1.
An unknown target and a blank one both resolve as not-found. Thin, but it is the answer that tells a model it invented a name, and it holds exclusive spans. P1 by the floor.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The snapshot comes back ordered by identifier. Real — an unordered listing changes between reads of the same set — but it is one ordering property of a read path already exercised by the admission rows. P2.

A finished agent stays resolvable with its final status while ceasing to be live. A sender holding an open question must be able to learn what became of its target; an entry that vanished is indistinguishable from one that never existed. P1.

The exemption that makes the limit usable: a workflow controller and its delegate are structurally deeper but cost no delegation depth, so the budget is spent on work rather than on orchestration. Asserted on both depths separately, which is the only way to tell the exemption from the limit simply not applying. P1.

A child's entry carries its ancestor chain, both depths, its declared type and its status. Those are the fields every later rule reads — the depth limit, the listing, and the routing — so a child admitted with the wrong ancestry is admitted into the wrong place in the tree. P1.

A root is admitted and described by what it IS — role and description both fall back to the agent kind — rather than being made to invent metadata. Every collaboration starts here, and an entry that came back with empty role and description would put blanks in front of the model choosing whom to address. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: An agent whose context names a different collaboration cannot register here. That is the isolation boundary between two conversations' agent trees; admitting one would make another collaboration's agent addressable from this one. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The delegation depth limit refuses the grandchild with the typed code. It is the bound on recursive spawning; without it an agent tree can nest without end. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A second registration of the same agent id is refused with the typed code and leaves the count unchanged — asserted, so a refusal that still mutated the map would fail. Two entries for one id would make resolution answer with whichever came first. P1.

Admission is all-or-nothing: an unknown parent is refused AND nothing is left behind — count zero and the id not findable. A half-registered child is an entry with a dangling ancestor that every tree walk then has to survive. P1.
Two writes against an id nobody holds return false. Negative returns on the mutation accessors. P2.

Constructing a bundle with an unusable option throws, so validation is not merely available on the options object but actually enforced on the path a host takes. This is where the class remarks land: a host that configures an impossible bound must fail the run that configured it, and Validate existing but never being called would satisfy every other test in this file. Catches a bad configuration reaching runtime and turning into refusals the model cannot explain. P1: the enforcement point, distinct from the validation rules it enforces.

All six defaults are pinned by value, and the default set is asserted to validate. Two of them are safety defaults rather than tuning: one ordinary delegation hop, and the NARROWEST transcript visibility mode — the comment says explicitly that it is the only mode which may ever be reached without an explicit choice, so a widened default would silently expose one agent's transcript to another in every host that configured nothing. Catches a default drifting to a more permissive value, which changes behaviour for every existing caller with no code change anywhere. P1: the default-configuration contract, and the surface a host inherits by saying nothing.

A delegation depth of zero is valid — the configuration for a collaboration that may not spawn at all. This is the non-vacuity partner for the negative-depth rejection: a validator using a positive-only rule would reject both and pass the invalid-options theory while making the no-spawn configuration unexpressible, which is the one a host reaches for to disable delegation. P2: a boundary-value variation whose value is bounding the adjacent rejection.

Six invalid configurations — a negative depth, three zeroed caps, a zero retention and an out-of-range visibility enum — each throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming the offending property. The parameter-name assertion is stated as the reason the test exists in this form: it is the only part of the diagnostic that tells a host which of six settings it got wrong. The undefined enum value is the case a range check alone would miss. Catches an impossible bound surviving construction and surfacing later as an inexplicable refusal to a model mid-conversation, which the class remarks name as the failure mode being prevented. P1: the validation contract, important failure handling at the configuration boundary.

The load-bearing guarantee of the hydration path: delivering into the root's live endpoint enqueues on the loop's input channel, which STARTS A TURN — a restart that woke the model to announce its own restart would burn a model run on every single hydration before the user typed anything. The absence is made non-vacuous by arranging an obligation owed to a dead agent for the reconciler to be tempted by. P1.
uncertainties: The test states, and I confirm from the body, that its own guarantee is partly unfalsifiable: it records a measured mutation (adding NotifyAbandonedObligationsAsync) that leaves the suite green, because that call's first guard is a ledger lookup a restarted process always misses. So it establishes that the reconciler AS WRITTEN delivers nothing, not that a delivery attempt would be caught.

rationale: The distinguishing case for :158 — 'report every open obligation' passes that row and fails this one. An obligation owed by an agent this process is running is still owed, and reporting it as dead is a false bereavement. P1.
An empty persisted set produces an empty report rather than treating everything registered as unaccounted for. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The reconciler's primary job: a name a previous process wrote down stays RESOLVABLE and says TargetNotLive, so a send is refused with a reason instead of being accepted for an endpoint nobody is behind. Both the report and the directory's own answer are asserted. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: The five-status sweep of the invalidation pinned at :76 — queued, running, completed, error, stopped all equally unreachable after the process died. A variation across an enum on behaviour already held. P2.
A second pass over the same set reports nothing. The consequence is a misleading operator report rather than wrong directory state — the agents are already tombstoned by the first pass. P2.

Since #705 the agent id is an ordinal minted per root, so two bundles really do both hold an agent-1: without the collaboration id in the key, one root's reconciliation tombstones another root's LIVE agent. Distinct from :110, which refuses a foreign set; here both bundles are real and the wrong one gets damaged. P1.

The case that happens on every hydration: the loop registers the root before reconciliation runs and the persisted set names it too. Tombstoning it would refuse the one agent that IS live. The opposite outcome from the same input shape as :76, and both are needed to pin the live/dead split. P1.

A persisted set is meaningless without its scope, and the case that proves it is a COLLISION — this bundle running its own live agent-1 while a foreign set names one too. Matching them would report another conversation's agent as one this process is running, and the guard inside MarkInvalidated cannot catch it because rebinding never reaches it. P1.
The second output of reconciliation: an obligation owed to an agent that did not survive is reported abandoned, which is how an operator learns a question will never be answered. P1.

The operator's whole view of a restart: all three buckets with counts and ids, on ONE line, because a trace that spans lines is one grep cannot pull whole. Eight product spans — diagnostics, held at P1 by the exclusive-span floor. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: An empty report still says something: a blank log line reads as a broken logger, not as a quiet restart. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A gated endpoint holds the hand-off open until the test releases it, so the sender is provably Running at admission and Completed by the time the failure settles — the interleaving is a fact rather than a race, which is what a narrow window like this needs. No notice reaches the finished sender, and the ledger still records DeliveryFailed. Both halves matter: restarting a finished agent to tell it about a message it can no longer act on costs a whole model run and produces nothing, while dropping the ledger record too would lose the fact entirely. Catches a delivery failure resurrecting completed agents. P1: the liveness gate on notification, a distinct rule from the failure classification.
requirements: in-process only; TaskCompletionSource-gated endpoint, no timing dependency

rationale: A permanently failed hand-off carries the target-gone code and is explicitly NOT retryable, with the code named in the notice body. The comment states the discriminator precisely — the two codes differ by VALUE, not by wording — so a sender branches on the code rather than on prose, and one that retried this case would burn turns on something that can never succeed. This is also the non-vacuity partner for the retryable row: an IsRetryable that always returned true would pass there and fail here. Catches the two failure classes collapsing into one. P1: the permanent failure path, with a distinct required response from the retryable one.

Two open questions in opposite directions are abandoned as the target leaves; both are closed, and exactly one is notified — the surviving sender, never the departing agent. The comment names why the construction isolates the right mechanism: the agent is abandoned WITHOUT being retired, so its directory entry still reads running, which means a pass here cannot be explained by a liveness gate and must come from the ToAgentId filter. The count assertion of two before the notify is what proves both directions were actually closed rather than one being silently skipped. Catches waking — and under a real endpoint, restarting — an agent that is on its way out, to tell it about its own question. P1: the notification-direction filter, distinct from the abandonment it accompanies.

Retiring an agent closes the questions addressed to it, and the asker is told, with the notice naming both the abandoned message id and the target-left code. Catches an asker waiting indefinitely on an answer the ledger already knows can never arrive — a workflow that stalls with no error and no timeout anybody set. P1: the retirement arm of the feedback contract, reached by a different trigger from a failed delivery.

A target that refuses the hand-off produces a ledger entry in DeliveryFailed with the RETRYABLE reason code, and a notice pushed to the sender's own endpoint. The class remarks frame the whole file correctly: admission is synchronous and delivery is not, so 'accepted' is a promise about responsibility rather than arrival, and the push is the only thing stopping that acceptance being the last the sender ever hears. Three notice properties are pinned beyond its existence — it comes from the system sender, it does NOT expect a reply (which would start a loop with nobody), and its body names both the message id and the code — so a sender can act on it rather than merely receive it. Catches a recoverable refusal that the sender never learns about, leaving it waiting on an answer that will not come. P1: the retryable failure path, important failure handling with a distinct required response.
requirements: in-process only; fake write endpoints, no real agents
uncertainties: Considered for the Collaboration nomination and declined: the ledger still records the truth when the notice is missed, and the component's stronger safety property — cross-collaboration refusal in TranscriptVisibilityPolicyTests — already carries a candidate. Recorded so the decision is visible rather than implicit.

rationale: After a failed send the sender receives a notice, the ledger holds exactly ONE entry — the original message — and the sender has no open inbound obligations. The ledger count is the load-bearing assertion: a notice admitted through the ledger would be a message the sender then owes something on, and a notice that itself failed would notify about the notice, which is an unbounded regress. Catches feedback becoming traffic that generates more feedback. P1: the out-of-band property of the notice channel, distinct from what any notice says.

The reply is admitted BEFORE the race so it already holds the claim — the comment explains why that matters: the contest under test must be between the two things that actually close a question, an answer landing and the target leaving, rather than between an admission and a closure, which cannot tie. Whichever wins, the entry must describe only that one: Answered carries a reply id and no reason code, Abandoned the reverse, and the abandoned count is pinned to 0 or 1 accordingly. A row showing both would mean two closers wrote over each other. The production shape is real — a sub-agent's answer handed over at the moment its manager retires it. Catches a question recorded as both answered and abandoned, so what a sender is told depends on which field it reads. P1: closure coherence between two independent terminal paths.

A Steer expects no reply, so delivering it is itself terminal and can genuinely race the failure path — the message type is chosen to make the contest real rather than constructed. Half the racers mark it delivered and half mark it failed; exactly one call reports success and the entry is closed. Counting successful REPORTS rather than inspecting the final state is the discriminating choice: a ledger that settled once but told every caller it had done so would leave a correct row and still let one caller record a delivery that another had already recorded as failed. Catches the outcome a sender is shown depending on which report it happened to read. P1: the exactly-once terminal transition, distinct from correlation claiming.

After the same sixteen-way reply race, the sender's inbox holds ONLY the winner's id and the ledger holds exactly two rows. The remarks give the consequence that makes this more than tidiness: a refusal that had already spent the target's backpressure budget would let retries starve real work, so a correlation refusal has to be decided before an identifier is minted or a slot reserved. Asserting the inbox contents by equality rather than by count is what proves the surviving slot is the winner's rather than an arbitrary loser's. Catches fifteen losing retries silently consuming a bounded inbox. P1: the no-cost-on-refusal contract, distinct from which reply wins.

Sixteen barrier-released racers answer one open question — what a retried tool call looks like from the ledger's side, several identical and individually valid replies. Exactly one is admitted, the losers all report CorrelationReplyInFlight with no message id, and then the test makes the distinction the whole design rests on: admission is a CLAIM, not a closure, so the question is still open and still names nobody until the winning reply is delivered. Only MarkDelivered moves it to Answered and records which reply closed it. Separating the two is what makes every retry behind the winner recoverable rather than a second answer reaching the asker. Catches an asker receiving several answers to one question, or a question closed by a reply that never arrived. P1: the exactly-once correlation rule under contention.
requirements: in-process only; 16 long-running threads on a Barrier, 8 repeats
uncertainties: The class remarks state that a refactor moving validation outside the lock would still pass every sequential test in AgentMessageLedgerTests. Per the standing rule that irreplaceability is a P1 floor and never a P0 argument, that is recorded and not used to raise this row.

rationale: Retiring a target abandons exactly the messages aimed at it, with the reason recorded, and leaves one aimed elsewhere open. Without it the sender waits on an answer that no longer has anyone to write it; without the scoping a departure would close unrelated conversations. P1.
Abandoning for an unknown agent or a blank id returns empty. A no-op boundary on the sweep above. P2.

Retiring a sender abandons the questions it was owed answers to and leaves another agent's question inbound. Left open, the target keeps being offered a question on behalf of somebody no longer there to read the answer, and can still spend a wait interrupt on it. P1 for the departure path in the other direction.
Abandoning from an unknown agent or a blank id returns empty. The matching no-op boundary. P2.

A sender's departure closes nothing when its only messages are an open steer and an already-answered question: the steer stays open and the answered question stays Answered. A steer is finished on delivery, so closing an open one races a delivery already in flight to cancel an obligation that was never there, and rewriting an answered entry falsifies what happened. P1 for the narrowness of the sweep.

With a cap of one and a long retention, three closed entries leave only the newest. Time-based retention alone does not bound a busy collaboration inside its retention window, and the oldest-first eviction keeps the history most likely to still be asked about. P1 for the second, independent bound.

Past its retention a closed entry is forgotten while an open one of the same age survives, with the clock driven rather than waited on. A closed entry is kept only long enough for a late caller to learn what happened; an open one is still needed however old, and evicting it would strand a live sender. P1 for the eviction rule that keeps a long conversation bounded.

The view excludes a question, a delegation whose answer is already in flight, and one addressed elsewhere, and is empty for the other agent. This is the list a refused task_update echoes back, so it must contain exactly the ids the ledger would then accept — a wider list sends the agent straight into another refusal, a narrower one hides the id it needs. P1.

Delivery closes a steer outright but only moves a question to Delivered. Handover is the whole lifecycle of a message nobody waits on and the halfway point of one somebody does; treating them alike either strands steers open forever or closes questions before they are answered. P1.

Admitting a response claims the question but does not close it — state still Accepted, still open outbound — and only delivery flips it to Answered with the response id recorded and the outbound view cleared. Closing on admission would tell the asker it had an answer that had not yet been carried anywhere. P1 for the two-phase closure the whole ledger rests on.
Delivering an already-closed message or an unknown id returns false rather than throwing or re-closing. An idempotence boundary on the transition the cases above pin. P2.

A failed delivery moves the entry to DeliveryFailed carrying the caller's reason code and clears the sender's open outbound. The reason is what the sender's obligations view shows, and the outbound clearing is what stops it waiting on a message that will never arrive. P1 for a terminal path a blocked sender depends on.

An answer that failed delivery releases its claim, so the question is answerable again — proven by admitting a second reply and delivering it to Answered, not merely by reading a flag. Closing on admission would strand the asker on a reply it was never given with no way to admit another. P1, and it holds a span no other measured declaration reaches.

The admitted notice carries the message id, both agent ids and the kind — enough to wake the target's owner, and nothing more. A wake-up signal is not a channel for message content, and widening it would push conversation text to every subscriber whether or not it is the addressee. P1.

Neither a self-delivery nor an unknown-target refusal raises the event. A notice for a message that was never admitted wakes an owner to find nothing in its inbox, and repeated under a retrying sender that is a wake-up loop driven entirely by failures. P1 for the negative that keeps the signal meaningful.

A handler that calls Find from inside the event actually gets the entry. A handler is a real caller's code, and the one job the event exists for is to make it look at what just arrived; raised under the lock it could only do so by deadlocking. P1 for a property no assertion on the notice alone would catch.

Both open views return oldest first, driven by a manual clock so the order is asserted rather than assumed from insertion, and the wrong agent's inbound view is empty. Callers pick the head of this list, so an unstable order means two readers act on different messages and the oldest obligation can starve. P1.

Once the answer is delivered a further reply is refused as CorrelationAnswered. Answered is terminal and needs no recovery, so the responder must be told to open a new exchange rather than to wait or resend — a distinct instruction from every other closed state. P1.

Replying to a question whose asker has gone is refused as CorrelationAbandoned. Nothing the responder writes can reach the asker, so the instruction is to find a live counterpart rather than to retry this correlation at all. P1 as the fourth distinct terminal recovery.

Replying to a question that was never delivered is refused as CorrelationDeliveryFailed. Nobody ever read the question, so the right recovery is to send the content again as a fresh message rather than to answer this id — different from every other closed state's advice. P1, and it holds an exclusive span.

A delivered steer is closed, so a reply to it reaches the closed branch — but the answer is CorrelationDoesNotExpectReply, not a generic already-closed. Telling a responder the exchange is over invites a retry; telling it the message never wanted an answer is the actual reason, and it matches what the still-open case reports. P1, and it holds an exclusive span.

A full inbox refuses with InboxFull and both the ledger count and the inbox count are unchanged. This is the recoverable refusal, so a phantom entry left behind would later be reported as outstanding work nobody sent and would keep a sender's obligations view permanently wrong. P1.

Five inline cases fix ExpectsReply from the message kind alone: question and delegation block the sender, steer, task_update and response do not. Whether a sender is waiting is not something a caller may assert about itself, and it decides who a wait can interrupt and what a departure must abandon. The reply-only kinds are given a real correlation so this stays a test about the kind rather than about correlation. P1.

A task_update against a delegation is admitted and the delegation stays open and still inbound. Progress is not a result: closing here would tell the delegator the work is finished while the delegate is still doing it, and the delegate could never report again. P1.

A successful admission records the entry as Accepted, expecting a reply and not closed, and the target's inbox holds exactly that message id. The inbox carries identifiers only — the queue is a claim on the target's attention, not a second copy of the conversation — so admission and reservation have to be one step or a message exists in one place and not the other. P1 for the ledger's primary operation.

Self-delivery is refused with SelfDelivery and the ledger count stays zero. Admitted, the agent wakes itself, owes itself an answer, and never makes progress. The count assertion is what proves the refusal left nothing behind. P1.

A correctly-sourced reply aimed at a third agent is also refused. The other half of the correlation's identity check: matching only the responder would let an answer close the question while being delivered to somebody who never asked. P1, and it holds 2 exclusive spans.

A third agent answering somebody else's question is refused as CorrelationNotAddressedToSender. Otherwise a bystander closes the question and the real target's answer is then refused as a duplicate — the asker resumes on the wrong answer and never gets the right one. P1, and it holds 2 exclusive spans.

Both response and task_update sent bare are refused as MissingCorrelation and the ledger stays empty. A reply-only kind only means something relative to another message; admitted bare it reaches the receiver as an orphan it cannot place and the ledger could never settle it. P1.
A correlation naming no known message is refused as UnknownCorrelation. A single-assertion lookup boundary among the correlation refusals pinned above. P2.

A reply to a still-open steer is refused as CorrelationDoesNotExpectReply. The open-message counterpart of the delivered-steer case, which carries the harder claim that the closed branch reports the same reason. P2.

A retried reply while the first is admitted but undelivered is refused as CorrelationReplyInFlight. This is the idempotency guarantee — a sender must not resume twice on one question — and the specific code matters because in-flight is recoverable if the first delivery fails, unlike the terminal states. P1.

A null inbox is how the directory says there is no such agent, and the ledger declines with UnknownTarget rather than inventing a queue nobody reads, leaving the count at zero. Without it a message to a typo would sit outstanding forever against an identifier that will never have a reader. P1.

Empty and whitespace senders and an empty target are all refused as InvalidSender. A blank identity admitted becomes an entry nobody can address, close or abandon, since every later operation keys on the id. On its own contract a validation boundary arguing P2; the exclusiveSpans floor places it at P1.

A task_update correlated to a question is refused as CorrelationNotADelegation, the question is untouched, and the target's inbox slot is still free for the answer that should have been sent. A question is answered, not progressed; admitting an update against one leaves the asker holding something nothing could ever close short of the target leaving. P1, and it holds 2 exclusive spans.

The interrupt claim is one-shot, returnable, and never settles anything: claim succeeds, the second fails, release restores it, and the question is still owed an answer throughout. Without the one-shot an agent that chose not to answer would spin instead of waiting; without the release a wait that lost its race to a timeout would consume the single interrupt the question gets and no later wait could ever see it. P1.

One session writes its roster down and shuts down; a brand new bundle over the same conversation — what a process restart produces — resolves the departed agents by BOTH name and id as TargetNotLive, while the live root still resolves successfully. The third assertion is the one that stops the rule overshooting: the root has a persisted row too, so a reconciliation that trusted the document over the live directory would mark the running agent gone and the conversation would refuse to talk to itself. Distinguishing not-live from not-found is the substantive part — a sender learns the agent existed and has ended, rather than that it never existed. Catches a restart losing every prior agent identity, so messages to them fail as typos. P1: the persist-then-reconcile round trip the feature is built on.

Attaching to a conversation whose metadata row does not exist yet — the ordinary first-turn case — writes nothing at all. The stated reason is the substantive one: the projection refuses to mint a row because an unstamped row, lacking the tenant, is unreadable by everyone afterwards, so a well-meaning create would poison the conversation permanently. Catches attach creating a tenant-less metadata row on every new conversation. P1: the refuse-to-create contract at the write boundary.
uncertainties: The name promises two things and asserts one. 'Persists nothing' is checked directly; 'still reconciles' rests only on the attach not throwing, with no assertion that the directory is usable afterwards.

rationale: An agent spawned after the handle is disposed does not reach the persisted roster. Catches a capture subscription that outlives its handle and keeps writing to a store the session no longer owns. P2: the lifetime bound on the behaviour the flush test pins, and its assertion is the same roster comparison reached under a simpler condition.

A store that parks every metadata write holds the flush open; Dispose is observed still incomplete after 250ms, then completes once the write is released, and the persisted roster contains the agent spawned AFTER the attach-time schedule. The comment argues the construction better than a summary could: asserting only on persisted content after Dispose returns is a detector the fast path usually beats, because an unflushed write still lands, just late — so parking the write makes the claim itself, that Dispose does not return while a capture is outstanding, the thing under test. The final roster assertion adds the second half: what it waited for is the LATEST roster, not the one scheduled at attach. Catches a shutdown that returns before its roster is durable, losing the session's agent identities. P1: the flush-on-dispose contract.
requirements: in-process only; gated store, 250ms negative observation
uncertainties: The not-yet-complete check is a 250ms observation. Unlike the vacuity risk the comment rules out, this direction fails safe: a Dispose that wrongly returned early would complete well inside 250ms.

rationale: After a restart has reported an agent gone, the re-capture drops it: the persisted document is asserted to contain the root ALONE, and a third session resolves the departed name as NotFound rather than not-live a second time. Reading the persisted projection directly rather than only the third session's resolution is what localises the property to the write side. Catches a roster document that grows forever, accumulating every agent a conversation ever had and re-reporting each restart's casualties on every subsequent restart. P1: the bounded-growth property of the persisted roster, distinct from the reconciliation it feeds.

Two conversations in one store each mint an agent-1 — which the comment notes is now genuinely the case since #705, not a contrived collision — and the second conversation resolves its OWN live agent-1 and its own name, while the first conversation's name is NotFound rather than not-live. Only the collaboration id separates the two documents, so this is the test of that separation. Asserting NotFound rather than merely a failure is what distinguishes proper isolation from leakage plus a liveness check: a directory that had read the other conversation's document would report the foreign name as not-live. Catches one conversation resolving another's agents, which routes a message into an unrelated conversation. P1: the collaboration-scoping contract on a shared store.
requirements: in-process only; one store, two collaboration ids

rationale: CreateRoot with no name yields a root named MainAgent. The mutation that must go red is restoring the old root default: that literal is what every child's preamble tells it to address, so a default that drifted would leave every reports-to clause pointing at a name nobody holds. P1.

A whitespace-only name falls back to MainAgent instead of throwing. A host reading an empty config value used to get an ArgumentException at collaboration construction, which took the whole conversation down for a blank setting. P1: the failure path a real configuration hits.
A configured name is used verbatim. The positive companion to the two fallback rows, asserting one property. P2.

Constructing a setup from one collaboration's bundle and another collaboration's context throws naming the mismatch. The bundle carries the shared directory and ledger, so accepting a foreign context would file this agent's rows under a collaboration it is not part of. P1: the isolation guard at the setup constructor, the seam every loop and sub-agent is built through.
A root setup exposes the bundle's options by reference and reports CanDelegate true. Accessor projections over state the directory rows already pin. P2.

With MaxDelegationDepth 1, the child setup reports CanDelegate false. The directory refuses the grandchild when it arrives; this projection is what lets the host withhold the spawn tool before the model tries, and a projection that disagreed with the directory would advertise a capability the next call refuses. P1: the projection guard on a delegated invariant.
Prepend over a null caller prompt yields exactly the composed identity, with no separator or trailing text. A shape variation of the prepend rule. P2.
requirements: in-process only; pure string composition over an in-memory directory

rationale: Compose with a null collaboration returns null. The null boundary on the composer, whose consequence Prepend_WithNoCollaboration_ReturnsThePromptUnchanged pins at the surface callers use. P2.
requirements: in-process only; pure string composition over an in-memory directory

rationale: With no collaboration the prompt comes back byte-identical. The mutation that must go red is dropping the null-collaboration guard: every legacy single-agent conversation would change behaviour on the next turn without any error. P1: the opt-in boundary for every conversation that never enabled collaboration.
requirements: in-process only; pure string composition over an in-memory directory

rationale: Prepend puts the identity sentence first and the caller's prompt last, asserted on both ends of the composed string. Order matters because the identity has to be read before any instruction that tells the agent whom to talk to, and the caller's prompt has to survive intact. P1.
requirements: in-process only; pure string composition over an in-memory directory

rationale: A root's preamble names MainAgent and its agent id and carries no reports-to clause. The root is the agent every child is told to address, so its own preamble has to agree with the name they are given. P1.
requirements: in-process only; pure string composition over an in-memory directory

rationale: When the parent is not registered in the directory, the preamble omits the reports-to clause entirely rather than printing an id. A wrong address is worse than a missing sentence, because an id here becomes a handle the model sends messages to; this is the branch a restart hits before the root re-registers. P1: the distinguishing case that stops the parent clause being emitted from the context alone.
requirements: in-process only; pure string composition over an in-memory directory

rationale: A child's preamble names the child by name and id and says it reports to its parent BY NAME, MainAgent. The parent's name rather than its id is the whole point: production logs show models addressing peers as lead, parent and manager, and the name is what the child can actually put in a SendMessage. P1: the primary content of the preamble.
requirements: in-process only; pure string composition over an in-memory directory

rationale: Null for an unknown target and for a live agent. The negative boundary of the accessor held at :153. P2.

#672: Resolve deliberately answers a tombstone with a null entry, so a caller recording ownership needs this second accessor to learn the identifier — and both spellings must give the SAME one, or the agent is keyed one way before a restart and another way after. P1.

The ambiguity rule has to follow the IDENTIFIER accessor too, not just resolution: naming either agent for a contested name would hand one of them ownership of the other's work. A separate code path from :136, and coverage records it adding new spans. P1.

Tombstones are keyed by (scope, agent id), not agent id. Since #705 every conversation has an 'agent-1', so a row from another root names a real agent that is none of this directory's business — tombstoning it here would refuse a name this collaboration is legitimately about to use. Both the refusal and the resulting not_found are asserted. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A second pass over the same persisted row reports no fresh work. The consequence named in the file is operator-trace growth on every hydration, not a routing error. P2.
The no-op half: a failed status update and a duplicate registration raise nothing. The negative complement of the row above. P2.

Every write that changes who is reachable — two registrations, a status update, a retention, an invalidation — raises the change signal, counted exactly. That signal is what drives the durable binding write and any live push, so a missed fire leaves the persisted view behind the in-memory one. P1.

A plain multicast invoke stops at the first throwing subscriber. The durable binding write and the live push share this list, so one broken push would cost durability — and the registration itself must not throw. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A re-spawn under a dead agent's name must both be ALLOWED and be what resolution reaches. Ordering inside Resolve is deliberately the single mechanism — the file records that a second guard inside MarkInvalidated would make the two mutations invisible to each other — so this is the only row that can hold it. P1.

The live ambiguity rule extends to tombstones — and the ids stay individually resolvable, which is the half that stops the rule from being implemented as 'poison the whole name'. Answering 'here is one of them' would attribute one dead agent's work to another. P1.
The same lookup by the id spelling rather than the name. The claim is held at :42, and :153 already asserts both spellings agree on the identifier path. P2.

The central claim: an agent a previous process spawned and this one cannot reach resolves as target_not_live, not as a success. A tombstone that resolved successfully would route a message to an agent whose process is gone. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: The discriminator that gives the whole feature its value: with a tombstone present, a name nobody ever held still answers not_found. A tombstone map that swallowed every miss would tell a model to 'spawn it again' for a name it simply mistyped. P1.
The record projection stamps the injected clock's instant. One field on a projection whose other fields are covered by the registration rows. P2.

A tombstone is resolvable but is not a member: GetAgents reads Snapshot, so listing one would offer a dead agent as somebody to talk to. The two read paths deliberately disagree, and this pins the disagreement. P1.

A child already registered by its parent's manager — with a working endpoint and a Queued status — is left completely untouched when its own loop is constructed: the agent count, the endpoint by REFERENCE, and the status all stand. The comment states the ordering that makes this necessary rather than pedantic: the parent had to know the child's endpoint before the child's loop existed, so a re-registration would either fail or, worse, replace a working endpoint with one pointing at a loop nobody drives. The reference-identity check on the endpoint is the assertion that catches the silent version; a count or presence check would not. Catches every message to a spawned sub-agent disappearing into an undriven endpoint. P1: the do-not-clobber rule at the loop/manager boundary, an important failure path.
requirements: in-process only; mocked provider, no run executed

rationale: Constructing a loop with a collaboration registers its own agent with the right name, a Running status and the Root kind, and exposes the setup by reference. Publishing at construction rather than at first run is what makes the agent addressable before it has done anything, which a peer sending to it immediately depends on. Catches a loop that never announces itself, so nothing in the collaboration can reach it. P1: the loop's primary collaboration responsibility, and the one thing the class remarks say the loop itself owns.

A loop constructed with no collaboration exposes none. Catches a default collaboration being manufactured for a standalone loop, which would give every single-agent conversation a directory and a ledger it never asked for. P2: the null-configuration boundary, asserted with a single null check.

A peer sends the published loop a question and the ledger records it Delivered — the round trip, not the presence of a row. The comment states the reason plainly: registration is only worth anything if the endpoint it published actually delivers, and a directory entry naming a broken or absent endpoint looks identical to a working one in every structural assertion. Catches a loop that appears in the roster but cannot receive anything, which is worse than being absent because senders are told their message was accepted. P1: the end-to-end reachability contract, distinct from the registration it depends on.

A loop constructed with a collaboration and a base system prompt holds a prompt that starts with the MainAgent identity sentence and ends with the base instructions. The mutation that must go red is passing systemPrompt unchanged to the base constructor. This is the one seam through which the preamble reaches a model at all: the composer can be correct and the agent still never learns its name, and the failure is silent - the model keeps running and addresses peers as lead and parent exactly as production logs showed before the feature.
