Missing a source is silent and one-directional: the reader returns an older timestamp, the cache reads Cold when it is warm, and the host pays for a full uncached prompt on a conversation whose cache was fine. Two guards make it non-vacuous — it starts by asserting null when nothing durable exists, so a reader returning a constant fails immediately, and it ends by asserting a different thread reads null, so a store-wide max fails too. Catches a max computed over too few sources or over the wrong thread. P1: the durable-activity contract underneath cache temperature.
requirements: in-process only; ConversationStoreHarness across all store kinds, fresh handle per step
uncertainties: Each source is advanced to a strictly newer time than the last, so the row proves each source is READ but never proves the reader takes the maximum rather than the last-checked source. A reader that simply returned the lifecycle timestamp whenever one exists would pass every step here.

rationale: Rows written before the seq column existed still yield the newest timestamp. Catches an activity reader that orders by seq and therefore reads nothing at all on a conversation that predates the column — a real population, and the failure would report every such conversation as cold forever. P2: a legacy-data variation on the behaviour the primary row establishes.
requirements: in-process only; seeds legacy rows through the harness
uncertainties: The 'memory' theory case returns early with a bare `return;` rather than being skipped, so that case reports as PASSING while asserting nothing. The comment gives a sound reason (no row can predate the binary in memory), but a reader of the results sees a green case that never ran.

rationale: When a live observation is available for a thread it supersedes the persisted one and the row reads Fresh; the sibling agent with no live observation still reads Stale. The sibling is the discriminator — without it a projection that marked everything Fresh, or one that ignored the live hook entirely, would satisfy the first two assertions. Precedence matters because the persisted observation is by construction one generation behind: a report that preferred it would show a user a context figure that is stale by exactly the turn they are watching, which is when they most need it. BeSameAs rather than equivalence proves the live instance itself is surfaced rather than a merged copy. Catches a live reading being ignored or mislabelled. P1: the live-over-durable precedence rule and the freshness labelling.

A loop running on a provider-side session (non-empty SessionMappings) reports Unsupported with no observation, freshness None and unknown cache temperature — spec 679 §9 says the host can neither observe nor compact a context it does not own. The discriminating assertion is the last one: its usage is still 200 tokens, 'spend is still spend'. Without it, the natural implementation of an exclusion is to skip the agent entirely, which silently under-reports the conversation's cost by however much the excluded loop burned — and excluded loops are exactly the long-running provider-side ones. Reporting Unsupported rather than None also matters to the caller: None invites a compaction attempt the host cannot perform. Catches an excluded loop disappearing from the spend total. P1: the exclusion contract and its cost carve-out.

An empty store and an empty roster still yield a report with exactly one row for the root, everything absent, zero totals and a null completeness. Catches a builder that returns no rows — or throws — for a conversation nothing has observed yet, which is every conversation on its first turn and would leave the context endpoint failing precisely when a user first opens it. P2: the empty-state boundary on the behaviour the build row establishes.

The whole read model behind GET /api/conversations/{id}/context is built on every store flavour from seeded durable state and checked field by field: roster order, parent linkage, execution kind, the latest observation and its provenance, freshness, cache temperature, per-agent compaction state with checkpoint id and rejection reason, per-agent usage, and the root total with its completeness flags. It is then rebuilt through a FRESH handle and asserted equivalent, which is the class's stated contract — the report must read the same before and after a restart. That re-read is what distinguishes a projection from a cache: a report assembled partly from in-process state would pass every field assertion above and diverge only after a restart, when the user sees a conversation that has apparently forgotten its own compaction and spend. Catches the read model losing rows across a process boundary. P1: the primary contract of the report.
requirements: in-process only; ConversationStoreHarness across all store kinds, fixed clock

rationale: Read an hour after the last durable activity, the root's cache reads Cold; an agent whose observations record caching disabled reads Unknown rather than Cold. The two outcomes are different claims and the distinction is the useful one — Cold means the cache has expired and the next turn will pay full prompt price, Unknown means the question does not apply because that loop sends without caching at all. Collapsing Unknown into Cold would tell a user a cacheless loop's cost is about to jump when nothing is about to change. This is the only row exercising the TTL comparison at all; the build row observes Hot immediately after seeding and never advances the clock. Catches a cache-temperature rule that never expires, or that reports a false expiry for loops that never cached. P1: a distinct projection rule rather than a variation on one already covered.
requirements: in-process only; clock advanced one hour via FixedClock
uncertainties: The TTL itself is never named. One hour is assumed to exceed it and the seed's own instant is assumed to be within it, so the row pins the DIRECTION of the rule but not its threshold; a TTL changed from minutes to tens of minutes would move nothing here.

rationale: Serialized under JsonSerializerDefaults.Web — what MVC actually uses — every enum on the report comes out as its NAME: execution kind, cost provenance, both completeness flags. The class comment explains the failure precisely: without a converter the web defaults ship these as integers, and a client cannot label an integer without holding a copy of the C# enum's declaration order, so the number silently remaps the day anyone inserts a member. That is a wire-compatibility break with no error at either end — the client keeps rendering, just with the wrong label on a cost figure. Pinning it on the report types only, leaving persisted usage shapes untouched, keeps the guard from over-reaching. Catches a serialization default turning a labelled contract into positional integers. P1: a cross-component contract with an HTTP client.
requirements: in-process only; pure serialization, no store
uncertainties: Constructs its own JsonSerializerOptions rather than reading the host's configured MVC options, so it pins the TYPES' own converters against the web defaults. A host that overrode the defaults differently is out of scope for this row.
ContextFreshness, CompactionStates and MeasurementProvenance appear on the report but are not among the four enums asserted here.

rationale: Thirteen fingerprint-pinned scenarios are each driven end to end in Off, Shadow and Compact — 39 full scripted runs covering restart adoption, legacy row backfill, parked runs resumed by an answer or a timer, sub-agent child compaction and two pricing regimes. Every run asserts the four zero-tolerance invariants (AC 4: no invalid tool pairs, no protected-state loss, no cross-thread reads, no raw-history loss) plus the mode's own contract — Off writes no state and runs no policy, Shadow records what it would have done but never touches the provider input, Compact activates and stamps an envelope only where the scenario expects it. That per-mode switch is what makes the matrix non-vacuous: without it a build where compaction never fired would satisfy every invariant in all three modes. Catches cross-mode regressions no single-behaviour test reaches. P3: a whole-feature operational journey across a scenario matrix, not a unit contract — it is the most expensive row in the component and its value is breadth, so it belongs after the targeted rows rather than before them.
requirements: in-process only; ScriptedProvider and ConversationStoreHarness, no network
WRITES TO DISK: the class fixture writes compaction-corpus-results.json and .md into CorpusPaths.ReportDirectory on disposal
serialized by [Collection("CompactionCorpus")], so it does not run in parallel with itself
uncertainties: Several assertions are conditional on scenario flags (ExpectRootCompaction, ExpectChildCompaction, MustSkipWith, ParksAtCall, Pricing). For a scenario with all flags off, the Compact arm asserts only CheckpointsActivated == 0, so the strength of an individual case varies widely across the matrix while every case reports identically as one passing test.

Numbers other than the invariants are deliberately NOT asserted — the class says they go to the report — so a quality regression that keeps the invariants but compacts far worse shows up only in a file a human must read.

rationale: The scenarios' fingerprints and the evaluator version must equal a committed manifest, and the scenario id list must be exactly a..m. This is the corpus's own integrity gate (D2): an edited scenario changes its fingerprint and the corpus refuses to run against inputs the manifest does not name until someone regenerates it deliberately. The id-list assertion is the part that matters most — it is the only thing standing between a silently deleted scenario and a matrix that shrinks without any test turning red, which is exactly how a corpus decays. The failure message names the file to copy, so the gate is actionable rather than merely obstructive. Catches drifted or missing corpus inputs. P2: a guard on the suite's own inputs rather than on product behaviour, and it derives its value from the P3 matrix it protects.
requirements: WRITES TO DISK: writes corpus.fingerprints.json into CorpusPaths.ReportDirectory before asserting
READS A COMMITTED REPO FILE: CorpusPaths.FingerprintsFile must exist relative to the test output
uncertainties: Depends on a committed file resolved through CorpusPaths, so it is sensitive to the test working directory in a way the other rows in this lane are not.

rationale: A candidate at or below an existing active boundary yields NoSafeBoundary rather than a cut. The active boundary marks what a previous checkpoint already compacted, so cutting there would summarise a summary and orphan the earlier checkpoint's own span. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A candidate past the end is clamped back into the thread. An input boundary on a search whose movement rules are pinned by the R1 and R3 fixtures. P2.

The current-instruction set is DERIVED from the rows at a given boundary rather than taken from anything a caller supplied, asserted on both sides of the second instruction so the answer changes with the boundary rather than being constant. A trusted value here would let a stale or hand-built request decide what the resumed agent is told to do. P1.

An empty thread has no boundary to cut at and is skipped with the typed reason rather than throwing or returning a cut at seq zero. P1 by the floor; on contract alone it is the degenerate input of the search.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Deferred calls and parked waits are counted into SEPARATE counters, seeded asymmetrically (two AskUserQuestion, one Wait) precisely so that a one-of-each seed cannot pass whichever counter each branch happens to increment. Those counts are what the checkpoint's recovery block reports and what V8 later validates against. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: An orphan call left by a dead stream ENDS its generation, so the boundary rule accepts it and only the pairing rule refuses it (#686 M16). A distinct exit from the paired case, reached by a real failure the fixture reproduces — the stream died and a later run carried the thread on. P1.

Assistant text and a tool call emitted in ONE generation, then the result: the cut may only fall after a generation's last row. This is a different atomic unit from the call/result pair — the fixture builds it by reusing the generation id explicitly — and splitting it discards half of a single model turn. P1.

A candidate landing on a tool-call row moves back before the pair, and the reported candidate seq is preserved separately from the chosen cut. Cutting between a call and its result leaves the tail opening with a result whose call is gone — a shape providers reject outright. P1 for rule R1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A candidate already at a legal boundary is accepted where it stands. Without it an implementation that always moved the cut earlier would satisfy every other R1 fixture, so this is what makes their assertions about WHERE the cut moved meaningful. P1 as the rule's non-vacuity anchor.

A Notify row is not an instruction, even though it enters the thread on the same side of the conversation. Quoting one as the current instruction would tell a resumed agent that a status notification is what it was asked to do. P1 for the classification rule the instruction quote depends on.

The flagship scenario the whole feature exists for: one instruction, a hundred tool turns, a mid-run cut at turn 60. It follows the decision all the way through — the chosen seq, the run id, the instruction row carried by REFERENCE, a clean recovery state — then builds the checkpoint and asserts what the projection actually dispatches: exactly eighty tail rows starting at turn 61, and an envelope whose second line is the verbatim current-instruction header carrying the original text. A cut that silently dropped the instruction would leave the agent working on a task it can no longer read. P1.
uncertainties: The strongest end-to-end claim in this file on consequence and assertion depth; held at P1 only because it is not an inP0Prefix member (LmMultiTurn's P0 candidates sit elsewhere).

rationale: A current run shorter than the floor is never split: the cut falls at the previous run's end, the current instruction is EMPTY because nothing of the current run was compacted, and the projection is asserted to carry all five run-2 rows. The empty-instruction half is the subtle one — quoting an instruction that is still present in the tail would duplicate it. P1 for rule R3.
The floor's arithmetic on a run long enough to split: the cut lands exactly where ten rows remain and TailTokens reports 100. An off-by-one here silently shortens every tail the feature produces. P1.

The release case: with a lookback of one, a correction older than that window may be split. Without it 'never split any run containing a correction' satisfies both protection fixtures above and the lookback would be dead configuration. P1 as R4's non-vacuity partner.

The same protection derived from the RUN LEDGER rather than from the rows: a run that followed an errored one is a retry and is kept whole. A different input path into the same rule — the ledger, not the message shape — so a fix applied to one does not cover the other. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A run the user corrected mid-flight is kept whole while it is recent. Splitting it can retain the correction while compacting the instruction it corrected, or the reverse — either way the agent resumes with half of an exchange whose halves only make sense together. P1 for rule R4.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A deferred AskUserQuestion at turn 30 refuses a cut at turn 60 and moves the boundary to just before it, keeping the placeholder in the tail and reporting a clean recovery state because nothing blocking was compacted. Compacting away a question the user has not answered yet strands the answer when it arrives. P1 for rule R6.

When the deferred call is the first row there is no safe boundary anywhere, so the selector SKIPS with the typed NoSafeBoundary reason and reports the deferred count. A different outcome shape from moving the cut, and the reason is what tells the policy why nothing happened instead of leaving it to guess. P1.

The second counter of the same CutBlockingState record, with the same construction, the same reason and the same assertion shape as the owed-continuation case. P2 as an additional input to a guard held at P1.

A blocking state the ROWS cannot show — an owed continuation known only to the loop — refuses the cut with the UnsafeState reason and carries the count into the recovery report. This is the input path that no amount of row inspection could discover, so it is a distinct source of refusal rather than a variation. P1.

The identical construction and identical assertions with the deferred tool changed to Wait. The by-tool distinction it rests on is pinned separately at P1 by the Observe fixture, which counts the two into different counters. P2 as a second tool under one rule.

With maxTail below minTail the selector keeps the floor and REPORTS the excess rather than enforcing the ceiling. Enforcing it would silently violate the guarantee that the current run keeps its floor, so the preference has to lose — and the flag is how the caller learns it did. P1 for rule R7.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The roster decides who exists; outcomes come from the real completion notifies FIRST and the model only fills gaps — asserted with a deliberate disagreement where the notify wins, a running agent with no outcome, and a model-only outcome that is kept. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Artifacts are scanned from real file tool calls across several tool spellings, unioned with the model's, and DEDUPED BY PATH with the scanned origin seq and the model's hash merged into one entry. Two entries for one file is the model editing a path it thinks it has two versions of. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The incremental form of :332 — rows before the previous boundary are not rescanned and the previous manifest's entries carry forward. A combination of the scan rule and the merge rule already held at :332 and :253. P2.

The user's own instructions are QUOTED WHOLE from the rows, with their seqs, rather than paraphrased by the model — the single section where a model rewrite silently changes what the agent believes it was asked to do. Both human rows across two runs are asserted, so a first-only or last-only implementation fails. P1.

Second-checkpoint merge (spec §2.5): the previous manifest's entries are kept with their headlines, the new span covers only the range past the previous boundary, and goals and instructions merge rather than replace. Rebuilding from scratch would discard the earlier headlines the model can no longer regenerate. P1.

Past the entry cap the OLDEST spans coalesce — merged run ids and a widened range — so the index stays bounded without losing coverage of any row. Dropping entries instead would make the oldest rows unrecallable. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 6 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A missing seq inside a run leaves the span contiguous rather than split. A robustness variation on the index construction pinned at :238. P2.

The recall index is the only way back to hidden rows: one span per run, contiguous from the first row to the cut, with a generated headline where the model supplied none. A wrong span sends a recall to the wrong rows and returns them as if they were the ones asked for. P1.

Instructions and decisions merge with the previous manifest's, deduped and ordered by seq — arranged so each list has an entry from each side and an exact duplicate to absorb. This is how a standing instruction ('never push') survives a second compaction; losing it is losing a constraint the user stated once. P1.

The recovery state travels from the cut into the manifest verbatim. Recomputing it as clean would have a checkpoint claim there were no deferred calls, parked waits or owed continuations at the boundary — the summary that a restart then trusts. Pinned on a hand-built cut, because the selector only ever produces a clean one. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.
Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The board is the authority on tasks: the nested tree is flattened in order, removed tasks are dropped, and the model's INVENTED task is absent entirely. A model-authored task list surviving into the manifest is a hallucinated work item the agent then pursues. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: With no board the model's tasks are kept but STRIPPED OF THEIR IDS — a model-invented id that looks like a board id is one a later tool call will try to act on. The distinguishing case for the rule above: 'ignore model tasks' passes :102 and fails here. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The prompt renders every row with its seq number and speaker, including the tool call's arguments and the tool result, and carries the previous manifest, the previous narrative, the sub-agent roster and the list of runs still needing a headline. The seq numbers are load-bearing rather than cosmetic: the manifest the model returns references rows by seq (QuotedItem.Seq, ArtifactRef.OriginSeq), so a prompt that omitted or renumbered them would yield a manifest whose quotes and artifacts point at the wrong rows — a checkpoint that reads plausibly and cites the wrong history. Carrying the previous manifest and narrative is what makes a checkpoint incremental rather than a fresh summary that silently forgets earlier goals. Catches a prompt that cannot support the references its own output format requires. P1: the input contract for the summarization.
uncertainties: Every assertion is Contain, so the prompt's ORDER and the absence of extra rows are unconstrained. A prompt that listed the rows out of sequence, or duplicated one, would still pass.

rationale: Three degenerate replies — empty, prose with no JSON, and a truncated object — all parse to null rather than to an empty manifest. Catches a parser that manufactures a blank summary from unusable text. P2: the unit-level input boundary underneath the SummarizeAsync throw row, reached through the same rule with three variations of malformed input.

A reply wrapped in conversational prose and a ```json fence is parsed, and every field of the manifest is mapped: instructions with their seq quotes, goals, tasks with status, artifacts with their origin seq, per-run headlines, per-agent outcomes and the narrative. Both halves matter. Fence tolerance is not leniency for its own sake — models routinely wrap JSON in prose, and a strict parser would turn a perfectly good manifest into the failed-call path and lose the checkpoint. Mapping EVERY field is what stops a silently dropped one: a manifest missing its artifacts still deserialises, still commits, and the loss only shows up as an agent that has forgotten which files it touched. Catches both an over-strict parser and a partially wired one. P1: the output contract of the summarization.
uncertainties: Decisions is present in the fixture JSON as an empty array and is the one field never asserted, so a parser that dropped decisions entirely would pass this row.

rationale: The provider call itself: exactly two turns, the first a System message carrying the summarizer's own SystemPrompt constant and the second a User message carrying the built prompt, no functions offered, the request's model winning over the constructor default, and the provider's UsageMessage handed back by reference. Functions being null is the assertion with teeth — a summarization that inherited the conversation's tool set could have the model attempt a tool call instead of producing a manifest, and it would also bill the whole schema on every checkpoint. Returning the usage is what lets a checkpoint's own spend be accounted rather than vanishing. The reply deliberately includes a thinking message, so the parser is proven to pick the content turn rather than the first one. Catches a checkpoint call built from the wrong turns, the wrong model or the wrong tool set. P1: the primary call contract.

A provider reply carrying no JSON object ('I cannot do that.') THROWS rather than resolving. The class summary states the rule as the distinction that matters: a reply without a JSON object is a failed call, not an empty manifest. The silent alternative is the damaging one — an empty manifest is a structurally valid checkpoint, so compaction would commit it and replace the conversation's instructions, goals, decisions, tasks and artifacts with nothing, discarding exactly the context the checkpoint exists to preserve, with no error anywhere. The raw rows survive — the corpus asserts zero raw-history loss in every mode — so a human reading the transcript could still recover, but the AGENT cannot: it continues the task from an empty manifest, and the work it does next is done in ignorance of what it was asked and what it already built. Catches a refused or malformed summarization silently becoming the agent's carried context. P1 with a P0 nomination: important failure handling on the one call whose output becomes the conversation's working memory.
uncertainties: DEMOTED in the end-of-slice P0 prune. Eighteen nominations across 347 in-scope rows is 5.2%, against the lane's healthy 2.4-3.1% band; ten survive. The nomination recorded above stands as the reason this row is the strongest in its component and is NOT withdrawn as an assessment - it is simply not a surviving candidate. Demotion reason: an empty checkpoint becoming working memory is damaging, but CompactionCorpusTests pins zero raw-history loss in all three modes, so what is lost is recoverable carried context rather than the record. Compaction also already holds three other nominations across its sub-components.

NOMINATED as the single Compaction P0 candidate after reading all six classes in the component (ProviderCheckpointSummarizer, ConversationContextReport, ContextObservationProjection, CompactionOptions, ConversationActivity, CompactionCorpus). Criticality justification: it is the only guard between an unusable provider reply and a structurally valid but empty checkpoint that becomes the agent's working memory mid-task, and it is a pure in-process unit test with no store, no clock and no provider, so it costs nothing to run first.

Contenders declined, with reasons. ContextObservationProjectionTests.Record_ForTheSameGeneration_KeepsBothAuthorsFields_InEitherOrder is a genuine lost-update guard but its damage is a wrong figure on a report, not a decision the agent acts on. Record_NeverOverwritesANewerSchemaRing is the only irreversible loss in the component, but what it loses is telemetry rather than work, and it needs a version-skew deployment to bite. CompactionCorpusTests.Corpus_HoldsEveryInvariant_InEveryMode carries the strongest invariants but is a 39-case journey, which is the wrong SHAPE for a small critical baseline.

Correction to an earlier draft of this row: it said an empty manifest is permanent context loss. That overstates it. The corpus pins zero raw-history loss in all three modes, so the rows survive; what is lost is the agent's carried context, not the record.

rationale: With no model on the request, the constructor's default model is used, and the response's usage is null when the provider sent none. Catches a null request model reaching the provider as a null model id. P2: the fallback arm of the model-selection rule whose positive direction the primary call row already pins, plus the absent-usage variation.

The wire shape the model actually reads, through the real handler: snake_case keys, the boundary seq, the match count, the tool_call_id, the row seq, the run id and the hint. A serializer default that emits camelCase leaves every field unreadable to a prompt written against the spec. P1.

An over-large limit is clamped to the configured maximum AND the answer says so — matched stays honest at six while returned is three, truncated is set and the hint tells the caller to narrow. A silently clamped answer reads as a complete one, which is how a model concludes the rest does not exist. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The bound that actually protects the thing recall exists to protect: the WHOLE answer is capped, dropping rows rather than only shortening them, so a broad query cannot spend the context window compaction just reclaimed. Per-row caps alone bound nothing across many rows. Rank 90 with 19 marginal spans. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: With nothing compacted the tool answers the typed nothing_compacted rather than an empty result set. The two are opposite facts to a model: 'there is no hidden history' versus 'the hidden history contains nothing matching' — and the second invites it to conclude the work never happened. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.
Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Two claims: the query matches without regard to case, and reasoning rows are never searched — recall is for conversation content, not for resurfacing the model's own private thinking into a later context. P1.

A second cap dimension over the same truncation machinery: the per-row character cap, with the seq embedded in the marker so the caller can ask again for that row. As a behaviour it is a variation on the clamping already pinned at :168 and I would have placed it at P2; it sole-covers one product span, so the floor decides the tier. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The containment invariant: recall reads only what compaction hid. An explicit from/to range past the boundary matches nothing, and an unfiltered read stops at the boundary. Leaking post-boundary rows duplicates content that is already in the live view. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A plain equality filter on the run id over the same read path, plus the role and type strings on the returned row. As a behaviour it is a further filter rather than a distinct read, so I would have placed it at P2; it sole-covers three product spans, so the floor decides the tier. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A tool-call id returns BOTH rows of the pair, with the call rendered as its name and arguments and the result as its output. A call without its result — or a result without the call that produced it — is unreadable, so the pairing rather than the filter is the behaviour here. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A profile prompt beats a constructor prompt on this loop. Catches an inverted precedence between the top two tiers. P2: a second point on the same cascade, on the same loop and the same seam the developer-instructions row already proves.

A profile prompt supplied alongside host developer instructions is what reaches the client as DeveloperInstructions after a real turn. The resolver test fixes the cascade; this is the only row proving the Copilot loop applies it on its start path, and it also pins the destination field, which is provider-specific — this loop carries the system prompt in DeveloperInstructions, so a correct resolution assigned to the wrong property would pass every resolver case and still run each profiled agent under the host's prompt. Catches the resolver being wired out of this loop, or its result landing nowhere. P1: the wiring seam for the Copilot loop.

Skills and sub-agents in a profile also trigger the once-per-loop unsupported warning, showing the deduplication is per loop rather than per unsupported FIELD. Catches a warning keyed to one field that fires again for another, or one that fires only for MCP. P2: a different unsupported-input set reaching the same rule and the same event id as the MCP row; the two differ only in which profile fields are populated.
uncertainties: Because both warning rows assert the same event id and the same count of 1, neither can distinguish 'warned once for this reason' from 'warned once for any reason'. A loop that emitted a single generic warning regardless of which fields were unsupported satisfies both.

rationale: A profile carrying all three unsupported input kinds at once still completes a turn. Catches an unsupported input throwing and taking the whole run down, which would make a profile that a sibling loop accepts into a hard failure here. P2: a robustness boundary combining the inputs the other rows cover singly.
uncertainties: The only assertion is that LastStartOptions is not null, so beyond 'the session started and nothing threw' this row constrains nothing. Its Codex counterpart is stronger because it also asserts the MCP dictionary stayed empty. Recorded as an assertion-strength gap; no change proposed.

rationale: A profile carrying MCP servers this loop cannot honour logs copilot.profile.unsupported exactly once across two turns. The disclosure is the important half: an operator who configured an MCP server in a profile and gets no warning has no way to learn it was ignored, and will read the resulting missing-tool behaviour as a model failure. The count of one is the second contract — a per-turn warning on a long conversation drowns every other diagnostic. Two turns is what makes the count mean deduplication rather than presence. Catches an unsupported profile input dropped in silence, and a warning that becomes per-turn noise. P1: the unsupported-input disclosure contract for this loop.
uncertainties: As in the Codex class, the loop's RunAsync task is started with a discard and never observed, so a fault in it would not fail the test.

rationale: The host's configured MCP dictionary reaches CopilotBridgeInitOptions.McpServers by REFERENCE. The comment states the risk precisely: this is a single forwarding line in OnBeforeRunAsync, and a silent regression on it drops every configured MCP server from the session/new ACP request. That failure is invisible from the outside — the session starts, the turn completes, and the agent simply cannot call the tools an operator configured, which reads as the model choosing not to use them. BeSameAs rather than equivalence is deliberate and stronger here: it proves the forwarding happens rather than an empty dictionary being reconstructed. Catches configured tool servers being silently dropped. P1: a cross-component wiring contract with the bridge.
requirements: in-process only; RecordingCopilotClient substituted via clientFactory
uncertainties: This row covers the loop's own SdkOptions.McpServers. Unlike the Claude and Codex loops, no row in this class covers merging a PROFILE's MCP servers with the host's — the profile MCP case appears here only as an unsupported input that triggers a warning.

rationale: An explicitly registered tool bridges through to the Copilot CLI's dynamic tool specs while neither client-only tool name appears. The positive control is what makes this the stronger of the two #246 guards in the lane: asserting 'ordinary_tool' IS present means a loop that bridged no tools at all fails, whereas the Claude counterpart's absence assertions would be satisfied by an empty surface. The rule matters because these two tools are registered only by MultiTurnAgentLoop's own constructor; if this loop injected them itself it would advertise to the model a way to ask the user a question that nothing here can route back, so the model would call it and the turn would stall or error on a capability the host never offered. Comparing against the providers' ToolName constants keeps the guard alive through a rename. Catches this loop inventing client-only tools. P1: a cross-component exposure boundary with a working non-vacuity control.

One scripted ACP stream — a thought chunk, two text chunks, a tool_call, a tool_call_update and the synthetic prompt/completed terminator — is asserted to translate into the loop's whole public message vocabulary. Several assertions carry real weight rather than restating the input. The two chunks 'Hel' and 'lo' must arrive as incremental TextUpdateMessages AND as a single aggregated TextMessage 'Hello', so both the streaming and the finalised views are pinned; a translator that emitted only one of them would leave either a UI with no live text or a transcript with no final message. The tool call must carry ExecutionTarget.ProviderServer, which is what tells the host this call is already being executed on the provider side and must not be dispatched locally — getting it wrong runs the tool twice. Usage must expose cached input tokens separately, which is what makes a cached turn's cost calculable. And every ordered message must have a MessageOrderIdx, without which consumers cannot reconstruct sequence from an async stream. Catches a provider event vocabulary translated incompletely or into the wrong shapes. P1: the primary translation contract for this loop.
requirements: in-process only; FakeCopilotClient replays scripted ACP envelopes, no bridge process
uncertainties: The MessageOrderIdx check is OnlyContain over a filtered set, so it asserts the field is PRESENT but never that the indices are distinct or increasing — a translator stamping the same index on every message would pass.
The enumeration is unbounded; a loop that never terminated the run would hang rather than fail.

rationale: After a run the Copilot session id extracted by the client is written to thread metadata under the copilot_session_id property. Without that write a host restarting has the conversation rows but no handle on the provider-side session that produced them, so the next turn silently opens a new one and the agent starts over — the same continuity failure the Claude loop guards with its session mappings, on a different key. Asserting the property key and its value, rather than merely that metadata exists, is what makes the record readable by the code that later resumes. Catches provider session identity not surviving the run. P1: the cross-process resume contract for this loop.
requirements: TIMING: a fixed 500ms sleep waits for metadata persistence that happens asynchronously after RunCompletedMessage
uncertainties: The 500ms delay is the only synchronisation with a write the loop performs after the run completes. It is generous, but it is still a guess: on a loaded machine a slow write reads as a missing one, and there is no signal the test could wait on instead.

rationale: A tool_call_update carrying status=failed becomes a ToolCallResultMessage with IsError=true and the specific error code copilot_tool_failed, and the run still completes. The direction of the failure is what makes this important: a translator that ignored the status field would hand the model the failure text 'kaboom' as a successful RESULT, and the model would reason on it as though the tool had worked — a fabricated success is far worse than a reported error. Pinning the error CODE rather than just the flag is what lets a host distinguish a provider-side tool failure from every other error class it handles. Catches a failed provider tool being reported as a success. P1: important failure handling in the translation path.
uncertainties: The failure text 'kaboom' is never asserted to reach the result, so whether the model is told WHY the tool failed is unpinned.

rationale: The constructor system prompt reaches the bridge as DeveloperInstructions, and the user's text reaches the provider VERBATIM as the run input. The second assertion is this row's distinct contribution: it pins that the loop does not wrap, template or annotate the user's prompt on the way out, which a provider-side agent would otherwise see as text the user never wrote. P2: the DeveloperInstructions half repeats what CopilotAgentLoopProfileTests already pins on the same field through the profile path, and the raw-prompt half is a single pass-through assertion rather than a distinct contract.
uncertainties: The input is a single user TextMessage. How a multi-message UserInput is rendered into the one string the provider receives is not covered by any row in this class.

rationale: A session/update carrying a kind the translator does not know must produce NO messages and exactly one Information-level diagnostic carrying structured properties — event type, dropped status, provider, provider mode and the unrecognised kind itself. Both halves matter and neither substitutes for the other: producing no messages is what stops an unknown event being fabricated into conversation content, and the structured diagnostic is the only way anyone learns the provider started sending something new. Asserting the PROPERTY VALUES rather than a formatted string is what makes the diagnostic queryable — a log line that reads well and carries no properties is invisible to the log queries that would surface a drift in the provider's event vocabulary. Pinning the level as Information rather than Warning is a deliberate choice about noise, and pinning the count at exactly one keeps a retry loop from flooding. Catches a provider event vocabulary drifting away unnoticed. P2: the unknown-input boundary on the translator.
requirements: pure unit test; hand-written ListLogger, JsonDocument fixture, no loop, no network
uncertainties: NO POSITIVE CONTROL anywhere in this class. 'Unmapped kinds must not produce messages' is asserted with no companion showing a MAPPED kind does produce them, so a translator returning empty for every event satisfies this row completely. If a partner exists it is in another class; within this file the claim is vacuous in one direction.

TIER NOTE for the coverage join: this is the only row in its file and may well be the only coverage of the translator's drop path. Tiered P2 on behavior alone, per the rule that irreplaceability never argues a tier up on its own. If the join shows exclusive spans outside the P0 prefix, the rubric's P1 floor applies to it mechanically — I am flagging it rather than pre-applying it.

ListLogger.IsEnabled returns true for every level, so a translator that guarded this diagnostic behind IsEnabled would look identical here to one that did not. On a host with Information filtered out, the drop would be silent and this row could not tell.

rationale: The deferral contract end to end: an IsDeferred placeholder with an empty result is published, the run completes, the provider is called exactly ONCE so no second turn fires against an unresolved call, and the pending set exposes it. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: The precondition guard: a new user input while a deferral is unresolved must NOT reach the provider. Verified twice over — the run comes back as an error naming the tool call, and the provider mock is still at one call. A request carrying an unresolved placeholder is not a valid request, and providers reject or mis-handle it. P1.
The pending entry carries function name, args and a deferral timestamp. Accessor detail on a set whose population is asserted at :29. P2.
The same disposal guard on the read accessor, which mutates nothing. P2.

Two deferrals in one turn: resolving the first starts its own child run (ADR 0004) that takes ZERO model turns, the run ids prove it is a new run rather than a re-completion, and only the resolution that clears the LAST unresolved call talks to the provider — which then sees both values. The interleaving rule that keeps a still-deferred placeholder from ever being sent. P1.

One restored Wait hits a genuine conflict — history already resolved it differently — and its throw used to abort the whole fallback loop, stranding every later entry forever. Per-entry isolation is asserted from both sides: the conflicting entry stays visibly parked with its two persisted rows untouched, and the innocent entry is still resolved and persisted. The highest exclusive-span row in this file. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 11 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: After a process restart the deferred registry is rebuilt from persisted history — id, function, args, run, generation and the original deferral instant all recovered. Without it, a deferral that outlived the process is unresolvable and the conversation is stuck with no way to answer it. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A Wait persisted while triggers were enabled, recovered by a process where they are disabled or rolled back: with no runtime to re-arm it, recovery must resolve it with a terminal trigger_disabled failure rather than leave it parked forever. Asserted on the persisted row, not just in memory. P1.

A tool handler's OperationCanceledException under a cancelled token must PROPAGATE, not be serialised into an LLM-visible tool error. The broad catch used to swallow user-initiated cancellation and hand the model an error message about its own cancellation, leaving the run to carry on. P1.

A second resolution with identical content is a no-op — no exception and, after a deliberate settle window, no third provider call. Resolutions arrive from webhooks and UI events that redeliver, so a duplicate must not start another run. P1.

External resolution replaces the placeholder and auto-resumes: a second provider call happens, that call's messages carry the resolved value (searched in both the singular and aggregated result shapes the middleware may produce), and the pending set empties. The whole point of deferral is that the answer reaches the model later. P1.

Resolutions arrive externally on arbitrary threads — webhook handlers, UI events — long after a host may have torn the loop down. Failing fast is what stops a disposed loop from mutating history that another process re-opening the same store is about to read. P1 for the mutating entry point.

A second resolution with DIFFERENT content throws rather than overwriting. This is the discriminator that stops the idempotency rule above from becoming last-write-wins — and a silent overwrite would change what the model was told after it had already been told something else. P1.
An unknown tool call id throws with the id in the message. A thin error path next to the two resolution rules it sits between. P2.

A deferral that outlived the process which created it still resolves through a fresh loop over the same store, and the persisted row stops being deferred. Delayed results are answered by humans and external systems on their own schedule, so outliving a restart is the normal case, not an edge one. P1.
A delayed result delivered as an error reports the tool as Failed with the message intact. Without it a failed external call reads as a successful tool in every lifecycle consumer. P1.

A disagreeing second result is rejected AND the committed value is unchanged in the store — both halves asserted, so an implementation that reported Conflict while applying the new value would fail. The model must not be told a different answer than the one it was already given. P1.

Eight concurrent deliveries of one result: exactly one Resolved, the rest Duplicate and nothing else, and — crucially — exactly ONE continuation, so however many callers race, the model is asked to continue once. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 5 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: ADR 0004 in one body: one child run per resolved result with unique ids and the real tool call as cause, none of them forks, exactly one provider call, the two non-final siblings complete as AwaitingSiblingResults with a turn count of ZERO, and the last one completes with a turn. The turn counts say in a subscriber's own vocabulary what the provider count says internally, so 'waiting' and 'did nothing' are the same story told twice. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The two-sibling form of the no-double-append check held at :305, which asserts it for the single result along with the cause and fabrication rules. P2.

The same result delivered twice is Duplicate, not Conflict. Delivery is by webhook, and a webhook that retries after a lost acknowledgement must not be told it failed — a caller that reads Conflict as an error escalates or drops a result that already landed perfectly. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: Resolved deliberately backwards: ownership of the continuation follows what is left OUTSTANDING, not arrival order. An implementation keyed on arrival order passes the forward case at :233 and fails here — this is the distinguishing case. P1.
An unknown tool call id answers NotFound. A thin negative on the outcome enum whose interesting members are covered above and below. P2.

The child's cause is the actual tool call — nothing synthetic is invented — no fabricated user message is appended to explain the result, and the resolved value appears exactly ONCE in the next request, counted across both the singular and aggregated shapes a request can carry it in. Carrying the cause and filling the placeholder must not both append. P1.

The tool belongs to the run that ASKED for it however long the answer took, and its completion is published before anything it caused — tool completed, child started, child's turn, child completed, in that index order. A subscriber that saw the child run before the tool completion would see a run whose reason for existing has not happened yet. P1.

Caller-initiated cancellation mid-write reports Cancelled, not StoreFailed. Both arrive as the same exception type, and blaming the store would have an operator chasing a health problem that does not exist. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The other half of that discrimination: an OperationCanceledException the CALLER did not ask for is the store failing. Calling it Cancelled would invite the caller to drop a result the store would happily take on retry — and the retry landing is asserted. Neither row alone pins the rule. P1.

A store failure leaves RETRY-SAFE state: the call is still outstanding, and the retry is reported Resolved rather than Duplicate — because the first attempt never committed. Getting that second half wrong tells the caller its result already landed when nothing was written. P1.

An entry restored from persisted history is pre-parked, so the child run id must exist by CLAIM time — before the commit — for the durable record to be able to name it, and the id the claim minted must be the id the cause carries. Catches a rebuilt entry that only learns it is parked at commit time, leaving the durable record written mid-commit naming no run at all. P1: the process-restart arm, a distinct entry point from a park observed live.

The other side of the same window, and the reason the guard cannot simply be "always start a child run": a result committing while its run is still going returns no cause, and the subsequent park is refused because nothing is outstanding. This is the non-vacuity partner for the regression case — a coordinator that minted a child run unconditionally would satisfy that test and fail this one. Catches a spurious child run per resolved call, which duplicates the provider request carrying the whole history. P1: the negative arm of the park decision, a distinct contract.

The claim is taken while the run is still going, the run then parks, and the commit lands after — the one interleaving the file's own remarks say the end-to-end suite cannot reach without racing a background run against a webhook. Driving the coordinator by hand makes the window a sequence of calls, so the regression is pinned deterministically rather than going quiet on a fast machine. All four post-conditions are asserted together: a cause is produced, it carries a child run id, it names the right tool call, and it owns the continuation. Catches a resolved result sitting in history with no run to carry it to the provider: no loop wake, no continuation, no answer — a conversation that silently stops replying with nothing logged as an error. P0: the coordinator exists for this window and this is the case that opens it. Coverage caveat: addsNothingNew means the same coordinator spans are traversed in other schedules, but none asserts the claim-before-park/commit-after-park interleaving and its child-run ownership, so overlap is not assertion redundancy.
requirements: in-process only; coordinator driven directly, no loop or provider

rationale: A second delivery for a call already mid-commit is refused, with a null claim and the IN-FLIGHT fingerprint returned to the caller. Returning the fingerprint rather than a bare false is the load-bearing half: it is how a caller tells an at-least-once redelivery of the same result from a genuinely conflicting second result, and a refusal without it forces the caller to guess. Catches two writers committing the same tool call concurrently, or a redelivery being treated as a conflict and dropped. P1: the exclusivity contract on the claim, a distinct primary behaviour.

Two calls from one turn, one claimed before the park and one entirely after: ordinals must still be 1 then 2 in COMMIT order, the child run ids must differ, and continuation ownership must fall to whoever clears the last outstanding call rather than whoever was claimed first. Asserting the owner in both directions — the first cause explicitly NOT the owner — is what makes it discriminating, since a coordinator that made every cause an owner would pass an owner-exists check. The dequeue order is checked separately so ordinal and delivery order cannot diverge. Catches a provider request built while another call is still outstanding, which is an invalid request, or two child runs sharing an id. P1: the multi-call ordering and ownership contract, distinct from the single-call park decision.

A resolution the store refused changed nothing, so its caller may deliver it again — but the retry must not forget the run ended meanwhile. Asserts the aborted claim leaves the call outstanding in the snapshot, that a second claim is therefore accepted, that by then the claim itself can see the park, and that the id the durable record already names is the one the cause carries. That last equality is the substantive one: a retry minting a fresh child run id would leave the durable record pointing at a run that never happens. Catches a delivery retry after a store failure being stranded exactly like the unhandled park. P1: the abort-and-retry arm, an important failure path distinct from the clean interleaving.

The worst shape of the same race — the whole turn's calls claimed, and only then the run ends. Every one comes back as a child run with a unique id, and the count of continuation owners is asserted to be exactly 1 rather than at-least-one, which is the assertion that catches every cause claiming ownership and issuing its own full-history provider request. Catches a fan-out of calls losing some results entirely, or multiplying the provider requests by the number of tools the turn used. P1: the multi-claim generalisation, distinct from the two-call ordering case because it fixes the owner COUNT rather than which one.
uncertainties: The OnlyContain non-null check would pass on an empty list, but the sibling assertions on causes[^1] and the owner count of exactly 1 fail on empty, so the test as a whole is not vacuous.

rationale: Recording a start is best-effort everywhere else; here it is the ordering that keeps the irreversible half safe. If the lifecycle write fails the provider must NOT be called (the next process would call it again and the model would see the conversation twice), nothing partial may be left behind, and the healthy successor carries it once under the same committed name. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The core durability claim: a result committed by a process that died before running it is carried exactly once by the process that replaces it, under the COMMITTED child run id — reusing that id is what makes a second crash idempotent. The result already in history is not appended a second time, and the persisted row stops being deferred. P1.

Severity is the product here: a host that restored deferred history the store never saw is a normal deployment, so the missing record is a WARNING about lost recoverability, not an error — and an error here trains an operator to ignore the case that is one. The continuation itself still starts. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The other side of that severity split: a record naming some OTHER run for this result is a real disagreement about which run carries it, and that is what error level is reserved for. Neither row alone pins the distinction. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The opposite direction: a continuation that already ran is not re-run by the next process. Without it every restart re-carries every past result. The negative is made deterministic rather than asserted on an absence — a run started by ordinary input can only begin once the recovered queue is empty, because delayed causes outrank input. P1.

P0 for capability containment surviving a restart. A run whose persisted receipt promised no spawning must not regain the Agent tool when a new process picks its owed continuation up — the suppression is read back out of durable metadata, and the recovered child's ADVERTISED function list is what proves it. The failure is a silent containment escape on the recovery path: an agent explicitly denied delegation gets it back by nothing more than a host restart, and nothing in the transcript says so. The row also carries the widest recovery path in the file — commit, recover, run the owed continuation to completion — so it doubles as this component's smoke test.
uncertainties: inP0Prefix member at greedyRank 20 with 104 new spans over a 3,268-span path.
Zero exclusive spans: the recovery machinery is re-covered by :241 and :331, so the row is chosen for its containment claim and its breadth rather than for being a sole cover.
Distinct component from this project's other P0s (input admission, tenant authorization, conversation ownership, sub-agent teardown, sub-agent observation).

rationale: The file's namesake race, built rather than waited for: a resolution claimed against a live run that finishes inside the durable write with the run parked. The record must name a child run — a child nothing recorded is one no restart can find — and the run that actually started must be the run the record names, since recovery keys off that id. P1.

An external store predating child-run naming is a fact about the deployment, not a delivery failure: the resolution proceeds without recoverability rather than being refused on every attempt forever. Asserted with a redelivery loop, and that exactly ONE attempt was needed — the discrimination against the refuse-and-retry rule at :82. The compatibility half is proven by the legacy façade compiling at all. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: What that deployment is TOLD: a warning naming the deployment limitation, no error, and emphatically not the contradiction message from :583. The continuation still reaches the conversation. A distinct log-severity path from :546 (old store versus missing record). P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Recovery writes a wake-up before the loop exists and the recovered run's own poll drains it; a flag that run forgets to clear leaves the loop ASLEEP FOREVER on a continuation it has already committed to running. Asserted through a later user turn and its own deferral, so the hang is reachable exactly as a restart produces it. P1.

The webhook shape: the caller that delivered a result is gone the instant the delivery returns, and the cause is already committed. A wake-up tied to the resolver's token dies with it and leaves the loop asleep on a queued cause. Arranged rather than hoped for — a queue of one and the loop held inside a child run make the backpressure real. P1.

A name committed by a process that died before running it is ADOPTED, not overwritten with a second run — two runs for one result send the conversation to the provider twice. A distinct concurrency path from the clean race above, and the assertion is on the started run's id, not merely on the record. P1.

A store that will not name the continuation refuses the whole resolution: the claim goes back, history is untouched, and the retry resolves and finishes the naming. Reporting a resolution that cannot record its carrier as having happened strands the result. Both the refused state and the retry's success are asserted, so 'refuse' cannot be implemented as a dead end. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 7 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Fail closed on purpose: an observer that throws blocks the enqueue entirely, so the caller gets a retryable error for a turn genuinely not taken. Swallowing would put the input in the channel with the host believing the agent idle — the exact defect the mechanism exists to prevent, reintroduced by the mechanism. P1.

The boundary the refusal must not cross: 'I have no entry for this conversation' is not evidence another agent holds it. Treating absence as a refusal fails every send to an agent the observer does not happen to track, including one it has not adopted yet — a total outage rather than a lost turn. P1.

Mint site one of two (#434): the accept is reported under the id the CALLER holds, so the ledger entry and the sender's receipt can retire each other, and the reported agent is the same instance — an observer that tracks agents by conversation compares that reference, so a wrong instance marks an agent that never took the input. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.
The file has almost no P2 because its rows are one per exit of a fail-closed protocol — report, enqueue, rescind — rather than variations on one behaviour.

rationale: SendAsync's other exit, which TrySendAsync does not have: a full channel parks on the write instead of refusing, and that await can still fail on a cancelled token or a channel completed underneath it. Same withdrawal, different failure shape, and the queue depth afterwards proves nothing was left behind. Ten exclusive spans. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 10 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The swap-race residual (#442): an observer parked in the report while the conversation's agent is replaced records nothing, yet this agent's channel is still open, so the enqueue used to SUCCEED — a turn sitting in an agent being torn down, in no ledger, with a receipt already handed to its sender. The refusal converts that into a failed send, and the row asserts the agent ASKED first, because a send that never reported would look identical. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The shape the three issue sites actually use: they send with no input id and discard the receipt. The minted id still exists and is what the ledger must hold — without this row those sites stay exactly as uncovered as they were before the fix. P1.

Issue site three's happy path through the collaboration write endpoint. The file's own remarks call the per-site rows regression guards rather than the mechanism's proof, and the accept itself is held at the mint sites above. P2.

The endpoint's own refusal path — its translation to a Refused disposition alongside the withdrawal — which is distinct product code from the mint sites and the widest single addition in the file's greedy order (10 new spans). A peer's refused delivery must not leave the host holding a turn that was never queued. P1.

Mint site two. The fix is structural — reporting from the only two places an acceptance can come into existence covers every caller by construction — so both places have to be pinned or the construction argument is half-proven. P1.

The rollback partner that makes reporting-before-enqueue safe: a refused send withdraws its own report, and ONLY that one — the two genuinely queued inputs stay reported. A standing report for a turn that was never queued leaves the conversation reading busy until the host's grace expires, refusing real handoffs for seconds. P1.

Ordering: the durable accepted-input write runs BEFORE the report, so a failure there means nothing was accepted by anyone — nothing to report and nothing to withdraw. Reporting first would leave the host holding an entry busy for a send that failed outright. P1.

The same refusal on the path that has a durable half: the accepted-input record written before the report has to be undone, or a caller polling by input id finds an acceptance for a turn that was never queued and never will be. It throws rather than returning null deliberately — null means 'retry this agent', and this agent is no longer the one the conversation holds. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 6 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: All three compaction lifecycle events — decided, applied, failed — must be registered as KNOWN types, publish exactly one event carrying their payload, and correlate to the thread, run and generation they came from. Running the same assertions as a theory over the three types is the right shape here: the failure mode for a new event type is that one of the family is added to the emitter but not to the known-types table, and an event that is not known is dropped or mishandled downstream rather than rejected at the source. The correlation triple is what makes the event usable at all — a compaction event that cannot be tied back to its run tells an operator that something was compacted somewhere. Asserting EventTypes equals exactly the one type, rather than merely containing it, pins that one call publishes one event. Catches an unregistered or uncorrelated compaction event. P1: the emission contract for the compaction event family.
requirements: pure unit test; recording publisher, no loop, no store, no clock
uncertainties: The payload is populated with seven fields and only four are read back. Tokens, Window, Reserve and CacheTemperature — the numbers a consumer would chart and the ones that make a decision reviewable — are set by the fixture and never asserted, so a serializer dropping them passes.

IsKnown is asserted against the theory's own InlineData constant, so it exercises the constants table rather than anything the finalizer does; it would catch a type removed from the table, not a type the emitter uses without registering.

rationale: With lifecycle services disabled, the finalizer reports that it published nothing. This is the off-switch for a subsystem a host may not want running at all, and the return value is what a caller uses to avoid doing follow-up work for an event that never went out. Catches a disabled lifecycle that publishes anyway. P2: the feature-off variation on the emission path.
uncertainties: The only assertion is the RETURN VALUE. Nothing observes that no event was emitted, because the disabled services carry no publisher to inspect — so an implementation that published through some other route and then returned false would pass. The row pins the report, not the absence.

rationale: A boot seed rides EVERY request, so reporting per request would announce the same file on every turn of a long conversation. Three requests carrying one system prompt produce one event. P1.

The incremental half: a second request carrying an old block and a new one produces a second event naming ONLY the new source, with rendered text that is only the new block. Repeating the old source would double-count it for any subscriber accumulating what the model has seen. P1.

The prompt-string seam that Codex- and Copilot-shaped loops dispatch through reports identically to the message-list seam — same rendered text, same source phase. Two loop shapes have to produce one event stream, or a subscriber's view of what the model was shown depends on which provider ran. P1.
The empty-case negative on the string-prompt overload. The overload's real behaviour is held at :193. P2.
A request whose text merely MENTIONS a context file publishes nothing. The negative is real but shallow; :285 holds the sharp form of the same rule with a tag that nearly matches. P2.
P2 on what the body can actually establish — a run that starts and completes with no reported request emits no context event.
uncertainties: The arrangement does not connect discovery to the agent: the block at :173 is built into a discarded local and is never handed to the loop, so the test asserts that an agent which was given nothing publishes nothing. It cannot distinguish an implementation that publishes from discovery from one that publishes from dispatch, which is the claim its name and comment make.

rationale: One phase constant, via a notify-carried block instead of the system prompt. The descriptor shape is held at :59 and the mid-session phase is asserted again at :193. P2.

The whole source descriptor in one place: boot phase, discovery kind, path normalised across separators SO TWO HOSTS AGREE, display name, dedup identity built from kind and normalised path, and the not-truncated flag. The dedup identity is what the once-per-source rules below key on, so its shape is load-bearing. P1.

A tag whose name merely STARTS with the block's tag name, and a bare mention of the opening tag in prose, are both not context blocks. A prefix-matching scanner would report arbitrary user text as delivered context — and the text here is exactly what a conversation about the feature contains. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 5 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The truncation flag: a subscriber reading a context_loaded event must be able to tell that the model saw LESS than the file holds, or it will attribute a model's ignorance of a rule to the model rather than to the truncation. P1.
uncertainties: inP0Prefix member (greedyRank 13, +136 new spans) but proposed at P1, not P0. Its own assertion is a single truncation flag; the 136 spans are an artefact of greedy ORDER — it is the first row of this file the prefix reaches, and :33 exercises the same emission path more thoroughly. The component is observability: a wrong or missing context_loaded event misleads a subscriber about what the model was shown, which is a reporting fault rather than a product failure, so it does not carry the criticality the other P0s do. Flagging it as the file's P0 candidate if the lead wants prefix-driven P0s here.

rationale: A block with no closing tag reports the whole block that preceded it and nothing else — a mangled tag reports LESS, it does not fail the send. The scanner runs on every outbound request, so an exception here would take down dispatch over malformed text. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Render and scan are inverse over a path containing a quote, an ampersand entity and angle brackets: text, normalised path, truncation flag, dedup identity and byte count all round-trip. The writer and the reader are separate code, and a divergence makes a path that renders fine come back as a different source — or as none. P1.

Two sources in one request are ONE delivery: sources in request order, rendered text the plain concatenation of the two blocks, and the hash over exactly that. The comment names the trap the assertion closes — the newline between the blocks belongs to the prompt, not to either block, so hashing it would cover bytes the model was never sent as context. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The event reports the BYTES that were sent: rendered text identical to the block, the UTF-8 byte count, the SHA-256 over that exact text, and the run and generation it belongs to. Everything a subscriber may conclude rests on those four fields agreeing with the request. P1.

Identity is the SOURCE, not its bytes: the same path re-rendered with different content is not a second delivery. Keying dedup on content would re-announce a file every time it was edited mid-session. A distinct rule from the boot-seed case above, and the one that fixes what the dedup identity is. P1.

One generation produces exactly TWO context observations — estimated before dispatch, measured once the provider reports usage — sharing one generation id and ordinal, persisted as ONE ring entry, and broadcast as a transient pressure frame. The pairing is the substance: the two payloads are checked to carry the same GenerationId and GenerationOrdinal, and the history is asserted to contain a single entry with the reason spelled out — estimated and measured are one generation. Without that, the obvious implementation writes two entries and every utilization trend downstream doubles its sample count. The measured payload's Utilization is pinned to an exact expression, 1000 / (200000 - 4000), so the reserve is proven to be excluded from the denominator rather than merely present in the payload; an off-by-a-reserve utilization is precisely the error that makes a compaction trigger fire early or late. It also follows the value out to the subscriber frame, so the persisted, published and broadcast copies are all checked. Catches miscounted or misattributed context measurements. P1: the primary per-generation observation contract.
requirements: in-process only; Moq streaming agent, InMemoryConversationStore, FixedCapacity resolver
bounded: 20s cts, plus a hand-rolled 100 x 20ms poll for the broadcast frame
uncertainties: The subscriber is attached and then the test sleeps a fixed 100ms before starting the run, rather than registering synchronously the way the Triggers and Recovery classes in this lane do (issuing but not awaiting the first MoveNextAsync). Under load the run can begin before the subscription attaches, and the frame assertions then depend on the 2-second poll finding a frame that was never published to this subscriber.

EstimatedInputTokens is asserted only to be greater than zero. The estimate's relationship to the measured value — the entire point of having both — is unconstrained, so an estimator returning 1 would pass.

LatestContextObservation is compared to the projection's own result with BeEquivalentTo. That pins the loop's in-memory view against the store, which is worth having, but both are read AFTER the run, so it cannot detect a view that was stale during the run and refreshed at the end.

rationale: Generation ordinals are a property of the CONVERSATION, not of the process: a first loop runs one generation and records ordinal 1, that loop is disposed, and a second loop over the same store records ordinal 2, with the history holding both entries. A reset ordinal is a quiet corruption rather than a loud one — the new process starts numbering from 1 again, so the ring holds two rows both claiming to be generation 1, and any consumer ordering or de-duplicating by ordinal silently discards or overwrites real observations. Asserting the ordinal after the FIRST loop, before the restart, is what makes the second assertion a continuation rather than a coincidence. Catches per-process generation numbering. P1: the restart-continuity half of the observation contract.
requirements: in-process only; two loops over one InMemoryConversationStore instance
uncertainties: The restart shares the same in-memory store OBJECT, so continuity that depends on state living in that instance rather than in persisted rows would survive for the wrong reason — the same caveat as the restart row in InterruptedDeferralRecoveryTests.

Only one restart and two generations are exercised, so the row pins that the counter does not reset; it does not show the ordinal is derived from persisted history rather than from a single carried-forward value.

rationale: With no capacity resolver configured the observation is still persisted with the real measured token count, but the window is null and — the assertion that matters — Utilization is NULL, 'an unknown window reads as unknown, never as a number'. This is tiered P1 rather than as an ordinary unconfigured-default variation because the assertion is a prohibition with a downstream consumer: utilization is what pressure and compaction decisions read, so a resolver-less host that defaulted the window to some constant would produce a plausible percentage computed against a window nobody knows, and compaction would fire on it. Persisting the measurement anyway is the other half — the host still gets its token counts, it just gets no ratio. Catches a fabricated utilization on a host with no capacity information. P1: the never-fabricate rule on the degraded configuration path.
requirements: in-process only; loop built directly rather than through the class helper, no lifecycle services at all
uncertainties: This loop is constructed directly rather than through CreateLoop, so it differs from the other rows in more than one variable: no capacity resolver, but also no publisher, no MaxToken and no PromptCaching mode. The PromptCachingEnabled false assertion therefore reflects the missing PromptCaching option, not the missing resolver, and the row is not a clean single-variable comparison against the first one.
A resolver that is PRESENT but returns null for the model — the more common shape, since Resolve is nullable — is not covered; only the wholly absent resolver is.

rationale: Multi-turn shape, which only the raw loop has: a tool call buys a second turn, ordinals run 1 then 2, each turn is its own generation so a subscriber can key state by generation id, the tool-call counts land on the right turns, and the run reports two. Ordinals are the subscriber's only way to order turns within a run. P1.
component: LmMultiTurn/turn lifecycle contract across all four loops

rationale: P0. Greedy rank 2 in the entire lane with 1097 marginal new spans over 3158 covered — no other single test in this lane reaches as much product per test, because this one row drives all four REAL loops (raw middleware pipeline, Claude SDK, Codex CLI bridge, Copilot CLI bridge) end to end against scripted provider streams. The claim is the load-bearing one for every lifecycle subscriber: a fragment is not a turn, so no number of deltas can produce a second turn_completed, and the one event carries the run's generation id. A duplicate turn event double-counts tokens, turns and cost for every consumer downstream.
