Non-vacuous by construction — it first asserts that deltas actually flowed, so a loop that silently dropped them cannot satisfy the count for the wrong reason.
component: LmMultiTurn/turn lifecycle contract across all four loops
uncertainties: Zero exclusive spans, which is expected: its file-mates drive the same four loops. Its argument is greedy reach, not sole cover.
The only P0 on the lifecycle contract; the failure and cancellation rows below sit on the same four loops and stay P1 so the P0 does not stack on one path.

rationale: Cancellation is a third stable outcome, neither success nor error, on all four loops — and the half-arrived answer is not counted as a message. Folding cancellation into Error makes every user-initiated stop look like a fault in the dashboards built on these events. P1.
component: LmMultiTurn/turn lifecycle contract across all four loops
uncertainties: Holds 8 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

A loop terminalizing every path through one shared exit would tell a subscriber that a generation which died succeeded. Rank 78, 20 exclusive spans. P1.
component: LmMultiTurn/turn lifecycle contract across all four loops
uncertainties: Holds 20 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The same answer delivered whole and delivered as deltas produces the same message count, tool-call count, ordinal and outcome on every loop. Fragments describe HOW an answer arrived; counting them as messages inflates every per-turn statistic in proportion to how chatty the provider's streaming happens to be. P1.
component: LmMultiTurn/turn lifecycle contract across all four loops

rationale: One ordinary turn described identically by MultiTurnAgentLoop, ClaudeAgentLoop, CodexAgentLoop and CopilotAgentLoop over four unrelated wire formats: the three events in order, the agent kind each loop honestly reports as its own, the model, the cause, turn one, the message and tool-call counts, the outcome, and the run and generation ids tying them together. A subscriber writes one handler against this shape for every loop. P1.
component: LmMultiTurn/turn lifecycle contract across all four loops

rationale: Every loop passes its provider's own token counts through onto the turn event, marked Complete. Four providers report usage in four shapes; the accounting stack reads only this one. A dropped or halved count is a billing number that is wrong and looks right. P1.

rationale: The correlation envelope on the turn event: thread, run and generation match the run that started, and a top-level run carries no parent run or sub-agent id. Unstamped or mis-stamped events cannot be attributed to a conversation at all, which is the difference between usage landing on the right row and landing nowhere. P1.

rationale: Sequential double completion emits one RunCompleted. The concurrent form at :120 asserts the same one-completion invariant through the same guard with eight racers and additionally checks exactly one caller is told it won. The sequential form is the weaker half, and coverage records it as adding no new spans. P2.
Eight concurrent completions of one run: exactly one returns true and exactly one RunCompleted is published. The in-process exactly-once guard, exercised in the shape that breaks it. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Disposal without a stop reports Interrupted, not Cancelled. The two outcomes are separate constants a subscriber acts on differently — a deliberate stop versus a host that went away — and this is the only row asserting the dispose path picks the second. P1.

A failed run must terminalise as Error and carry the message. A subscriber that sees Completed for a run that failed reports success for work that did not happen — and the error text is the only thing telling anyone why. P1.

The precedence rule of the ForAgent merge, all four cases: null and Disabled both stay Disabled — so passing a disabled bundle can never accidentally enable lifecycle — the loop's agent kind is stamped over the host's, and the host's model id wins over the loop's guess while the guess still fills a null. Every host wiring a loop goes through this. P1.

The true branch of the WasForked flag plus the parent run id on the correlation. The false branch and the correlation shape are already asserted at :60 through the same payload construction, and coverage records this as adding nothing new. P2.
The other direction: a publisher that throws must not break the run — the run still persists as Completed. A subscriber's fault reaching the loop would let anyone listening kill the work. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The empty case of the reconciliation pass — nothing dangling, nothing emitted. A negative variation of the reconciliation behaviour held at P1 above, adding no new spans. P2.
uncertainties: Name and assertion disagree: the name promises reconciliation runs once across restarts, while the body starts and stops the loop twice with nothing dangling and asserts no events were published at all. Tiered on what the body actually asserts.

rationale: A run left non-terminal by a previous incarnation is reconciled on the next boot: published as Interrupted, persisted as Terminal, and gone from the non-terminal list. Without it a crash leaves a run that is forever in flight to every reader of the store. P1, and the highest exclusive-span row in this file.
uncertainties: Holds 8 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Two finalizer incarnations both believing they own the run — the shape a restart overlapping its predecessor produces. The tie is broken in the STORE, not in either process's memory, so the in-process guard above cannot decide it. Distinct mechanism, distinct failure. P1.

Every event from a spawned agent carries the full lineage: own thread, parent thread, parent run, spawning tool call, and sub-agent id — checked on all events, not just the first. That correlation is the only thing that lets a consumer rebuild the run tree; dropped on the completion, a sub-agent's end cannot be attributed to its parent. P1.

The pairing contract a subscriber is allowed to assume, asserted whole in one place: exactly RunStarted then RunCompleted, matching run and generation ids, agent kind, cause, outcome, one source stream, ascending source sequence, unique event ids, and correlation carrying the run id on both. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Cancelling the loop terminalises the run it interrupted as Cancelled, both published and persisted. Without it, cancelling leaves a run that started and never completed — the exact dangling state reconciliation then has to clean up on the next boot. P1.

A lifecycle store that throws on every call must not suppress the events: both are still published with the right run id. Lifecycle is observability, and a degraded store taking the event stream down with it is the failure mode this rules out. P1.

Store-only wiring still drives the run to Terminal/Completed in the store. That is a shipped configuration — persist for reconciliation, publish to nobody — and no other row asserts the store half without a publisher present. P1 on the persistence claim.
uncertainties: The 'publishes nothing' half is vacuous — the RecordingLifecyclePublisher at :39 is never passed to the agent (the services bundle at :42 carries only LifecycleStore), so its event list is empty regardless of product behaviour. The persistence half is real and is what this row is tiered on.

rationale: Lifecycle is off unless asked for: an unwired loop reports disabled AND the store holds no run rows. Every loop in the product runs this configuration by default, so a regression that switched it on would put lifecycle writes on every host that never opted in. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: The derived child bundle drops the parent's ModelId while keeping the same publisher, sequence allocator and approval gate by reference, and both a null and a Disabled parent derive to the Disabled singleton. The dropped model is the substantive one and the comment gives the mechanism: carried forward it would beat the child's own resolved model in ForAgent's null-coalescing, so every sub-agent event would claim a model the child never called — corrupting per-model cost attribution across the tree. Keeping the approval gate by reference matters equally: a gated parent did not ask for ungated children. P1: the derivation contract itself, distinct from whether the spawn path calls it.

Across every event one spawn produces, the distinct non-null sub-agent ids collapse to exactly one. Catches an id minted per event or per stage, which would make a subscriber see a crowd of one-event agents instead of one agent's stream and break every grouping keyed on it. P1: the grouping key's stability, distinct from the lineage fields' correctness.
uncertainties: Filters out null sub-agent ids before the distinct count, so an event stream that carried the id on only one event would still report exactly one.

rationale: With capacity 1, a second spawn queues behind a blocked first; the parent's current run is changed WHILE it waits, and when it finally starts it must report the run that accepted it rather than the one in flight when capacity freed. Changing the parent run between accept and start is exactly the window a capacity queue opens, and only a lineage captured at accept time survives it. Catches a queued child attributed to an unrelated later run, which misplaces it in the tree — the same class of defect as the restart case but reached through the capacity gate rather than a rebuild. P1: the queued-spawn arm, a distinct path to the same invariant.
requirements: in-process only; gated provider, bounded 10s wait

rationale: The parent is moved on to a different run before the child is restarted, and every run the child publishes must still carry the ORIGINAL spawning tool call and parent thread, must never carry the later run, and must keep one sub-agent id across the restart. The setup is what makes it decisive: re-deriving lineage at rebuild time would read the parent's by-then-current run and lose the tool call outright, silently re-parenting the whole sub-tree. It also pins the subtler rule that the second run's parent is the FIRST run rather than the spawn, so an in-thread cause outranks lineage and a subscriber walks the chain. Catches an agent tree that reassembles wrongly from the event stream — every cost, every transcript and every completion barrier keyed on that tree then attributes to the wrong parent. Nominated P0: the file exists for this regression and it is the one case where the derivation is called at the wrong moment. Confirmation held pending the facts join.
requirements: in-process only; mocked parent agent and provider

rationale: A host-code spawn carrying no tool call still reports the parent run and a sub-agent id, with the tool call id null. Catches a lineage derivation that treats a missing tool call as missing lineage and drops the parent run with it, which would orphan every host-initiated sub-agent in the tree. P1: the host-spawn arm, a distinct entry point from a model tool call.

A spawned child's run_started correlation carries the parent thread, the parent run, the spawning tool call id and a non-blank sub-agent id — and, in the same assertion block, its OWN thread and run differ from the parent's. Both directions are needed: lineage says where the child came from, not who it is, and a child that reported the parent's thread as its own would collapse the two agents in every consumer. Drives a real child loop through the manager rather than the derivation helper, which the file's remarks justify — the derivation was never the risky part, the spawn path forgetting to call it is. P1: the lineage baseline the other cases vary.

A manager created with no lifecycle services spawns a child and the publisher records nothing, pinning that an unobserved parent produces unobserved children rather than a child that wires itself up independently. P2: the assertion is weaker than the contract it names, so it is a boundary case over the wiring the other tests establish rather than a distinct guarantee.
uncertainties: Close to vacuous: the RecordingLifecyclePublisher it asserts on is never handed to the manager, which is constructed with lifecycleServices null. An empty result is therefore guaranteed by construction rather than by the behaviour under test — a child that DID publish could only do so to a publisher it was never given. The stated contract would need the publisher wired and the child's inheritance suppressed some other way.

rationale: A tool name the host never registered is rejected WITHOUT consulting the gate. The comment states the reason plainly — ordering, not politeness: the call cannot execute whatever the answer, so asking would spend a human's attention, or a remote approval round trip, on something already doomed. Asserting WasConsulted is false is the whole substance; the error result alone would pass on an implementation that asked first and rejected after. Catches an approval prompt raised for a call that can never run. P2: an ordering variation on the reject path, secondary to whether the gate blocks at all.
uncertainties: Unlike the refusal row, this one asserts only IsError and never the error code, so it cannot distinguish 'rejected because the tool is unknown' from a failure for any other reason — including one raised by the approval path it is trying to prove was skipped. The WasConsulted check carries the row; the result assertion adds little.

rationale: A denying gate must stop the handler from running AT ALL — the assertion's own because-clause says it: a refusal must block execution, not merely annotate it. The row then pins the three things that make the refusal usable rather than merely effective: the result is flagged IsError with the Denied error code, the reason and tool name come back through the ORDINARY result channel so the model can choose something else instead of watching the loop unwind, and the gate was consulted for exactly that one tool. The class remarks state why an integration row is required and not just the preparer's own unit tests — a preparer nothing calls is a decision nothing enforces — so the property under test is that the loop asks, on the real dispatch path. The tool is named delete_everything for a reason: if this inverts, the gate is decorative and every denial in the product is ignored while the UI reports the call was refused. Catches an authorization decision that does not actually gate. P1 with a P0 nomination for the approval-gate component.
requirements: in-process only; Moq streaming agent, no store, no timers, two scripted turns
uncertainties: NOMINATED as the single P0 candidate for the approval-gate component. Criticality justification: this is an authorization boundary, the one consequence class where a green suite and a broken product are indistinguishable from the outside — a decorative gate refuses in the UI and executes anyway. It is also the broadest row here, since it fails for EVERY denial rather than for a particular payload, and the cheapest kind of run in this lane: two scripted turns, no store, no clock, no provider. Verified against the existing candidate list: the two Lifecycle candidates already nominated cover the turn contract and restart lineage, not approval.

Contender declined, with reasons. AnApprovedCallRunsOnExactlyTheBytesTheApproverSaw is the confused-deputy row and is equally severe where it bites — approve one payload, execute another — but it bites only when something mutates arguments between decision and dispatch, whereas an inverted refusal breaks every denial unconditionally. If the lead weights payload integrity over gate effectiveness, that is the row to swap in.
The refusal message is matched by substring, so its structure is unconstrained.
Only one gate is configured. ToolApprovalOptions takes a LIST of gates, and the semantics when several disagree — first denial wins, all must allow, ordering — are exercised by no row in this class.

rationale: The handler must receive exactly the argument JSON the approver was shown — 'what was decided and what executed must not diverge'. This is the confused-deputy shape: a gate that inspects one payload while a different one reaches the tool converts human or policy approval into a rubber stamp, and the divergence is invisible because both halves report success. Comparing the handler's captured string against the RECORDED request's Arguments.Json, rather than against the fixture constant, is what makes it a decision-to-execution comparison rather than two independent equality checks. Catches an approved call executing on payload the approver never saw. P1: the integrity half of the approval contract.
uncertainties: The comparison pins AGREEMENT between the gate and the handler, not fidelity to what the model actually requested. A preparer that rewrote the arguments before showing them to the gate would present the rewritten bytes to both and pass. The no-approver row asserts the handler sees the original constant, which covers the ungated path only; nothing pins the original bytes through a gated one.

rationale: With no lifecycle services at all, the tool runs on the original arguments and returns a non-error result — the loop behaves exactly as it did before approval existed. This is the feature-off path, and it carries a second job the class depends on: it is the positive control for the refusal row's zero-invocation assertion. Without it, a dispatch path that never invoked handlers under ANY configuration would satisfy 'invocations == 0' for entirely the wrong reason. It is also the only row that pins the handler receiving the untouched fixture arguments, which is what the gated integrity row cannot show on its own. Catches an optional feature that changes behavior when it is switched off. P1: the unconfigured-default contract, and the non-vacuity partner for the gated rows.
uncertainties: 'lifecycleServices: null' is the only off shape covered. A bundle that is present but carries a null Approval preparer is the configuration a host is far more likely to produce, and no row exercises it.

rationale: A batched two-call message plus a singular one counts three tool calls, and the result message counts toward messages but not toward calls. Providers differ in which shape they emit and middleware rewrites between them, so a counter that saw a batch as one call would under-report every provider that batches. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The idempotence latch on the ordinary close path: a second close reports nothing. A repeated event double-counts a turn a subscriber already saw finish. P1.

Eight racing completions: exactly one caller is told it won AND exactly one event is published. The two assertions are separate claims — a latch could publish once while telling several callers they won, which is how a loop ends up believing it still owns a closed turn. P1 for the compare-and-set under contention.

Three turns report under their own generation ids in order, with ordinals 1, 2, 3 and a run count of three. Ordinals that repeated or drifted would make two turns indistinguishable to a subscriber aggregating by them. P1.

The ordinary path with the whole payload pinned: the exact event ORDER (run started, turn completed, run completed), the run and generation ids, an ordinal starting at 1, the outcome, the message and tool-call counts, a null error, and the run's own turn count agreeing. Everything a subscriber is allowed to assume, in one place. P1.

Messages arriving before the turn opens and after it closes are ignored; only the one inside the window counts. Both sides are seeded in one body, so an implementation that simply counted everything for the run, or that kept accepting after the close, fails. That post-close half also protects the exactly-once report from being reopened. P1.

Cancellation escapes the loop without ever reaching a completion call — the case the test calls out as exactly what the sweep exists for — and it is driven through a real running loop and StopAsync rather than through the seam directly. The outcome is Cancelled, and the full event sequence is asserted. P1.

Disposal reports the open turn as INTERRUPTED — a third distinct outcome, and the one that says the process went away rather than that anything decided to stop. Disposal without a stop is what a host shutdown looks like. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A turn still open when the run errors is swept, reported with the run's outcome and the error message, and KEEPS the count of what it produced before it died. Without the sweep that turn is never reported at all and a subscriber waits forever for an event that is not coming. P1.

The positive half of the same mapping: present detail counts are carried. Two field assertions over the projection whose dangerous direction — inventing zeros for absent detail — is held at P1 above. P2.

Absent cache and reasoning detail comes through as NULL, not zero, alongside the totals the provider did report — and completeness is stamped Complete. A provider reporting no cache detail is not a provider reporting zero cached tokens, and collapsing the two turns an unknown into a measured claim of zero. P1.

A run stopped by its turn ceiling reports MaxTurns at the run level while its open turn reports Completed: the run stopped BETWEEN turns, so the turn itself was fine. Letting the run's outcome flow into the turn's would mark a perfectly good turn as failed on every capped run. P1.

A run that performs no model turn — the non-final delayed-result sibling of ADR 0004 — emits NO turn event and reports a count of zero. Synthesising a turn here would invent model work that never happened, in the events downstream billing and telemetry read. P1.

Text, reasoning and tool-call DELTAS are not messages, and a fragment of a tool call is not a requested tool call — only the complete message that supersedes them counts. Since the CLI translators push deltas through history and the raw loop does not, counting them would make message_count mean something different per provider, which the file states is the one thing this event may not do. P1.

A turn the loop already closed is not re-reported when the run then FAILS, and it keeps its Completed outcome rather than inheriting the run's error. The sweep and the loop are two independent reporters of the same turn, so this is the seam between them, and rewriting a finished turn's outcome would misattribute a run-level failure to a turn that succeeded. P1.

Two finalizers over one run: the first wins the terminal transition, the second is told it lost, and only ONE run-completed event reaches subscribers. Two terminal events for one run would close the same run twice with contradictory outcomes downstream. P1.
uncertainties: The method name says the loser's TURN is not reported, but the assertion counts RunCompleted events; the in-file comment states turn reporting is deliberately idempotent per finalizer and it is the run that must end once. Taken at the comment's word.

rationale: No usage message observed leaves the payload's usage null. A boundary on the same projection. P2.

With no lifecycle services wired, the whole turn flow runs and the lifecycle reports itself disabled — no publisher, no events, no throw. This is the default configuration for every consumer that has not opted in, so a seam that assumed its services were present would break every existing agent at once. P1.
The same substring contract for the second control frame, whose loss means the client never discards an abandoned partial. A separate type and a separate emitted string from :256. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The pre-Trigger four-argument positional shape must still construct, with Trigger defaulting to null. Adding a positional member to a record silently breaks every existing positional call site, and this is what keeps the old shape compiling and behaving. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The pre-Trigger four-value Deconstruct still binds even though the record now carries a fifth member — the read half of the same compatibility promise, and a separate overload from the constructor above. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 6 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Four properties delegate to the wrapped assignment. P2.
The message reports the System role. P2.
The same record fully populated. P2.
Record construction with defaults null/false. P2.
Fork fields and the run-id alias on a fully populated message. P2.
The unset fork defaults. P2.
The message reports the System role. P2.

The chat client routes this control frame by a RAW SUBSTRING match on the serialized payload, and the discriminator comes from a type-name fallback that nothing in the type's own source states. A rename or a tweak to that fallback is a SILENT client outage — the frame still ships and still parses, the client just stops resyncing after a drop. P1.

Finding #4: the enum's wire converter must be discoverable from the TYPE — a [JsonConverter] attribute, as Role does it — not depend on each caller remembering to register it on its own options. Asserted with bare production options and no manual converter, which is the only arrangement that can tell the two apart. P1.
The same record with every positional argument supplied. P2.
Record construction with defaults null. P2.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: Passing a subAgentTemplateSource to the loop constructor must actually route through SubAgentToolProvider, so a TryRegister on that shared source surfaces on the NEXT turn's request options. The comment states precisely what this buys and it is the reason the row exists separately from the middleware-level one: if a refactor drops the fallback or has the loop construct its own private source, every unit-level provider test still passes and only this row fails, because it pins the chain at the seam the production sample actually wires. Turn one is asserted NOT to contain 'reviewer' before the registration, which is what makes turn two's containment a change rather than a coincidence. Catches a constructor parameter that is accepted and then ignored. P1: a cross-component wiring contract that unit tests structurally cannot see.
requirements: in-process only; real MultiTurnAgentLoop over a Moq streaming agent, no store
bounded: 10s cts; the run task is observed in a finally so cancellation does not surface as an unobserved exception
uncertainties: The loop is constructed with an EMPTY SubAgentOptions.Templates dictionary and a separately seeded shared source. That is the wiring under test, but it also means the row never covers the ordinary case where both are populated, which is where a merge order or a duplicate-key conflict would show up.

capturedOptions is a plain List appended from the mock's callback on whatever thread the loop invokes it, and read from the test thread. The turn boundaries are established by draining ExecuteRunAsync to completion, which orders the writes in practice, but the list itself is unsynchronised.

rationale: A discovered template whose name collides with a BUILT-IN seed must not replace it: TryRegister returns false and the Agent tool description still carries the built-in's text with none of the impostor's. The comment calls this a trust-boundary pin and the fixture makes the threat model explicit — the colliding template's system prompt is literally MALICIOUS and its description EVIL — because templates arrive from discovery, which is outside the process's trust boundary, while seeds are the host's own. If first-wins inverts, an external source silently substitutes its own system prompt for a trusted agent name, and every later spawn of 'researcher' runs attacker-supplied instructions under a name the operator believes they configured. Nothing downstream can detect that: the spawn succeeds, the name is right, the tool description is the only visible artefact. The row asserts both the refusal and its effect, which are separate claims — a source that returned false and stored anyway would fail the second. Catches a discovered template hijacking a built-in agent. P1 with a P0 nomination for the template-source component.
requirements: in-process only; middleware invoked directly with a Moq IAgent, no loop, no store, no timers
uncertainties: NOMINATED as the single P0 candidate for the template-source component. Criticality justification: this is the only trust boundary in the sub-agent surface, and the failure substitutes externally supplied instructions for a trusted agent under the operator's own configured name — the worst consequence class in this slice, and undetectable downstream. It is also among the cheapest rows here: one middleware invocation, no loop, no store, no clock.

FOR THE LEAD, family-level ranking, since I have now touched four SubAgents-family components and the one-per-component rule is only as good as the scoping. If the family gets ONE slot, my order is: (1) this row, trust boundary; (2) the descendant-question relay row in SubAgentIntegrationTests, a silent tree-wide stall; (3) the recursion guard, resource exhaustion bounded by MaxConcurrentSubAgents; (4) ListAgents, a wrong snapshot. I declined (2) on scoping grounds and nominate (1) on the same reasoning applied consistently — a trust boundary outranks a stall.

MATERIAL GAP in this row's proof. Every effect assertion reads the Agent tool DESCRIPTION, which is a proxy for which template is active. Nothing spawns the colliding name, so an implementation that refused the description change while storing the impostor's AgentFactory or SystemPrompt would pass. The refusal assertion (added is false) carries the real weight; the description checks corroborate it but do not exercise the executed template.
First-wins is checked only against a SEED. A collision between two DISCOVERED templates, where neither is privileged, is undefined here.

rationale: A template registered mid-session surfaces in the request options the injection middleware hands the agent on the next turn, with no middleware rebuild. The class summary names the whole chain this pins as one wired path — mutable source, tool provider, contract building, injection middleware — so a regression in any link fails here rather than nowhere. The before/after structure is what gives it force: turn one asserts the new name is ABSENT, the registration happens, turn two asserts it is present along with the seed and the new template's own description text. Checking the description text and not merely the name pins that the model receives enough to choose the agent, which is the point of activating it at all. Catches a mid-session registration that requires a restart to take effect. P1: the primary mid-session activation behavior.
requirements: in-process only; middleware invoked directly, no loop
uncertainties: The SAME MiddlewareContext instance is passed to both InvokeAsync calls. The row's claim is about two successive turns, and a middleware that mutated or cached state on the context would behave differently here than against two independently built contexts.

Only registration is exercised. Whether a template can be REMOVED mid-session, and disappears from the next turn's options, is covered by no row — and a stale template that outlives its source is the same class of defect in the other direction.

rationale: Asserts the three constructor-set properties: ThreadId echoes the argument, CurrentRunId starts null, IsRunning starts false. Field initialisation with no behaviour behind it, and ThreadId_ReturnsConfiguredValue restates the first third of it. P2 as a baseline shape check, not because it is unimportant.

Named for an update but asserts null before the send and null again after a fixed 500ms delay; the in-run value is never observed, so what it actually pins is that the run id is cleared on completion. P2 — the interesting half of the behaviour is not reached by the assertions.

Disposal stops the loop and a second DisposeAsync does not throw. Double-dispose is the ordinary shape here — every test in this file disposes after a using-scoped cancellation — so idempotency is a real contract, not a curiosity. P1.

The other side of the same fallback: it must not trip on a prior in-flight run's completion before our run has started. Modelled with an agent that strips receipt ids on the first run only, so run #1's completion arrives uncorrelated while run #2 is ours. Without the deferred grace logic the iterator yield-breaks early and the caller silently loses its own answer. P1.

The run-scoped enumeration: send an input and enumerate exactly that run's assignment, body and completion, terminating on its own completion rather than running forever. P1 for the primary request/response projection over a loop that is otherwise pub/sub.

An implementation may publish a RunAssignmentMessage with empty InputIds (the dequeue-deferred publish path), leaving the iterator with nothing to correlate on. Without the grace-period fallback the enumeration never terminates and the caller hangs, so the test wraps it in WaitAsync to fail rather than bleed into the outer timeout. P1 for important failure handling, and its 14 exclusive spans put a floor under that anyway.
uncertainties: Holds 14 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies regardless of the tier the behaviour alone would earn.

rationale: Two inputs queued before the loop starts must be drained into one run carrying both receipts, not two runs. Synchronised on the subscriber's own observable side effect (a re-published probe actually arriving) rather than a delay, and the wait completes even when batching breaks so the HaveCount(1) goes red instead of hanging. P1 for the batching contract that decides how many LLM turns a burst of inputs costs.

Copying a ConcurrentDictionary is not atomic: Count is read under the locks and CopyTo taken under them again, so a subscriber leaving in between leaves a default(KeyValuePair) — a null channel the fan-out dereferences. Reproduced by volume (16 drainers, continuous churn, 20k publishes) with a 60s ceiling so a wedge fails instead of hangs. It surfaced originally as an intermittent NullReferenceException out of an unrelated test's DisposeAsync. P1 for a real concurrency failure on the publish path every disconnect can trigger.

One message may carry several calls, so a single pass is not enough: dropping the message that held call B also orphans call A's result, which was correctly paired until then. Only a sweep iterating to a fixed point removes A's result too; a one-pass sweep leaves a dangling tool_result and the provider rejects the replay exactly as before. P1 for the termination condition of the sweep.

A $type written by a newer binary is not bit rot: during a rollback window every such row is dropped, and the operator has to tell that apart from a damaged record. The test pins both directions — the unknown-type log names the discriminator and the row id, and the corruption message must not also fire. P1, with 7 exclusive spans putting a floor under it.
uncertainties: Holds 7 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.
Diagnostics-only: the row is skipped either way and only the log distinguishes the two causes. Held at P1 pending the lead's answer on diagnostics-only contracts.

rationale: The older and likelier route to the same broken shape, with no corruption anywhere: PersistMessageAsync appends one row at a time and swallows an append failure, leaving a permanently half-written exchange. A sweep gated on 'a record was skipped' would leave this route unrepaired, so the test proves the mechanism is blind to why the partner is missing. P1 for a second, independent origin of the invariant.

A call and its result are two separate 1:1 rows, so skipping one per #489 orphans the other, and nothing downstream repairs it — RestoreHistory is a bare AddRange and the transformation middleware passes an unpaired half through verbatim. Providers reject both shapes and the same row fails on every recovery, so the thread stays wedged across restarts. Four InlineData cases cross which half is damaged with the singular and plural call shapes, because a sweep keyed on one shape no-ops against the other. P1 for the pairing invariant recovery has to preserve.

The same safety rule on the other extractor arm. The plural shape filters its ids through a different code path than the singular one, so a guard removed there fails silently unless this case exists. P1 as the second arm of a two-arm guard, not a variation of the first.

The safety counterweight to the deleting rules: a call with no usable id cannot be matched either way, so the sweep must pass it through rather than invent a verdict. The whitespace case is not hypothetical — AnthropicRequest.IsExpectedMissingToolCallId uses IsNullOrWhiteSpace to declare a provider-server call legitimately id-less, so a sweep using IsNullOrEmpty would hunt for a partner that was never written and delete a call the provider accepts. P1 for the rule that stops the repair from becoming the data loss.

Pairing asks whether a partner exists, not how many. A refactor to 1:1 matching would consume the id on first match and silently drop the second answer. Reachable in a real store because the two result shapes take different persisted ids — the singular a deterministic tcr:{threadId}:{toolCallId}, the plural a random Guid — which the test asserts before relying on it. P1 for a safety rule with a concrete route into production data.

An operator scanning at Information must not read 'Recovered 1 messages' and miss that the other rows were lost, so the summary states attempted/unreadable/unpaired and rises to Warning whenever anything was dropped — including rows dropped by the pairing sweep, not just rows that failed to deserialize. Diagnostics are the only signal that silent history loss happened, so P1; held at P1 rather than promoted, consistent with the open question raised to the lead about diagnostics-only contracts.

'Nothing was restored' must have one answer: the all-corrupt load has the same observable outcome as the zero-row branch, so it must not return true. A boundary combining two already-covered branches, with no caller behaviour asserted beyond the bool. P2.

#489: one undeserializable row must not abort recovery of the healthy rows around it. The corrupt row sits deliberately between two healthy ones, so a whole-list abort loses the sibling after it. SubAgentManager.RestartRunAsync recovers through this same method, so the per-record degradation also decides whether a sub-agent restart survives a bad row. P1 for the degradation rule the rest of this region builds on.

A plural ToolsCallResultMessage answers its calls just as the singular one does; reading only the singular shape leaves those calls looking unanswered and deletes them as soon as any unrelated row is skipped. The fixture includes a corrupt unrelated row so the sweep provably ran and still kept the pair. P1 for the recognition arm that decides whether valid history survives.

RestoreHistory appends, so a second recovery duplicates the whole conversation (2N messages). This pins the idempotency guard for the caller that pre-warms with an explicit RecoverAsync and then starts the loop. P1 for the failure mode that silently doubles everything sent to the provider.

The agent pool starts loops via RunAsync and never calls RecoverAsync, so unless RunAsync rehydrates the persisted conversation the model loses all prior context after a restart even though every message is still on disk. Polls the working history rather than sleeping. P1 for the recovery entry point the production caller actually uses.

A second RunAsync on a running loop throws InvalidOperationException naming 'already running' rather than starting a second loop over one input channel. P1 for the guard on double-start, with 2 exclusive spans putting a floor under it.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The same enforcement invariant on the second entry point. Both overloads hand back a SendReceipt the host relays as a guarantee, so a caller must not be able to get an honest answer from one method and a silently-unstamped one from the other by picking the blocking overload. P1 as a second route to the same guarantee, which is exactly where a guard goes missing unnoticed.

Deterministic proof that SendAsync does not wait on run-loop processing: a start gate stalls the loop before it reads the channel, three sends complete, ExecuteCallCount is 0 and PendingInputCount is 3. It replaced a wall-clock threshold that flaked at 152ms under a loaded solution run. P1 for the defining property of the fire-and-forget send, proven without a timing race.

The fire-and-forget send contract: SendAsync hands back a receipt with a non-empty ReceiptId, the caller's InputId preserved, and a QueuedAt near now, while the loop is running. P1 for the primary caller-facing shape of the send path.

The receipt a caller holds must appear in the InputIds of the run assignment the loop publishes, which is the only way a subscriber knows which run answers its send. P1 for a cross-component correlation contract; ExecuteRunAsync's whole termination rule is built on it.
Round-trips the caller's InputId and the null case. A field-level variation of the receipt shape already covered by SendAsync_WhenNotRunning_QueuesMessage. P2.
Brackets QueuedAt between a before and after timestamp. A field-level boundary on the same receipt. P2.
IsRunning is true after RunAsync and false after StopAsync. Lifecycle state that pools and hosts branch on, so P1 for the primary stop transition.

A registered subscriber observes the full run envelope: the RunAssignmentMessage, the loop's own published text, and the RunCompletedMessage. This is the fan-out's primary behaviour end to end, and it is the mechanism every host reads a run through. P1.
A single property echo already asserted inside Constructor_SetsProperties. P2 as a redundant accessor check.

SendReceipt.SpawningSuppressed is an enforcement statement, not an echo of the request. An agent that does not override EnforcesSpawnSuppression has no spawn machinery to police, so accepting a flagged input must leave the receipt false; a host relays that field to its caller as a guarantee, and echoing the request would manufacture one nothing is keeping. P1 for a contract whose failure mode is a false statement about what is being enforced.

The update rebuilds ThreadMetadata from scratch after every completed run and carries Properties across by hand, so a field left off that list is destroyed by the first turn. Here the conversation's title and preview. P1 for a data-loss path on the hot completion route.
The same preserve-on-rebuild rule applied to a sibling field. A field variation on the behaviour PreservesExistingProperties already pins. P2.

Ownership is stamped once at creation and never repaired (spec 8.3), and this method is downstream of every conversation because it runs after every completed run. The four owner columns were never added to its hand-carried list and SaveMetadataAsync upserts all four unconditionally, so the first completed turn nulls the tenant and the owner; under Identity:Enforce=true a null-tenant row reads as absent and the conversation 404s for the person who just created it. Carries its own non-vacuity assertion that LatestRunId changed, proving the row was actually rewritten. P1.
uncertainties: Would be a strong P0 candidate on consequence alone — ownership loss makes a freshly created conversation 404 for its creator under Identity:Enforce=true — but this project's inP0Prefix set holds no member in this file (best greedyRank 64), and the enforced prefix rule keeps P0 inside the prefix. Flagging for the lead rather than promoting unilaterally.

rationale: Combines the update half with the preserve half, both asserted separately elsewhere in this region. P2 as a combination case.

A loop constructed with NO defaultOptions — exactly how a sub-agent or workflow-delegate loop is built — must still send the provider a real max_tokens, and one above 4096. The class traces the full chain and it is the same defect the argument-guard class catches from the other end: a null budget lets the Anthropic provider apply its raw 4096 default, a tool_use block carrying a real file body or script exhausts it, the provider stops with max_tokens and truncates the streaming argument JSON mid-string, and the loop executes the corrupt args. The main agent already dodges this by configuring a budget explicitly, which is precisely why the unconfigured construction is the shape worth pinning. Capturing the options the provider actually RECEIVES, rather than reading the loop's configuration, is what makes this about the request rather than about a field. Catches an unconfigured loop inheriting a provider default too small for tool arguments. P1: the per-turn budget floor, and the prevention side of the truncated-argument defect.
requirements: in-process only; Moq streaming agent, no store, single turn
uncertainties: Related to the P0 nominated in ToolCallArgumentGuardTests (TruncatedToolArgs_DoNotReachHandler_...), which guards the SAME defect family from the far end. This row prevents the truncation; that one stops the harm whatever caused it. I kept the nomination on the guard because it holds for every cause of malformed arguments, not only for an exhausted budget.

BeGreaterThan(4096) is a bare lower bound and the actual floor is never pinned, so a floor of 4097 — useless against the failure described — passes. There is also no upper bound, so a floor large enough to be a cost problem passes too.

The complementary case is uncovered and it is the one a floor typically gets wrong: a host that supplies its own SMALLER MaxToken deliberately must not have it raised. Nothing here shows the floor defers to an explicit value.

rationale: Exactly two public constructors exist. Catches a third overload silently reintroducing an ambiguous or redundant shape, which the other rows cannot see because each looks only for a constructor MATCHING its own predicate and would still find it. P2: a closure guard over the surface the two shape rows describe; it constrains the count, not any behaviour.

The prior constructor's default values are pinned — 50 turns, 100 and 1000 channel capacities, persistRunLedger false, a null system prompt — and the overload is confirmed to have no descendantQuestionSink parameter at all. Defaults are baked into caller assemblies at compile time, so changing one silently gives newly compiled consumers different behaviour from existing ones against the same package. Catches a quiet retune of a published default. P2: values on the signature the existence row already pins, and the weakest of the three compatibility claims because it breaks nothing at load time.

On the prior constructor, exactly the first three parameters are required and all seventeen others remain optional. Catches an optional parameter becoming required, which breaks every short-form call site in every consumer at compile time. P2: an attribute of the signature the existence row already pins, and a source-compatibility claim rather than the binary one.

The exact twenty-parameter CLR signature that shipped on origin/main is asserted to still exist, by reflection, with the same parameter types in the same order. The class explains why source-level compilation is not the relevant check: MultiTurnAgentLoop ships in a packable NuGet, and appending a parameter to its only constructor changes the constructor metadata token, so an already-compiled consumer binds to a method that no longer exists and throws MissingMethodException the first time it constructs a loop. Nothing in this repository's own build would notice — every in-tree caller recompiles. Pinning the full type sequence rather than the arity is what catches a parameter type widened or two adjacent parameters swapped, both of which keep the count intact. Catches a binary-breaking change to a published package. P1: the binary-compatibility contract for the package's public entry point.
requirements: in-process only; pure reflection over the loaded assembly, nothing is constructed
uncertainties: The expected signature is a hand-maintained Type[] in the test file, so it records what someone believed shipped rather than what a published package actually contains. Nothing here compares against a real prior assembly.

rationale: The new overload exists carrying includeAskUserQuestionTool and includeNotifyClientTool as REQUIRED bools plus optional descendantQuestionSink and compaction parameters. The requiredness is the load-bearing detail and the comment reasons it out correctly: a required parameter with no supplied argument makes an overload inapplicable rather than merely lower-priority, so a three-argument call site can never become ambiguous between the two constructors. Give those flags defaults instead and every existing short-form call in every consumer stops compiling at once — a source break affecting callers who changed nothing. Asserting the optional parameters' types and null defaults alongside pins the rest of the shape. Catches the new controls being added in a way that breaks existing call sites. P1: the overload-design contract that makes the back-compat constructor viable.
uncertainties: The no-ambiguity property is argued in the comment, not exercised: nothing here compiles a short-form call site, so the claim rests on the C# overload-resolution reasoning being correct rather than on an observation.

rationale: When the underlying agent throws mid-stream, the completion still arrives carrying IsError=true AND the fork metadata — WasForked=true with ForkedToRunId pointing at the completed run. The error path is where fork provenance is most likely to be lost and most needed: a natural implementation stamps the fork fields on the success branch and returns a bare error completion from the catch, so the caller that forked a run learns it failed but not which of its outstanding forks failed. Asserting all three fields on the same message is what distinguishes 'the error path publishes a completion' from 'the error path publishes the SAME completion'. Catches fork correlation being dropped exactly when a caller needs it to attribute a failure. P1: important failure handling on the fork signal.
requirements: in-process only; mocked IStreamingAgent whose stream throws
uncertainties: This is the only row in the whole fork family covering the error path; the Claude, Codex and Copilot loops have no equivalent, so their error-path fork stamping is unpinned.

rationale: The raw-LLM loop threads a caller-supplied ParentRunId into its RunAssignment and reports WasForked=true with ForkedToRunId equal to the completed run's id. The class states its own scope precisely: the rule is shared via MultiTurnAgentBase.ResolveBatchParent, and this row exists to check the wire-up at THIS loop's run-start and run-complete sites. It is the fourth of four loops carrying the same wiring, and the one with no SDK bridge in the way, so a failure here points at the shared path rather than a provider adapter. Catches fork provenance dropped on the raw loop. P1: the fork-signal wiring for the raw-LLM loop.
requirements: in-process only; Moq IStreamingAgent, empty FunctionRegistry

rationale: An unparented run on the raw loop reports WasForked=false and a null ForkedToRunId. Catches every run being labelled a fork. P2: the negative arm of the rule the positive row establishes, and its non-vacuity partner on this loop.
uncertainties: None of the three rows in this class bounds its ExecuteRunAsync enumeration, so a loop that never completed a run would hang rather than fail.

rationale: The same window on the ERROR path: a run whose generation throws still reports the input that queued while it ran. The comment names the specific defect shape, and it is the one a fix to the success path would miss entirely — the error completion omitted the argument, silently defaulting to 0. A defaulted optional parameter is invisible at the call site, which is why this needs its own row rather than a shared assertion. The consequence is if anything worse here than on the success path: a failed run is followed by a run for the queued input through the same provider, so tearing the provider down after a failure turns one recoverable error into a second, different failure the user cannot connect to it. Asserting IsError true alongside the pending count keeps the row honest about which path it exercised. Catches a defaulted pending count on the error completion. P1: the error-path half of the same contract.
uncertainties: Only ONE queued input is covered by either row, so PendingMessageCount is pinned at 1 and never at a value that would distinguish a real count from a hardcoded one. A loop that returned 1 whenever anything was queued would pass both rows.
No row covers the complementary case — a run completing with NOTHING queued reports 0 — which is the direction SubAgentManager acts on destructively.

rationale: A message that arrives while a run is in flight must be advertised on that run's completion — PendingMessageCount 1, HasPendingMessages true — so the completion reads as non-terminal. The class documents the live failure this replaced in full: the loop hardcoded 0, so a message landing while a run finished produced a 'terminal' completion, SubAgentManager disposed the sub-agent's owned provider and its HttpClient, and the follow-on run's first request threw ObjectDisposedException. The window is made DETERMINISTIC rather than hoped for — the provider is gated mid-generation so the second message provably lands after the turn loop's pre-turn input poll, which is the only window where the input is still unassigned at completion. Both the count and the derived flag are asserted, since consumers branch on the flag while the count is what carries the information. Catches a completion that lies about being terminal. P1: a cross-component contract between the loop's completion signal and the sub-agent lifecycle.
requirements: in-process only; a hand-written gated IStreamingAgent, no store, no Moq
bounded: 30s cts and 15s waits; fully gated, no sleeps
uncertainties: Was a contender: the documented consequence is a real observed production failure. Declined on consequence class — it fails LOUDLY, as an ObjectDisposedException on the very next request, so an operator learns about it immediately. The nominations in this slice guard failures nothing downstream can detect.

The consequence chain stops at the completion message. That SubAgentManager actually keys its provider disposal on this flag is stated in the comment and asserted nowhere here, so the row pins the signal, not the behavior that consumes it.
Neither row observes the FOLLOW-ON run. The claim that the queued input becomes a subsequent run through the same provider — the reason the completion must not be terminal — is not exercised.

rationale: The second null-argument boundary on the same constructor. P2.
Null-argument validation with the parameter name asserted. P2.
The third null-argument boundary on the same constructor. P2.

The wrap-up turn is a TURN as far as observers are concerned: two turn-completed events, the wrap-up's own message and tool-call counts, a run turn count of two, and exactly two provider calls. A wrap-up invisible to lifecycle would make the run's reported turn count disagree with the model calls actually billed. P1.

When a run exhausts its turn budget mid-tool-loop, one final synthesising turn runs and the model's summary becomes the last content message. Without it the run ends on a bare tool result — the user's last visible message is raw JSON from a tool, with no statement of what happened. The test identifies the wrap-up turn by the instruction the loop injects, so it is checking the real mechanism. P1.

The model ignores the wrap-up instruction and asks for another tool. The loop must NOT execute it — asserted by the exact execution count, two, matching the budget — and must still close the run on a deterministic assistant status. Executing it would make the turn cap unenforceable by a model that simply keeps calling tools. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 5 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The wrap-up turn's own provider call fails. The turn is reported with the Error outcome AND still carries a message, because the deterministic fallback status is emitted anyway. A run whose last act failed silently would end on the tool result the wrap-up existed to replace. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 6 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The agentic loop itself: the model asks for a tool, the loop executes it from the registry, publishes the result, calls the provider AGAIN with it, and ends on the final text. This is the behaviour the whole component exists for. P1.

#693: the context-window advice must be earned by the EXCEPTION, not by the size of the history. A disposed HttpClient is a lifecycle defect, and the run error must report it without telling the user to buy a bigger-window model — advice that sends them to fix the wrong thing while the real fault stays in the log. P1 for the false-positive direction.

The true-positive direction: a stream abort over a very large history keeps the overflow advice and hedges it as 'likely'. The fixture is shaped deliberately so the in-turn retry does not absorb the failure and it reaches run-level classification — without this the #693 fix could have been a blanket removal. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: BUG H3b: locally-executed tool results are published OUT OF BAND, bypassing the transformation middleware that stamps ordering, so without an explicit stamp they reach subscribers with a null MessageOrderIdx and the client's merge logic — keyed partly on it — drops them. The result vanishes from the UI while the run looks fine. P1.

Each agentic TURN must advertise its own generation id, captured off the options the loop passes the provider. The client's merge key is kind-runId-generationId-messageOrderIdx and the ordering index resets every turn, so a run-scoped id makes turn N and turn N+1 collide and later turns' text collapses onto the first block (#105/H1 over-corrected from per-message to per-run). The assertions pin non-empty AND distinct, which is exactly the middle position. P1.
The simplest complete run through the raw loop: an assignment, the assistant text, and a completion message, in one enumeration. Every other test here presupposes this path works. P1.

A provider that SAYS it overflowed gets the advice even with a ten-character history, using the exact error string the retry helper builds around Anthropic's body. A classifier keyed only on history size would miss the one case where the answer is certain. P1 as the third distinct branch.

A tool the PROVIDER executed server-side must not be run again locally: the call is published with its execution target intact, no local result is produced, and the provider is called exactly once — no second turn, because there is nothing to feed back. Executing it locally would duplicate a real side effect and feed the provider a result it never asked for. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The fire-and-forget entry point returns a receipt carrying a non-empty id and ECHOING the caller's input id. That echo is how a client correlates its optimistic local message with the run the loop starts, and nothing else in this type checks it. P1 for the correlation contract, thin assertions notwithstanding.
uncertainties: Named for a RunAssignment; the in-file comment records that SendAsync is fire-and-forget and returns a SendReceipt. The assertions match the comment, not the name.

rationale: The broadcast path: a subscriber attached before the send receives the assignment, the assistant text and the completion — a different delivery route from the enumerable ExecuteRunAsync returns, and the one the streaming host actually consumes. It polls for the completion rather than sleeping a fixed interval, which the in-file comment records as the fix for a real CI flake. P1.

The recovery control tells the client where to resume, so it must name the last run actually delivered. Stamping identity before attempting the write lets the message that overflowed — and was therefore never delivered, and here belongs to a different run — set the resume point, telling the client it is caught up on a run it never saw. P1.

Tracking run and generation as independent fields lets a run-2 message inherit run-1's generation, producing a resume pair that never existed. The cursor must advance atomically, so a message moving to a new run carries that run's generation even when it has none. P1 for a corruption no single-field assertion would catch.

Disposal publishes a shared completion so later callers can await the same teardown, but the first caller awaited a different task — the teardown's own — so a failing teardown faulted both, and with a single caller (the common case) nobody ever observed the published one. The finaliser then re-raised it on TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException, a fault from a correctly disposed agent surfacing later and somewhere else. The test identifies its own exception by reference because that event is process-wide and shared with every parallel test, and forces the finaliser with two collect/wait passes. P1 for a failure that lands on unrelated code.

Channel completion used to run after OnDisposeAsync on the same straight-line path, so a descendant whose cleanup threw skipped it entirely and every connected client was left parked on an await-foreach over a channel nobody would ever complete — a hang with no error on an agent that is already gone. The failure must still be reported, not converted into silence. P1.

Channel teardown runs from disposal's outermost finally, and a finally that throws replaces the in-flight exception — so an escaping hook failure would tell the caller 'a subscriber hook failed' while the actual fault, the descendant's own cleanup, vanished. Both failures are distinct instances so the assertion is on identity, not on type. P1 for exception precedence during cleanup.

Teardown completed one subscriber's writer and then ran its hook, per subscriber in a single pass, which made each client's hook a gate on the next client's stream ever ending — one throwing hook and every subscriber after it hung forever. Completing all writers first is the fix. Three subscribers, so 'every stream after the first' is a real claim, and every hook is proven to have run. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The second unguarded step, and the one that lands where subscribers are most likely to be connected: terminalization exists precisely for an agent disposed with runs still open. An armed clock fails only the terminal timestamp, so the setup calls succeed and the failure is attributable to that step alone. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product span, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Truncation is a property of one run's buffer, so the next run must serve its replay normally; otherwise a single oversized run poisons every later one for the life of the pooled agent. P1 for the reset of the truncation flag, which is separate state from the buffer reset.

The distinguishing case for the seed: it is a starting point, not a pin. A fix that stamped the replayed run unconditionally, or froze the cursor once seeded, would report run-1 here and tell the client to resume from a run it has already moved past. P1 — without it the two seeding tests admit an implementation that is wrong in the other direction.

StopAsync sat outside disposal's only guarded region, so an agent whose loop had faulted — the single most likely reason anyone disposes one — threw there and skipped channel teardown entirely, parking every connected client forever. The fault is driven through real production control flow (RunAsync observes and rethrows it, leaving the run task faulted as it would be live) rather than by overriding disposal, and the primary failure must still reach the caller. P1.

A plain bool guard lets the second caller return while teardown is still mid-flight, so an await-using hands back a half-disposed agent. Disposal must be idempotent AND awaitable: every caller observes the same single teardown, completed. Driven by a gated OnDisposeAsync so the concurrent arrival is deterministic rather than timed. P1.

Publisher hot-path regression: the fan-out used to await every subscriber's WriteAsync through Task.WhenAll, so one full bounded channel hung PublishToAllAsync indefinitely and stalled the live run for everyone. Now the full subscriber is dropped. Each publish is bounded by a per-call timeout so a re-regression fails rather than hangs, the fast subscriber is proven to keep pace, and the dropped one still drains its buffered backlog in order before receiving exactly one terminal SlowConsumer recovery control stamped with the run and generation it was caught up on. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product span, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The withheld-replay route into the same emptiness: this subscriber receives no buffered messages at all, only the leading advisory, so that advisory is the one thing that can seed its cursor. A distinct delivery path from the replayed-prefix case, reached whenever the bridge is truncated. P1.

A replayed message is delivered as surely as a live one, so it must advance the delivery cursor. Recording only live writes leaves a subscriber that replayed all of run-1 and then received only runId-less content — which finalized tool_call messages really are, 0 of 267 across the recorded traffic carry a runId — stamped with nothing at all, handing the client a resume point naming no run. P1.

A capped buffer loses the run's earliest messages, and a prefix that silently omits part of a run is undetectable by the client — so the replay is withheld entirely and the client is told to reload authoritative history. The advisory LEADS the stream rather than ending it: ending would force a reconnect that lands on the same truncated buffer and is advised again, for the rest of the run. P1 for the contract and its loop-freedom.

Diagnostics: 500 deltas against a single-slot cap must not warn, while one canonical entry over the same cap must. The truncation itself is already observable to subscribers as a ReplayTruncated advisory and is held at P1 by the two cap tests, so this pins the operator-facing signal only. P2.

A single subscriber registering while a publisher runs, asserting a contiguous duplicate-free run. The sibling Subscribers_registering_against_a_contended_publisher documents in detail why one subscriber cannot actually enter the register-and-snapshot window — nothing outside SubscribeAsync can schedule a publish into a few-instruction gap — so this exercises the ordinary path rather than the lock. P2, with the lock property held at P1 by that sibling.

Ordering inside teardown: remove the subscriber, then complete its channel. Reversed, a publish racing the completion instant still finds the subscriber present, fails its write against the completed channel, and evicts it as if slow — stamping an ordinary shutdown with a resync control the client will act on. The race is driven through a real hook at the exact instant rather than by sleeps, and the scenario is kept single-threaded by yielding the replay entry synchronously. P1.

Three disposals of a failing agent all see the same exception instance. The claim is the corollary of the unobserved-task test and is additionally asserted as a second-caller check inside A_failed_teardown_still_ends_every_live_subscriber_stream, A_run_loop_fault_resurfacing_through_StopAsync and A_lifecycle_terminalization_failure. P2 as the narrow restatement.

The advisory was latched by one per-run bool, so whichever subscriber reached the truncated state first spent the only warning ever issued. This process runs several subscribers on one agent — the transcript mirror and the sub-agent forwarder subscribe alongside the browser — so an internal consumer could swallow the browser's warning and leave it with an empty replay and a live tail it cannot distinguish from a complete stream. Both subscribers stay registered afterwards, which is what keeps advising everyone loop-free. P1.

ExecuteRunAsync's own subscriber is subject to the same slow-consumer eviction, and ending its iterator silently is indistinguishable from an ordinary run completion — so a caller collecting its output reports a truncated run as a successful one. It must yield the same terminal control SubscribeAsync does. P1 for the second consumer of an eviction path whose failure mode is a silent wrong answer.
uncertainties: Holds 6 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Deltas are excluded before byte accounting runs at all, so fifty deltas each ten times the whole byte budget must not threaten it while a canonical message still enters and replays faithfully. Without the ordering, ordinary streaming would truncate every run's replay. P1 for the interaction between the classification filter and the byte bound.

Combines a live subscriber registered before the run with a second one reconnecting mid-run, then checks a later message reaches both. Each half is held at P1 elsewhere in this file (mid-run replay, and the fan-out no-duplicate rules). P2 as the combination.

The other side of the runId-keyed reset: a genuinely new run must clear the prior run's buffer, or a subscriber joining during run-2 replays run-1's stale content as if it were current. The blocked second read proves nothing was left behind. P1.

A generous count cap with a tiny byte budget proves the byte bound stops buffering first — a count-only cap lets a run of large messages consume unbounded memory long before 10,000 of them arrive. Same three-point shape as the count cap: full replay under budget, a live sentinel proving the exact boundary, and the crossing message flipping the run to truncated. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product span, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The count cap is a memory bound on a long-lived pooled agent. Pinned at three points: a buffer filled to exactly the cap replays in full with no advisory, a live sentinel proves the snapshot ended exactly there rather than leaving a remainder, and the cap+1'th canonical message flips the run to truncated so a later joiner is told to resync. P1 for the bound and the transition out of it.

The classification table every other rule in this file rests on: five fragment shapes are not canonical (including a JSON argument fragment, which arrives as an argument-bearing tool-call update rather than a distinct type) and eight complete/control/accounting shapes are. A message type on the wrong side either floods the bridge with fragments or drops real content out of every replay. Thirteen MemberData cases in one declaration. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 18 exclusive product spans, the highest in this file, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: #171: an out-of-band notification folded into the active run publishes a WasInjected assignment carrying the SAME runId, and the reset keys on a new runId rather than on every assignment. Otherwise every injected notification silently wipes the in-flight run's replay and the next reconnect loses everything published before it. P1.

Nothing stopped a later subscriber from registering into a dead fan-out map, where its channel is never written to and never completed, so the caller waits forever. Rejecting with ObjectDisposedException turns a hang into an answer. P1.

The same rejection for the window that actually happens in production: a client connecting between teardown passing the subscriber map and disposal finishing. Reproduced deterministically from inside the teardown loop via the subscriber-completed hook, so it is a real interleaving rather than a timed approximation. P1 for the race half of a guard whose after-the-fact half is trivial.

The negative half: with no active run the first read must not synchronously yield the finished run's messages, because the client already holds those through persisted REST history and a replay would duplicate them. Asserted on IsCompleted rather than a delay, so it is a statement about synchronous availability, not about timing. P1.

The defining resume contract: a client that reconnects mid-run replays the in-flight run's canonical messages and then keeps streaming live. Without it the visible stream simply froze after a conversation switch or refresh, because the pooled backend run kept going while the fresh subscriber saw only what came after it. Also pins the asymmetry the bridge rests on — 10,001 streaming deltas published first never enter the buffer and so cannot evict the canonical text, while live fan-out still delivers deltas unfiltered. P1.

The frozen-tool-pill resume: a client that switches away mid-tool-call rebuilds the unresolved pill from REST history and resolves it only if the resumed stream replays both the call and its result. Text-only replay leaves the pill stuck forever. P1 for the message classes the client's resume render path depends on.

The register-and-snapshot atomicity the _replayLock exists for, reached by contention rather than by a widened window: 32 dedicated threads parked on a gate the publisher itself opens, then 30,000 non-yielding publishes. The invariant is exact, not statistical — replay covers the run from its assignment, so every subscriber must end with the whole run exactly once, a replay prefix and a live suffix meeting with no overlap and no gap. It carries its own non-vacuity guard: registeredDuringBurst must be greater than zero, so a run in which every subscriber arrived late fails instead of passing quietly. Its own comment is honest that only one relocation of the registration is reliably caught here (the other went red once in eleven runs), which is exactly the kind of scope statement a maximum-coverage tier should not overstate. P1.

A stop arriving during the PRE-LOOP startup window — history recovery, ledger and lifecycle reconciliation, usage hydration, OnBeforeRunAsync, all of which run before RunAsync assigns the loop task — must wait for that work rather than seeing two null fields and returning as a no-op. The fixture is built so the failure is observable rather than inferred: startup is provably entered (a TCS fired) and provably unfinished (its gate is still closed), and the startup work ends in a conversation-store WRITE, so a stop that returns early is visible afterwards as a write it did not wait for. The gate is deliberately not cancellable, and the comment explains why that matters — a writer already past its own cancellation check is exactly what a stop has to wait out, and a cancellable gate would let the fix be 'cancel it' rather than 'wait for it', losing the write. The closing assertion is the real proof: after the stop returns, the startup write is complete. Catches a stop that abandons in-flight startup persistence. P1: important failure handling on the shutdown boundary.
requirements: in-process only; a MultiTurnAgentBase subclass gated on TaskCompletionSources, InMemoryConversationStore
bounded: 30s on every wait; costs a fixed 500ms observation window
uncertainties: Was a contender. DECLINED because MultiTurnAgentBase already carries a candidate in this slice (the accepted-input rollback in TrySendAsyncDurabilityTests); treating the base type as ONE component with one slot is the line that keeps the one-per-component rule meaningful, given how finely I have been scoping elsewhere. Recorded so the lead can swap if the stop boundary is judged the more critical of the two.

The 500ms window is honest about what it is — the class comment calls it only an upper bound on the bug, since the old no-op returned in microseconds — but it is still a fixed sleep, and it costs half a second on every run of the suite.

RunLoopAsync returns immediately in this fixture, so the stop is only ever waiting out STARTUP. A stop arriving after startup completes but before the loop task is assigned — the other half of the described window — is not exercised.

rationale: A stop whose timeout expires against a loop that ignores cancellation must NOT clear the state saying a run is live: StopAsync returns, but IsRunning still reads true. The old behavior logged the timeout and cleared the tracking anyway, which is the dishonest-boundary shape the class is named for — the agent reports stopped while its loop is still running, so a supervisor is free to start a second loop against the same conversation, and two runs then interleave on one thread's history. Constructing an unstoppable loop rather than a slow one is what makes the timeout deterministic: the stop CANNOT succeed, so the only question left is what it reports. Catches a timed-out stop that lies about the outcome. P1: important failure handling when the stop cannot be honoured.
requirements: in-process only; a loop that never observes its token, released explicitly so disposal does not hang
uncertainties: No row anywhere in this class shows IsRunning going FALSE after a stop that succeeds. As written, an implementation whose IsRunning was hardcoded true would pass this row, so its non-vacuity depends entirely on coverage living elsewhere. The positive control belongs here.

Only IsRunning is checked. Whether the timed-out stop reports the failure to its caller at all — a return value, an exception, a log — is unasserted, so a caller has no tested way to learn the stop did not take.

rationale: 3200 registrations across 32 writers, each in its own keyspace so the only valid outcome is that everything landed — a lost write shows as a short count rather than hiding behind a collision. The snapshot publication gate under real contention. P1.
Initial state of the default constructor. P2.

Enumerating Templates while another thread registers must not throw, because SubAgentToolProvider.CreateAgentDescriptor enumerates it while the discovery webhook registers into it. A collection-modified exception there fails the tool descriptor the model is about to be handed. P1.

A rebind publishes a NEW snapshot and leaves the old one untouched — a reader holding the previous snapshot keeps seeing the old factories and a null characteristics factory, while the new snapshot's entries route explicit model selection to the rebound agent and report ownership. Mutating in place would change the catalog under a descriptor build already in flight. P1.

The source must not retain the caller's dictionary: removing an entry from the seed afterwards leaves the catalog intact. A retained reference would let an unrelated caller retroactively delete a sub-agent the loop is already advertising. P1.
