The seeded constructor exposes what it was given. Strictly subsumed by :67, which asserts the same containment AND the defensive copy. P2.

A template registered after a rebind picks up the current factories, including routing an explicitly-selected model to the rebound agent. The TryRegister counterpart of :154, and the row coverage ranks highest in this file. P1.
uncertainties: inP0Prefix member (greedyRank 35), but no P0 is proposed from this file: it holds zero exclusive spans anywhere, the component is small (no row exceeds 77 covered spans), and the file's most critical claim — the first-wins trust boundary at :94, where a discovered template must not shadow a built-in — sits on a NON-prefix row. Prefix membership selects candidates; it does not confer P0, and promoting this row would pin the rebind plumbing rather than the boundary that matters.

rationale: A rejected duplicate is not copied, observed through a counting copy constructor. Rejection itself is held at :94; this adds that the rebind path does no wasted copy on the way. A refinement of an already-covered path. P2.

The sub-agent template trust boundary, and this row is the only declaration in the lane to assert it: TryRegister refuses a duplicate name and leaves the existing template's content intact. Mechanism, corrected after lane-daemon challenged the original citation and I verified both halves in source: the test's own comment cites WorkspaceSubAgentLoader.MergeBuiltInWins, but that method enforces its boundary with builtIns.TryAdd on a plain dictionary (WorkspaceSubAgentLoader.cs:308-328) and never calls TryRegister — it is an analogy, not the mechanism. The mechanism is the only product caller, ContextDiscoveryController.cs:337, whose else-branch reads 'First-wins collision with a built-in OR an earlier discovery on this conversation.' That is the webhook discovery path, which is where a workspace-authored template actually arrives. It asserts the CONTENT as well as the false return, so a registration that overwrote the body while reporting refusal still fails; change TryRegister to SetItem and both assertions fail. Undetectable defect if this row is dropped: a workspace-supplied template registered under a built-in name silently replaces it, and every later spawn of that name runs an attacker-chosen system prompt and factory while the caller believes it invoked the built-in. The component LmMultiTurn/sub-agent template registry holds 16 rows and no P0, and no other declaration there asserts shadowing — the nearest neighbour asserts factory rebinding, which is a different claim. P0 outside the prefix under the bounded both-directions exception. LINE 53 EXCEPTION, stated not assumed: addsNothingNew is true over its 26 covered spans and it holds no exclusive spans, so by coverage alone this row contributes nothing. That is a statement about traversal: the registry's dictionary operations are walked by every other test in the file, and none of them asserts that a duplicate registration is refused with the seed's content intact. Admissible under line 48 because the component would otherwise have no P0 pinning its essential contract, and the contract here is a trust boundary no measurement can express.
The primary add path — returns true and the entry is visible. P1.
Argument validation on TryRegister's name. P2.
Argument validation on TryRegister's template. P2.

An entry upserted AFTER a rebind must carry the current characteristics factory, proven by routing an explicitly-selected model through it and getting the rebound agent back. An upsert that kept the seed's factories would silently send a refreshed sub-agent to the old provider. P1.

The trusted-reseed counterpart of first-wins: a host refreshing entries it built itself must be able to replace them, which TryRegister would pin forever. The two policies live on one dictionary and only these two rows separate them. P1.
Upsert on an absent name adds it — the fall-through of the replace path above. P2.
Argument validation on Upsert. P2.

The same rule on the Codex translator: a NotifyMessage in the input batch reaches the prompt with its marker and kind rather than being skipped. This is a separate builder with its own message-type switch, so it can regress independently — a fix applied to one translator does not reach the other, which is exactly why the pair exists rather than a single parameterised row. Catches asynchronous events silently not reaching a Codex model turn. P1: the notify-to-prompt contract for the Codex translator.
requirements: in-process only; pure static prompt builder
uncertainties: Same substring-only weakness as its Copilot sibling: the notification's detail and source identifiers are never asserted.

rationale: A NotifyMessage in the input batch must have its envelope appended to the Copilot prompt, carrying the notification marker and the kind. The class explains the failure it replaced and why it was invisible: these CLI loops build the prompt from the input BATCH rather than history, and previously skipped any non-TextMessage with an unsupported_message_type warning — so a sub-agent completion notification was dropped on the floor with only a warning to show for it. The parent then never learns its child finished and waits on an event it was already sent. Asserting the KIND as well as the marker is what pins that the notification is identifiable rather than an anonymous blob. Catches asynchronous events silently not reaching a CLI model turn. P1: the notify-to-prompt contract for the Copilot translator.
requirements: in-process only; pure static prompt builder, no loop or client
uncertainties: Both rows assert only two substrings. The envelope's detail ('sub-agent done'), its source tool name and its tool call id are all supplied by the fixture and none is asserted, so a builder emitting the marker and kind while dropping the payload would pass — and the payload is the part the model needs to act on.

rationale: A notification delivered to an IDLE loop wakes it: exactly one turn runs, the NotifyMessage itself reaches the model in that turn's message list, and its pill is published live on the loop's output with the producer's GenerationId intact. Three separate failures are excluded at once — a notification that wakes nothing (the agent never learns its sub-agent finished), one that wakes a turn but strips the envelope (the model is prompted with no idea why), and one that is persisted but never surfaced to the UI. Asserting the exact GenerationId 'notify:fixed' rather than mere presence is the deliberate part: identity preserved end to end is what lets a client correlate the pill with the tool call that produced it, and a loop that re-stamped its own id would satisfy every weaker check. Catches an out-of-band notification that reaches neither the model nor the client. P1: the primary idle-delivery behavior for notifications.
requirements: bounded: MessageCollector waits 10s and rethrows a diagnostic TimeoutException
uncertainties: The collector's completion counter is a volatile int incremented outside the lock that guards the message list, while Snapshot takes that lock. The two are therefore not read consistently — a run completion can be counted before its message is visible to a subsequent Snapshot. Harmless for these assertions, which re-read after the wait, but the parked sibling's disjunction reads both under the same assumption.

rationale: A notification arriving while the loop is parked on an unresolved deferral must be folded into history and delivered on resume, NOT rejected by the deferred-guard as a run failure. The class summary calls this the one edge, and the row proves both halves: while parked it asserts no extra provider call, no error completion and the Wait still deferred; after the host fires it asserts turn two sees BOTH the resolved wait result and the notify. Without the fold, a background sub-agent completing while its parent waits either kills the parent's run or is dropped — and the parent is precisely the actor that is parked waiting for it, so this is the exact moment the notification matters most. The synchronisation is the strongest in this lane: the wait polls the DECISION'S OWN SIDE EFFECT (the pill published by TryAppendParkedInputsAsync) rather than sleeping, and its comment records that a fixed delay previously raced under CI load and let the fire land before the notify was parked. The disjunction on callCount>1 and error completions means a regression trips the wait immediately and fails at the assertions instead of burning the timeout. Catches a notification killing or bypassing a parked run. P1: important failure handling at the notify/deferral intersection.
requirements: in-process only; Moq streaming agent, ManualLoopTriggerSource, default in-memory store
bounded: Wait.UntilAsync default and a 10s completion wait
uncertainties: Only ONE notify is delivered while parked. Whether several notifications arriving during a single park all survive the fold, and in order, is not covered here or in the ordering class, which fires against running operations rather than parked ones.

rationale: An explicitly EMPTY id list adopts nothing. Collapsing empty into 'no restriction' is the difference between a no-op and moving every quarantined conversation in the deployment — and it is the ordinary shape of an empty-list bug. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Adoption selects on the SOURCE tenant, which is what makes a second run a no-op rather than a second move: the follow-up call naming a different destination finds nothing, and the row adopted first is not re-stamped into tenant B. Without that, a retried maintenance command relocates conversations again. P1.

The same oversized-list claim on the adoption path, with q2 as the declared non-vacuity partner: it is in the source tenant and NOT in the selection, so a restriction that silently stopped restricting under the new binding would adopt it too and the test would fail rather than quietly pass. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: SQLite refuses a creation-ordered listing rather than approximating one, because thread_metadata has no created_at column and re-deriving it in SQL would be a second copy of CreationTimestampOf free to diverge. The refusal message is asserted to name both the missing column and the helper, so the reader is told what to do about it; the other two stores answer normally in the same body. P1 for a deliberate capability gap that must stay loud.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product span, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: P0 for the tenancy-maintenance baseline. It runs the rehearsal and the apply against the same seed — two quarantined rows plus one real one that must not move — and asserts that the rehearsed id set IS the set the apply moves, not merely that both return two. Criticality: this is the dry run an operator reads before authorising a bulk cross-tenant move of live conversations, so a rehearsal that reported a different row set than the apply would move is a rehearsal of nothing, and the move it precedes is not reversible by re-running it. It exercises both maintenance entry points across all three stores and holds the file's only exclusive coverage of that path.
uncertainties: inP0Prefix member, greedyRank 27, and holds 9 exclusive product spans that nothing else in the lane reaches.
Paired with the P0 at :192; that one covers the listing predicate, this one the ownership-maintenance writes.

rationale: A grant set of 32,767 ids — one past the ceiling this engine actually enforces, not the 999 the issue quotes — both completes and still filters, with an ungranted peer row present so a clause that collapsed to 'match everything' under the new shape fails the second assertion while passing the first. The test's own remarks record that a 1,200-id draft was worthless because the bundled SQLite raises the limit to 32,766. P1.

An app-only caller matches on app id and must NOT take the grant branch, seeded with a grant it would wrongly honour. A grant names a person; a service credential is not one, and letting one collect grants turns a machine identity into a user's proxy. P1.

Publication is scoped to the tenant that published it. The tenant filter runs first, and a published branch placed ahead of it turns 'published to my organisation' into 'published to everyone' — a one-line ordering change with no local symptom. P1.

The outer boundary, seeded in the only shape that proves the tenant conjunct exists: the SAME owner id stamped into the OTHER tenant and listed AS that owner, so the row is excluded by tenancy alone. Any row owned by somebody else is already excluded by the owner conjunct, which is why the obvious version of this test stays green with the tenant clause deleted. P1 for cross-tenant isolation.

The AUTHORIZATION filter runs before the page is cut: nine peer rows newer than the caller's single one, and a page of five. Filtering an already-trimmed page returns nothing, so the user's own conversation vanishes from her sidebar while the row is intact on disk. A separate clause from the presentation exclusion pinned at the top of this file. P1.

The listing predicate has to mirror EVERY allow branch of spec 7.4, and the tenant-published branch had no counterpart here. The point read already allows the row, so its absence made the two disagree in the worst direction: a 200 on the direct link and silently missing from the list. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The grant branch in both directions from one seed: a shared conversation appears for the user holding the grant and is absent for the same user without it. The negative half is what stops a grant branch that admits every Shared row regardless of who holds a grant. P1.

Spec 7.1 principle 4, checked from both a user scope and an app-only scope. The C# stores are where this goes wrong because null == null is true in managed code, and getting it wrong hands every unclaimed conversation in the tenant to every app-only caller at once. P1.

The happy path, which this file's own remarks call the least interesting claim in it. Owner matching is exercised inside the tenant-admin, app-only, published, private-peer and filter-before-paging cases, each of which adds a branch this one does not. P2 — not unimportant, but already reached by stronger cases.

Both halves of the untenanted rule in one body: the background sub-agent scan opts into tenant-or-untenanted so a tenanted root's not-yet-stamped descendant is not dropped, while a CALLER-facing scope must not admit that same row. Getting the second half wrong hands unclaimed conversations to an arbitrary tenant member; getting the first wrong makes descendants invisible to the scan that maintains them. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 5 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The declared non-vacuity partner for the published branch, seeded with both an explicitly Private peer row and an unset one. A branch that admitted every same-tenant row would satisfy the published test while handing every member's private conversations to every other member of the tenant. P1 — the case that makes the allow branch falsifiable.

The admin branch of spec 7.4 mirrored into the listing, with a tenant-B row present to pin that admin does not mean global. Omitting the branch produces the worst available outcome — an EMPTY list for a tenant admin while the point read on the same rows allows — which reads as data loss rather than as a permissions bug. P1.

The four owner columns survive a write and a read on each store. This is the vacuity anchor for every filter claim below it: without it a store that silently persisted nothing would satisfy each must-not-appear assertion in this file for the wrong reason. P1 for what it protects rather than for what it asserts.

Two independent narrowings — the presentation exclusion and the authorization scope — compose in one statement, and the seed makes each failure visible on its own: the caller's agent-owned rows are all newer than her real ones and outnumber the page, so an exclusion applied after LIMIT returns an empty page, while another user's row is the newest in the tenant, so a scope dropped while editing the exclusion returns it. Runs against the SQLite, file and in-memory stores from one theory body, which matters here because the predicate is spelled twice — once in SQL and once in managed code — and the sample ships the FILE store while the spec's predicate is written in SQL. P1.

P0 for the scoped-listing baseline. It drives the whole authorization-and-exclusion predicate end to end on all three stores (452 covered spans, the widest reach in this file) while pinning that an excluded prefix is compared literally: the SQLite clause is a substr comparison precisely so that a % or _ in a prefix is not a wildcard. Criticality: the failure this prevents is a query that SUCCEEDS and returns the wrong set — rows silently deleted from a user's own sidebar with no error anywhere — and it is the shape a rewrite to NOT LIKE would reintroduce invisibly. The assertion is an exact id set, not a count, and the kept ids are chosen to be exactly what those wildcards would have swallowed, so the rank is not carrying a weak test.
uncertainties: inP0Prefix member, greedyRank 14 of the project's 36-member prefix — the highest-ranked declaration in this file.
Paired with the P0 at :656 on tenancy maintenance. The two sit on different components — the listing predicate and the ownership-maintenance writes — so this is not two P0s stacked on one code path.

rationale: The 8.5.4 startup repair claims every unstamped row for the quarantine tenant and claims ONLY those — the already-tenanted row is asserted unmoved. A repair that over-claimed would sweep live conversations out of their real tenant on the next boot. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 42 exclusive product spans, the highest in this file, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Offset paging issues one query per page, so rows that compare equal with no defined tie-break can be returned twice or never — and the row never returned is simply missing from the sidebar. The tie-break is spelled twice (ConversationListOptions.Order and SQLite's ORDER BY) and the seed order is neither ascending nor descending by id, so no store passes by echoing insertion or filesystem order. P1.

The unscoped overload is a SEPARATE statement in every store, so a fix applied to the scoped one proves nothing about it — and this is the overload the sample's own sidebar takes whenever identity enforcement is off, which is the default deployment. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 18 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Eight separate store instances over one directory each write the same thread's metadata fifteen times; none throws, no temp file survives, and the resulting file loads as a whole document. The leftover-temp assertion is the one that catches a writer dying between its write and its rename, which a not-throwing check alone would miss, and the successful reload is what distinguishes a whole document from an interleaving of two. Nothing is shared between the writers but the filesystem, which is the point — the per-instance semaphore offers no protection here at all. Catches a conversation's metadata being corrupted into unparseable JSON by concurrent hosts. P1: the end-to-end durability shape the other two decompose, and the only row here that observes the file's integrity rather than one hazard.
requirements: writes under the temp directory; 8 concurrent writers x 15 writes
uncertainties: This is the one row in the file that IS race-based, which the class remarks argue against for the other two. It can go green on a fast box without the writers actually overlapping; its temp-file and whole-document assertions still hold value, but it does not by itself prove the hazard was met.

rationale: A handle is held open with FileShare.None on the deterministically-named temp path for the target — what a concurrent writer holding its own output looks like to everyone else — and the store must still complete its write. The remarks explain why a deterministic name is the defect rather than an implementation detail: there is only one such path per target, so every writer to a file contends for it, and the write cannot even reach the rename because WriteAllTextAsync onto the held path fails first. Reloading and asserting the new value is what makes it more than a does-not-throw: a store that swallowed the failure would pass the throw check and lose the write. Catches two stores over one directory — a shape the remarks name two existing test classes as constructing — silently dropping each other's metadata. P1: the temp-name contention contract.

A real FileStream taking exactly the sharing a concurrent File.ReadAllTextAsync would take is held on the destination, then released partway through the store's retry budget; the write must still land. Two properties of the construction do the work: holding a handle rather than racing threads means the hazard is present on every run instead of on a slow box, and releasing AFTER the first rename attempt means the test distinguishes a retry from a fixed sleep and from a handle that was already gone. The failure it pins is reported rather than theoretical — UnauthorizedAccessException from Windows MoveFile via UpdateMetadataAsync under CompactionStateProjection, because FileShare.Read withholds the delete access REPLACE_EXISTING needs. Catches a metadata write lost whenever anything reads the file at the wrong moment. P1: the rename-retry contract, an important failure path the per-instance lock structurally cannot cover.
requirements: writes under the temp directory; Windows file-sharing semantics are what the case turns on
uncertainties: `released.Should().BeTrue()` is set on the preceding line and can never fail; it documents intent rather than checking anything.
The 60ms delay before releasing the handle is a timing assumption: on a machine where the store's first rename attempt has not yet run, the test would pass without exercising a retry.

rationale: A second append must accumulate rather than replace, checked through a load rather than through the file. Unlike the in-memory store this is a read-modify-write of a whole file, which is precisely where an append silently becomes an overwrite and the earlier turns of a conversation disappear. P1.
Asserts the messages.json filename inside that directory. Same class of layout statement. P2.
Asserts the on-disk layout — a directory named for the thread. A storage detail already implied by every round trip in this type. P2.

A thread id carrying characters no filesystem accepts must still round-trip: the write sanitises it and the read resolves the same sanitised name. Without both halves agreeing the write either throws or lands somewhere the reader never looks — and unsanitised path characters are also how a thread id reaches outside its base directory. P1.
An empty batch must not create the thread directory at all. The listing enumerates directories, so an empty write would otherwise mint a permanent phantom conversation on disk. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Named for atomicity but the assertion reaches only temp-file hygiene: no *.tmp remains in the thread directory after a write. It says nothing about what a reader sees mid-write or after a crash, which is what atomic means here. P2 for what it actually verifies.

Construction creates the base directory. Every writing test in this type depends on it implicitly, so what this adds is the explicit statement. Its teardown is deliberately not in a finally, because Purge throws when it cannot detach and a throw from a finally replaces the assertion failure unwinding through it. P2.
Null-argument validation on the constructor. P2.
Idempotent delete of an absent thread. P2 as a boundary on the operation above.

Deletion removes the whole thread directory, messages and metadata together, and the test proves the directory existed first so the assertion is not vacuous. A partial delete leaves the thread listed with nothing behind it. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Ties need a defined total order. Here the mechanism is explicit: the file store enumerates directories and the filesystem hands them back ascending — the exact opposite of the expected order — so without the tie-break the tied rows come back reversed and this fails for the right reason. P1, and a stronger red-without-the-fix argument than the in-memory twin's.

The file-specific arm: a metadata.json that will not parse must degrade to minimal metadata for that thread rather than dropping it from the listing or failing the whole call. One damaged file must not hide a conversation or take the sidebar down with it. P1 — a distinct branch from the missing-file case.

A thread directory with no metadata.json must still be listed with minimal metadata synthesised. Metadata is written at run completion, so a conversation whose first run has not finished would otherwise be invisible to its own owner. P1.

The compatibility pin for callers that pass no options: nothing excluded, last-used order. The agent-owned row is seeded newest on purpose, because a store that quietly applied a default exclusion would look correct on every other assertion in this file. P1.

Both ways an id can fail to carry a timestamp are seeded — a pre-timestamp thread-{guid:N} with no delimiter, and a delimited id whose segment does not parse — and both fallback values are placed above the parseable rows, so treating an unparseable id as zero orders them last and fails. Losing either row from the listing is the defect this ordering exists to prevent. P1.

The Created sort mode derives its key from the thread id rather than from LastUpdated, with the two orderings seeded to disagree completely so a branch that quietly did nothing cannot pass. P1 for a distinct ordering contract on this implementation.

Its own note is explicit that it does not prove the tie-break and stays green without one: a single run enumerates the store consistently, so the pages line up either way. What it guards is the paging arithmetic over a tied set. P2, taking the test at its own word.

The interleaved seed, which is what separates filtering before the page from filtering after it — filtering afterwards still returns rows, just a different half-page depending on the offset. The assertion is that all three pages concatenated equal the whole kept set in order. P1 for pagination continuity under exclusion on the file store.

The listing projection must carry the Properties bag — title and preview — through a JSON round trip on this store, not just through an in-memory copy. Dropping it leaves every conversation showing as untitled while the data is still on disk. P1 for a projection guard on the serialising implementation.
Limit trims to the newest n. The paging behaviour that actually breaks is held at P1 by the exclusion and tie tests below. P2.
Offset skips the newest rows. Same reasoning as the limit case. P2.

Exclusion runs before Skip/Take on this store too. The seed makes every excluded row newer than every kept row, so an implementation that filters after paging returns nothing at all. Same production shape as the in-memory twin — 302 threads, 256 agent-owned, five usable rows out of fifty — but this is the file store's own ordering and paging code. P1.

The file store's own listing: every thread directory comes back. This is a separate implementation of the listing contract from the in-memory store's, over directory enumeration rather than a dictionary, so it needs its own exerciser. P1.
Empty-store boundary on the file store's listing. P2.
Default most-recent-first ordering, computed by the file store from metadata it has just read off disk. Seeded out of creation order so directory order cannot pass for a sort. P1.

A messages.json that is not valid JSON returns empty rather than throwing. The alternative takes down every caller that touches that thread — including the agent loop's startup recovery — with an exception nothing downstream expects. P1 for the degradation rule on the read path.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Absent-thread boundary on the message read. P2.
Load orders by timestamp regardless of write order, seeded out of order so file order cannot pass for a sort. This is what makes a recovered conversation read as it happened. P1.

A corrupt metadata.json returns null rather than throwing, which is the same answer the absent case gives and is what callers already branch on. Throwing here would make one damaged file fatal to the thread. P1 for the second degradation rule, on a separate read path from the messages one.
Absent-thread boundary on the metadata read. P2.
Asserts the metadata.json filename. Layout statement, like its message-file sibling. P2.

The serialisation round trip that everything about a thread outside its messages depends on: run ids and the session mappings that tie a conversation to its external session. A field that fails to serialise is silently null on the next load. P1.

The same durability claim on the accepted-input table, which is a separate file: after a restart this is what decides whether a conversation reports busy or idle, so its loss is not the same failure as losing the run ledger. P1.
An empty set rather than a throw for a thread with nothing accepted. P2.
Newest first after a disk round trip, proven with an out-of-order insertion sequence so file enumeration order cannot be mistaken for the sort. P1.
uncertainties: Restates on the file store an ordering rule InMemoryRunLedgerStoreTests also holds; kept at P1 because the sort must be re-established after a read from disk, where write order is not a promise.

rationale: Null for an unknown run id. On its own reading this is a lookup boundary I would have placed at P2; it sole-covers one product span, and the floor decides the tier rather than my judgement of its weight. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The accepted-input side table written and read back through the file store — the durable half of the acceptance mechanism the #434 family depends on. P1.

Removing an id that was never recorded neither throws nor creates a file. A defensive boundary on the call above, which I would otherwise have placed at P2; it holds two exclusive product spans, so the floor decides. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Retirement removes exactly the named input and leaves the sibling alone. An input that can never be retired leaves the conversation reading busy for the host's whole grace window. P1.

The one claim only this store can make and the entire reason it exists: a SECOND store instance over the same directory reads the entry back. An in-process cache that never reaches disk passes every other row in this file and loses the ledger at the first restart. P1.
Upsert means update, not append — on disk the second write must replace the first, or the listing shows a run once per status transition and the ledger file grows without bound. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 7 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The durable ledger's baseline: an entry survives serialization to disk with its thread, run id, status and input ids intact. This is the file the host reads on restart to decide what was owed. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: The store's primary write: appending to a thread that does not exist yet creates it and holds every message. Everything else in this type reads what this wrote. P1.
The second branch of the same write — a thread that already has messages accumulates rather than being replaced — asserted with the same count check. P2 as the sibling branch.
Null-argument validation on the second parameter. P2 as a sibling of the same rule.
Null-argument validation with a parameter-name assertion. P2.

An empty batch must not materialise a thread. Otherwise a caller that persists nothing still creates an entry that shows up in listings and thread-id enumeration as a conversation with no content. P1, and its exclusive spans put a floor under it.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A test-support reset that empties both maps. Real callers do not clear a live store. P2.
Idempotent delete of an absent thread. P2 as a boundary on the operation above.

Deletion has to clear BOTH maps: metadata surviving a delete leaves the conversation listed and loadable with no content behind it, which reads to a user as a deletion that did not happen. P1 for the two-store invariant.

The union of message-bearing and metadata-only threads, read off the enumeration helper. The same union is what ListThreadsAsync_CreatesMinimalMetadataForThreadsWithoutExplicitMetadata holds at P1 on the caller-facing surface. P2.

Ties on LastUpdated need a defined total order, or the result merely echoes whatever the backing ConcurrentDictionary enumerated. Rows are saved in an order deliberately unequal to the expected one, since LINQ's sort is stable and would otherwise make the assertion a description of insertion order. This is the test that actually goes red without the tie-break. P1.

A thread that has messages but no metadata row must still be listed, with minimal metadata synthesised. Metadata is written at run completion, so a conversation whose first run has not finished — or whose metadata write was lost — would otherwise be invisible to its own owner. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 8 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The compatibility pin: every pre-existing caller passes no options, so the exclusion feature must not change what they receive. The agent-owned row is seeded NEWEST on purpose, because a store that quietly applied a default exclusion would look correct on every other assertion in this file. P1 for the default-path guarantee.

Both ways an id can fail to carry a timestamp are seeded: a pre-timestamp thread-{guid:N} with no delimiter at all, and a delimited id whose segment does not parse. Losing either row from the listing is the very defect this ordering exists to fix, and both fallback values are placed ABOVE the parseable rows so an implementation treating an unparseable id as zero orders them last and fails. P1.

A second sort mode that derives creation time from the thread id rather than reading LastUpdated. The two orderings are seeded to disagree completely — exact reverses — so a Created branch that quietly did nothing cannot pass. P1 for a distinct ordering contract.

Its own note is explicit that it does not prove the tie-break and stays green without one: a single run enumerates the store consistently, so pages line up either way. What it guards is the paging arithmetic over a tied set. P2, taking the test at its own word.

The interleaved seed, which is the case that separates 'filtered before the page' from 'filtered after it' — filtering afterwards still returns rows here, just a different half-page depending on where the offset lands. Asserting the concatenation of all three pages equals the whole kept set in order is what a non-empty first page would not. P1 for pagination continuity under exclusion.

The listing is a projection, and a projection silently drops whatever it forgets to carry: here the title and preview, which is exactly what the sidebar renders. A dropped Properties bag leaves every conversation showing as untitled while the data is still on disk. P1 for a projection guard.
Limit trims to the newest n. The paging behaviour that actually breaks — interaction with exclusion and with ties — is held at P1 by the three paging tests below. P2.
Offset skips the newest rows. Same reasoning as the limit case. P2.

Exclusion runs before Skip/Take, not after. This is the store-level shape of a live failure: LastUpdated is bumped by every completed run and background agents run constantly, so agent-owned rows crowd the front of the ordering — on a deployment of 302 threads, 256 of them agent-owned, a caller that trimmed first and filtered second got five usable rows out of fifty and lost every older conversation. The seed makes every excluded row newer than every kept row, so filtering after paging returns nothing at all. P1.
The listing's primary behaviour: every thread with metadata is returned. This is what the conversation sidebar is built from. P1.
Empty-store boundary on the listing. P2.
The default ordering, seeded out of insertion order so a stable no-op sort cannot pass. Most-recent-first is the whole affordance of the sidebar. P1.

Two loads return different list instances, so a caller mutating what it got cannot reach into the store. The assertion is reference inequality of the outer lists only, which does not reach element sharing. P2.
Absent-thread boundary: an empty list rather than null or a throw. P2.

The tie-break inside one millisecond. A turn emits several messages faster than the clock resolution, so without a secondary key a tool call and its result can come back reversed — a shape providers reject outright. P1 for the second ordering key, not a variation of the first.

Load orders by timestamp regardless of append order, which is what makes recovery reconstruct the conversation as it happened rather than as it was written. Seeded out of order (3, 1, 2) so insertion order cannot pass for a sort. P1.
Absent-thread boundary on the metadata read. P2.

An edited message keeps its original position: the store ignores the caller's timestamp on replace. Honouring it would move the message to the end of the conversation on the next load, silently reordering history around it. P1.

Replacing an id the thread does not hold throws and names the id, rather than appending it as a new message or silently doing nothing — either of which turns an edit into invisible data loss or duplication. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The missing-thread arm of the same guard, naming the thread id. A separate lookup from the message-id arm, and the floor applies here too. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Upsert semantics on the same key, asserted through one field. P2 as the second branch of the save already held at P1.
The metadata round trip that thread listing, recovery and ownership all read through. P1 for the primary save/load path.

Ten concurrent appends of ten messages each must total a hundred. This store backs in-process hosting where several loops and the transcript mirror write the same thread, so a lost update here is silently lost conversation. P1 for the concurrency contract.
The whole-store reset performing the same clearing as :138, on a method that exists for test setup. P2.

Deleting a conversation clears BOTH side tables — the ledger by thread, the entry by run id, and the accepted inputs — so a deleted conversation leaves nothing behind that a later lookup could resurrect. Eleven exclusive spans, the widest sole-cover in this file. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 11 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: An empty set rather than null for a thread with nothing accepted. P2.
Newest first, proven with an out-of-order insertion sequence so insertion order cannot be mistaken for the sort. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: An empty list for an unknown thread. P2.
Null for an unknown run id. P2.
The accepted-input ledger's baseline write and read — the store side of the acceptance mechanism the whole #434 family depends on. P1.
Removing an id that was never recorded does not throw. A defensive boundary on the call above. P2.

Retirement actually removes. An accepted input that can never be retired leaves the conversation reading busy for the host's whole grace window, which is the failure mode the rescind paths exist to avoid. P1.
The ledger's baseline: an entry persists and reads back whole, with its input ids in ORDER. The run ledger is what a restart reads to decide what was owed. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: Upsert means update, not append: the status advances and the listing still holds ONE row for the run. Appending instead would show every run once per status transition to anything that lists them. P1.

Ownership of the mutation gate is the open HANDLE, never the file's existence — a host killed outright cannot delete its gate file, and a store reading existence as 'a mutation is in flight' would refuse every later completion and retraction of that admission permanently. Both directions asserted: the orphaned file does not block, and a genuinely held handle does, with the stand-down driven on an injected clock instead of a ten-second sleep. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 5 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The narrow window where a prior holder's mutation is already durable but its gate handle has not finished closing. The caller here owns its reservation and has every right to succeed once the gate frees; a store with no retry sees the held handle once and is refused for good. A different retry site from :504, arranged directly rather than raced. P1.

A refused exclusive create cannot be interpreted by looking at the record afterwards, because the winner may retract in the same instant — deciding 'refused and nothing there, so this is a store fault' fails a send whose id is free and returns a 500 for an input that could simply have been granted. Driven in the shape it occurs in rather than stubbed. P1.

DirectoryNotFoundException derives from IOException, so a vanished thread directory lands in the collision-retry arm on every attempt with the read answering synchronously — a tight loop holding a core for the whole settle budget and never looking at its token, inside the very code path that exists to remove a starvation source. Cancellation is the observable that separates yielding from spinning, and the tree is taken away by an atomic rename because a recursive delete leaves a gap in which the create legally wins. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: P0 for the input-admission baseline. It pins the reason the acceptance record exists separately from the accepted-input marker: the agent loop DELETES that marker as soon as it folds an input into a run, and a caller retrying after the drain must still be told what the host granted. If the record did not outlive the drain, a repeated idempotency key would queue a SECOND turn — a duplicate model run with duplicate side effects, silently, on the ordinary retry path every client has. One test drives reserve, the ledger's record and remove, and the read-back across all three shipped store implementations, and its 195 new spans at rank 9 make it the widest single admission claim available.
uncertainties: inP0Prefix member at greedyRank 9 — the highest-ranked prefix row in this lane's remaining LmMultiTurn files — contributing 195 new spans, the largest marginal contribution of any row in this file.
Zero exclusive spans: other rows re-cover parts of this path, so it is chosen for breadth and consequence, not for being the sole cover of any span.
Sits on a different component from this project's other P0s (sub-agent teardown, conversation ownership), so the P0 set is not stacking on one code path.

rationale: The invariant the entire read side rests on: a record that can be OPENED can be READ. A dedicated OS thread opens every record it finds during a contended reserve/retract sweep; refused opens are ignored as the claim holding the file shut, and its own open count is asserted so a run that saw nothing cannot pass as clean. The real defect was a winner creating the record and flushing from a continuation, which handed losers IOException for a perfectly admitted input. P1.

A settled record read back through a fresh store object, including the enum. Reading another store object's write is already asserted at :216, and the reserve-then-outcome-then-read sequence at :141. The residual claim — that the enum is not stored positionally — is a serialisation detail on an otherwise covered path. P2.

A record left empty or half-written by a host that died mid-claim is still an ADMITTED input — the name was taken by an exclusive create somebody won. Once the settle budget is spent, both the read and a fresh reserve must FAULT rather than answer 'never admitted', because that answer queues a second turn for an input already granted. Driven on an injected clock with a fail-loud cap, so a widened budget cannot quietly become a hang. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Two callers retracting with ONE token over forty rounds: exactly one may be told it removed the record. Two trues mean two callers go on to re-take the id, so a later delete lands on the new owner and a third send queues a duplicate turn — and a read-then-delete implementation reports exactly that. P1.

Eight independent file stores racing for each of twenty ids. The file's own reasoning is why this is not a duplicate of :216 — a two-caller race can step over a microsecond-wide check-then-act window by luck, and File.Move(overwrite: false) reads as create-if-absent while being a stat-then-rename that silently replaces. Only a wide repeated fan-out separates a genuine O_CREAT|O_EXCL from a lucky one. P1.

The token guard, both verbs at once: a stranger's reservation id can neither record an outcome nor release the admission, and the owner's record is left exactly as it was. Without it a late release from a retracted-and-re-admitted send deletes the NEW owner's record and lets a third send queue a duplicate turn. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Null for an id that was never admitted — the answer that lets a send proceed at all. Thin, but it is the negative every admission decision starts from, and :659 exists precisely because a WRONG null here queues a duplicate turn. P1 as the positive control that null means absent.
Recording an outcome under the matching reservation replaces the stored record, and the replacement is what a later read returns. The settle half of the admission lifecycle. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Compensation: the owner retracting frees the id, and a later send is then admitted for it. A send whose work never got queued must not burn the idempotency key forever — that is a legitimate request permanently refused. P1.

The admission primitive across all three shipped stores: the first caller is told it owns the input by a null return, and the second is answered from the STORED record rather than from its own request — which is what lets a retry learn what the host already granted. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The cross-process claim tested the only way that means anything: two INDEPENDENT store objects over one backing, sharing no in-process lock, contending with both admissions minted first. Exactly one wins, the loser is handed the winner's record, and the stored record is one racer's rather than a merge. A store whose atomicity came from a private semaphore passes every single-object test and fails this one. P1.
Restores a text message and checks the same five fields the round-trip test at :343 checks with harder content. P2 as the subsumed half.
Restores a tool call, subsumed by the round-trip at :370 which asserts the same fields over nested argument JSON. P2.

The only exerciser of restoring a tool RESULT with its correlation id and payload intact. A result that came back with the wrong id, or as the wrong type, breaks the pairing every rehydrated history depends on. P1.

#680 forward-compatible rehydration: a row written by a NEWER build with a discriminator this one cannot resolve is skipped and reported with a typed exception, while the tool call and result surrounding it both come back and stay in order. Without it, one future row aborts the load of the entire conversation — after a rollback, permanently. P1.
The restoring batch overload, asserting types and one field each. Same reasoning. P2.
Empty-input boundary on the batch restore. P2.

A full round trip over text containing angle brackets, ampersands and both quote characters. Serialisation is where those either survive verbatim or come back escaped, doubled, or truncated — and the message body is the conversation itself. P1.

Nested-object and array arguments survive as an EXACT string. Tool arguments are JSON inside JSON, which is where double-encoding lives; a body that came back re-escaped would be rejected by the tool on replay while looking correct in storage. P1.

The full column projection in one place: thread and run ids from the call, role, agent, generation id, ordering index, the type discriminator, and the serialised body. Every persisted row in the product is produced by this mapping. P1.

Two conversions of the SAME message get different row ids. The id is the store's primary key, so deriving it from content would make a repeated message — an identical retry, a duplicated turn — collide with and overwrite the earlier row. P1.
Discriminator plus a substring check on the serialised body. The round-trip test at :370 restores the same message type and asserts its fields exactly. P2.
The same shape for tool results — discriminator and substrings — where the restore test at :198 asserts the actual fields. P2.

The parent run id is carried from the message onto its own column. That column is what links a sub-agent's rows to the run that spawned them, and nothing else in this type covers it — dropped, the run tree cannot be rebuilt from storage. P1.

The row is stamped with the current time, bounded by readings taken either side. Timestamp is the primary sort key every load orders by, so a converter that left it at zero would tie every message in a conversation and collapse ordering onto the secondary key. P1.
The batch overload over three messages, asserting discriminators only. A map over the single conversion held at P1. P2.
Ten messages keep their ordering index at their list position. A batch variation of the index passthrough already asserted in the single-message conversion. P2.
Empty-input boundary on the batch conversion. P2.

The foundation the checkpoint machinery stands on: seq is monotonic and GAP-FREE across separate appends, the watermark follows it, an empty thread reads zero, and both are scoped per thread. Every boundary, cut and range in the compaction stack is expressed in these numbers. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

Every row in this file is P1: it is a small spec-pinning suite where each row holds a separate clause of §2.2/§8.3/§12.1 over every store flavour, and none is a variation of another. Recorded rather than forcing a P2 quota.

rationale: A caller-supplied Seq is discarded and the store assigns its own. The fork between the two plausible implementations: honouring the caller lets any writer collide with an existing number or jump the watermark, and gap-free numbering is what the stale-watermark guard reads. P1.

Rows written before seq existed are numbered on the first append, in the order a reader already saw them, and the numbering is STABLE — a second append and two fresh handles leave every legacy number exactly where it was. A backfill that renumbers on each open moves history underneath any boundary already recorded. P1.

The tie the ordering rule does not cover: message_order_idx restarts per generation, so two legacy generations can share a millisecond AND an index. The backfill breaks such ties by rowid and the load must break them the same way, or the order a reader saw before the first append is not the order seq records after it. Ids are chosen so neither lexical nor reverse-insertion order coincides with rowid order. Rank 112, 13 marginal spans. P1.
uncertainties: The test states its own limit: dropping the rowid tiebreak passes today because the sorter preserves the rowid-ordered scan it is fed. Only REVERSING the tiebreak fails it, so this pins a contract SQL does not promise rather than proving the current query.

rationale: A checkpoint lives in the same table as ordinary messages, so it must survive persistence with its type discriminator, its column metadata and every manifest field, AND the resilient restore must not mistake it for a tool call or a tool result while pairing rows. A checkpoint that cannot be read back is a conversation whose compacted half is gone. P1.

The bounded read behind recall and replay: both bounds inclusive, the limit respected, an out-of-range window and an INVERTED range both empty rather than throwing or returning everything, and another thread's rows never reachable. The only row covering this API. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The distinguishing case, and the file says so: a row appended LATER carrying an EARLIER timestamp still loads second. (timestamp, idx) is not a total order — a clock step or two rows in one millisecond breaks it — so the read must order by seq. A timestamp-ordered load reorders history under a boundary that was computed on seq. P1.

A pending tool-result placeholder is replaced in place: same seq, same position between its neighbours, new payload, and the watermark does NOT advance because a replacement is not an append. Re-appending instead would move the resolved result to the end of the transcript, away from the call it answers, and inflate the watermark that the checkpoint guard compares against. Thirty-seven exclusive spans, the widest sole-cover in this file. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 37 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The watermark is read from the STORE, not remembered by the handle: a second process appends and the first handle's next read sees the higher number. The file names this as the precondition the checkpoint guard relies on — a cached watermark makes the stale_watermark rejection unreachable and lets a checkpoint commit over rows it never saw. P1.

An accepted input already listed on a Completed run produces no second row — the ledger still contains exactly one entry, and it is the original. This is what makes orphan detection a coverage test rather than a presence test: a reconciliation that synthesised a row for every accepted input would pass the orphan case and duplicate every input here. Asserting the surviving row's id as well as the count rules out the original being replaced by a synthetic one. Catches every restart doubling the thread's run history and re-marking completed work as interrupted. P1: the coverage predicate, distinct from the synthesis it gates.
requirements: in-process only; relies on IsRunning as the completion signal for reconciliation

rationale: Completed and Errored runs both survive reconciliation unchanged. This is the bound on the dangling-run rule and its non-vacuity partner: a reconciliation that marked EVERY row Interrupted would satisfy the dangling test completely and only fail here. Catches finished history being rewritten as interrupted on every restart, which would make a thread's own record of what succeeded unreliable and could re-drive completed inputs. The completion inference is stated rather than timed — reconciliation is awaited before the loop task is assigned, so a running agent proves it already ran. P1: terminal-status finality, a distinct contract from the transition it bounds.
requirements: in-process only; relies on IsRunning as the completion signal for reconciliation

rationale: A run left Queued or InProgress by a crash is reconciled to Interrupted when a fresh process starts, covering both non-terminal statuses. The setup is what makes it a crash simulation rather than a state edit: the store is seeded BEFORE the agent exists, so nothing in the process could still be running that run, which is exactly the inference reconciliation itself is entitled to make. Catches a thread wedged permanently by a crash: an InProgress row nobody will ever complete keeps the send guard closed, so the conversation refuses every new input with no error a user could act on, and no amount of restarting clears it. Nominated P0: reconciling dangling runs is the essential baseline of restart recovery, and this is the only row that observes it. One nomination for this component rather than one per class. Confirmation held pending the facts join.
requirements: in-process only; in-memory store, polled 5s bound
uncertainties: DEMOTED in the end-of-slice P0 prune. Eighteen nominations across 347 in-scope rows is 5.2%, against the lane's healthy 2.4-3.1% band; ten survive. The nomination recorded above stands as the reason this row is the strongest in its component and is NOT withdrawn as an assessment - it is simply not a surviving candidate. Demotion reason: a run left in the wrong terminal state is wrong in a place an operator reads - the ledger the status API answers from - rather than hidden. The survivors fail where no one is looking.

rationale: After a stop and a second RunAsync on the SAME instance, exactly one row still covers the orphan input. Reconciliation is a per-process concept, so a guard tied to the call rather than the instance would synthesise the orphan again on every restart of the loop and grow the ledger without bound. The first-start count of one is asserted before the second start, so the final count of one is provably stable rather than never having been two. Catches a restart-safe operation that is not idempotent. P1: the idempotency contract, distinct from the reconciliation behaviours it protects.
uncertainties: The stability assertion is preceded by a fixed 100ms sleep rather than a polled condition, so an erroneous second reconciliation slower than 100ms would not be observed. The test's own comment acknowledges the sleep is there to give a wrong implementation a chance to act.

rationale: A store that throws on the first ListRunLedgerAsync — the exact call reconciliation makes — must not stop the agent starting, and a genuine input sent afterwards runs to Completed. Two details make it real rather than a does-not-throw: the assertion reads the INNER store so it never trips the decorator's one-shot fault, and the call count is checked to be non-zero, which proves the fault was actually reached rather than the test passing because reconciliation never ran. Catches a transient storage blip at startup bricking the agent entirely, turning a recoverable read failure into a dead conversation. P1: an important failure-handling contract on the startup path.

An input accepted with no ledger row covering it — a crash between the 202 and StartRunAsync — is given a synthetic Interrupted row scoped to its thread. The stated design reason is the substantive part: synthesising the row means the input id resolves through the ordinary lookup, so no caller needs a restart-specific code path to explain a missing run. Catches an accepted input that resolves to nothing forever, so a client polling the id it was handed gets a permanent not-found for work the server acknowledged. P1: the orphan-input arm, a distinct crash window from a dangling run.
The terminal transition updates the SAME row to Completed and keeps its input ids — losing them at completion loses the correlation a sender's receipt is retired by. P1.
The error flag variation of the terminal write held at :109. P2.

The write-through proved by EFFECT rather than by inspecting a field that has no getter: a run driven through a real loop lands in the ledger carrying the caller's input id. This is the wiring every recovery path depends on. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: The interesting half of that gate: a store that satisfies IConversationStore but not IRunLedgerStore is rejected AT CONSTRUCTION. Accepting it would leave a host that believes it persists run state silently keeping none, discovered only after a restart loses runs. P1.
Null store with ledger persistence on is rejected. Argument validation over thirty-eight spans. P2.
The gate does not fire when ledger persistence is off. The negative guard on the check above. P2.
The case that distinguishes a union from an append — the row above asserts containment, which an appending implementation also satisfies. Here the duplicate count is pinned at one. P1.
An empty injection returns before any store write, leaving UpdatedAt untouched. An early-return boundary. P2.
With no ledger store the call neither throws nor writes. A configuration guard. P2.

Injected inputs are UNIONED into a live run's row: replacing instead would drop the ids the original send is waiting to have retired, leaving those acceptances outstanding forever. Widest single addition in this file (12 new spans). P1.

The InProgress row is written as the run STARTS, carrying every input id in the drained batch — that row is what a restart reads to decide the run was in flight and what it owed. The two inputs are enqueued before the loop runs so the batch is deterministic rather than a race the assertion happens to win. P1.

Four racing attaches with four different names: one wins, and every caller comes away naming the winner rather than the name it proposed. A caller told its own name won when it did not would address a continuation that does not exist. P1 for the third of this store's three compare-and-set paths.

A late caller proposing a different child is handed the committed name and the stored name does not move. It has to adopt the winner rather than start a second continuation for the same result. The stronger half of the pair on consequence, and the one that would let two children exist if it failed. P1.

The primary attach: a resolution that carried no child run id can be named later, and naming the continuation must not disturb the resolution itself — the fingerprint and resolved timestamp are asserted unchanged. That separation is what makes attach safe to call after the fact. P1.

P0 for the durable-continuation baseline of this store. It walks the whole lifecycle a resumed host depends on — start a run, defer a call, resolve it without a child, name the child, then name it AGAIN — and pins that the retry is handed back the same continuation rather than starting a second one. Criticality: this is the write that decides whether a lost acknowledgement costs a duplicate child run, which is real duplicated model work and real duplicated side effects, and the guarantee has to hold identically across a dictionary, a file and a SQLite row. Its assertions reach both the returned name and the persisted state, so the rank is not carrying a weak test. Also the file's highest-ranked declaration by measured coverage.
uncertainties: The only inP0Prefix member in this file (greedyRank 7 of the project's 36-member prefix).

This file is an interface conformance suite — one declaration per contract clause of IRunLifecycleStore — so almost nothing in it is a variation of something else and the P2 tier is nearly absent here by construction, not by inflation.

rationale: Attaching to a call that was never deferred names nothing. P1 by the floor; on contract alone it is the absent-key boundary of the rule above.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A call with no result yet has no continuation to carry one, so attach returns null and stores nothing. Naming one would let recovery start a child run for a result that never arrived. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The cross-thread guard on attach, mirroring the one on resolve: another thread naming this call's continuation is refused and the stored child id stays null. Two operations key on the same (thread, call) pair, so each needs its own guard — one of them silently accepting is how a continuation ends up owned by the wrong conversation. P1.

The live-run listing filters out what has terminalized. A terminal run leaking into it is a finished run that recovery would resume — re-running work whose effects already happened. P1 for the filter, distinct from the ordering rule.

The recovery listing is deliberately ordered OPPOSITE to the display listing — oldest first — because resuming outstanding runs in the order they started is what keeps their effects in the order they were requested. The seed inserts newest-first so insertion order cannot pass. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The per-thread listing returns only that thread's runs, newest first, with a third thread's run seeded to prove the scoping. Cross-thread leakage here would show one conversation's runs inside another. P1.
An unknown run id loads as null rather than throwing or synthesising a row — the answer recovery branches on when deciding whether a run ever existed. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Deferrals are numbered in commit order (1, then 2), come back in that order, and both show up as unresolved. The ordinal is how a caller correlates a late result to the call it belongs to, so a store that numbered them by anything else would mismatch results to calls. P1.

Re-recording the same tool call id hands back the record already committed — the same ordinal and the original tool name, not the second caller's differing one — and leaves exactly one deferral stored. Without this a retried deferral doubles the outstanding work a run believes it is waiting on. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 7 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Deferring a call against a run the store never saw throws rather than creating an orphan deferral no run will ever resolve or wait on. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 11 exclusive product spans, the highest in this file, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Reusing a run id that has already terminalized throws, rather than resurrecting a finished run in place. Terminal is a one-way state and this is the transition that would undo it — including the outcome and turn count already recorded against it. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 6 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A second start for the same run — a retry, a reconnect, a host correcting the lineage it first reported — refreshes the description while keeping work already committed against it. A store that replaced the row instead of upserting would drop deferrals a caller is still waiting on. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Starting a run that is already described as Terminal is refused, so the store never holds a run that was born finished and would be skipped by the live-run listing the moment it was written. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Every field of a started run survives the write and read: thread, run and generation ids, the parent run and thread, the spawning and causing tool calls, the sub-agent id and cause kind, plus the derived initial phase, null outcome, null terminal time and empty deferral list. This lineage is how a restarted host reattaches a child run to the parent that spawned it, so a column silently dropped by one store orphans the child. Declared once on the abstract base and executed against all three IRunLifecycleStore implementations (in-memory, file, SQLite) through the three sealed fixtures at the foot of the file, so one frozen declaration is three runs over three storage engines. P1.
The same rejection for a missing run id, which is the primary key every later operation addresses. P1 by the floor.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A run with no thread id is rejected at the write rather than stored as an unreachable row: every read path is keyed by thread, so such a row could never be listed or resolved again. P1 by the floor; on contract alone it is argument validation.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Four racing terminalizations and exactly one true. This is the compare-and-set the once-only rule rests on, and it must hold identically in a dictionary, a file and a SQLite row — three engines with three completely different concurrency stories. P1.

Terminalization happens once: the first call wins and reports true, the second reports false AND changes nothing — the stored outcome, turn count and terminal timestamp all stay the first call's. A second call that overwrote them would rewrite how a run ended after the fact. P1 for the store's central once-only guarantee.
Terminalizing a run that was never started reports false rather than throwing or creating a terminal row from nothing. P1 by the floor.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A result arriving after the run has terminalized still resolves. Deferred calls outlive their run by design — that is what deferral means — so refusing here would discard every late result and leave the deferral permanently unresolved in the durable state. P1.

Four racing resolutions with four different fingerprints: exactly one reports Resolved, and none reports NotFound. The second assertion is what stops a losing caller being told the call does not exist — it lost the race, which is a different fact and leads to a different recovery. P1.

A second, DIFFERENT result for the same call reports Conflict and changes nothing at all. This is the case that separates 'a retry of the same answer' from 'a second, contradictory answer', and only the fingerprint can tell them apart. Silently taking the newer one would let a stale duplicate rewrite a settled result. P1.

The primary resolution: the outcome is Resolved and the stored deferral carries its resolved flag, timestamp, fingerprint and child run id, with the unresolved projection now empty. That projection is what tells a resumed run whether it is still waiting on anything. P1.

The same result delivered twice reports Duplicate and the FIRST resolution stands — its child run and its timestamp — rather than the later delivery overwriting them. A redelivered result is the ordinary case after a reconnect, and taking the second would repoint the continuation at a child that no longer matches what was already reported. P1.
Resolving a call that was never deferred reports NotFound rather than creating a resolved deferral out of nothing. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The same call id addressed from another thread reports NotFound. The resolution is keyed by (thread, call), so this is the guard that stops one conversation resolving another's outstanding work — a sibling route on the same identifier, which is exactly where scoping goes missing. P1.

After the factory is disposed and pools are cleared, the containing DIRECTORY must be renameable and the database file must exist at the new path. The comment answers the obvious vacuity objection head-on and correctly: the factory pools, so ClearAllPools is required even when disposal is right, but the defect bypassed the pool entirely — base.Dispose was never invoked, so the connection was neither closed nor returned, and pool-clearing cannot release a handle the pool does not know it owns. That makes ClearAllPools the precise dividing line rather than a mask. Choosing a directory rename over a file delete is deliberate: it is the operation publish-launch.ps1's atomic swap performs over a deployed database, and the one that actually failed in CI. Catches a deployment swap failing with access denied. P1: the handle-close contract on disposal.
requirements: creates and renames a directory under the temp directory; Windows file-locking semantics

rationale: Three full saturate-then-release cycles at maxConnections, then one more acquisition under a 10-second token. The cycle count is reasoned rather than arbitrary — one cycle would pass even if permits were released only once, so three is what shows the pool is still whole after repeated use. Asserting against a timeout instead of awaiting plainly is the difference between a failing test and a hung suite. The consequence is stated exactly: nothing ever reposts a lost permit, so a factory that loses maxConnections of them blocks forever on the next acquisition with no error anywhere — a process that stops doing work while looking healthy. Catches a permit leak on disposal. P1: the permit-return contract, distinct from the handle-close contract in the same disposal path.
requirements: creates SQLite files under the temp directory; 10s bound on the probe acquisition
uncertainties: The class remarks argue no store-level test can observe these obligations. Per the standing rule that irreplaceability is a P1 floor and never a P0 argument, that claim is recorded but is not used to raise this row.

rationale: Synchronous Dispose is exercised three times at maxConnections 1, then BOTH directions of the permit count are checked: one more acquisition must succeed, and a second concurrent acquisition while the first is alive must be refused on a 500ms token. The over-cap assertion is what makes this more than a duplicate of the async case — at a cap of one the permit count is directly observable, and a double-release would silently raise the real concurrency limit above the configured cap, the opposite failure and equally quiet. The sync path is reachable through `using` and through DbConnection's own async-to-sync fallback, so it is not a hypothetical entry point. Catches a permit released twice or not at all on the synchronous path. P1: the exactly-once release contract, a distinct guarantee from the async path's at-least-once.
requirements: creates SQLite files under the temp directory; 500ms and 10s bounds

rationale: The store's primary write on a thread that does not exist yet, read back through its own loader. Everything else in this type presupposes it. P1.

A second batch accumulates rather than replacing: two runs, five rows. In SQL this is the difference between an insert and an upsert on the thread key, and getting it wrong deletes the earlier turns of a live conversation. P1.
The second null-argument boundary on the same method. P2.
Argument validation with the parameter name asserted. P2.
An empty batch writes nothing and creates no thread. Without the early return an empty insert statement either throws or mints an empty thread row that then appears in the listing. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Idempotent delete of an absent thread. P2.

The WHERE clause, with a second thread present and asserted intact. A delete missing its predicate empties every conversation in the database, which is the single most destructive defect available in this type. P1.

Deletion clears BOTH tables, asserted through the two readers. A delete that cleared only messages leaves a metadata row that the listing still returns — a conversation that opens empty and cannot be removed. P1.

All eleven persisted columns asserted individually after a round trip, parent run and generation id included. Those two are what reconstruct the run tree, and a column silently dropped by the reader is invisible until something downstream tries to walk it. P1 for the column mapping.
Absent-thread boundary on the message read. P2.

The merged conversation store's baseline: message order is the one contract here whose failure is silent and total. src/LmMultiTurn/Persistence/MessageSequence.cs:30 is the single definition of append order for all three backends - `.OrderBy(m => m.Timestamp).ThenBy(m => m.MessageOrderIdx ?? 0)`, documented at :4 as existing so the backends 'cannot drift' (#680). SQLite calls it at SqliteConversationStore.cs:81, freezes the result into `seq` at :96, and LoadMessagesAsync replays `seq` at :309. The defect: delete the `.ThenBy` at MessageSequence.cs:30 and rows written inside one millisecond come back in whatever order the caller assembled them. A streamed generation writes several rows inside the same tick, so this is the ordinary path, not an edge case. Nothing throws and no status changes - the store returns a scrambled conversation and every later turn is fed it. Independence, each sibling verdict read from its own body: under that deletion Sqlite :130, InMemory :92 and File :143 all stay green, because each builds its messages at now, now+100 and now+200, so a lost secondary key cannot reach them; the remaining 54 rows of the component never construct two rows sharing a timestamp. Note the one other detector honestly: InMemoryConversationStoreTests :117 is the same shuffled same-timestamp case against the shared helper (verified at :124-141) and also goes red. It stays P1. That is the argument for promoting here rather than leaving the component empty - the contract has exactly two detectors and a P0-only selection would run neither. Stated, not assumed (rubric line 53): addsNothingNew is true, and the exception is claimed deliberately. This row and LoadMessagesAsync_ReturnsMessagesOrderedByTimestamp reach an identical 260-span set while asserting different orderings; coverage counts spans reached and never which ordering was asserted, so the whole of this contract is invisible to it. Outside the greedy prefix and carrying no rank (rubric line 48): its P0 rests on the contract above and on no coverage standing, which is why the mutation above, not a rank, is what argues it.
Load orders by timestamp with the rows inserted out of order, so insertion order cannot pass for a sort. Message order is the conversation, so a missing ORDER BY reads the history back scrambled. P1.
Absent-thread boundary on the metadata read. P2.

A second save for the same thread updates in place rather than failing on the key or leaving the first row to win the read. Metadata is rewritten on every turn, so an upsert that is really an insert either throws immediately or freezes the conversation's metadata at its first value. P1.

CurrentRunId and LatestRunId are distinct columns and both must survive. Nothing else in this type touches latest_run_id, so a mapper that dropped it would go unnoticed here and resume the wrong run. P1.
The open properties bag — title and preview live here — survives the JSON round trip. Dropping it leaves every conversation showing as untitled while the data is intact in the row. P1.

The session-mapping dictionary survives serialisation into its column, asserted per key. These map a conversation to the provider-side session it resumes; losing them silently starts a NEW provider session on the next turn, which reads as the model forgetting everything. P1.
Save then load, asserting the thread id came back. The overwrite case below performs the same round trip and additionally checks a field that changed. P2 as the subsumed half.
