Repeated operations across both tables must not re-run schema creation destructively or fail on it. A CREATE that is not guarded takes the whole store down on the second operation of every process. P1 for the initialisation path, with the caveat recorded above.
uncertainties: Its assertion is a message count, so what it really shows is that this interleaving of appends and metadata saves completes without a schema error — not idempotence in general.

rationale: The same concurrency mechanism with the contention removed: five writers on five different thread ids. P2 as the easier variation of the case above.

Ten concurrent appends of ten rows each to ONE thread, with all hundred rows required afterwards. This is the contended case — the same connection and the same thread key — and lost rows here are lost turns of a conversation. P1.

Deleting a non-existent wait on a never-initialised schema does not throw, covering the entry point a cleanup path reaches first when nothing was ever saved. Catches lazy init being wired into save and load but not delete, which would fault teardown on a fresh database. P2: an entry-point variation on the lazy-init contract the save case pins, and the assertion is a does-not-throw rather than an observation of state.

A saved wait is gone after delete. Catches a delete that reports success without removing the row, so a resolved wait is re-armed on the next restore and fires again. P2: the third leg of the basic round trip, over the save-and-load baseline; the cross-thread test already exercises delete under the harder condition.

Two threads save a wait under the SAME wait id and both survive with their own labels, and deleting one thread's row leaves the other's intact. The comment gives the reason the collision is real rather than hypothetical: wait_id is the model-assigned tool_call_id, which is not globally unique, so identity must be keyed on (thread_id, wait_id). Asserting the delete in isolation as well as the save is what covers both halves of the key — a store scoped correctly on write but not on delete would pass the first assertions and fail the last. Catches one conversation's armed wait silently overwriting or deleting another's in a shared store: cross-conversation data loss with no error and no way to notice. P1: the identity-scoping contract for this store.
requirements: in-process only; shared-cache in-memory SQLite, real schema
uncertainties: Was a contender for a Persistence P0 on a cross-conversation data-loss argument. Resolved after reading the remaining four Persistence classes: the nomination went to SqliteResourceGrantStoreTests.ARoleTheConstraintNeverAllowed_IsAbsentFromBothReaders, because a disagreement between two readers of an access-control column is a stronger criticality argument than a wait row overwritten across threads. This row stays P1 with no nomination.

rationale: A store constructed with no prior explicit schema initialisation still saves and reads back. The recorded regression is a caller-ordering hazard rather than a logic bug: every construction site that forgets the initialiser fails at first write, in production, on a table that does not exist. Making init lazy and idempotent inside the store removes the ordering requirement from every caller at once. Catches a wait that cannot be persisted at all on a fresh database, which means no wait survives a restart. P1: the initialisation contract, distinct from the read-write behaviours it enables.
requirements: in-process only; factory with no schema initializer call

rationale: Re-saving an existing wait with a CLAMPED maxFires and refreshed timeout and armed-at updates all three, not just the fire count and status. The test name states the defect it excludes, and the construction is chosen so each column moves in a distinguishable direction — a partial upsert would leave the original maxFires of 5 standing. That column matters most: it is the restore path re-arming a wait with a reduced remaining budget, so a dropped clamp restores the ORIGINAL budget and lets a bounded wait fire more times than it had left. Catches a restart resetting a nearly-exhausted wait to full. P1: the upsert completeness contract, distinct from insert and from scoping.

A saved wait is loadable under its own thread and ABSENT under another. The paired negative is what makes it a scoping test rather than a round trip — a load that ignored thread_id entirely would satisfy the positive alone. Catches a restore handing one conversation another's armed waits, which would arm triggers against a thread that never asked for them. P1: the store's primary read-write contract and the baseline the other rows vary.

An Editor grant written through the store's own API reads back as Editor from the point read AND as a single Editor row from the listing. The test says why it exists and why it is ordered first: without it, a store returning nothing from either reader would satisfy every agreement assertion in the unrecognised-role case, since 'both empty' is trivially agreement. Catches a grant that cannot be read back at all, and anchors the file's agreement claim to a positive. P1: the store's primary read-write contract and the non-vacuity anchor for the fail-closed row.

A role value the table's CHECK constraint would refuse is seeded by direct SQL — the constraint dropped for the insert, because GrantAsync could not produce such a row — and both readers must then deny it: the point read returns null and the listing is empty. The recorded defect is a genuine divergence, not a hypothetical: the listing used to answer Viewer for the same row the point read denied, so one row meant 'no access' to the check that gates the operation and 'viewer' to the share list the owner is reading. The remarks say precisely when it becomes reachable — a row restored from a build predating the constraint, or a manual edit during an incident — which is also when nobody is watching. Both readers are asserted in one test because agreement is the property; either alone is satisfiable by a wrong-but-consistent answer only if the other is checked too. Catches an authorization decision that differs by which code path asks. P0: fail-closed agreement between the two readers of an access-control column is the criticality argument for this store. Coverage caveat: addsNothingNew means allowed-role cases traverse the same reader spans, but none seeds a legacy-invalid role and asserts denial from both readers, so overlap is not assertion redundancy.
requirements: writes a temp-directory SQLite file; no network, no credentials
raw SQL seeding rebuilds the table without its CHECK constraint

rationale: An unreadable row and a valid Viewer grant sit on the same resource, and the listing returns exactly the valid one. The subject ids are chosen so the bad row sorts FIRST — aaa-first against zzz-last — which is what makes the case discriminating: a break instead of a continue, or a guard one level out, truncates the list at the bad row and hides everything after it. Skipping a row must not become skipping the read. Catches a single corrupt grant silently emptying an owner's entire share list, so access that still exists becomes invisible to the person managing it. P1: the row-granular degradation contract, distinct from what any single row resolves to.
uncertainties: Asserts the surviving row only. It does not separately assert that the point read for the skipped subject denies access, though the sibling test covers that subject in isolation.

rationale: Empty set for an unknown thread. P2.
Thread scoping on the accepted-input query — a separate statement from the ledger listing, and one where a leak would make one conversation's idempotency keys suppress another's inputs. P1.
Thread scoping on the listing — one conversation's runs must never appear in another's. P1.
Empty listing for an unknown thread. P2.
Newest first, with the three rows deliberately written out of order so insertion order cannot be mistaken for sort order. The listing is what a caller reads to find the current run. P1.
Null for an unknown run id. P2.

Recording the same (thread, input) twice neither throws nor duplicates. This is the ordinary retry path — a client resending an input it already sent — so a primary-key violation here would surface as an error for a request that should simply be recognised. P1.

The accepted-input marker is written and comes back in the listing. That marker is what the admission path reads to decide whether an input was already taken, so a write that did not land would let the same input queue twice. P1.
Removing something that is not there does not throw. P2.
The drain: the marker is removed once the input is folded into a run. Without removal the set grows without bound and every later admission decision reads a longer list. P1.
Interleaved writes across both tables complete and the counts add up. A smoke test whose individual operations are each already covered above. P2.

The upsert semantics the name promises: a second write for the same run id replaces status and input ids AND leaves exactly one row. An insert-only implementation would accumulate a row per status transition and make the listing report a run many times. P1.

Every column of a ledger entry survives the round trip, timestamps included — the helper truncates to millisecond precision because the store stores Unix milliseconds, so the assertion is exact rather than approximate. The primary write-and-read path. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: Empty input-id list boundary on the round trip above. P2.
Four input ids instead of two. A list-size variation of the round trip. P2.

Non-vacuity for the refusal above, and the boundary between them is exactly one integer: a refusal that also rejected an ordinary current database would satisfy :260 and break every process on the deployment. P1.

The rollback case (#386): an older binary opening a file a newer one migrated must REFUSE, because it cannot migrate down and cannot know what changed — reading it as 'already current' hands the older code tables and columns whose meaning it does not know, on the one store that holds customer conversations. The version is pinned in the message so an operator can see which file they have. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The per-step guard INSIDE the loop, which the row above never reaches because it exits at the already-at-latest fast path. Stamped at 1, the runner must skip step 1 and apply the rest — detected by a table step 1 would have created. A different guard from :163 despite the similar-sounding claim. P1.

The only case that can tell 'the runner consults user_version' from 'every statement happens to be idempotent': an EMPTY database stamped at the latest version must come back still empty. Re-running the current steps cannot distinguish those, and the distinction is what makes a future ALTER or a data-inserting step safe. P1.

A database an earlier build created reads user_version 0 even though step 1 effectively ran; the runner has to recognise that, apply the rest, and keep the pre-existing row intact. Getting it wrong either re-runs step 1 against live tables or strands an existing customer database on an old schema. P1.
A fresh install actually has the tables — conversations, metadata, notify waits and the tenant registry. The first thing a new deployment depends on. P1.
A fresh database ends stamped at the latest version, plus a change-detector on the constant itself. Every row below asserts that stamp on its way to a stronger claim. P2.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: A row inserted between two initializations survives the second. Data safety on the re-run path, which :315 establishes far more strongly on the path that actually alters tables. P2.
Two runs in a row leave the version at the latest. The weaker form of the idempotence :163 and :234 establish with cases that can actually distinguish implementations. P2.

Cross-tenant identity collision made structurally impossible at the schema level rather than trusted to the store — two tenants cannot claim one Entra directory — while still permitting several rows with no directory behind them, which the legacy tenant needs. Both halves are required: the index without the partial clause would block the legacy rows entirely. P1.

The real customer upgrade: stamped at the last version before the owner columns, with rows already present, through the one step in the ladder that is an ALTER TABLE. Every prior column value is asserted unchanged row by row, and the new tenant column must be NULL rather than defaulted — null is what the startup repair looks for, so a defaulting migration makes those conversations permanently untenanted and invisible to the repair. P1.

#347: an operator can paste a directory id in any shape Guid.TryParse accepts, but a token's tid claim is always the D form — so the id is canonicalised ON WRITE and the stored value reads back canonical. Without it, provisioning with a braced or upper-case id creates a tenant that no sign-in from that directory can ever match, and the failure looks like 'we have never heard of you'. P1.

The normaliser is not a validator: a non-GUID placeholder is still accepted and still matches case-insensitively. Real — it keeps seeded deployments resolving — but a tolerance boundary on the canonicalisation held at :257. P2.
The duplicate check runs on the CANONICAL form, or a second tenant claims a directory already taken simply by re-shaping the id — the claim guard at :162 defeated by punctuation. P1.

A suspended tenant is RETURNED, with its status, rather than being filtered out as if it did not exist. The caller has to tell 'your organisation's access is suspended' apart from 'we have never heard of you', and only the store returning the row makes that possible. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Spec 4.4's explicit-provisioning rule: a lookup for an unknown directory returns null and — asserted by counting rows in SQL — creates nothing. A store that auto-provisioned on first sign-in would let any Entra directory in the world make itself a tenant. P1.

Admin-ness is false before binding, true after it, and false in a SECOND tenant that named the same person — asserted with both tenants provisioned for the same UPN, which is the arrangement where a query keyed on user id alone would wrongly answer true. Cross-tenant admin is privilege escalation across an isolation boundary. P1.

Provisioning writes the tenant with every field intact AND names the first admin with a NULL user id and NULL bound_at — read straight from SQL, because the store never returns that row. That null is the precondition the entire binding rule below depends on: the admin is named before they have ever signed in. P1.

A duplicate internal tenant id is refused with the typed outcome and leaves NOTHING behind — the tenant count is unchanged and, checked in SQL, no second admin row was written. A partial write here would name an admin for a tenant the call did not create. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A second tenant claiming a directory that is already claimed is refused, nothing is written, and the impostor id resolves to nothing. Admitting it would put two tenants behind one directory, and every sign-in from that directory would then resolve to whichever row the query happened to return. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A second repair pass rewrites nothing. The already-canonical row is already excluded and counted at :307. P2.

Two rows that fold onto one value would violate the unique index, and the repair runs on EVERY startup — so throwing here is a host that cannot boot with no in-product way out. The colliding row is left byte-for-byte as it was and, critically, is COUNTED, so the startup log can warn that a tenant was left unreachable instead of silently reporting a smaller rewritten total. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Rows written before normalisation existed — or by a build rolled back to one — keep whatever shape they were given, and only this repair can reach them. Three legacy shapes are rewritten, the already-canonical row is neither touched nor counted, and each value is read back raw. P1.

The UPN is consulted exactly ONCE because it is mutable and re-assignable: the first sign-in binds the durable user id and the instant, and a later sign-in claiming a DIFFERENT oid for the same UPN changes neither. Without that, an attacker who gets a departed admin's UPN reassigned to them inherits tenant admin. P1, and the positive complement of the P0 below.

P0 for the tenant-admin authorization baseline. It is the negative that makes admin binding an authorization decision at all: a user who was NEVER NAMED as first admin cannot bind, and is not reported as an admin afterwards — both halves asserted, so a bind that silently failed while IsTenantAdmin still said true would not pass. Criticality: the failure mode is privilege escalation in a multi-tenant product — whoever signs in first becomes the tenant's administrator, with no in-product way to undo it, and every later authorization check in that tenant inherits the mistake. The row also happens to be the cheapest wide cover of the provisioning and binding path (rank 17, +111 spans).
uncertainties: inP0Prefix member at greedyRank 17, contributing 111 new spans — the second-largest marginal contribution among this lane's remaining prefix rows.
Zero exclusive spans: the bind path is re-covered by :175 and :223, so this row is chosen for consequence and breadth rather than for being the sole cover of any span.
Sits on its own component (multi-tenant authorization); the other LmMultiTurn P0s are on input admission, conversation ownership and sub-agent teardown, so the P0 set is not stacking on one path.

rationale: The named UPN matches regardless of case. A comparison variation of the bind path above, which already provisions with mixed case at :95. P2.

Six cases fix the whole system-prompt cascade in one place: profile beats the constructor prompt, the constructor prompt beats developer instructions, developer instructions are the last resort, all-null resolves to null, profile beats both when all three are supplied, and a WHITESPACE-only profile prompt is skipped rather than winning. The whitespace case is the one that earns the row — an empty-string check would let a profile with a blank prompt silently erase whatever the host configured, which is the worst outcome available here because the agent then runs with no system prompt at all and nothing reports an error. Three separate loops (Claude, Codex, Copilot) each wire this resolver, so the rule is fixed once here and only the wiring is checked per loop. Catches a precedence inversion or a blank prompt winning. P1: the shared resolution contract behind every loop's system prompt.
uncertainties: The whitespace case is covered only on the PROFILE argument. A whitespace-only constructor prompt or developer-instructions value is not exercised, so whether the same skip rule applies to the lower tiers is unpinned.

rationale: An AggregateException holding a disposed-client fault and a genuine prompt-too-long 400 classifies Overflow at a small estimate. Both halves matter: flattening happens, and the resolution is strongest-wins rather than first-wins, so a lifecycle fault ordered ahead of the real overflow cannot mask it. Catches a parallel or retry path wrapping its faults and losing the remediable one. P1: the aggregation contract, a distinct primary behaviour over the single-exception arms.
uncertainties: Asserts strongest-wins with the overflow second in the list; the reverse ordering is not exercised, so first-wins ordering that happened to agree here would also pass.

rationale: Seven transport faults that carry no evidence the RESPONSE was aborted — a device-not-ready IOException, HostUnreachable, a ConnectionError that never opened a connection, and bare 502/503/504/408 statuses — stay NotOverflow at twice the large estimate. This is the precise line the classifier has to hold: an aborted response on a big history is evidence of size, but a connection that never opened is evidence of availability. Catches the size heuristic being applied to every transport fault, which would remediate an outage as if it were an overflow. P1: an important negative boundary distinct from the abort family it sits next to.

Five real provider shapes — Anthropic's 400 prompt-too-long body, OpenAI's context_length_exceeded, the Responses API wording, a bare Anthropic 413 where the status alone suffices, and the Responses error surfaced as a plain InvalidOperationException — each classify Overflow at BOTH a small and a large estimate. Asserting at the small estimate is what carries the contract: it proves the token estimate cannot veto an explicit provider statement, so a conversation the estimator underestimates is still remediated. Catches an overflow the loop fails to recognise, which retries the identical oversized request until the run dies. Nominated P0 as the positive half of the classifier's essential contract; the negative half is the lifecycle-fault row. Confirmation held pending the facts join.
uncertainties: DEMOTED in the end-of-slice P0 prune. Eighteen nominations across 347 in-scope rows is 5.2%, against the lane's healthy 2.4-3.1% band; ten survive. The nomination recorded above stands as the reason this row is the strongest in its component and is NOT withdrawn as an assessment - it is simply not a surviving candidate. Demotion reason: COMPONENT DUPLICATE - ProviderErrorClassifier carried two candidates, which the one-per-component rule forbids and which I should have caught when the second was nominated. The false-positive direction survives (LifecycleAndProgrammingFaults_AreNeverOverflow_EvenOnAHugeHistory) because misreading a programming fault as overflow hides the real bug behind pointless compaction; this direction fails loudly as a rejected request.

rationale: Seven lifecycle and programming faults — disposed client, unresolved deferred tool call, bad argument, unsupported streaming, null reference, JSON conversion, and a retry helper wrapping a disposed client — all classify NotOverflow at five times the large-history estimate. The wrapped case is the decisive row: it proves the classifier unwraps rather than matching on the outer message, so a retry helper cannot launder a lifecycle fault into an overflow. Catches the failure the #693 contract exists to prevent: a genuine bug on a long conversation being read as a context overflow, which sends the loop into compaction remediation and permanently hides the real defect behind a plausible-looking recovery. P0: this is the criticality argument for the component, not merely a distinct behaviour. Coverage caveat: addsNothingNew means other cases traverse the classifier spans, but none distinguishes a wrapped lifecycle/programming fault from genuine overflow on a huge history, so overlap is not assertion redundancy.
requirements: in-process only; pure classification over constructed exceptions

rationale: 401, 403, 404, 429 and 500 on a doubled large history all stay NotOverflow. Catches the classifier keying on history size whenever the server answered at all, which would read an auth failure or a rate limit as an overflow and send a long thread into compaction instead of surfacing a credential or quota problem. P1: the answered-but-not-about-size arm, distinct from the transport families.

A null exception throws ArgumentNullException rather than returning a verdict. Catches a null silently classifying as NotOverflow, which would read as a decision rather than a caller bug. P2: an argument-guard variation on the entry point, not a distinct classification behaviour.

Seven abort shapes — HttpIOException and HttpRequestException with ResponseEnded, the bare premature-end message, the forcibly-closed IOException, ConnectionReset and ConnectionAborted socket codes, and an abort wrapped by the retry helper — yield LikelyOverflow on a large history. Matching the socket CODE rather than its text is the portable choice, since Windows and Linux render the same code differently. P1: the tie-break arm where history size legitimately contributes, distinct from both the explicit-overflow and never-overflow arms.

The same seven abort shapes at one token below the large-history threshold classify NotOverflow. Paired with the large-history row this pins the boundary exactly: the two tests differ only in the estimate, so together they prove size is the tie-breaker and neither verdict is a constant. Catches an ordinary network blip on a short conversation being remediated as an overflow, which would compact a thread that had no size problem. P1: the other half of the tie-break pair.

When a provider stream dies on the same turn that holds an unresolved deferral, the run must PARK rather than launch a recovery continuation — because a continuation would have to carry a tool result that does not exist yet, and the effect it is waiting on has a human on the other end. The row's construction answers the hardest question a test like this faces, and its comment states it outright: the provider call count stays at 1 either way, because a recovery attempt is rejected by the turn precondition, so the count alone cannot tell a park from a failed recovery. The distinguishing assertions are the run's OUTCOME — not failed, no error, because parking is a normal successful end — plus the deferral still outstanding and the handler having run exactly once. It then follows through: the answer arrives, a child run continues the conversation, and the second request is checked to CARRY the tool result rather than re-ask for it, with the tool invocation count still one. Catches an interrupted turn that either loses a pending client effect or surfaces a spurious error. P0 because losing or duplicating the pending human effect silently corrupts the conversation. Coverage caveat: addsNothingNew means other cases traverse the same interruption and deferral spans, but none jointly distinguishes parking from a rejected recovery and verifies one post-answer continuation, so overlap is not assertion redundancy.
requirements: in-process only; Moq streaming agent scripted per attempt, InMemoryConversationStore, HttpIOException as the transport fault
bounded: 10s waits on each run completion
uncertainties: Was a P0 contender: it is the row that keeps a pending human answer from being lost to a transport fault. DECLINED on scoping — the Recovery family already carries a candidate in this slice (InterruptionAfterACompletedToolCall_SettlesItOnceAndNeverReExecutesIt), and that one guards the harder consequence, a completed side effect running twice. Same treatment as the SubAgents descendant-question row: recorded, not nominated. FOR THE LEAD: if Recovery warrants two slots, this is the second.

The GenerationAbandonedMessage assertion pins that the client is told to drop partial output, but nothing checks the abandoned generation's identity, so a message naming the wrong generation would pass.

rationale: The in-process half of the same rule: the park spends the input's one recovery, and the CHILD run that resumes it inherits the spent budget, so its own interruption buys no third attempt and the run fails with stream_interrupted_after_recovery. The class remarks explain why this forces real child runs rather than a single run — a parked input resumes in a DIFFERENT run, so a budget stored on the run silently refills at every park, and an input that can refill by parking loops forever against a broken transport one client round-trip at a time. Asserting the failure rather than a success is the correct shape here: the desired behavior is that the loop gives up, and a row that asserted eventual success would be satisfied by the runaway. Catches a recovery budget scoped to the run instead of the input. P1: the in-process budget-inheritance contract.
uncertainties: Unlike its two siblings this row never checks ToolInvocations, so it does not exclude the deferring handler running again on the resumed attempt.

Both budget rows pin that a SPENT budget is not refilled. Neither shows that a fresh logical input gets its own recovery — the positive control for the budget existing at all — which lives, if anywhere, in the stream-recovery class rather than here.

rationale: The recovery budget belongs to the logical input and must survive a PROCESS RESTART: the parked run spent the input's one recovery, a new loop picks the conversation up from the store alone, and the resumed input still gets no second attempt — it fails with stream_interrupted_after_recovery on its own interruption. The comment explains why this boundary, not just the in-process one, is the one that matters: a deferred client tool exists precisely so an answer can arrive minutes later, from a human, in a process that has since restarted, so the restart is the LIKELY path rather than the exotic one. A budget refunded by restart buys one extra provider call per restart, forever, against a transport that is already broken. The restart is modelled honestly — the loop is disposed and rebuilt over the same store, with the counters deliberately living on the harness so they span both processes — which is what makes 'the second call' mean the same thing before and after. It also re-checks that the completed client effect is not re-executed. Catches a per-input budget that is really per-process. P1: important failure handling across the restart boundary.
requirements: in-process only; the restart replaces the loop over a shared InMemoryConversationStore, no real process boundary
uncertainties: The restart is a new loop over the SAME in-memory store instance, so anything the budget might rely on that lives in that object graph rather than in persisted rows survives for the wrong reason. A true restart reads a fresh store from durable storage; this one cannot distinguish persisted state from process state that happens to be shared.
Only one restart is exercised. The stated fear is a refund 'once per restart, forever', and a second restart-and-resume cycle — the shape that would show accumulation — is not run.

rationale: A genuinely truncated SSE body — cut on a frame boundary, then ended with the exact HttpIOException HttpClient raises when a body stops early — must still be classified as recoverable after passing through a REAL provider client, a real agent and a real HTTP transport. The remarks state what every other recovery test has to assume and this one checks: those tests hand the loop the exception it classifies, so a single catch in the client or the agent that re-wrapped the fault into an InvalidOperationException, or worse a TaskCanceledException the classifier reads as user cancellation, would silently turn every recoverable blip into a failed run and no mock-agent test could see it. Reaching a second POST is itself the proof, and RequestCount is asserted to be exactly 2 rather than at least 2, so a retry storm fails too. The fixture is built to keep the truncation as the only variable: it delegates to the shared test SSE handler so the surviving prefix is byte-for-byte what the stack normally parses, and cuts on a frame boundary so the prefix stays parseable. It then checks the retry delivered the whole reply and that the replacement carries a NEW generation id, so a client can discard the abandoned one wholesale. Catches a recoverable transport blip misclassified anywhere in the provider stack. P1: the only end-to-end proof of the classification the whole recovery family depends on.
requirements: NO NETWORK despite the real HttpClient: the handler delegates to OpenAiResponsesTestSseMessageHandler in-process and the base address is never dialled
real provider stack: OpenAiResponsesAgent over OpenAiResponsesClient, InMemoryConversationStore
bounded: 30s cts, chosen deliberately so a lost recovery fails instead of hanging
component: LmMultiTurn.Recovery (classification through the real provider stack)
uncertainties: Was a contender: it is the only row proving the fault survives the provider stack with its classification intact, and it is load-bearing for every mock-based recovery test. Declined because the Recovery family already carries a candidate in this slice, and because this is the most expensive row in the family — a real client, a real transport and a full SSE parse — which cuts against a P0's job of running first and cheaply.

The final check is AllSatisfy over RunCompletedMessage, which passes on an EMPTY sequence. If the run ever completed without publishing a completion into this collection, the 'invisible to the caller' claim would hold vacuously. The earlier ContainSingle assertions make an empty collection unlikely but do not exclude a missing completion specifically.

The remarks are explicit that OpenAI Responses is only the vehicle and the property belongs to all three providers. The Anthropic and OpenAI-chat stacks each have their own SSE reader and event mapping, and neither is covered by this or any sibling row — so the re-wrapping defect described could exist in them today and this suite would stay green.
The reply is verified by splitting on single spaces and counting four words, which couples the assertion to the scripted fixture's whitespace rather than to its content.

rationale: An attempt that delivered only a usage report before dying is retried rather than continued: no continuation instruction appears in the second request. The message ORDER is the load-bearing construction and the comment explains it — usage comes first with fragments trailing, because the joiner flushes a fragment run into a real TextMessage as soon as a different type follows it, so fragments-then-usage would deliver genuine content and would not test this at all. Catches usage being counted as completed output, which would instruct the model to continue from a reply the user never saw a word of, stranding the turn. P1: the boundary between the retry and continuation arms, and the case that decides which one applies.

An attempt that streamed only fragments before dying is retried exactly once under a DIFFERENT generation id, and the retry is equivalent to the original request with no TextUpdateMessage and no assistant TextMessage carried into it. The client additionally receives a GenerationAbandonedMessage naming the first generation, so it knows which unfinalized blocks to drop. The distinct generation id is what keeps the replacement from colliding with the abandoned attempt on the client's merge key. Catches a partial assistant reply being persisted as if it were real output, so the model is later conditioned on words it never finished. P1: the empty-attempt arm of recovery, distinct from the continuation arm.

The stream dies AFTER a complete tool call is emitted, so the tool's execution is already in flight when recovery begins — the exact shape that doubles a side effect if mishandled. The handler's execution count is asserted to be exactly 1, the visible result appears exactly once, and the settled result is carried into the continuation request, which is what makes re-issuing the call unnecessary rather than merely discouraged. Reading both the single and aggregate result shapes means the assertion cannot pass by looking in the wrong place. Catches a recovery that re-runs a completed effect: the tool here is a read, but the same path runs writes, payments and deletions, and a duplicated one is not recoverable after the fact. P0: idempotence of committed effects across recovery is the criticality argument for this component. Coverage caveat: addsNothingNew means other recovery cases traverse the same loop spans, but none begins after a complete tool call and jointly asserts one execution, one visible result and continuation reuse, so overlap is not assertion redundancy.
requirements: in-process only; mocked streaming agent and a real function registry

rationale: When a complete message landed before the interruption, the continuation request keeps that message, drops the trailing fragment, and carries an internal continuation instruction. Three assertions fix the instruction's scope precisely: present in the second request, absent from the first, and absent from everything the subscriber saw — so it is never rendered to the user as a bubble they did not write. Catches an internal prompt leaking into the visible transcript, or a continuation that re-sends only the original request and loses completed work. P1: the continuation arm, distinct from the full retry.

The transport fails byte for byte as in the recovered cases, the only difference being that cancellation was requested first, and a tool that never completes is registered. The comment names why that construction is decisive: recovery's first act is an UNCANCELLABLE wait for every tool the attempt dispatched, so entering recovery here would wedge the loop forever — which makes the drain returning at all a real test of the cancellation guard rather than one that passes because everything downstream throws anyway. Asserted with a 30-second race against the drain, plus exactly one provider request. Catches a cancelled run being answered with a second provider call, or hanging permanently on teardown. P1: the cancellation guard on the recovery path, an important failure-handling contract.
requirements: in-process only; bounded by a 30s race, not a sleep

rationale: A provider that dies on every attempt produces exactly two requests and then a failed run whose error carries the stable classification stream_interrupted_after_recovery. Bounding the budget at one automatic recovery per logical input is what stops a persistently broken provider being retried indefinitely at the user's expense, and the named classification is what lets a caller distinguish this from an ordinary failure. Catches an unbounded retry loop. P1: the retry budget, distinct from the recovery behaviours it bounds.

A clean run makes exactly one provider request, emits no GenerationAbandonedMessage, and returns its single assistant message. This is the control the whole file is read against: without it, a recovery path that fired on every run — abandoning a generation and re-requesting each time — would satisfy every other test here, since they all assert on what the SECOND attempt contains. Catches recovery triggering when nothing was interrupted, which would double every provider call in normal operation. P1: the non-vacuity anchor for the file, and a distinct contract in its own right.

An attempt holding ONLY a usage message is canonical enough to keep for history but must NOT read as having canonical messages, because the retry-versus-continue discriminator is built on that flag. The comment draws the distinction the rest of the class depends on: usage is accounting, it delivered no content and ran no effect, so an attempt holding only usage produced nothing worth continuing from and must still read 'retry'. Getting this wrong is not visible at the point of the mistake — the attempt looks productive, recovery chooses to continue, and the continuation is built on a turn that produced nothing, so the model is asked to carry on from an empty turn. Asserting BOTH sides on the same object (CompletedMessages has one entry, HasCanonicalMessages is false) is what pins the two senses apart; either alone reads as a plain true or false. Catches an accounting-only attempt being mistaken for delivered work. P1: the rule that separates the two meanings of canonical.
requirements: pure unit test; no loop, no store, no clock, no async
uncertainties: The row pins the FLAG, not the decision. That an attempt with HasCanonicalMessages false actually causes a retry rather than a continuation is asserted by the recovery classes, not here, so this is one half of a two-part argument.

rationale: Four shapes each set HasCanonicalMessages on their own: completed text, completed reasoning, a tool call, and a tool result. The set is chosen to span the two things the flag is meant to mean — content the user saw, and an effect that ran — so a discriminator that recognised only text would fail on the tool shapes. Its structural job is to be the positive control for the two negative rows: without it, an implementation whose flag was always false would pass both the fragment row and the accounting-only row. Catches a canonical-content discriminator that misses a message kind. P2: variations of one rule, and the both-directions partner for the negative cases.
requirements: pure unit test; four theory cases
uncertainties: The theory data omits the shapes most likely to be misclassified: an EMPTY completed text message, and a tool result flagged IsDeferred — the latter being a placeholder rather than a ran effect, which is exactly the distinction the class cares about elsewhere.

rationale: When a fragment is followed by the canonical message that subsumes it, only the canonical join is kept — one completed message, never both. This is the substantive half of the fragment rule: keeping both would write the partial text into history alongside its own completed form, so the conversation replays 'par' immediately before 'partial then whole' and the model sees its own stutter as real prior output. Observing the fragment FIRST and then asserting a single completed message is what makes this a de-duplication check rather than a plain append check. Catches streaming deltas leaking into persisted history. P1: the canonical-join rule.
uncertainties: The single retained message is never inspected, so 'only the canonical join is kept' rests on the count. An implementation that kept the FRAGMENT and dropped the canonical message would satisfy ContainSingle.

rationale: Text and reasoning DELTAS are rejected by Observe, leave HasCanonicalMessages false and keep CompletedMessages empty — 'fragments are deltas, not completed work'. Covering both the text and the reasoning update shapes is the point, since a discriminator written against one and not the other is the likely partial fix. Catches streaming deltas counted as delivered work. P2: the negative boundary on Observe, with the substantive fragment rule carried by the canonical-join row.
uncertainties: Other update-shaped messages that could arrive mid-stream — a tool-call argument delta, for instance — are not covered, so the rule is pinned for two fragment kinds rather than for fragments as a class.

rationale: Two callers of SettleToolTasksAsync must observe the SAME wait rather than starting a second settle, and the wait must not complete while a tracked tool is still running. The reference-equality assertion is the load-bearing one, and its because-clause says why: a second caller starting its own settle would await the same tool tasks twice, and on a path where settling has side effects that is a duplicate effect rather than a duplicate wait. Pairing it with IsCompleted false before the gate is released makes the wait's meaning concrete — it is genuinely outstanding, not an already-completed task returned twice. Gating one of the two tasks on a TaskCompletionSource makes the whole row deterministic with no sleeps. Catches a settle that is neither shared nor complete. P1: the idempotence contract on tool settling.
requirements: pure unit test; deterministic, gated on a TaskCompletionSource, no sleeps
uncertainties: `starts.Should().Be(1)` proves almost nothing. The counter is incremented inside a Task.Run delegate that runs exactly once by construction, whatever SettleToolTasksAsync does with the resulting Task, so this assertion cannot fail for the defect it appears to guard. The reference-equality check is the real evidence of exactly-once.

The method name promises every tracked task is AWAITED; what is asserted is that the returned wait completes and that both tasks are still tracked. A settle that returned after the gated task alone, ignoring the other, would pass since the second task completes on its own.

rationale: A tracked tool task that faulted must surface its exception out of the settle rather than being absorbed. A swallowed tool failure is the worse outcome by some distance: the attempt settles cleanly, the turn proceeds, and a tool that never produced a result is treated as though it had. Asserting the exception TYPE and message rather than merely that something threw pins that the original fault propagates rather than a wrapper that loses the cause. Catches tool failures disappearing at the settle boundary. P1: important failure handling on the settle path.
uncertainties: Exactly one task is tracked, and it is already faulted before settling. The interesting shapes are uncovered: one failure among several tasks (is the rest awaited, or abandoned?), and a task that faults AFTER the settle begins.

rationale: A batch whose inputs all carry a null parent resolves to no parent and no fork. Catches an unforked batch being reported as a fork, which would re-parent an ordinary turn. P2: the negative baseline, and the ordinary case rather than a distinct behaviour — the explicit-fork positive is where the contract lives, and this is its complement.
An empty batch returns no parent and no fork rather than throwing. Catches an unguarded First on an empty sequence at a point the loop reaches on every batch. P2: the degenerate input boundary.

An empty parent string is not a fork. Catches a run forked onto an empty-string ancestor, which resolves to nothing downstream and would fork against a parent that cannot exist. P2: an input-shape variation on the no-parent baseline.
uncertainties: Covers the empty string only; a whitespace-only parent is not exercised, so which of the two the implementation normalises is not pinned here.

rationale: A batch carrying three DIFFERENT parent run ids resolves to the first and emits exactly one warning naming the winner. Both halves are needed: the resolver must not fail on an ambiguous batch, and the operator must be able to see that a fork parent was silently discarded — an ambiguity resolved quietly is a run attached to the wrong ancestor with nothing in the log to explain it. Asserting a SINGLE warning also pins that the ambiguity is reported once rather than per conflicting element. Catches a batch of forks from different parents being merged into one run with no trace. P1: the conflict-handling arm, the only failure path this helper has.
requirements: in-process only; capturing logger, probe subclass exposing a protected member

rationale: With a null before and after the only real parent, the parent is still found. Catches a resolver that reads only the head of the batch and misses a fork declared by a later input. P2: a positional variation on the explicit-fork case rather than a distinct contract.

Two inputs naming the SAME parent resolve to it with no warning. This is the non-vacuity partner for the mixed-parents case: a resolver that warned whenever more than one parent was present would satisfy that test and fail this one, so it is what makes the warning a conflict signal rather than a batch-size signal. Catches log noise on every legitimate multi-input fork. P2: a variation whose value is bounding an adjacent assertion rather than pinning a behaviour of its own.

One input naming a parent yields that parent AND the explicit-fork flag. The flag is the substantive half: it is how the caller distinguishes a caller-declared fork from an ordinary continuation, so returning the right id with the flag false would still attach the run to the wrong shape of history. Catches an explicit fork being treated as a normal turn. P1: the positive contract the helper exists for, and the case every other row here varies.

The #529 defect: the configured default sub-agent model is set to something other than the parent's, and the assertion is on what reached the factory rather than on what the option holds — plus the explicit flag, without which the factory hands back the parent and silently discards the configured model, and a selection source of conversation-default so an operator can tell 'the configured model won' from 'nothing was configured and the child inherited'. Those two were indistinguishable. P1.

The conversation default changes which model runs but keeps the inherited effort floor, unlike a per-spawn or per-template choice. A conversation-wide operator setting expresses no per-task intent, so dropping the floor here would quietly buy a model upgrade at the price of an effort downgrade — often a net loss. P1 for the distinction between the two kinds of model choice.

The conversation default beats a model the template itself declares. This is the rung that is a judgement rather than an obvious ordering: template markdown is authored in a workspace the operator does not edit and the host cannot read, so a template-declared model winning silently overrides the model the operator is paying for. P1.

A conversation-wide effort floor beats the inherited effort on parent-model reuse. The floor is the operator's standing instruction for this conversation, so an inherited value winning would make the setting inert exactly where children are cheapest to under-power. P1 for the precedence.

An explicit spawn model suppresses the inherited effort but not the conversation floor: the child runs the chosen model at the floor. The two effort sources are deliberately different in this respect, and collapsing them would either ignore the operator or over-nudge a deliberately different model. P1.
The floor also survives a tier-resolved model. The second selection kind through the survival rule the explicit-model case pins. P2.

A genuinely different explicit model still wins outright and the tier resolver is never consulted (call count zero). This scopes the normalization to same-as-parent restatements only; applied broadly it would demote every deliberate per-spawn model choice whenever a tier was also supplied. P1.

A differently-cased restatement of the parent's model normalizes like an exact-case one, matching the tolerant id comparison used elsewhere in this manager. A casing variation of the rule pinned above. P2.

With the parent on a strong model, a mechanical-tier request still resolves to the mechanical model. The opposite regression: a normalization that quietly let the parent's own model stand would make every child inherit the now-stronger primary and spend accordingly. P1 as the guard in the other direction.

A same-as-parent override with no tier alongside is still honoured as spawn-model. Only a restatement supplied together with a tier is redundant filler; without one there is nothing to defer to and the caller really did say 'run this on my own model'. P1 for the other half of the normalization's precondition.

A calling model that restates its own id as the explicit model argument while also supplying a tier has the restatement treated as filler, so the tier wins: the resolved tier model, tier-resolved true, explicit false, selection source spawn-tier and the effective tier visible. Spawn-model has the strongest precedence, so left as-is this redundant self-reference made every child of a review conversation resolve to the primary agent's own model regardless of the tier its author chose. P1.

An explicit model choice leaves reasoning un-nudged: effort null and the explicit flag true. The inherited floor was shaped for the parent's model, so carrying it onto a deliberately different one applies a setting chosen for a provider that is no longer in play. P1.

An explicit override alongside a tier skips the resolver entirely (call count zero) yet is still built transport-correctly for the override's own id, with the pre-shaped reasoning withheld. Short-circuiting the resolver is the easy half; the trap is concluding that no tier means the plain template factory, which builds the controller's transport and hard-fails on a cross-vendor override. P1.

A per-spawn model beats the conversation default and is reported as spawn-model. The parent deciding at dispatch time for this one task is a stronger signal than a standing preference; inverted, the operator setting would override every deliberate per-task choice in the conversation. P1 for the top of the ordering.

A template that explicitly declares the same model the parent happens to run is still marked explicitly selected. Deciding provenance by comparing ids would erase the author's intent whenever the two coincide, and the factory then hands back the parent instead of building the template's own provider. P1.

A template-declared explicit model is also built through the model factory rather than the controller's provider. The same transport-correctness rule as the tier case, reached from the template rather than the spawn. P2.

On parent-model reuse with no template effort and no model choice, the child inherits the parent's reasoning floor so it thinks like the launching conversation. Without it a delegated sub-task silently runs at the provider default while its parent runs high. P1.

With no model chosen anywhere the characteristics carry the parent's model and IsModelExplicitlySelected false. The flag is what tells the factory to hand back the parent agent rather than build a new provider, so an inherited spawn reported as explicit pays to construct a duplicate of the parent. P1 for the default rung.

Factory metadata and template metadata are merged, and on a shared key the template wins. Both sides carry provider request properties, so a merge that let the factory overwrite would silently discard whatever the template author configured for this agent. Asserted on the options that reached the provider. P1.
A template with no default options still gets options created to carry the factory's metadata. The null boundary of the merge above. P2.

The characteristics factory receives the resolved spawn model, the template's typed effort, and the explicit-selection flag as one value. This is the whole interface between routing and provider construction; anything wrong here builds the child on the wrong model with the wrong reasoning. The legacy factory is wired to throw, so the characteristics path is provably the one that ran. P1.

The plain-path characteristics factory receives the tier-resolved model with the conversation floor, returns a provider whose shaped reasoning reaches the request, and the agent snapshot reports both the requested and the shaped effort. The snapshot pair is what lets an operator see that a floor was asked for and actually applied rather than silently dropped by a provider that could not express it. P1, and it holds 16 spans no other measured declaration reaches.

With a model override the pre-shaped metadata is not seeded. Shaped reasoning is transport-specific, so handing it to a different model sends provider-specific keys to an endpoint that does not accept them. The negative that keeps the inheritance from becoming a cross-transport failure. P1.

A plain-path delegate with no model override receives the parent's pre-shaped reasoning metadata on its request options. Asserted on what reached the provider, not on what the option holds. P1 for the plain path's inheritance.
A per-spawn tier also beats the conversation default, reported as spawn-tier. The adjacent rung of the ordering the explicit-model case pins. P2.

A template that declares its own effort keeps it over the conversation floor, low included. The template author knows this agent's job; a floor that could only raise would make every cheap mechanical helper think as hard as the conversation's most expensive step. P1 for the top of the effort ordering.
The same template-wins rule against the inherited floor rather than the conversation one. A second source through an ordering already pinned. P2.

A template whose model came from its own authored tier is built for that model, and the snapshot carries the effective model id, the authored tier, and a model-selection source of template-tier. The snapshot is what a presentation layer shows beside the raw Agent argument, which for this spawn is misleading; without the effective fields an operator reads the request rather than what ran. P1, and it holds an exclusive span.

A per-spawn intelligence tier reaches the factory as a tier-resolved model on the resolved id, with the resolver called exactly once for that tier, the explicit flag false, and effort null. The tier is how the Agent tool and workflow tasks ask for a capability rather than a name; reported as inherited it hands back the parent and the tier does nothing. P1.

On the plain path a resolved tier is served by a provider built for that model through TierAgentFactory — the template's own factory is wired to throw and does not run — the resolved id becomes the request model, and the controller's pre-shaped reasoning is not seeded. Building the controller's transport for another vendor's model posts to the wrong endpoint and hard-fails at the provider. P1.

An unmapped tier leaves the plain path unchanged: the template's own factory runs, the inherited reasoning is seeded, and TierAgentFactory is wired to throw and is never consulted. A host with no route for a tier must degrade to the previous behaviour rather than fail the spawn or build a provider for a null model. P1.

With no characteristics factory the legacy factory is called exactly once. Every template authored before the characteristics path exists takes this route, so losing it breaks all of them at once; the count assertion also rules out building the child's provider twice. P1.
The record still deconstructs to model and effort after gaining its provenance flags. A source-compatibility boundary for existing callers. P2.
A null agent is rejected at construction with the parameter named. A null-guard boundary. P2.
The agent guard also fires through a with-expression, the copy path where a record's init validation is easiest to lose. A second entry point into the guard above. P2.
Null extra properties are rejected at construction with the parameter named. A null-guard boundary. P2.
The extra-properties guard also fires through a with-expression. The fourth null-guard boundary on the same record. P2.

A descendant parking on AskUserQuestion must surface to the ROOT conversation as exactly one DescendantQuestion notification — a distinct kind, never the generic ClientNotification and never conflated with the SubAgentCompletion relay a background spawn also produces. The count is asserted as exactly one, which is the right shape for a notification: zero means the tree stalls forever waiting on a question nobody was asked, and a duplicate means the client navigates twice or renders a phantom pending question. Two further assertions make the provenance real rather than assumed: the notification's SourceToolCallId equals the spawn receipt's agent id, so it is attributed to the descendant that actually parked; and the ROOT's own deferred-call registry is asserted EMPTY, which is what proves the notification came from the descendant tree rather than from the primary's own AskUserQuestion handling — the one confound that would make the whole scenario prove nothing. It exercises the production wiring end to end, root loop through SubAgentManager to the default delivery sink. Catches a parked descendant question that never reaches the conversation a human is watching. P0 because a missing notification stalls the whole descendant tree with no visible question. Coverage caveat: addsNothingNew means other sub-agent cases traverse the same wiring spans, but none asserts exactly one descendant-question notification with real descendant provenance and an empty root deferral registry, so overlap is not assertion redundancy.
requirements: in-process only; Moq parent and child agents, no store configured
bounded: 20s run cts and a 10s Wait.UntilAsync on the notification
uncertainties: STRONG P0 contender, declined on scoping rather than on merit. Its consequence clears the bar I have been applying — a descendant parked on an unasked question stalls the whole tree silently, which is the hang class. But the SubAgents family already carries two candidates in this slice (ListAgents snapshot, recursion guard), and nominating a third turns the one-per-component rule into no rule at all. FOR THE LEAD: if SubAgents is scoped as ONE component with one slot, this is my recommendation among the three, because a stall is worse than a wrong snapshot and the recursion guard's defect is bounded by MaxConcurrentSubAgents. If it stays scoped as three sub-components, this row should get a slot too.

The observer records only DescendantQuestion notifications. The class summary's claim that the kind is never the generic ClientNotification and never conflated with SubAgentCompletion is therefore only half checked: a run emitting the right notification AND a spurious generic one alongside it would pass.

ObserveAsync issues but does not await the first MoveNextAsync so the subscriber registers synchronously — the same iterator-detail dependency noted on NotifyRestoreLoopTests. Sound here, and its comment explains the CancellationToken.None choice, but it rests on when SubscribeAsync's iterator first suspends.

rationale: The default synchronous spawn, end to end: the parent calls the Agent tool, and the tool result IS the sub-agent's final answer rather than a JSON spawn receipt, with the parent then producing its closing text and the run completing. The substantive assertion is the one on the result's CONTENT — the sub-agent's own words come back as the tool result — because that is what distinguishes synchronous delegation from the background mode, where the same call returns a receipt to poll. Getting this backwards is not a crash: the parent receives a receipt it does not understand, narrates that it dispatched an agent, and the actual answer never enters the conversation. Catches synchronous sub-agent results not reaching the parent. P1: the primary sub-agent orchestration path.
requirements: in-process only; Moq parent and child agents
uncertainties: Almost every assertion here is a lower bound — NotBeEmpty, Contain — so the row pins that the expected messages are present but nothing about counts or ordering. A run that spawned the sub-agent twice, or emitted the tool result before the tool call, would pass unchanged.

The negative half of the stated contract ('not a JSON receipt', 'no second parent relay turn') is asserted nowhere: parentCallCount is tracked for scripting but never checked, so an implementation returning BOTH a receipt and the final text would satisfy every assertion.

rationale: The background flow: a spawn with run_in_background true returns a JSON receipt carrying an agent_id immediately, and the parent's next turn polls it with CheckAgent and gets back a status. The row's real value is that the parent's second scripted turn PARSES the agent id out of the receipt and calls CheckAgent with it, so the receipt is proven machine-readable by a consumer rather than merely non-empty — the id round-trips through the same path a real model would use. Catches a background spawn whose receipt cannot be polled. P2: a variation on the spawn path, and weaker than its neighbours as written.
uncertainties: The assertions are the weakest in the class: HaveCountGreaterThanOrEqualTo(2) for the results, and a CheckAgent result located by two substring probes for 'status' and 'template' with neither value ever checked. A CheckAgent returning a status of the wrong agent, or a stale one, passes.

The agent-id extraction has a silent fallback to the literal 'unknown'. If the receipt failed to parse, the second turn would call CheckAgent with 'unknown' and the row would then depend on whether that error result happens to contain both substrings — the failure would not be reported as a missing receipt.
The method name claims the tools are registered and callable while the doc comment describes the background receipt flow; the assertions match the name, not the doc.

rationale: One undeserializable persisted row, placed ahead of the healthy ones so a whole-list conversion aborts before reaching them, no longer throws out of SendMessageAsync: the row is skipped and the restart runs to completion. A single bad record otherwise makes a conversation permanently unrestartable, which is unrecoverable for the user without editing the store. P1.

A restart failed at history recovery — through a store whose LoadMetadataAsync is armed to throw, injected at the first step after the epoch CTS is disposed and before the replacement run is armed — leaves the agent restartable: the next attempt reports 'resumed' and runs to completion. The failure cleanup keeps the agent registered but disposes both the epoch CTS and the live loop, so without re-arming each the agent stays advertised while permanently unable to accept a message, the next restart cancelling a disposed CTS and then sending into a disposed loop. P1, and it holds 6 exclusive spans.

Six inline cases cover the template/add/remove matrix, including the null base set and removal narrowing an added set. The result is the child's tool authority, so an over-wide set hands a sub-agent capabilities the template deliberately withheld and an over-narrow one silently breaks it. P1 for the full truth table.
Removing from nothing throws with an actionable message, since a removal with no base set silently means either everything or nothing. A single boundary over the matrix above. P2.

A child whose provider throws relays an envelope tagged [Error] rather than [Completed]. The distinction is what stops the parent treating a failure as an empty success and moving on; the matcher checks the tag specifically. P1.

A finished background child relays a SubAgentCompletion NotifyMessage to the parent wrapping its result in the named sub-agent envelope. The background path's entire value is this relay: without it a child's answer reaches nobody. P1.

The #246 descendant-question notification fires exactly once per parked question — with the right kind, the descendant's own agent id in SourceToolCallId and the awaiting-answer wording — and re-observing the parked spawn does not re-deliver it, while the child stays Running. Zero means a client never learns a question exists; more than one makes it re-announce and re-navigate to the same prompt. P1 for both bounds and the non-terminal status together.

A child that parked on its own AskUserQuestion must never be relayed as '[Completed] ... (no text response)'. Its run terminates with nothing pending, so the completion handler takes the same terminal branch a finished run would; telling the parent the child finished with nothing to show, when it never got to finish, sends the parent on to the next step without the answer. P1.

Zero and negative OutputChannelCapacity are rejected at construction, where the host hands its options over, rather than where a spawned child finally builds its bounded channel. Deferred, the misconfiguration surfaces as an ArgumentOutOfRangeException from inside a live stream and reads as a broken sub-agent run rather than bad configuration. On its own contract a validation boundary arguing P2; the exclusiveSpans floor places it at P1.

Disposal with a background agent present does not throw. The assertion is only that no exception escapes — the capacity and row-retirement consequences of disposal are pinned by the collaboration admission tests — so this is a smoke boundary. P2.
uncertainties: Asserts only that DisposeAsync does not throw; it does not observe what disposal did to the running agent.

rationale: A completed background agent's peek carries agent_id, template, task, status and a non-empty recent_turns containing the assistant text the run actually produced. The wait is on the specific terminal status rather than the presence of a 'status' key, which every payload has from the instant of spawn, and the turns half is asserted so a regression that stopped recording them cannot pass silently. P1 for the observation surface a parent reads between turns.

After an answered question has settled its caller, the next text-free run is genuinely terminal and returns the placeholder. The latch's other edge: outliving the answer's result would mean an agent that once asked a question could never finish a text-free run again, blocking its caller forever. The continuation is shaped as zero model turns deliberately, since a thinking-only run is rejected by the separate discriminator and so could not tell a cleared latch from a stale one. P1.
A message to a completed agent — confirmed completed first — restarts it and reports 'resumed'. The other half of the same call's behaviour, and the one that rebuilds a torn-down pipeline. P1.

A follow-up injected into a still-running background agent gives one monitor two run completions; the slot was acquired once at spawn so it must be released once. Releasing per completion over-releases the SemaphoreSlim, which throws inside the monitor and flips the agent to Error. The blocking provider makes the two runs distinct rather than one batch, and the agent settling 'completed' is the observable difference. P1.

Messaging a queued agent by id and by name both throw with text naming 'queued' and CheckAgent. A queued agent has no loop to receive anything, so accepting the message would drop it silently; naming the observation tool gives the caller a way to wait for the start it is really waiting for. Both addressing modes are asserted because they resolve through different lookups. P1.

A caller-supplied name addresses the agent as well as its generated id, and the receipt echoes the name. Models refer to children by the names they chose, not by opaque ids, so name resolution is the addressing path that actually gets used. P1.

A message to a still-running agent is injected in place and reports status 'message_sent'. In-place injection is a distinct outcome from a restart, and the status is how the caller knows which one happened. P1.
Messaging an unknown id throws ArgumentException naming it. A single-assertion lookup boundary alongside Peek's. P2.

An ambiguous segment throws from SpawnAsync with a message listing both candidates so the controller can re-issue an exact name. The negative side of the same seam the bare-name case pins, over a resolver branch already covered. P2.

A background spawn returns immediately with a JSON receipt carrying agent_id, template and status 'spawned'. The agent_id is the handle every later Peek, SendMessage and wait is keyed by, so the receipt is the whole interface to an async child. P1.

A foreground spawn cancelled while queued throws OperationCanceledException and the provider is verified never to have been called with that task's text. Cancelling a queued entry that later starts anyway spends a permit on work the caller abandoned, and the verification is on the specific prompt so a different agent's run cannot satisfy it. P1 for the must-not.

Two zero-turn runs in a row: only the first may be absorbed, and the second settles both the continuation and the original caller. A latch left armed absorbs every later text-free run, so the caller never settles and the permit never returns. Its siblings each have only one run for the latch to swallow, where an unconsumed latch and a consumed one behave identically. P1 for the bound that separates them.

The production ordering: the answer lands before the monitor classifies the parked run, so the resolution empties the deferred-call registry before the probe reads it and the probe reports no question pending for a run that parked one. Forced through a classification-time seam rather than raced — resolving as soon as the registry shows the call loses that race nearly every time and would exercise the safe path while appearing to prove the dangerous one — and both the hook firing and the resolution outcome are asserted, so the test cannot go vacuous. P1.

The foreground path stays blocked while the question is outstanding — proven non-vacuously by waiting for the descendant-question notification first, which only the parked branch emits — keeps its permit so a second spawn queues, and settles with the real answer once the deferred call is resolved. Treated as terminal, this returned the placeholder almost instantly and tore down the loop, losing the answer forever. P1.

It drives the #262 window that opens the instant a deferred AskUserQuestion is resolved — emptying the loop's live registry — and closes only when the answer-triggered work produces text. A completion landing inside it reported 'no question pending' for a benign reason, so the terminal gate settled the one-shot latch with the '(no text response)' placeholder and permanently discarded the human's answer, because a TaskCompletionSource settles once. Three staged runs, an independent completion subscription and mid-flight state assertions make the window deterministic rather than timed. P0 because the regression silently and permanently loses a supplied answer. Coverage records greedy rank 4 with 614 marginal spans; rank is supporting evidence only.

When the answered run is the agent's last word and produces only thinking, the caller settles on its own and a second spawn succeeds under maxConcurrent 1, proving the permit came back. This is where the fix turns into something worse than the bug if over-applied: with no later run to settle it, the task never completes, the agent never leaves Running, and MaxConcurrentSubAgents shrinks permanently — silently, because this branch raises no notification. Nothing nudges the agent here, matching production. P1.

The forced race followed by a zero-turn resolution run: absorbing the asking run must leave the latch armed, because the run its resolution triggers can itself need absorbing. Genuinely distinguishing — neither sibling covers it — but it is the combination of two halves each already pinned, so P2 by scope rather than by importance.

With the pool saturated a further background spawn is accepted with status 'queued' and a stable agent_id, rather than rejected with 'Max concurrent sub-agents reached'. Rejecting made the caller's only recovery a retry loop it had no signal to time. P1 for the defer-queue's primary behaviour.

The handle a queued spawn returns is immediately real across every observation surface: TryPeek reports queued, KnownAgentIds contains it, KnownAgents lists it under its name so an unknown-target correction can offer it, CheckAgents resolves it by id and by name, and ListAgents reports Queued. A handle that only some surfaces know is worse than no handle, because the caller cannot tell a queued agent from a lost one. P1, and it holds 6 spans no other measured declaration reaches.

With a pool of one, the queued second spawn actually starts and reaches completed once the first frees its permit — both peeks asserted. Accepting a spawn into a queue nothing drains is a black hole that looks healthier than the old rejection while being strictly worse. P1 for the pump that makes queueing meaningful.
A spawn after DisposeAsync throws ObjectDisposedException rather than admitting an agent nothing will ever monitor. A single-assertion lifecycle boundary. P2.

With MaxQueuedSubAgents 1 the third spawn throws SubAgentQueueFullException. Queueing instead of rejecting is only safe if the queue itself is bounded; otherwise a model in a retry loop grows it without limit and every entry holds a live agent record. P1 for the bound that makes the defer-queue safe.

End to end: a bare segment name whose template is registered under a plugin prefix spawns and returns the child's result. The resolver being correct proves nothing if SpawnAsync never consults it, and this is the positive proof of that seam. P1.

A provider that throws surfaces as SubAgentExecutionException naming the template, and still no parent relay. The caller is blocked on this call, so swallowing the failure into a relay would leave it waiting for a result that arrives somewhere else. P1 for the failure half of the synchronous contract.

A synchronous spawn returns the sub-agent's final text directly and the parent's SendAsync is never called. The result flows back as the tool result in the same parent turn; a relay would inject a duplicate of an answer the parent already has. Primary path plus the invariant that separates it from the background path. P1.
An unregistered template name throws ArgumentException naming it. A single-assertion boundary over the resolver whose branches are pinned individually below. P2.
An explicitly supplied name is kept exactly; the readable-name fallback only fills in when the caller omits one. The negative boundary of the derivation the previous case pins. P2.

A spawn with no name still surfaces a readable handle derived from the template, distinct from the raw id, and that derived name is a first-class address SendMessage accepts. A derived name that no lookup honours is decoration; asserting the round trip is what makes it a handle. P1.

A delivery arriving right after a background completion is refused, the total parent relay count stays exactly one, and the agent settles 'completed' rather than 'error'. The exactly-once count and the no-error settle add a boundary over the completed-target case above, which already pins the refusal and the absence of a restart. P2.

A delivery to a completed sub-agent returns TargetNotDeliverable, the provider is verified called exactly once so the agent was not restarted, and no relay reaches the parent. Restarting on late context resurrects a finished child and charges a model call for information nobody asked it to act on; a spurious relay tells the parent the child finished twice. P1.

Directory context routed to a running sub-agent lands in that sub-agent's own next model call — asserted on the actual argument of the second GenerateReplyStreamingAsync — and never on the parent. Delivering to the parent instead puts one child's context into a conversation that has no use for it while the child that needed it never sees it. The two-turn shape (block, tool call, second turn) is what makes the injected message observable. P1, and it holds 6 exclusive spans.

An id belonging to no sub-agent of this manager returns NotOwned, distinct from TargetNotDeliverable: the injector keeps looking, or drops without marking seen, so a gateway redelivery can still route it later. Collapsing the two makes an unrouted discovery indistinguishable from a deliberately dropped one. On its own contract a boundary arguing P2; the exclusiveSpans floor places it at P1.

Two agents sharing a segment under different plugins do not auto-resolve; both come back as suggestions. This is what bounds the prefix tolerance: guessing between two real agents silently runs the wrong one, which is worse than the mis-prefixed name the feature exists to forgive. P1.

A key that is an exact ordinal match is never re-routed by segment logic, even when another key shares its trailing segment. This is the precedence rule: a resolver that tried segments first would satisfy every other accepting case here and still route a correctly-named request to the wrong agent. P1 as the distinguishing case.

Four inline cases cover every accepting branch of the resolver: exact, case-insensitive exact, bare skill segment, and a wrong plugin prefix with the right segment — all landing on the qualified key with no suggestions.
