Authored workflows and controller models routinely name an agent by a bare or mis-prefixed name, and without recovery the run silently collapses to general-purpose. P1, and it holds 3 spans no other measured declaration reaches.
A name matching nothing returns false with an empty resolution and no suggestions. The negative baseline of the resolver whose accepting and ambiguous branches are pinned above. P2.

With no model available anywhere, the template's own options object is returned BY REFERENCE with its model still empty. The reference identity is the substantive check — it proves no copy was made and no field rewritten when there was nothing to apply. Catches a resolver that rebuilds options unnecessarily and drops fields on the way. P2: a no-op boundary of the inheritance rule the other rows establish.

With all three sources populated and mutually distinct, the per-spawn override wins. Supplying all three at once is what makes the result identify one rung of the precedence chain rather than merely showing the override is read. Catches a caller's explicit model choice being ignored in favour of a template default, so a spawn deliberately routed to a different model silently is not. P1: the top of the precedence order.

A template with no options at all resolves to the PARENT's model rather than null. The class summary records the production failure this prevents in full: without inheritance the provider agent falls back to its own hardcoded default, which was observed as a sub-agent sending claude-3-sonnet-20240229 to a backend that only serves the parent's model and getting HTTP 400 model_not_supported. Asserting the result is non-null before reading the id matters because null is the legitimate answer in the sibling case, so the two outcomes are genuinely different code paths. Catches every built-in sub-agent failing outright on any host whose backend serves one model. P1: the inheritance rule that the whole class exists for.

A template that carries other options but leaves ModelId at its default empty string still inherits the parent's model, AND keeps its own Temperature. The comment names the trap: ModelId defaults to "" on GenerateReplyOptions, so a null check alone would treat a blank as a deliberate choice and skip inheritance — the same production failure as the no-options case, reached by the far more common configuration. The preserved Temperature is the second half: applying the parent model must not discard the template's other settings, which a wholesale replacement would. Catches inheritance that only works for templates configuring nothing at all. P1: the blank-versus-absent distinction, a distinct rule from the precedence chain.

With nothing configured at any level the result is null rather than a fabricated empty options object, preserving the prior inherit-provider-defaults behaviour. Catches an empty options object being passed down and overriding provider defaults with blanks. P2: the degenerate-input boundary, and the negative that keeps the non-null assertion in the inheritance case meaningful.

With no override, the template's model beats the parent's. This is the rung that makes inheritance a fallback rather than an override: a resolver that always returned the parent model would satisfy the two inheritance tests and fail only here, and a split-model configuration — a cheap sub-agent under an expensive parent — would silently run every sub-agent on the parent's model. Catches inheritance overshooting into a policy. P1: the middle rung of the precedence order, and the bound on the inheritance rule.

With a template restricted to a name the parent lacks, the warning would fire without wildcard expansion, so its silence under '*' is evidence the expansion happened. A second reading of the expansion the theory already asserts directly. P2.

An add list whose entries match no parent tool logs exactly one unmatched warning. Silent narrowing is how #635 stayed invisible: the child runs, produces nothing useful, and nothing in the log says why. P1 for the diagnostic that makes it findable.
An add list naming a real tool and the wildcard logs no unmatched warning. The paired negative of the diagnostic above. P2.

Through the real Agent handler, an add_tools string of a lone separator leaves the toolset unfiltered. It used to parse to an empty but non-null array, which the spawn path reads as a filter matching nothing rather than as no filter — the same hole as the wildcard, one layer up, and only visible when production code does the parsing. P1.

A dispatch prompt referencing the board, sent to a template whose tools list contains none of the task tools, logs the warning. This is the floor under the whole feature: the agent is being ordered to do something it structurally cannot, and without the line the run just fails to do its job with no explanation. P1.

A board-referencing prompt to a template that does have the task tools logs nothing. The other axis of the two-condition trigger: without it a warning keyed on the prompt alone would fire on every correctly-equipped board dispatch. P1, and it holds 2 exclusive spans.
At the unit seam the wildcard expands from the inheritable roster rather than being kept as a name. The mechanism behind a rule already pinned end to end through two spawn paths. P2.

The mode's enforcement is applied last: not even a spawn-time removeTools strips a required tool. Ordering is the whole content of the guarantee — a union applied before removal would satisfy the previous case and still let one spawn argument defeat the mode. P1.

A restricted template's enabled set is unioned with the mode's required tools. The #623 defect was exactly that the per-template filter silently dropped tools the dispatch prompt ordered the agent to use. P1 for the rule at its unit seam.

Unset required tools leave the previous behaviour byte for byte, and no filtering at all stays null rather than becoming a list. The second half is the load-bearing one: required tools narrowing an inherit-all template into a two-name list would strip every other tool from every host that never opted in. P1 for the opt-in boundary.

A deliberate 'tools: []' deny-all reaches an empty resolved toolset — asserted reached, not assumed — and logs no empty-toolset warning. A warning that fires on correct configuration trains people to ignore it, which costs the diagnostic its value on the collapse it exists for. P1 for the false positive.

The deny-all suppression is not a blanket over the template: a spawn that asks for a tool on top of 'tools: []' and receives none of it is still a collapse, because the caller wanted something. Without this the false-positive fix would silence the diagnostic for every spawn against a deny-all template. P1.

The enforcement travels through ForChildLoop to a grandchild: the child's own manager runs on inherited options and its equally restricted grandchild still carries the required tool. The #623 incident was observed one level down, so a guarantee that holds only at depth one misses the case that produced it. P1.

The same assertion shape with a known-good explicit value discriminates: the named tool is present and the unnamed one is absent. This is what proves the harness reads the real resolved toolset rather than something that would satisfy a Contain assertion whatever the spawn did. P1 as the wildcard theory's non-vacuity anchor.

The same empty resolved toolset reached from a template that named a tool and got none of it does log the warning. The pair is the discriminator rather than either half alone: a fix that could not tell a deliberate deny-all from a collapse would be incomplete in one direction or the other. P1.

A template that inherits everything really does show all three names through the same accessor, so the wildcard theory's all-three assertion is a reachable outcome. The second half of a non-vacuity proof whose discriminating half sits above. P2.

Three accepted spellings and three rejected ones, including null. The rejections carry the weight: 'all' is a legal tool name and add_tools has no group language, so a predicate that accepted either would silently grant a child every tool the parent has whenever a model guessed at syntax. P1 for the accept/reject boundary of a privilege-widening predicate.
The predicate accepts AskUserQuestion and NotifyClient and rejects two ordinary tools. The unit seam behind the count rule the warning tests pin end to end. P2.

The second trigger: the prompt never mentions the board, but the host's assignment probe knows a task is already assigned to this spawn's name. Prompt text alone misses the ordering where the primary assigns first and dispatches with a neutral instruction. P1, and it holds an exclusive span.

The same toolless template with a prompt that mentions no board logs nothing. A warning that fired on every restricted template would be noise on the majority of correct spawns. P1, and it holds 2 spans no other measured declaration reaches.

A parent exposing only the two never-inherited tools can hand a child nothing, so an empty child toolset there is structurally unavoidable and not a narrowing to report. A boundary of the count rule pinned above. P2.

Same template, same spawn, one inheritable tool added to the parent, and the warning fires reporting one inheritable tool. The paired positive keeping the silence above from passing on a spawn that failed outright. P2.

Four accepted phrasings including the incident's literal spaced imperative, and two rejections including null. The predicate decides whether the floor fires at all, and both directions matter: too narrow and the incident recurs silently, too broad and every dispatch warns. P1 for the accept/reject set.

The same over-grant and warning when the remove_tools string is parsed by the Agent handler rather than handed in pre-split. The handler seam is already proven exercised by the lone-separator case. P2.

The second way 'withhold these' produces the opposite: the entry matches, is removed, and is put straight back by the required-tools union. Deliberate precedence, but silent from the caller's seat until this line existed — and it must be a different line from the no-op one, which stays quiet here because the entry did match. Both counts are asserted. P1.

The required-tools union re-adds a NAME; it cannot conjure a tool. On a parent exposing no contract or handler for the mode-required tool the name survives into the resolved set while the child still does not have it, and the operator was told 'restored ... the sub-agent still has them' — a false statement about narrowed tool authority that also suppresses the accurate no-op line. The child's resolved toolset is asserted directly, and the sibling differs by one variable: the pre-fix name-set predicate passes there and fails here. P0 because an operator acts on this determination at the exact moment authority was narrowed. Coverage records greedy rank 29 with 80 marginal spans; rank is supporting evidence only.

An entry never in the base set that comes back through the union is reported as restored, not as a no-op, because the caller's question is whether the tool is there and it is. The two lines partition by observable outcome, so drawing the wrong one states the opposite of the truth. P1 for the partition rule the P0 case above then narrows.

Same harness, same accessor, one variable changed to an exact tool name: the removal really happens and the warning really stays quiet. Without it the group-pattern warning could be an artifact of the test never reaching the code, and the silence could be an artifact of a failed spawn. P1 as the discriminator for both.

'remove_tools: *' means removing a tool literally named '*' — deliberately still a no-op, since wildcard language on this side alone is the asymmetry that made F-001 reachable — but not a silent one. A second spelling through the warning the group-pattern case pins. P2.

The #638 F-001 headline: 'add_tools: *' with a group pattern on the remove side reads as 'everything except the board tools' and produced the opposite — every board tool granted, no warning. Both halves are asserted, the over-grant and the warning, so it cannot pass on a spawn that never resolved. P1: a privilege narrowing that silently widens instead.

Same harness, same spawn, the mode declaring no required tools: the tool is genuinely withheld and the restored line stays quiet, so the fired warning next door is caused by the union and nothing else. A paired positive. P2.

A required name absent from the parent's own contracts is not materialized on the child, while a required name the mode does hold is. A mode cannot grant what it does not have, and an implementation that registered required names unconditionally would hand a child a tool with no handler behind it. P1 for the authority ceiling.

A spawn that ends up with no inherited tool at all logs exactly one empty-toolset warning. A child with an empty toolset cannot do the work it was dispatched for, and the failure otherwise reads as a bad model rather than a bad filter. P1.

Through the real spawn path, a template whose tools list strips the task tools still registers them on the child. The unit rule proves nothing if the spawn path applies the filter somewhere else, and the filter site is where the defect lived. P1.

With no RequiredToolNames the same restricted template keeps only its domain tool and neither task tool. The opt-in pin through the real path: without it an implementation that always granted the task tools would satisfy the union case and quietly widen every existing template. P1.

With a parent holding five contracts of which two are structurally never inherited, the line says three inheritable tools and specifically not five. The number is what a reader uses to judge how much was lost, and counting the never-inherited pair makes the warning overstate what was available. Asserts the number, not merely that a line was logged. P1.

With three remove entries of which two withhold nothing, the single line names 2 tools and lists exactly those two, excluding the one that really did withhold. A line reporting 1 or 3, or naming the matched entry, sends the reader after the wrong argument. Asserting the number and the membership rather than that some warning fired. P1.

An add list naming nothing the parent has still leaves the mode's required tools in place, and still narrows away the domain tool. Pinned with an unmatched literal rather than the wildcard, because the wildcard now grants everything and would satisfy the assertion for the wrong reason. P1: a spawn-time mistake must not be able to strip what the mode guarantees.

The #623 incident's verbatim dispatch line cites no hyphenated tool name and no board phrase, and must trigger on the marker heuristic alone — no assignment probe is wired, pinning the ordering where the primary dispatches before assigning any task. A heuristic that misses the line that caused the incident is the one case it had to catch. P1.
The wildcard supplies the base set that makes 'everything except X' expressible, since removeTools without one throws. A composition of two behaviours each pinned on its own. P2.

All three documented spellings of the all-tools wildcard grant every tool the parent exposes, and none of them survives as a literal name. The #635 defect added '*' to the enabled set as a tool NAME, matched no parent contract at the intersection, and left the sub-agent with no inherited tools at all — the opposite of what the caller asked for. Asserted on the child's resolved toolset. P1.

The wildcard also works when the string is parsed by the Agent handler rather than handed in pre-split. The same claim as the theory above through a seam the lone-separator case already proves is exercised. P2.
The receipt flag is false when nothing was asked and true when it was, on an enforcing loop. Every enforcement row above already asserts the same flag on the way to a stronger claim. P2.
The same receipt statement on the sibling entry point. P2.

The scoping claim in one body: the spawn tool is gone on the suppressed run, back on the next, and the read and follow-up tools are never withdrawn on any of the three. A suppression that leaked past its run would silently stop an agent fanning out for the rest of the thread. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: The interleaving a caller cannot control — it only learns the host queued its message — so a flagged input routinely lands mid-run and is injected between turns. Deriving suppression from the batch that STARTED the run left exactly the turn the flagged input asks about free to spawn, after the receipt had already promised otherwise. The race is constructed rather than waited for, and the release afterwards is polled, not assumed. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Hiding the contract is not enforcement: the model can replay a spawn call from earlier history, so the handler refuses it too and no sub-agent is started. Without this the guarantee holds only for a well-behaved model. P1.

A suppressed notification arriving at a RESTORED parked run is folded into persisted history under that run — the restart path for the parked-fold case, where a run object rebuilt by recovery has to be a valid target for the fold. The widest single addition in the file (rank 43, 52 new spans). P1.

A notification arriving while the conversation is parked cannot start a turn, so it is folded into history and delivered by the RESUME — and the suppression it asked for has to ride along, because that resume is the only run its receipt can be about. The unsuppressed parked run is asserted first, so the later absence is a change rather than a constant. P1.

The latch owns a reference-counted scope, so a run that ends by THROWING must release it exactly as a clean one does. A leaked scope strips the spawn tool from every later turn on the thread and shows up only as an agent that mysteriously stopped fanning out. P1.

A resumed run is a NEW run id, so the latch has to be carried across deliberately — otherwise the guarantee evaporates at the first deferral, which is precisely where a barrier-following synthesis waits. Both model calls are asserted, and the resumed turn signals AFTER its contracts are recorded so the assertion cannot race the call it is about. P1.

The pause can last as long as whatever the deferral waits on, so a restart in between is ordinary: the marker is durable next to the deferral and restored with it, and the acknowledged guarantee outlives the process that made it. Written as two real loops over one store, with the persisted deferral waited for rather than assumed and the restored deferral checked as a precondition so the assertion cannot pass for the wrong reason. P1.

An external snapshot supplies a domain tool the delegate should inherit and a name that collides with the controller's own control-plane tool, which is also on the exclusion list. The delegate inherits the domain tool with its handler, does not inherit the excluded name even though it appears in BOTH the controller registry and the external snapshot, and the controller's own surface still exposes it. The double source of the excluded name is the discriminating construction: an exclusion applied at only one of the two merge inputs would leak it. Catches a workflow control-plane tool reaching a delegate, which lets a delegate rewrite the state machine driving it. P1: the external-merge contract, a distinct primary behaviour over the local filter.

The external-tool merge emits a debug log, asserted as a count greater than zero against a message prefix, deliberately content-free so the log carries counts rather than tool names. Catches the merge becoming silent, which would leave an operator unable to tell whether a delegate's surface came from the controller or the launching conversation. P2: an observability property over the merge whose functional contract is pinned separately, and the assertion is a lower bound on a message match rather than a statement about what was merged.
uncertainties: Asserts only that at least one Debug line matches the prefix; it does not check the counts in the message, so a log reporting the wrong numbers would pass.

rationale: The filter drops a named contract and keeps the rest. Catches the exclusion helper itself being wrong. P2: the unit beneath the snapshot tests, which exercise the same filter through the path that actually calls it; a break here fails those too.

A null and an empty exclusion list both return every contract unchanged. Catches a null being treated as exclude-everything, which would silently strip a sub-agent's whole tool surface for hosts that configure no exclusions at all — the default configuration. P2: an input-shape variation on the filter unit, though its consequence is wider than the positive case it accompanies.

The snapshot a spawn hands down keeps the domain tool and excludes both the configured NonInheritedToolNames entry and the Agent-family tools. Asserting on the snapshot rather than on a spawned child's surface tests the value actually passed at the boundary, which is where an exclusion is either applied or lost. Catches a launch or orchestration tool leaking into an inherit-all template. P1: the inheritance boundary itself, distinct from the parent-surface and recursion-guard assertions that read the same snapshot for different reasons.

With an inherit-all template and an exclusion configured, the parent's own surface still carries both its domain tools AND the self-registered Agent family. Catches an exclusion implemented by removing the tool from the shared registry rather than from the inherited snapshot, which would disarm the parent as a side effect of protecting the child. P1: the parent-side half of the exclusion contract, the direction that is easy to break silently because the child-side assertions would still pass.

The parent advertises Agent, CheckAgent and SendMessage to itself, while the snapshot handed to a spawned sub-agent contains the domain tool and none of the three. Asserting both halves in one test is what makes it a guard rather than an absence: a build that simply failed to register the family would satisfy the exclusion and fail the parent assertion. The mechanism is ordering — those tools are registered after the inheritable snapshot is taken — and the test pins the observable consequence rather than the ordering. Catches a sub-agent that can spawn sub-agents, which is unbounded recursive delegation: an unpayable bill and a machine out of processes, from one model deciding to delegate. Nominated P0: the recursion guard is the criticality argument for the whole inheritance surface. Confirmation held pending the facts join.
requirements: in-process only; mocked provider, no spawn executed
uncertainties: DEMOTED in the end-of-slice P0 prune. Eighteen nominations across 347 in-scope rows is 5.2%, against the lane's healthy 2.4-3.1% band; ten survive. The nomination recorded above stands as the reason this row is the strongest in its component and is NOT withdrawn as an assessment - it is simply not a surviving candidate. Demotion reason: third of the four in the SubAgents family ranking. Unbounded spawning is capped in practice by MaxConcurrentSubAgents and presents as obvious load; the family's slot goes to the trust boundary.

rationale: Each template's key, Description and WhenToUse must appear in the Agent tool description, because that text is the only thing the parent model reads when choosing a sub-agent type. A template missing from the catalog is a capability the model cannot reach at all. P1 for the descriptor's primary content.

Pins the Claude Code parity parameter set present (subagent_type, prompt, description, name, model, run_in_background, add_tools, remove_tools) and the legacy names gone (template_name, task, agent_id). A parameter absent from the contract cannot be supplied by the model however the handler behaves, so this is the schema every other spawn behaviour depends on. P1.
Two substring assertions on the name parameter's guidance text. The auto-derivation it documents is enforced elsewhere; this pins only that the wording mentions it. P2.

#641 F-005. This description is the only half of #638 the model reads, on every spawn, and therefore the only half with a path to preventing an over-grant rather than reporting it afterwards — the SubAgentManager warning fires after the child already holds the tools the caller meant to withhold. Three load-bearing claims are pinned: exact names only, no wildcard or group pattern, and the add_tools '*' composition that replaces it. P1 because a silent wording regression here restores the whole over-grant class.
Two substring assertions on steering wording that nudges the model to continue a live child rather than spawn a fresh one. Guidance quality, with no enforcement behind it. P2.

The same TryRegister visibility rule read off the subagent_type parameter's enum list instead of the tool description. A second projection of the behaviour GetFunctions_AfterTryRegister_ReflectsNewTemplate already holds. P2.

Which policies a child loop inherits: the conversation-wide type policy is passed through by reference, while the workflow-local name gate, unit selection and metadata resolver are cleared. A leaked name gate would reject every grandchild spawn whose name the parent workflow never registered. P1 for the inheritance boundary between a workflow and the loops it starts.

#77 mid-session activation: when the discovery webhook registers a template into the shared source, the next GetFunctions must surface it in the Agent catalog. The memo is keyed on the source's snapshot reference precisely so TryRegister invalidates it; a memo that outlived the change would make newly discovered agents permanently invisible for the session. P1 for the invalidation direction of the memo.

The memo's over-granting direction, pinned on its own. The sibling test builds its first surface inside the scope and so exercises only the way out, where a stale memo under-grants; this is the way in, where a stale memo hands the spawn tool to exactly the turn a caller was promised could not start children. It carries its own premise assertion that an unsuppressed build is really in the memo, so it cannot pass for the wrong reason. Both directions ride on one memo-key conjunct today, which is an implementation coincidence, not a reason to drop the fail-open side. P1.

ToolCallInjectionMiddleware re-invokes the function-set factory on every LLM call, so without the memo this provider rebuilds the whole sub-agent surface — template catalog text and all — once per turn from inputs that change perhaps twice a session. Reference equality across two calls is the memo's primary behaviour; its invalidation guards are pinned separately. P1.

Counts the four tools and names them. The same list is asserted, in both directions, by SuppressSpawning_DropsOnlyTheSpawnContract and GetFunctions_BuiltBeforeSuppression, which carry the behaviour that can break it. P2 as a bare surface-shape check.

A refused call created nothing, so there is nothing for the key to protect; remembering the failure would poison that key for the rest of the session and make the recovery the error text asks for — fix the name, call again — impossible to carry out. P1 for the release rule on the refusal side, with 11 exclusive spans putting a floor under it.
uncertainties: Holds 11 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The counterweight to the release rule: subagent_failed is raised when the run ENDS in error, so the child was created, executed, and may already have called a tool, written a file or messaged a peer. Treating it like the refusals would free the key and let a repeat run the whole thing again — exactly the duplication the key exists to prevent. The replay stays an error carrying the same code, because returning it as a plain result would tell the model its retry succeeded, and Times.Once on the child's streaming call proves no second run happened. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The representative of the throw-side of this surface's error partition: a missing required argument is a caller/host fault and comes back as ArgumentException, while a model mistake such as an unresolvable type comes back as a recoverable tool result. P1 for that partition; its four siblings across Agent, SendMessage and CheckAgent are recorded as P2 variations of the same rule.
The second required-argument case on the same handler, asserting the same throw shape as HandleAgentToolAsync_MissingPrompt. P2 as a variation of a partition already held at P1.

A type policy that returns null for this type must not suppress an authoritative workflow-unit selection underneath it — the fall-through has to reach tier 4, not the caller's 1. Precedence chains fail exactly here, where a non-applicable higher rule swallows a lower one. P1.

The case that distinguishes the rule in WorkflowSelectionOverridesPlaceholderOptionalModelValues from 'always discard a zero tier': with no workflow selection in play, modelIntelligence 0 is a real request and must reach the resolver as 0. Without this, the placeholder-erasure fix could be implemented as a blanket zero-drop and nothing would notice. P1 as a distinguishing case, not a variation.

With the single permit taken and no queue slots, the next spawn returns queue_full as a recoverable error rather than throwing. Saturation is an ordinary operating state under MaxConcurrentSubAgents, so the model has to receive a code it can wait on. P1 for important failure handling on the spawn path.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A model retries the call whose outcome it could not see, and without a key that retry is indistinguishable from a genuine second delegation — a second agent that costs a full run, may act on the world twice, and reports back as an answer nobody asked for. The replay returns the FIRST receipt so the id the model holds stays right, and says so in a nested 'replay' object rather than a top-level 'code' that would collide with the result's own vocabulary. P1 for the primary idempotency contract.

A host that correlates spawn results by exact name supplies a SpawnNameGate; when it rejects, the handler must surface spawn_name_unmatched as a recoverable error and not spawn, so the caller re-issues the exact name rather than looping on a silently discarded duplicate. subagent_type is valid in the fixture, which proves the rejection came from the gate and not from unknown_subagent_type. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The harder half: two identical tool calls in one turn, rather than a sequential retry. A ledger consulted only after the work completes lets both spawns through because both look unseen while both are running, so the claim has to be taken before the spawn. Both callers must come back holding the same agent id. P1 for the concurrent route into the same duplication.

P0 for the routing-authority boundary on every spawn. Three things at once: the type policy is handed the CANONICAL key ('code-reviewer:architecture-review') rather than the abbreviation the model wrote, so a host policy keyed on real template identity is actually reachable; the policy's tier replaces BOTH caller-authored fields, so a model cannot route its own review onto a cheaper or costlier model than the host decided; and the recorded ModelSelectionSource says 'type-policy', so what actually decided the model is auditable afterwards. Criticality: this is the point where host authority over model selection either holds or silently defers to the caller, and it decides real spend on every child. Also the file's highest-ranked declaration by measured coverage (greedyRank 32, inP0Prefix).
uncertainties: The only inP0Prefix member in this file (greedyRank 34); the rest of the file's declarations sit outside the prefix, so this is the one P0 candidate available here.

rationale: The recoverable side of the partition: an unresolvable subagent_type is a model mistake, so the handler returns a result carrying unknown_subagent_type and the available catalog rather than throwing — the loop hands the model something to self-correct with instead of the run collapsing to general-purpose. P1.

Ordering: the routing policy runs only after a canonical type resolves. Two InlineData cases cover both ways resolution fails — a name matching nothing, and a skill segment ('shared') matching two plugins ambiguously — and both must reach unknown_subagent_type with zero policy invocations. A policy consulted on an unresolved name would route on a string the host never accepted. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product span, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The idempotency wrapper reads idempotency_key out of the arguments before the handler runs, which puts a JSON parse in front of every guard the handler owns. Unparseable arguments are the handler's question: a key that cannot be read is simply no key, and answering with a parse exception would replace a coded refusal the model can act on (spawn_suppressed here) with an unhandled fault. P1 for the ordering between the wrapper and the guards behind it.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The complement that makes the key opt-in: two identical delegations with no key are two delegations. Deduplicating on the arguments instead would silently collapse a deliberate fan-out of identical workers into one, which no error would ever report. P1 as the case that distinguishes the mechanism from argument-hashing.

A workflow unit's authoritative selection carrying a null tier must erase the caller model's placeholder empty-string model and zero tier, so the TierModelResolver is never consulted. Otherwise a model that fills optional fields with defaults silently overrides the unit's routing. P1 for a distinct precedence rule on the spawn path.
Required-argument validation on the CheckAgent handler. P2 as a variation of the partition held at P1.
Required-argument validation on the SendMessage handler. P2 as a variation of the partition held at P1.
Required-argument validation on the SendMessage handler, same throw shape as the Agent handler's. P2 as a variation of the partition held at P1.

A follow-up addressed to a child that is spawned but still waiting for a permit is a recoverable error, not an exception out of the handler. The queued state is normal — the spawn receipt that gave the model the id said 'queued' — so a model addressing it has done nothing wrong; letting the manager's exception escape gives the model no code to branch on and no instruction to wait. Returning the collaboration surface's own target_not_started keeps one vocabulary for one condition across both surfaces. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 6 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Two substring assertions on SendMessage's steering wording. Same class as the other guidance-text checks. P2.

The synthesis turn of a recursive review must not be able to start new children while still being able to read what they delivered and nudge one, so suppression drops Agent and keeps SendMessage, CheckAgent and WaitAgent — and the scope ends, with the next build advertising spawning again. P1 for the barrier's primary behaviour in both extent and duration.

Nested scopes with a double-disposed inner one: the second dispose must not decrement the depth again and re-advertise spawning while the outer scope still expects it hidden. Another fail-open route into the same barrier, reached by ordinary using-scope nesting. P1.

Contracts are rebuilt per turn but handlers are a construction-time snapshot on the loop, so hiding the contract still leaves the handler reachable when the model replays an Agent call from earlier history. The handler must answer spawn_suppressed rather than start a child after the barrier. P1 for the enforcement half of a guarantee the contract half only advertises.

CheckAgent called with the name a spawn was given returns a non-error payload carrying that agent's id and name. SendMessage took a name and CheckAgent did not, so a model that had just messaged analyst was told analyst did not exist the moment it checked on the same agent; the two tools now resolve a target the same way and the id path is unchanged. P1: the name arm of the CheckAgent handler.

A running key is pushed past the ledger's bound by MaxRemembered completed fillers, and a second reservation of that key must still BLOCK. The assertion is deliberately not 'returned a replay' — the comment says returning ANYTHING there means it did not wait, so IsCompleted being false is the only formulation that catches a caller handed a claim. The consequence is stated as an asymmetry: forgetting a finished key costs a stale answer nobody can act on, while forgetting a running one costs the guarantee itself, and the next caller spawns the second agent the key existed to prevent. The test then completes the first call and confirms the waiter receives the replay rather than a claim, so blocking is not merely a deadlock. Catches a duplicate spawn under retry, which is a doubled sub-agent and doubled spend. P1: the exclusivity guarantee at the eviction boundary.
requirements: in-process only; pure ledger, 10s bound on the resumed wait

rationale: A FINISHED key pushed past the bound is forgotten and becomes claimable again. The comment names its role exactly: non-vacuity for the sibling — keeping running claims must not turn into keeping everything, which would make the ledger grow without limit for the lifetime of a long conversation. Asserting a fresh claim AND a null replay is what distinguishes forgetting from returning a cached result. Catches an unbounded ledger. P1: the bound itself, and the constraint that keeps the exclusivity rule from becoming a leak.
Allocation happens after validation, so a rejected spawn leaves the user's first agent as agent-1. A gap in a never-reused sequence is cosmetic. P2.

Two conversations both mint agent-1; their TRANSCRIPTS must not collide. The thread id carries a digest of the root, identical for every spawn in one conversation and different across conversations — asserted in both directions plus the reconstruction from the public helper. A shared tag across conversations is one user's sub-agent writing into another's transcript. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The rowless host (a CLI, or a conversation that exists only as messages) has no counter to continue from, so numbering resumes above the highest child transcript UNDER THIS ROOT'S SCOPE — another conversation's agent-9 and a legacy-shaped thread are deliberately excluded, and the spawn must not invent the root's metadata row. Both the scan and its scope filter are distinct mechanisms from the persisted counter. P1.
The same transcript scan reached by a different absence — the row exists but carries no counter. A variation on :175. P2.

The counter outlives the process: a new manager over the same root hands out agent-3, never agent-1 again. Restarting into a reused ordinal means two different agents sharing one transcript and one addressable id. The persisted property and its value are pinned, not just the returned id. P1.
The derived display name for an unnamed spawn. Cosmetic beside the id contract above, which the same spawns already pin. P2.

The non-vacuity partner of :255 and the enforcement-off path: a helper that stamped unconditionally satisfies every assertion above while inventing identity metadata on deployments that never asked for it. The distinguishing case, so it carries the same tier. P1.

One sequence and one scope for the whole family: a grandchild built from the parent's real ChildOptions draws the root's next ordinal and lands in the root's thread scope. Per-manager numbering would give two family members the same id, which is the collision the ids exist to prevent. P1.

#705's primary contract: the agent id is an ordinal in strict spawn order, unaffected by template, explicit name or background mode, and it is what the tools actually resolve — the row goes on to look the agent up through TryGetAgent, which is the path SendMessage and CheckAgents use. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: #385. A subagent-* thread is minted inside the spawn and never through the provisioning route that stamps ownership, so without this it persists with a null tenant — which under Identity:Enforce reads as an absent row and makes the sub-agent's transcript unreadable to the person whose conversation spawned it. Tenant and owner inherit; Visibility deliberately does NOT, because 'Shared' is a publication decision about the parent that nobody made about this transcript. The root's own identity columns are checked undisturbed. A P0-grade consequence on a file with no prefix member, so it is left at P1 and flagged.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The storeless fallback still numbers from one. A configuration variation on the numbering pinned at :69. P2.

#275: provenance is resolved from the SPAWNING manager, not captured once at the root. The fixture gives the manager a parent that is itself a sub-agent — the exact shape a grandchild's spawning manager has — and asserts both halves a root-captured factory got wrong: attribution to its own parent thread, and a describe callback that resolves against its own live roster. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The static id helper in isolation — textual tag reuse and a deterministic digest. Thirteen product spans; the behaviour it describes is exercised end to end by :214 and :106. P2.

An allow-list naming two collaboration-only tools alongside Spawn yields Spawn ALONE. The allow-list must therefore intersect the shape rather than add to it, which the comment states as the risk: listing a name the shape does not emit must be inert rather than conjuring a tool with no manager behind it. That failure is worse than a missing tool — the model is advertised a capability whose handler has no backing manager, so it calls something that cannot work. Catches configuration becoming a grant mechanism in its own right. P1: the intersective property of the allow-list, distinct from which subset it selects.
requirements: in-process only; provider construction only, no spawn

rationale: An empty allow-list yields no tools, distinguishing an empty set from a null one. Catches empty being treated as unset, which would grant the whole family to a host that explicitly granted nothing — the opposite of what it configured. P2: the empty-input boundary, and the complement of the null default.

A null allow-list emits all four tools. This is the legacy path every host that never narrows takes, so it pins that the option is additive configuration rather than a behaviour change — a null treated as an empty set would silently strip delegation from every existing host at once, with no configuration change to point at. Enumerating all four by name rather than checking a count also fixes the composition of the default shape. Catches an opt-in narrowing that is not actually opt-in. P1: the compatibility default.

An allow-list of one name yields exactly one tool. This is the case the class remarks are written about: a host whose UI lists Agent, SendMessage, CheckAgent and WaitAgent as separate checkboxes previously had no way to grant one of them, because the provider emitted a whole shape and ticking a single box silently granted the family. The remarks state the principle plainly — the runtime grant has to match the granularity the host advertises, or the choice it offers is fiction. Catches a user who granted only the ability to spawn also handing over messaging and waiting. P1: the granularity contract the option exists to provide.

A two-name allow-list yields exactly those two, with an explicit assertion that an unnamed sibling is absent. Catches a filter that keeps the named tools but fails to drop the rest. P2: a cardinality variation on the single-name grant, reaching the same rule with more entries; its added value is the explicit exclusion assertion rather than a distinct contract.
The sink survives into child loop options, deliberately unlike the spawn-authority hooks. Fourteen product spans of option propagation. P2.

The seams are hit from tool dispatch, descriptor building and spawn construction on different threads, so a racy counter under-reports exactly when the run is busiest — the case the measurement exists for. Two hundred parallel iterations across three counters, asserted to exact totals. P1.
A fresh sink reports zeros so a reader can tell 'measured, nothing happened' from 'never measured'. Twenty-three product spans on the sink's initial state. P2.
Instrumentation is opt-in and defaults to null. Six product spans. P2.

A fresh, emptier sink is exactly what a host RESTART produces, and letting it win would report a conversation that spawned two agents as having done no coordination work at all. Unrelated properties in the same bag are also left intact — a projection that rewrote the bag would silently drop another feature's data. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Both artifacts — the aggregate work row and the per-spawn timings — survive into the property bag, which is the only surface an offline scorer ever sees. Anything not written there does not exist as far as scoring is concerned. P1.
uncertainties: inP0Prefix member at greedyRank 24 with 90 new spans, and I am NOT proposing it for P0. Zero exclusive spans, 118 covered, and the component is the opt-in evidence layer: the file's own remarks state the sink is null by default so an unconfigured host behaves byte-for-byte as before. A failure here costs an eval scorer its numbers; it costs no user any data or any behaviour. Third prefix member I have declined on criticality, consistent with the calls on ContextLoadedEmissionTests and MutableSubAgentTemplateSourceTests.

rationale: One corrupt property reads as not-measured rather than taking the whole projection down, and a null metadata row does the same. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Two counters accumulate independently. An additional accumulator alongside the spawn totals above. P2.

The sink's arithmetic: phase totals accumulate, each individual timing is retained in order, and a reconstruction counts BOTH as a reconstruction and as a spawn — it pays the same construction cost, and 'how much of this run was re-construction?' is the question the measurement exists to answer. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Both directions of the memo, which is what makes this a measurement rather than a restatement of it: a repeated identical call must add NOTHING (or the sink inflates every long run by its turn count) and a changed template set must add exactly ONE (or the sink goes silent and reports a saving that is really a blind spot). The two fail to different numbers, so a stuck counter satisfies neither. P1.

The seam measured through a REAL spawn rather than by calling the sink directly: template, reconstruction flag, the phase timings ordered sensibly against the total, and the numbers the tool-registry question is actually about — how much tool surface each spawn re-materializes. Thirteen exclusive spans. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 13 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: An empty target list returns an empty batch with all counters at zero rather than throwing or summarising the whole roster. Catches an empty selector being treated as select-all, which would return every agent to a caller that asked about none. P2: the degenerate-input boundary.

A name differing only in case does not resolve. Catches a case-insensitive lookup matching an agent the caller did not name, which in a collaboration where names are model-chosen would silently address the wrong worker. P2: a comparison-semantics variation on the resolution the batch tests establish, asserted with one entry.

A batch of four targets — an id, a name, an unknown, and the id repeated — returns four entries in the SAME order, each echoing its own target, with the resolved agent id per position and a null for the unknown. Positional correspondence is the substantive contract: the caller is a model matching results back to the things it asked about, and a batch that deduplicated, reordered or dropped the unknown would shift every subsequent answer onto the wrong request. Keeping the duplicate rather than collapsing it is the case that catches a well-meaning distinct. Catches a model being told the status of an agent it did not ask about. P1: the batch correspondence contract, and the row that covers all three hazards at once.
requirements: in-process only; mocked provider, bounded teardown

rationale: A single spawned agent resolves with its target echoed, its id, its name and a live status, and is reported found. This is the positive baseline the not-found cases are measured against — without it, a CheckAgents that found nothing at all would satisfy every absence assertion in the file. Catches a roster read that cannot resolve an agent the manager itself just spawned. P1: the resolution baseline for the batch read.
uncertainties: Status is asserted as one of running or completed, which the comment attributes to timing. That is honest about the race but means the row does not pin which status a just-spawned background agent should report.

rationale: A resolved entry carries the template name it was spawned from and the task it was given. Catches a status read that identifies an agent but cannot say what it is doing, which leaves a model unable to decide whether to keep waiting. P2: additional fields on the entry the resolution baseline already returns.

A five-target batch with two unknowns and one duplicate reports five requested, two not found, and three found entries. Catches summary counters that disagree with the entries they summarise, so a model reading only the summary draws a different conclusion from one reading the list. P2: a larger-input variation on the counts the correspondence test already asserts, and its own comment concedes it only verifies that found entries are not counted as not-found rather than pinning their statuses.

Four content fields the collaboration surface added — role, description, a typed message body and the sub-agent's own reply — are proven present in the system and then proven absent from BOTH the rendered log lines and every structured property value. Two design choices make it strong. First, the directory is interrogated to confirm it is holding the very sentinels the log must not show, so the guard cannot pass because the values never arrived. Second, checking rendering and structure separately closes the gap the comment names: rendering alone misses a value attached to a placeholder a formatter drops, structure alone misses content interpolated into the template. The message is sent through the real SendMessage tool and asserted delivered, so the manager's own write path is exercised rather than a directory lookup. ADR 0009 says logs carry identifiers, types, outcomes and lengths only. Catches user and model content reaching durable logs. P1: the privacy contract over the widened collaboration surface.
requirements: in-process only; TestAgentFactoryOverride substitutes a fake agent, capture-all logger
uncertainties: Strong criticality argument for a SubAgents P0 — an EUII leak into logs is durable, exfiltrates outside the process boundary and cannot be undone once shipped — but SubAgents already carries two candidates under the one-per-component rule I adopted mid-pass. Raised for the lead's pruning pass as a SUBSTITUTION contender against the two standing SubAgents candidates, not applied here.
Uses the production hook SubAgentManager.TestAgentFactoryOverride, so the real agent factory path is not the one logged.

rationale: The spawn task and the relayed follow-up prompt — the two pieces of typed user content the interactive focus feature carries (WI #194) — must not appear in any log the manager emits, at ANY level. The class summary explains why this is broader than the transport-level test that already exists: that one observes only the WebSocket manager's logger, so a leak in the core manager passes it. NotBeEmpty on the captured lines is a real non-vacuity guard: a manager that logged nothing at all would otherwise satisfy every absence assertion in the file. Catches a user's typed prompt in a durable log. P1: the original EUII contract for the spawn and relay paths, distinct from the collaboration fields.
requirements: in-process only; capture-all logger, test agent factory override
uncertainties: Weaker than its sibling in one specific way: this row checks only the RENDERED lines (Snapshot), not the structured property values (StructuredSnapshot) that AssertNoSentinelWasLogged checks. A task or prompt attached as a log property but not interpolated into the template would pass here and fail only in the collaboration row. Recorded as an assertion-strength gap; no change proposed.

rationale: The positive half of the privacy contract: a spawn must log its FINAL effective routing as structured properties — selection source, template name, spawn name, requested versus template intelligence, effective model id and intelligence, requested and shaped effort. Without it the two absence rows would be satisfied by a manager that logged nothing operable, leaving no way to explain after the fact which model a delegated run actually used or why. Two details give it teeth: Single() on the template-tier selection source fixes that exactly one routing decision is recorded rather than several competing ones, and asserting nulls for the requested intelligence and shaped effort distinguishes 'not supplied' from 'defaulted'. Catches routing that is unexplainable, and pins the metadata-only shape ADR 0009 permits. P1: the observability contract that bounds the redaction rule.
uncertainties: SpawnName is asserted to be the literal 'workflow:1:task' while the spawn TASK is a sentinel. A spawn name is author-supplied free text like role and description, so this row asserts one such field is present in logs while its sibling asserts two others must never be. That distinction is presumably deliberate (a name is an identifier here) but the file does not state it.

rationale: The mutation guard for the ceiling's VALUE: its own comment records that setting the production constant to zero passed all 1252 tests before this existed, because every sibling test overrides the ceiling AND uses a task that never finishes, so none can tell 'abandoned instantly' from 'waited, then abandoned'. This one deliberately does not override, and its run task finishes shortly after cancellation with an observable side effect. P1 — without it the bound could be silently reduced to nothing.

P0 for the sub-agent teardown baseline. It reproduces a three-deep deadlock end to end: disposal cancels the spawn pump's token first, that token is the very one a background QUEUED spawn's SendAsync is blocked on, unblocking it lands in the failed-spawn cleanup, and that cleanup's own await of a run task which ignores its token was unbounded — so the cleanup hangs, the pump awaiting it hangs, and disposal awaiting the pump hangs. Criticality: the observable failure is a host process that never exits, from a spawn that never finished registering, and the fix is a bound at a call site distinct from the one #373 already covered. The path it drives is the widest in this file (729 covered spans): real permit acquisition, deferred queueing, the pump's dequeue and start, and the cleanup path — and the assertion is elapsed time under a short overridden ceiling, which is the same production code path with a smaller number.
uncertainties: inP0Prefix member, greedyRank 12 of the project's 36-member prefix, and 5 exclusive product spans.

This file is a curated regression suite — one test per named defect (F1, F2, F3, F5, #373, #396, #404 and the review blockers), each with its own reproduction — so it carries almost no variation material and P2 is nearly absent by construction rather than by inflation.

rationale: #373: disposal awaited each sub-agent's run and monitor tasks with no ceiling, so one run task that ignores its token hung DisposeAsync — and every host shutting down behind it — forever. The fixture simulates exactly that task and asserts disposal returns well inside the ceiling. P1 for the bound at DisposeAsync's own await site.

The same window entered from the other side: the MANAGER is disposed while a spawn sits at registration. Registration is rejected with ObjectDisposedException and the constructed agent is still disposed once. A different trigger and a different failure type from the caller-cancellation case, and the one that decides whether host shutdown leaks a live sub-agent. P1.

Cancelling in the window between acquiring the permit and registering the agent: the spawn throws, NOTHING is listed, and the already-constructed agent is disposed exactly once. Leaving it unregistered but alive leaks an agent nothing can reach or stop. P1.

The permit half of the pending-completion rule: with a limit of one, a nonterminal completion must NOT free the slot, so a second spawn defer-queues — and once the terminal completion lands the pump starts that queued spawn on the released permit. Both directions in one body, so neither 'never releases' nor 'releases early' passes. P1.

F3: with a single slot and the completed sub-agent's parent relay deliberately blocked, a fresh spawn must still acquire the slot — proving release happens BEFORE the relay. Releasing after would let one slow consumer of the parent's inbox stall every future sub-agent in the process. P1.

F5: a subscription that fails outright must FAULT the completion latch, with the original exception, rather than leave it unresolved. Anything awaiting the sub-agent's completion otherwise waits forever for a run that is already dead — and the test bounds its own await so a regression hangs one test, not the suite. P1.

A restarted monitor can fault BEFORE the restart arms Running. The fault must be recorded against the run GENERATION so arming observes this generation's terminal and refuses to overwrite Error with Running — otherwise the manager advertises a dead run as live and callers keep sending into it. The fixture gates the restart send so the fault-then-arm ordering is deterministic, not hoped for. P1.

F2, the race the per-epoch guard redesign exists for: epoch 1 has released its slot but its subscription is still open and blocked, exactly as a real agent's is, when epoch 2's restart send fails. A shared or reset-in-place guard lets epoch 1's late release consume epoch 2's slot; the fixture makes that ordering deterministic and the capacity probe would show the corruption. P1.

#404's second unbounded await: when a restart's own send fails after the replacement tasks started, the catch cancels and awaits them, and that await must be bounded too — or the exception it is trying to surface never escapes. The test asserts both the elapsed bound and that the InvalidOperationException actually propagates. A fourth distinct await site, and each had to be bounded separately. P1.

#404: the restart path awaited the finished run's tasks before rebuilding, and that await was unbounded unlike every sibling teardown. A token-ignoring run task wedged the restart and the caller's SendMessageAsync with it — a user's follow-up message hanging forever on a run that already finished. P1 for the bound at the pre-rebuild await.

The inject send is linked to the run's lifecycle token, and terminal disposal cancels it. That must not surface as caller cancellation, because the thing being dropped is the USER'S MESSAGE: the continuation has to re-enter the decision loop and deliver the prompt to the restarted run. Asserted through the real manager boundary, with the prompt's arrival at the restarted agent checked rather than just a status. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The discriminating counterpart: an OperationCanceledException from the agent's own send, with NEITHER token cancelled, must propagate instead of being retried. Retrying anything that looks like cancellation risks duplicate delivery or an unbounded loop, and the exact send count is asserted to prove no retry happened. P1 — the case that stops the fix above from becoming a blanket retry.

F1: the spawn's own SendAsync fails after the monitor already owns the gate. The slot must be released EXACTLY once — a missed release leaks capacity until restart, a double release corrupts the semaphore and lets more sub-agents run than the limit — and the probe is honest about being indirect: fill the pool exactly, then show the next spawn defer-queues. The partial registration is also rolled back, so the failed name resolves to nothing. P1.

On graceful completion the manager pushes the terminal status through the child's own store causally, verified on UpdateMetadataAsync for the child's scoped thread id rather than on any write. Choosing the atomic member is what separates the manager's push from the child's own post-run SaveMetadataAsync, so the assertion cannot be satisfied by behaviour that already existed. Catches a terminal state that lives only in memory and is lost on restart. P1: the graceful arm of the durable terminal transition.

All four statuses are classified in one theory: Completed, Error and Stopped terminal, Running not. Enumerating every case with a negative among them means neither an always-true nor an always-false classifier passes. This is the canonical set so callers reading snapshots — the in-process review completion source among them — do not each re-derive the three-of-four terminal set and disagree. Catches Error or Stopped being omitted, under which a failed child is waited on forever. P1: a small but load-bearing shared classification, cheap and complete.

Two real sub-agent loops are driven into opposite lifecycle states at once — one whose provider completes and one whose provider blocks until cancelled — and the snapshot must report both, each with its name, template, task, status, scoped thread id and activity stamp. The determinism is structural rather than timed: the finisher is joined on ObserveCompletionAsync and the runner blocks on an infinite delay, so neither status is a timing race. Catches a read seam that reports only running or only finished children, which is what every consumer of the roster reads. Nominated P0: the essential baseline of the presentation-only read seam this file exists for. Confirmation held pending the facts join.
requirements: in-process only; mocked streaming providers, bounded teardown
uncertainties: DEMOTED in the end-of-slice P0 prune. Eighteen nominations across 347 in-scope rows is 5.2%, against the lane's healthy 2.4-3.1% band; ten survive. The nomination recorded above stands as the reason this row is the strongest in its component and is NOT withdrawn as an assessment - it is simply not a surviving candidate. Demotion reason: lowest of the four in my SubAgents family ranking (recorded on the trust-boundary row in MidSessionTemplateActivationTests). A wrong roster snapshot is read by a model that can re-check it.

rationale: A completed child that is restarted back to Running must clear its terminal timestamp. The test waits for the timestamp to be set before restarting, so the later null is provably a clearing rather than a value that was never written. Catches a restarted agent reporting the PRIOR run's terminal instant, which violates the snapshot's own contract that Running has no terminal timestamp and would let a completion barrier treat a live agent as finished. P1: the restart arm of the terminal-timestamp contract.

In one snapshot the completed child carries a terminal timestamp and the still-running child carries null. Asserting both in the same snapshot is what makes it discriminating: a field that was always null or always set would fail one arm. The contract records WHEN a child reached its terminal transition rather than only THAT it did, so the instant can be stamped durably without drifting on a later idempotent refresh. P1: the terminal-timestamp contract, distinct from the status the baseline snapshot already reports.

A sub-agent whose SubscribeAsync throws outright must still push its terminal transition through the child's own store, exactly as a graceful completion does. The verification is on the ATOMIC UpdateMetadataAsync member specifically, which the comment justifies precisely: a child's own post-run save only ever calls SaveMetadataAsync, so asserting UpdateMetadataAsync proves the manager itself did the push rather than the child incidentally doing it. Catches the recorded defect where a monitor-faulted child that never writes again leaves its persisted metadata claiming running forever, indistinguishable from a genuinely active agent. P1: the fault twin of the completion push, and the arm whose absence is invisible in a snapshot.
requirements: in-process only; mocked conversation store with verified interactions

rationale: A sub-agent whose LOOP has been marked disposed is rebuilt with a fresh instance on the next continuation, and TryGetAgent must return that post-rebuild instance. The trigger is now an explicit arrangement, not a consequence of finishing: under loop-lifetime ownership a completed agent disposes nothing and a follow-up REUSES the same instance, so the test sets the exact rebuild condition RestartRunAsync reads on the real SubAgentState the monitor classified the run against, then sends. Reference identity is asserted four ways — the pre-restart resolve IS the first created instance, marking alone swaps nothing, the post-rebuild resolve IS the second, and is NOT the first — with independent instance counts of one before the continuation and two after. That combination is what makes it a real identity test rather than a status check. Catches a stale instance being handed to callers after a rebuild, so messages are sent into a disposed agent. P1: the instance-currency contract, distinct from resolution itself.
requirements: in-process only; fake agent factory override, bounded Wait.UntilAsync

rationale: Resolution by generated id and by caller-supplied name both succeed and return the SAME live instance by reference, while an unknown key returns false with a null out value. The reference-identity assertion is the substantive one: two lookup keys returning equal-looking but different instances would split state between callers. Catches a non-throwing resolve that throws, or a name index that resolves to a copy. P1: the resolution contract, the other half of the read seam beside the snapshot.

A background sub-agent whose run produces the text 'done' is observed by id and yields exactly that. This is the whole point of the seam the class describes: a host-side trigger source (#144) that did not spawn the agent must still be able to await its completion by id and receive the result. Asserting the RESULT rather than merely that the await returned is what distinguishes observing a completion from observing a latch — a seam that resolved with null would satisfy any weaker formulation while giving the trigger source nothing to act on. Catches an out-of-band observer that cannot read a finished run. P1: the primary behaviour of the observation seam.
requirements: in-process only; mocked streaming agent, bounded teardown via Wait.ForTeardownAsync
uncertainties: The await is not itself bounded inside the test; the class relies on Wait.ForTeardownAsync only for disposal. A seam that never resolved would hang this test rather than fail it, unless an outer runner bound fires first.

rationale: Observing an id the manager never issued throws ArgumentException rather than returning. The alternative failure is the quiet one: resolving null for an unknown id would let a trigger source holding a stale or mistyped id conclude the run finished with no result, which is a wrong answer rather than an error. Catches a stale id reading as a completed run. P2: the unknown-input boundary on the behaviour the positive row establishes.
requirements: in-process only; manager with no agents spawned

rationale: Toggling the parent-relay flag for an unknown id throws rather than silently succeeding. A no-op here is worse than an exception because the caller believes it suppressed (or enabled) the automatic relay and only discovers otherwise when the parent is notified — or is not — long after the call returned. Catches a configuration call that reports success while changing nothing. P2: the same unknown-id boundary applied to the sibling method on the seam, so it varies the entry point rather than the contract.
uncertainties: No row in this class exercises SetNotifyParentOnCompletion on a KNOWN id, so the flag's effect on relay behaviour is untested here; only its guard is. The absence is recorded, not proposed for change.

rationale: A ReplayTruncated advisory LEADS the stream and the live tail — answer text then run completion — follows on the same subscription; the monitor must ignore the advisory and return the real answer. This is the bound on the terminal rule and its non-vacuity partner: a monitor that terminalised on any StreamRecoveryMessage would pass both severed tests and fail every healthy run whose only sin was joining late. Asserting the answer text rather than merely that nothing threw is what proves it kept watching rather than merely surviving. Catches a truncation advisory failing healthy delegations. P1: the non-terminal arm, and the discriminator between the two reasons.
requirements: in-process only; test factory override, 10s bound

rationale: A SlowConsumer recovery advisory arrives and the stream then ends CLEANLY — the fake mirrors the real publisher, which calls TryComplete() rather than TryComplete(ex). That is exactly why the defect was invisible: no exception reaches the monitor's catch, so it falls out of its await foreach, resolves nothing, and every WaitAgent, WaitForAgents and AwaitCompletionAsync caller blocks forever on a run nobody is watching. The test requires a throw carrying the reason in its message, which the comment defends as the only clue the caller gets. The whole thing is bounded at 10s so a regression fails one test rather than hanging the suite. Catches a permanently stuck delegation. P1: terminalisation of a severed monitor, important failure handling.
requirements: in-process only; TestAgentFactoryOverride substitutes a fake agent, 10s bound
uncertainties: Uses a production test hook, SubAgentManager.TestAgentFactoryOverride. The class remarks justify it — the real fan-out only emits these messages under backpressure conditions that cannot be staged deterministically — but the substitution means the real publisher's completion behaviour is asserted only by the fake mirroring it.

rationale: Faulting the latch is only half the contract: the agent's own record must go terminal too, asserted as status error through Peek. Without it CheckAgent and ListAgents keep reporting a running sub-agent that no longer exists, so a parent polling the roster instead of awaiting the latch waits on a corpse. The comment also explains why the observation is deterministic rather than raced — the status is stamped on the same path, before the latch resolves, so awaiting the throw is sufficient synchronisation. Catches a terminal state visible to one reader and not another. P1: the roster-visible half of terminalisation, distinct from the latch.
requirements: in-process only; test factory override, 10s bound

rationale: The restart flag must FALL exactly when the replacement is delivered, or the next epoch's ordinary drop is treated as a restart and the observer awaits a signal that never comes — a hang instead of a clean end. The lifetime rule the two decision rows above cannot express. P1.
The teardown spelling of the same flag-clearing rule held at :451. P2.
The decision table's drop case: stream ended, no restart in flight, nothing signalled — EndStream, decided from state rather than from a clock. P1.
A third input combination — the signal fired before the decision — reaching the same AwaitReplacement outcome as :419. P2.

The opposite outcome from the same inputs but for the restart-intent flag: a restart in flight means wait for the imminent signal however long the dispose takes. The explicit intent flag is what replaced a wall-clock grace period, and these two rows are the pair that pins it. P1.

The atomic read seam: the agent and the awaitable that fires when THAT agent is replaced are captured together, the signal taken with a0 resolves to a0's replacement and never to a0 itself, and each swap installs a fresh signal for the next epoch. Every observer decision below reads this pair. P1.

5,000 swaps raced against 5,000 snapshots through a barrier, counting the one observable a torn two-read pair produces — a signal that already resolved to the very agent it was handed with. Zero occurrences is the atomicity claim, and it is unfalsifiable from the single-threaded row above. P1.

The proof that no wall-clock heuristic survives: a gate holds the old instance's dispose open between the point it ends the observer's stream and the swap that delivers the replacement, and the observer is asserted STILL RUNNING in that window. The previous two-second grace would have expired and killed a perfectly valid focus stream on a slow machine. Deterministic — the gate, not a delay, defines the window. P1.

P0 for the sub-agent observation baseline. A rebuild disposes the child's loop between ending the observer's stream and swapping in a fresh instance; an observer bound to the old instance must not end when that instance's stream closes — it has to follow the swap and stream the second run. Reaching that rebuild is now an explicit arrangement rather than a consequence of completing: under loop-lifetime ownership a plain terminal completion disposes nothing and a follow-up reuses the live loop, so the test marks the loop disposed on the real SubAgentState the monitor classified the run against — and asserts that arrangement did not itself end the observer — while the dispose the observer reacts to remains the genuine one the rebuild performs. The failure is user-visible and silent: the focus stream simply stops, so a person watching a sub-agent sees it go dead on the ordinary continue-the-task path with nothing reported as an error. The test proves the whole chain rather than the seam alone — it gates the follow-up on the observer having already drained run 1, so the swap is observed mid-subscription rather than re-resolved afterwards, and it asserts the two runs' texts arrive IN ORDER on one uninterrupted enumeration, which is what rules out an early end plus a reattach.
uncertainties: inP0Prefix member at greedyRank 22, contributing 98 new spans over an 863-span path — spawn, owned-provider completion and disposal, follow-up relay, restart, instance swap and the observation seam, end to end.
Zero exclusive spans: :486 and :627 re-cover much of this path from their own angles, so the row is chosen for breadth and consequence rather than for being a sole cover.
Distinct component from this project's other P0s (input admission, tenant authorization, conversation ownership, sub-agent teardown).

I tiered ContextLoadedEmissionTests' prefix row at P1 as observability while proposing this observation-seam row at P0. The distinction is the consequence, not the word: a wrong context_loaded event misreports what a subscriber is told AFTER the fact, whereas this seam failing means the live output a person is watching stops arriving.

rationale: In the window between a restart's dispose and its swap the registry still hands out the OLD, disposed instance, and subscribing to it throws ObjectDisposedException at the first MoveNextAsync. That is an ordinary transition, not a failure — escaping it reaches the client as a stream-failed frame and an abnormal socket close for a child about to stream perfectly well. The enumerator is driven on the test thread deliberately, because a backgrounded observer can lose the race to the swap and pass either way. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The counterpart to :627 and the reason it is safe: ONLY ObjectDisposedException means 'this instance is gone, look for its replacement'. A genuine fault and a cancellation both reach the caller unchanged — asserted for each — because absorbing them would send the observer to await a replacement that is never coming, turning a fast visible failure into a stream that hangs until the connection dies. P1.

Teardown signals every state's replacement awaitable with null, so an observer blocked on a still-running child unblocks instead of waiting forever for a swap that will never come. Again asserted with the observer's token un-cancelled, which is what separates ending cleanly from being killed. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The backpressure DROP path: a slow subscriber removed while the instance stays alive gets no replacement signal and no restart flag, so the observer must END — promptly and deterministically, not on a timeout — or the focus socket never closes and the client cannot reconnect and replay. Asserted with the observer's own token proven un-cancelled and the child still registered, so 'it ended' cannot be the test cancelling it. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: #362 reproduced exactly — gate armed, restart parked inside a dispose the manager's own teardown awaits, gate never released — proving the bound turns a run-wide wedge into one named TimeoutException that names both the subject and the caller. The assertion is structural rather than temporal, and it verifies the teardown is still blocked afterwards, so a bound is not mistaken for a fix. P2 as a harness guard.
uncertainties: Its subject is the shared test-utility teardown bound (Wait.ForTeardownAsync), not product behaviour, so it is tiered as infrastructure. It is not low-value: the failure it prevents aborts the whole assembly. Worth the lead's attention if infrastructure guards should sit above P2.

rationale: The relayed record's ProviderAttemptId must equal the sub-agent's OWN loop thread id plus the generation — not the bare agent id. The comment gives the mechanism and the stakes: the parent relay and the sub-agent's own capture describe the SAME provider call, so a differing key records one call under two ids, which the comment calls a cross-conversation dedup landmine. Asserting against the production helper that builds the id, rather than a hardcoded string, means the two sides cannot drift apart without this failing. Catches every sub-agent's spend being counted twice in a conversation total — a billing number that is silently wrong in the direction of over-charging.
