P1: the dedup identity of a relayed usage record.
requirements: in-process only; mocked provider and sink, bounded teardown

rationale: Folding descendant usage fires the ledger's aggregate-changed callback carrying the descendant total, which is the source of the live usage banner. Asserting the callback saw 140 rather than merely firing is what distinguishes a notification from a correct one. Catches sub-agent spend that is folded and persisted but never announced, so a delegating conversation's banner stays frozen at the parent's own usage until a reload. P1: the live-notification arm of the relay, distinct from the fold and from persistence.

A split-model configuration sets the sub-agent's model on the TEMPLATE's DefaultOptions rather than a per-spawn override, and the captured usage record must name that model. The comment states the failure precisely: otherwise a sub-agent's spend is mis-attributed to the dispatcher or parent model. That matters because per-model attribution is what makes a cheap-worker-under-expensive-parent configuration measurable at all — mis-attribution moves real money between line items while the total stays right, so nothing looks wrong. Catches spend attributed to a model that was never called. P1: the model attribution of a relayed record, distinct from its identity or its total.

Descendant usage causes the supplied persist delegate to run, so a sub-agent's spend reaches durable storage rather than only the in-memory ledger. Catches descendant usage that is visible live and lost on restart, which under-reports exactly the conversations that delegated the most work. P1: the durability arm of the relay, distinct from the fold and the notification.
uncertainties: Lower bound only: the persist count is asserted greater than zero, so a relay that persisted on every observation rather than coalescing would pass unchanged.

rationale: With no usage sink configured the sub-agent still runs and returns its answer. Catches a null sink faulting the relay and taking the sub-agent's result with it, which would make usage accounting a hard dependency of delegation rather than an optional one. P2: the unconfigured boundary, asserted only on the returned text.

A sub-agent's UsageMessage reaches the ROOT conversation's ledger: the total is the sum of both token sides, the root conversation id is preserved, and exactly one per-model entry records one attempt. The attempt count of exactly 1 is the assertion that catches a fold applied twice, which the attempt-id test then localises to the key. Catches sub-agent spend never reaching the conversation it belongs to, so a delegating conversation under-reports everything its workers did. P1: the relay's primary behaviour and the baseline the other rows vary.

An override the host's validator rejects is DROPPED and the sub-agent inherits the parent model, with an explicit second assertion that the bogus id never reaches the provider. The class summary explains why a model supplies bad values routinely: the Agent tool exposes model as an unconstrained string, so a controller LLM fills it with an invented id, a value belonging in another field, or a typo, and passing it through hard-fails at the provider — a wasted spawn plus its tokens. Catches a model's guess becoming a request model. P1: the validation-and-drop contract, important failure handling at a model-controlled input.

A dropped override with a tier factory wired must behave exactly as if no override had been given: the parent model reaches the provider, the tier factory is never invoked, and the template factory is. Asserting the tier factory list is EMPTY is the discriminating part — a manager that routed the rejected id through the transport-aware factory would ask the host to build a provider for a model it just said it did not recognise, which is at best a wasted lookup and at worst a resolution failure inside the host. Catches the drop and the routing decisions being made from different inputs. P1: the interaction between validation and factory selection, which neither of the two single-concern rows covers.

With no validator configured, even an unrecognisable override passes through unchanged. This is not an edge case but the DEFAULT path — every host that has not opted in takes it — so it pins that the feature is additive rather than a behaviour change. If dropping unknown overrides became the default, every existing host would silently lose per-spawn model selection with no configuration change and no error. Catches an opt-in gate that is not actually gated. P1: the compatibility default, a distinct contract from the validated paths.

A validated override must be built through the host's TRANSPORT-AWARE tier factory, asserted three ways: the tier factory was asked for exactly that model id, the parent/template factory was NOT used, and the override still reaches the provider as the request model. The middle assertion is the one that catches the defect — a delegate that reused the parent provider would satisfy the model-id check while POSTing to the wrong endpoint, which the comment names as the claude-sonnet-4.6-on-Responses storm. The scenario is real rather than constructed: an Anthropic-transport override under an OpenAI-Responses parent. Catches every cross-transport override hard-failing at the provider after the spawn and its tokens are already spent. P1: transport-correct routing for a validated override, distinct from whether the override survives validation.
requirements: in-process only; recording provider mocks, bounded teardown

rationale: A recognised override still wins over the parent model. This is the non-vacuity partner for the whole file: a manager that dropped EVERY override would satisfy both fallback tests and make the feature useless, and only this row fails. Catches validation overshooting into a blanket refusal, which would silently disable per-spawn model selection for every host that configures a validator. P1: the accept arm of validation, and the bound on the drop rule.

When a descendant parks on its own AskUserQuestion, the default relay into the parent must REPORT its accept under the same receipt id the parent's channel actually holds. The class remarks state the correlation discipline and why either fact alone is worthless: a relay rerouted onto the loop's raw enqueue path still delivers the input, so asserting delivery stays green, and asserting merely that the observer heard something would be satisfied by any other accept on the thread. So the row finds the queued input, reads its receipt id, and requires THAT id to have been announced. The comment also picks out why this site is the dangerous one — it fires while the whole spawn tree is otherwise idle, which is precisely when a grantee handoff reads the entry releasable, the #418 shape. Catches an accept site rerouted off the ledger while still appearing to work. P1: a per-site regression guard on an accept path no host call site can cover.
requirements: in-process only; a REAL MultiTurnAgentBase parent with its loop never started, Moq sub-agent
bounded: 10s Wait.UntilAsync, bounded teardown via Wait.ForTeardownAsync
uncertainties: The class is explicit that these rows do not prove the mechanism — InputAcceptanceObserverTests does, at the mint sites — so their value is entirely as site guards. That is a reason to keep them and a reason not to treat either as the component's primary coverage.
The observer assertion is a Contain over a snapshot, so extra or duplicate accepts announced for the same relay would pass unnoticed; only the presence of the correct pairing is pinned.

rationale: The same correlation applied to the other accept site: a background spawn's result is delivered onto the pooled parent as a real turn by a monitor task the host never sees, and that accept must be announced under the id the channel holds. The comment names the consequence precisely — the host cannot record this accept because it does not know it happened, so if the relay stops announcing, nothing else in the suite or the host notices, and a grantee handoff landing between the accept and the run that would start it hits the #418 hole again. Using a REAL MultiTurnAgentBase parent rather than the Moq IMultiTurnAgent the other sub-agent suites use is what makes this reachable at all; the remarks say so outright, since a mock's SendAsync is a stub and the mint site under test never runs. Catches a background-result relay that delivers without being ledgered. P1: the second per-site guard.
uncertainties: The helper's remark records that the relay REPORTS before it enqueues, which is why it accumulates drained inputs rather than waiting once. The ordering itself — report first, enqueue second — is therefore relied upon but never asserted, and a relay that enqueued first would leave a window in which the input exists with no announcement.
The relay is located by notify KIND only. If both relays a parked spawn produces carried the same kind, the row could correlate against the wrong queued input.

rationale: #644's factory-supplied half verified by EXECUTION rather than inference: the child demonstrably still holds a tool the host supplies per agent, so remove_tools could not withhold it, and reporting that entry as 'withheld nothing' tells the dispatcher the delegate lacks a capability it has — false in the one direction that matters. The child loop's own registered surface is checked first, which is what makes the classification claim true rather than assumed. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 6 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A rejection raised while PROJECTING the receipt happens after the spawn was admitted to the collaboration, so it must give the slot back — otherwise every such spawn permanently shrinks the root-wide cap until the pool admits nobody. A cumulative resource leak with no error of its own. The message is pinned, not just the exception type, because the collaboration exception derives from the same base and would pass on an admission failure that never reached the queue. P1.

The false-positive guard for :101: two sets are in play — every name the parent exposes decides 'unmatched', the inheritable ones decide the empty-toolset signal — and collapsing them reports AskUserQuestion as a typo. The consequence is dispatcher noise rather than the under-reporting this file exists to prevent. P2.

Live capacity and depth, including can_delegate false for a child at the depth limit — the field a dispatcher reads before sub-delegating. Running counts, totals and both caps are pinned as values, so a receipt echoing configuration instead of live state fails. P1.

#671's core claim: the receipt reports what the delegate HOLDS, not what the template asked for. A template-metadata receipt tells the dispatcher a delegate has a tool that never materialized, which is precisely the silent work debt the receipt exists to end. The source discriminator ('registered') is pinned alongside. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: A queued spawn has no loop, so it must PROJECT its tools and say so — reporting an empty surface would have the dispatcher read 'this delegate has no tools' and route the obligation elsewhere. The mismatch it already knows is still reported on the queued path. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 1 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The capability-collapse flag: an add_tools that inherits nothing leaves a delegate with no tools at all, and the flag is asserted alongside the real absence it describes. A distinct signal from the unmatched array — a dispatcher reading only the latter sees one bad entry, not a delegate that can do nothing. P1.

A third classification code: an entry defeated by the mode's required-tools union (#623) rather than matching nothing. Intentional precedence, and the dispatcher's belief about the delegate ends up correct either way — unlike the over-grant at :147 and the unremovable tool at :206, which is why those two carry the tier and this variation does not. P2.

#638 F-001 at dispatch time: remove_tools has no group language, so 'everything except the board tools' silently OVER-GRANTS. The row asserts the over-grant the array describes is real — the tool is still on the surface — and that the exact-name entry did withhold its own. A capability the dispatcher believes was withheld and was not. P1.

The primary mismatch signal — the add_tools entry that matched nothing is named, the one that matched is not, and a next_action points at the field to fix. Without it a mistyped or group-shaped entry silently grants nothing. P1.

The discriminator that makes every other row's tools array mean something: the receipt is the child loop's REGISTERED surface, not a re-derivation that could drift from it. Asserted by equivalence against the live loop. P1.
The paired silence, covering all four signals at once: without it every mismatch assertion in this file passes on a receipt that reports a mismatch unconditionally. P1.
The omission counterpart of :255 for a non-collaborating spawn. P2.

A spawn rejected by tool-set validation must leave NO conversation row behind. The class documents the exact ordering defect and its production toll: the child's tenant and owner metadata were stamped by InheritAsync — a durable write that creates the thread directory — before BuildEnabledToolSet threw, and the failure path never removed the row, producing nine metadata-only ghost directories in production. The row is careful about the thing that would make it prove nothing, and says so: the parent is given a real tenant because with a null parent tenant InheritAsync is a no-op and the ghost could never form, so the pin would be vacuous. It then asserts on the actual filesystem — the set of thread directories is exactly the parent's — rather than on a store abstraction, which is where a partial write would hide. Checking ListAgents is empty closes the in-memory half. Catches a rejected spawn leaking durable state. P1: important failure handling with a durable side effect.
requirements: TOUCHES THE FILESYSTEM: FileConversationStore under a fresh Path.GetTempPath() directory, deleted best-effort in teardown — the only row in this slice that is not purely in-process
in-process otherwise; Moq parent and provider, no network
uncertainties: The row cannot distinguish the two possible fixes. Validating BEFORE the durable write and writing-then-compensating both produce this end state, and they differ where it matters: a compensating delete leaves the ghost behind if the process dies between the write and the compensation, which is the same failure the row exists to prevent.
Only ONE rejection reason is exercised. Any other validation that runs after InheritAsync — an unknown template, a concurrency limit — would leak the same way, and none is covered.

Directory cleanup swallows IOException as best-effort, so a run that cannot delete its temp tree leaves it behind silently. Harmless for correctness, but it accumulates across runs on a machine where the store keeps handles open.

rationale: Single-flight restart: of three concurrent continuations exactly one restarts and the other two await it, with the awaited signal proven still pending and then released to all. Two callers entering the restart both rebuild a provider for one agent. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A continuation arriving during a pending terminal disposal is routed to a fresh-provider RESTART rather than injected through the provider being torn down. Injecting there writes into a provider about to be disposed, which loses the message with no error anywhere. P1.

The lease invariant the rest of the file builds on: a terminal disposal cannot flip terminal — and therefore cannot dispose the owned provider — while an admitted inject send is still in flight. Both halves are asserted, that the disposal is still parked AND that the status has not moved. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.
Almost no P2 here: each row is a separately reported blocker or a distinct lease/restart state, not a variation on one behaviour.

rationale: Cancel runs callbacks synchronously and aggregates any that throw, and that must not abort the lease drain or the terminal transition — a provider left neither disposed nor poisoned is one a later restart happily reuses. The callback is proven to have fired, so the swallow is exercised rather than assumed. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Blocker B: an admitted send wedged on a stalled provider must be cancellable by the disposal itself, through the lifecycle token, even when the CALLER's token can never fire — the fixture uses CancellationToken.None deliberately. Without the link the disposal parks forever and the agent is never reclaimed. P1.

Blocker A: a FAILED terminal disposal leaves the dispose guard reset, so the poison flag — not the disposed flag — is what makes a continuation rebuild rather than reuse a partially-disposed provider, and a fresh provider clears it. The row pins exactly that the two flags disagree in this state. P1.

Blocker C: a fast restarted run can go terminal before the restart's own arm-Running publish executes, so that publish is generation-guarded — otherwise it overwrites the terminal state and the next continuation injects into a dead run whose provider is already disposed. Includes the live control, so a guard that always refuses fails too. P1.

The context lease shares the very counter terminal disposal awaits, so a disposal cannot dispose the owned provider while an admitted context send is in flight. Twenty-three new spans — the widest addition in the file, and the claim that ties the newer lease into the older invariant. P1.

A finished sub-agent refuses context AND leaves the single-flight restart claim untouched, so a genuine continuation still owns the restart. A refusal that consumed the claim would leave the next continuation awaiting a restart nobody is performing. P1.

The out-of-band context lease admits into a running sub-agent WITHOUT overwriting the parent-relay preference the way BeginContinuation does — mutating it silently drops or doubles the sub-agent's own completion relay to its parent. P1.

The third admission state — terminating, status still Running — refuses. The terminating state itself is set up and exercised at :53 and :28; this row adds the refusal for the context lease specifically. P2.
A substring assertion on the tool description that steers the model away from workflow ids. Prompt surface; a regression costs a wasted tool call the error path below already explains. P2.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: An abandoned turn must not leave a tool call blocked on a child that never finishes — the caller's token ends the wait. Without it a cancelled turn leaks a wait for the lifetime of the child. P1.
A timeout abandons the OBSERVATION only — the agent is still running and is reported so. A timeout that cancelled the child would destroy work the caller merely stopped waiting for. P1.
A failed child is as terminal as a finished one: the wait ends and reports error. If only success ended the wait, the outcome the caller most needs to hear about would be the one that hangs it. P1.

The tool's reason to exist: block without polling until the child is done, and return its RESULT — a wait that ends without the result costs the caller another turn to fetch it, which is the cost the tool was added to remove. P1.

The accept side of that validator: a numeric string is honoured, because models routinely emit integers as strings and this parser always took them. It is the distinguishing case — a validator that rejected ALL strings would pass every rejection above and break working callers. P1.
The empty-roster form of that error still carries the code and a non-empty explanation, rather than degenerating into a bare or blank message where there is nothing to list. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: Six unusable shapes — non-numeric, empty string, wrong JSON type, zero, negative, negative-as-string — all used to parse to null, indistinguishable from omitted, and became the UNBOUNDED wait the caller passed a timeout to avoid. A cap asked for and not applied is an error, and the rejection names what would have worked. Driven with raw JSON so the wire shapes a model emits are exercised as they arrive, against an agent that never finishes, so a regression hangs rather than merely asserting wrong. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 6 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The same unavailable verdict reached by the other route — disposal cancelling a queued spawn with the manager's token rather than the caller's. A second route to the shared assertion held at :201. P2.

Where 'the wait ended' and 'the agent finished' come apart: a queued spawn removed from the queue before a start that then throws leaves the id in NEITHER table, so the observation faults and the post-wait peek misses. The verdict is a third status with a detail line — reporting completion would tell the model its child succeeded while handing it nothing, and the empty peek result reaching the JSON parser is a crash. The race is made deterministic by releasing the permit only after the handler is parked. Widest addition in this file (rank 63, 34 new spans). P1.

An omitted cap and an EXPLICIT NULL both mean 'no cap' and must survive argument validation on the identical path — models routinely emit null for a parameter they chose not to set, and rejecting it as a malformed integer breaks the tool's default use. Non-vacuous: the wait is asserted still parked before the gate opens. P1.

WaitAgent called with the name a spawn was given returns completed for that agent. Its own argument guard was the only thing rejecting a name - the wait it guards has always resolved one - so a model that spawned analyst and waited on analyst was told no such agent existed by the half of the call that never needed the id. P1: the name arm of the tool's primary path.

A mistyped target returns unknown_agent whose text names the spawned agent by the NAME its receipt reported and, after it, the id. Replaces the ids-only correction row: listing ids alone is what taught models the ordinal was the address. Without a usable candidate list the model guesses, and each guess is a turn. P1.

A roster over MaxListedAgentIds announces showing N of M, includes the first entry and omits the ones past the cap - so the cap is applied, not merely announced. A silently truncated list invites the model to conclude its target does not exist and spawn a duplicate. A bound on the listing the P1 row pins. P2.
An agent whose name equals its id is printed once, not as agent-3 (agent-3). A legacy spawn with no name reports its id as its name; the formatting variation for that shape. P2.

The same roster in two input orders yields one identical sentence, ordered by name. A model refused twice should read the same sentence twice rather than infer the roster changed. An ordering property of the listing the P1 row pins. P2.

An empty roster produces the sentence saying there are no other agents to address, rather than a listing that trails off after its colon. This is the text every refusal ends with in a conversation that has spawned nothing yet, which is the common case; SendMessage_ToAnUnknownTarget asserts it verbatim through the tool. P1.

The shared sentence lists every agent as name (id), asserted exactly. Four refusal sites share it - SendMessage, WaitForAgents, CheckAgent and WaitAgent - so this is the one place the vocabulary a model learns peers' addresses from is pinned; the name leads because it is the handle the caller should use, and the id trails for when a name is not enough. Production showed 61 conversations taught the ordinal by a sentence that named nobody. P1: the primary content of the sentence.

A tool whose contract declares required parameters must not run when the argument payload is an EMPTY STRING — the second shape the max_tokens truncation took, where Bash args arrived at 0 bytes. The comment names the precise gap this closes: `FunctionArgs ?? "{}"` guards null only, so an empty string was dispatched straight through. That is a distinct code path from the malformed-JSON case and would survive a fix aimed only at parse failures, which is why the pair exists. Deciding on the CONTRACT's required parameters rather than on the payload alone is the design being pinned, and it is what lets the parameterless case still run. Catches a required-argument tool invoked with no arguments at all. P1: the empty-payload half of the guard.
uncertainties: Only the empty string is covered, though the comment mentions null alongside it. Whitespace-only args — the other way a degenerate payload arrives — are exercised by no row.
A contract with a mix of required and optional parameters, called with args supplying only the optional ones, is the interesting middle case for a contract-driven guard and is not covered.

rationale: A genuinely parameterless tool called with empty args is legitimate and must still execute, with a non-error result. This is the guard's over-fire control and its comment says so — the guard rejects empty or malformed args only when the contract declares required parameters. Its structural job is what earns it a place: the two rejection rows assert that a handler was NOT invoked, and without a row proving a handler IS invoked under the same harness, a guard that blocked every call whatsoever would pass both. Catches an argument guard that breaks parameterless tools. P2: the both-directions partner for the guard, a variation on the same rule rather than a distinct behavior.
uncertainties: Tiered P2 as a control, consistent with how the other non-vacuity partners in this slice were tiered (for example the no-seed row in CodexAgentLoopInitialThreadIdTests). Its coverage value is higher than P2 suggests, since the two P1 rows in this class are vacuous without it.

rationale: Tool arguments cut off mid-string by a max_tokens stop must never reach the handler, and the call must come back as an LLM-visible recoverable error so the run survives and the model can retry. The fixture is the observed payload, not an invented one: a Write call truncated after ~71 characters to a valid JSON PREFIX with no closing brace. That prefix shape is what makes this the dangerous case rather than merely the broken one — a lenient deserializer can bind file_path successfully and default content, so the tool writes a real file with wrong contents, and the class doc states the harm exactly: executing a side-effecting tool with truncated args is the actual harm. Both halves are asserted, and both are needed: handler-not-invoked alone would be satisfied by a loop that crashed the run, and the error result alone by a loop that executed and then reported an error. Catches a destructive tool executing on a payload the model never finished emitting. P1 with a P0 nomination for the argument-guard component.
requirements: in-process only; Moq streaming agent, no store, no timers, two scripted turns
uncertainties: NOMINATED as the single P0 candidate for the argument-guard component. Criticality justification: the failure produces an irreversible side effect outside the process — a file written with truncated contents, a shell command run half-formed — from input that is malformed rather than wrong, so nothing downstream can detect it. Same consequence class as the approval-gate nomination and, like it, cheap: two scripted turns, no store, no clock. Verified against the existing candidate list: no other row in this slice claims this component.

Contender declined. EmptyToolArgs_ForFunctionRequiringArgs_... covers the same defect family and its comment says it is the shape that actually shipped past the null-only guard, but empty args cannot bind anything, so the realistic outcome there is a deserialization failure rather than a partial execution. The truncated prefix is the one a lenient parser accepts.

The row does not assert WHAT the error says. The class's stated purpose is that the model can retry, which needs the result to identify the malformed-argument cause; any error at all satisfies the assertion as written.

The guard's decision point is not observed, only its effect. Whether the rejection happens at the shared dispatch choke point named in the class summary, or somewhere else that happens to produce the same outcome, is not distinguished.

rationale: A 20KB deferred resolution must be bounded BEFORE it is fingerprinted, persisted and published, and the bounding must not break idempotence: a byte-equal redelivery still reports Duplicate, the second resolve does not throw, and no third provider request is made. The ordering in the name is the substance — fingerprint after bounding, not before — because the two orders diverge exactly on redelivery, which is the case that matters for a resolution arriving twice from a retrying caller. Checking all three copies (published, persisted, and the text carried by the NEXT provider request) is what closes the usual half-fix, where the visible copy is trimmed and the one replayed to the provider is not. The final requests.Count assertion is the non-vacuity guard on the idempotence claim: without it, 'did not throw' would pass on an implementation that quietly started another run. Catches an oversized deferred result reaching history, or bounding that breaks duplicate detection. P1: the deferred ingress path, distinct from the executor one.
requirements: in-process only; Moq streaming agent, InMemoryConversationStore
bounded: 20s run cts, two 10s drain waits, 10s persistence poll
uncertainties: The comment states the mechanism outright — the redelivery 'bounds to the same canonical text, so it is a duplicate' — and that mechanism has a hazard nothing here tests. Two DIFFERENT oversized payloads sharing a 512-byte prefix also bound to the same canonical text, so the second would be classified Duplicate and discarded. Fingerprinting after truncation makes distinct results collide by construction; the row exercises only the byte-equal case, where the answer is right for both orderings.

AssertBounded checks that the marker prefix appears and the text ends with ' bytes]', so the marker's SHAPE is pinned but the byte figure it reports is never compared against the real original length. A marker reporting the wrong size would pass everywhere in this class.

rationale: When a tool handler throws with a 20KB message, the error result must be bounded in all three copies — published, persisted, and the text the NEXT provider request replays — while still being flagged IsError. Exception messages are the ingress nobody sizes: a stack-carrying or payload-echoing exception is written by code that never considered it would be sent to a model, so this is where an unbounded result is most likely to originate. Asserting that requests[1] carries exactly the published bounded string, rather than merely something short, pins that history holds ONE canonical text rather than a trimmed display copy beside a full stored one. Catches an oversized handler failure inflating every later request. P1: the error ingress path for tool results.
uncertainties: Was the bounding component's P0 contender as the likeliest real source of an oversized result. Declined on consequence class: an unbounded result inflates requests and eventually draws a provider rejection, which is loud, recoverable and already approached from another angle by the two ProviderErrorClassifier candidates in this slice. Nothing durable is lost or corrupted and no boundary is crossed, so it does not clear the bar the other nominations meet.

Nothing asserts that the ORIGINAL exception text is recoverable anywhere — a log, a diagnostic field — so as written the class is equally satisfied by an implementation that discards the untruncated message entirely.

The bounded copy is never checked for the leading content of the original; only the cap, the flag and the marker are pinned. A bounding that returned the marker alone, dropping all 512 bytes of actual message, would pass all three rows.

rationale: A result the PROVIDER produced for a tool it ran itself — Anthropic web_search, code execution — is bounded at history ingress, and its ExecutionTarget survives the bounding as ProviderServer. The comment names why this path needs its own row: there is no executor on our side to trim it, so every other bounding site in the loop is bypassed, and the only remaining chokepoint is the shared AddToHistory ingress. It also explains the coverage this buys — the loop only ever sees an IMessage sequence, so streamed and non-streaming-mapped provider responses arrive identically and one row covers both. The second run is not decoration: it proves the BOUNDED text is what the next request replays, which is the whole point, since an unbounded server-tool result silently inflates every subsequent request until the provider rejects the conversation. Catches provider-executed results entering history unbounded. P1: the third and least-guarded ingress path.
requirements: in-process only; no registry functions at all
uncertainties: The claim that this covers BOTH streamed and mapped non-streaming responses rests on the argument in the comment, not on an exercised second shape. It is a sound argument — the loop's input is an IMessage sequence either way — but it is reasoning, not coverage, and it would stop holding the moment a mapping path handled provider-server results before the loop saw them.
The published copy is not asserted here, unlike the other two rows; both ExecuteRunAsync enumerations discard their messages. Only the persisted and replayed copies are checked.

rationale: Firing an armed notify-mode wait puts a <trigger>-tagged USER turn carrying the fire payload into persisted history, delivered through the loop's ordinary queue gate. This is the base delivery contract the whole ordering file builds on: the no-interrupt rows all order a fire against something else and would be satisfied by a fire that never arrived at all, so a positive delivery row is what makes them mean anything. Reading the envelope back from the conversation store rather than from the message stream is deliberate — it proves the injected turn became part of the durable conversation the next request is built from, not merely something a subscriber saw go past. Asserting the payload 'fire-1' is in the text pins that the fire's own content reaches the model rather than a bare wake-up. Catches an armed notify wait whose fires go nowhere. P1: the primary notify delivery contract.
requirements: in-process only; Moq streaming agent, InMemoryConversationStore, ManualTriggerSource
bounded: 5s per run completion and a 5s Wait.UntilAsync on history
uncertainties: The helper's own remark records a precondition caveat: RunCompletedMessage fires whether or not the injected run's provider call succeeds, so waiting on run completion does not by itself prove the injected turn was processed successfully — the history assertion is what carries the weight.
The envelope is matched by substring ('<trigger>' and the payload), so its structure is unconstrained; a malformed envelope containing those substrings would pass.

rationale: A notify fire issued while an LLM stream is open — the generation has started and yielded nothing — must appear in history after that generation's assistant message, delivered as a fresh <trigger>-tagged user turn rather than injected into the turn in flight. The gating is what makes the scenario real: a TaskCompletionSource holds the stream open so the fire is proven to occur mid-generation, not merely nearby in time. Preempting here would splice a user turn into a partially streamed assistant message, which corrupts the transcript and, on a provider that validates turn alternation, breaks the next request outright. The WaitForHistoryAsync helper also closes a vacuity hole its own comment names: on a history that never filled, 'index of X greater than index of Y' degenerates into comparing two -1s, so the wait ensures the ordering assertion is reached only once both messages exist. Catches a trigger preempting an in-flight generation. P1: the no-interrupt guarantee on the generation path.

A notify fire issued while a tool handler is genuinely mid-execution — the handler is blocked on a TaskCompletionSource, so the tool provably has not returned — must still appear in history AFTER that tool's result. This is a different loop path from the generation case and the comment traces it: because the turn HAD a tool call, the run does not end, it polls for new input and folds the queued fire into the SAME run as a second turn. Interrupting here would produce a history in which a tool call is followed by a user turn and only later by its own result, which is a malformed tool-call/result pairing that providers reject outright. The class remarks also record the discipline that makes the whole file trustworthy: it asserts on final history ORDERING, never on wall-clock timing, and gates the in-flight operation so the fire is proven to arrive while it is open. Catches a trigger preempting a running tool. P1: the no-interrupt guarantee on the tool-execution path.

With a block-mode wait parked as deferred and a notify wait armed in the same turn, firing the notify wait must leave the block wait's deferred tool call completely untouched. The assertion is unusually careful and its own comment says why: presence-by-key would pass for a regression that mutated the entry in place — overwriting FunctionArgs, DeferredAtUnixMs or GenerationId while keeping the id — so the row captures the entry BEFORE the fire and compares by record value-equality afterwards, proving every field is unchanged rather than merely that something is still keyed. The consequence of cross-talk is severe and silent: a notify fire that resolved or corrupted a parked block wait would unpark a run that is still waiting on a condition that has not happened, and the model would proceed on a result it never received. Catches one wait's delivery leaking into another wait's parked state. P1: isolation between the two wait modes, and the best-constructed assertion in this class.
requirements: in-process only; Moq streaming agent, InMemoryConversationStore, ManualTriggerSource
bounded: run completions are awaited through LoopSubscription, history through Wait.UntilAsync with a 5s deadline
component: LmMultiTurn.Triggers (notify does not touch block waits)

rationale: Three fires issued back to back surface as three <trigger> turns in the order they were fired. This is a different property from the two no-interrupt rows: they order a fire against an in-flight operation, this one orders fires against EACH OTHER. Losing it produces a conversation in which asynchronous events are narrated out of sequence — the model is told a later thing happened before an earlier one, and reasons on a causal order that never occurred. The row deliberately asserts on relative content ordering and not on how many runs the loop batched them into, which keeps it from breaking on a legitimate batching change. Catches out-of-order or coalesced trigger delivery. P1: the FIFO delivery contract for notify fires.
uncertainties: Each fire is awaited only until its own enqueue returns, so the three enqueues are effectively sequential rather than concurrent. The row pins that a FIFO queue is preserved through delivery; it does not exercise concurrent producers racing at the enqueue point.

rationale: Three non-restorable notify rows are restored into a loop whose input channel holds ONE, with recovery driven deliberately before RunAsync starts the reader. Recovery must complete without blocking, and the two rows whose terminal envelopes could not be enqueued must be RETAINED for the next recovery rather than deleted. The comment documents the exact defect this replaced: restore-time delivery went through a blocking enqueue, so a full channel with no reader left WriteAsync waiting forever — a startup deadlock, the worst failure shape available, because the host never finishes coming up and there is nothing to observe. The retention half is equally deliberate: deleting a row whose envelope was never accepted loses the notification permanently, so the rule is delete-only-on-accept. Bounding RecoverAsync with WaitAsync(5s) is what makes a regression fail as a timeout instead of hanging the whole suite. Catches a recovery deadlock and silently dropped notifications. P1: important failure handling on the startup path.
requirements: in-process only; InMemoryConversationStore and a Dictionary-backed INotifyWaitStore double, no SQLite
uncertainties: The retained count is asserted as terminalRowCount - channelCapacity, which assumes exactly channelCapacity envelopes fit. That is true for a channel drained by nobody, but it couples the assertion to the channel's exact free capacity at that instant rather than to the weaker and more robust property the rule actually states — that no row is deleted unless its envelope was accepted.

rationale: A thread with ZERO persisted message rows but an active notify-wait row is recovered, and the wait is re-armed under its ORIGINAL wait id and then proven to still deliver. The zero-messages setup is the point, not an edge case: notify waits live in their own store keyed only by thread and are not backed by a deferred tool-call placeholder in history, so a restore path gated on message count would silently skip them — and a wait armed on the very first turn has no messages by construction. The row also refuses to stop at re-arming: it fires the restored sink and follows the fire all the way to a <trigger> envelope in persisted history, which is what separates 'a sink object exists' from 'the wait works'. RecoverAsync's own return value is asserted false, pinning that the restore ran despite the message-count-driven return staying unchanged. Catches notify waits lost across a restart. P1: the notify-wait restore contract, which is separate from the block-wait one.
requirements: bounded: 5s on the run-completed drain and 5s on the history wait
uncertainties: The subscription is established by issuing but not awaiting the first MoveNextAsync, with a comment explaining that this registers the subscriber synchronously ahead of the iterator's first suspension point. That is a real ordering fix for a real race, but it depends on an implementation detail of SubscribeAsync's iterator rather than on an observable contract; if that iterator ever suspends earlier, the race returns silently as an intermittent timeout.

rationale: Six argument shapes are rejected with ArgumentException: a malformed duration, a malformed instant, delay and deadline supplied together, non-JSON, a JSON array, and a wrong value type. The contradictory-args case is the discriminating one — it is well-formed JSON with two valid fields, so only a rule that rejects ambiguity catches it, and a parser that took the first field it recognised would pass every other case here. The test name states the consequence directly: a silent fallback arms the wait against its CEILING instead, so a request for a two-minute timer becomes a ten-minute one with no error anywhere. Catches a mis-specified timer firing at the wrong time rather than failing. P1: the argument-validation contract, an important failure path distinct from firing.
requirements: in-process only; pure arm-time validation, no timing

rationale: A five-second timer is disposed and then observed not to fire within 400ms. The contract it names — a disposed timer must not fire into a wait that is gone — is real and worth pinning, but the observation window cannot establish it. P2 on the strength of the assertion rather than the importance of the contract; the demonstrating construction would be a short delay disposed just before it elapses, or a fake clock advanced past the deadline after disposal.
requirements: in-process only; 400ms observation of a 5s timer
uncertainties: Near-vacuous as written: the delay is 5s and the observation window is 400ms, so an implementation where DisposeAsync did nothing at all would also see no fire in that window. The test cannot distinguish 'disposal suppressed the fire' from 'the timer had not yet elapsed'. Flagged as a strengthening candidate, not a removal candidate.

rationale: A 200ms delay fires within a 5-second bound. The bound is a WaitAsync on the sink's completion rather than a sleep, so a timer that never fires fails on the timeout instead of passing quietly. Catches the ordinary relative-delay timer never firing, which strands every block-mode wait built on it until its ceiling. P1: the source's primary behaviour and the baseline the other timing cases vary.
requirements: in-process only; real 200ms wall-clock delay, 5s bound

rationale: Empty args make the timer fire at the wait's ceiling deadline. Catches a timer with no arguments never firing at all, leaving the wait to be torn down by the runtime's own ceiling rather than resolving. P2: an argument-shape variation on the delay case, reaching the same fire through a different instant source.

Armed with an ArmedAt thirty minutes in the past and a five-minute delay, the timer fires at once rather than computing a negative interval. This is the restore-after-restart shape: a persisted wait is re-armed with its ORIGINAL armed-at, so every resumed timer whose moment has passed takes this path. Catches a negative-duration timer that throws on arm or waits the wrong span, which would drop every already-due wait on process restart. P1: the elapsed-arm arm of the resolution, and the one a restart actually exercises.

The write side the whole file depends on: arming in notify mode persists a row carrying the wait id, thread, kind, args, label, max fires and a zero fire count. Nothing above can restore what was never written, and a row missing args or max fires restores into a different wait than the one the caller armed. P1.

A cancelled wait's row is removed at the terminal transition, so the next restart does not resurrect a wait the user explicitly cancelled. The live-path counterpart to the restore-time deletions above. P1.

A deadline that passed while the process was DOWN resolves as timed_out rather than being re-armed on its original TTL. Re-arming an elapsed wait either fires it late against a deadline the caller already gave up on or leaves it live indefinitely. Rank 126 with 10 marginal spans. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 6 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The crash window between persisting the final fire count and deleting the row: restore must drop such a row SILENTLY. Re-arming it with a clamped budget of zero produces a wait that can never fire again yet never self-terminates until its TTL, and notifying again duplicates an envelope the conversation already received. All three assertions — not re-armed, nothing notified, row gone — are needed to separate those outcomes. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: With neither store nor thread id configured the restore is an inert no-op rather than a throw. A configuration boundary on the entry point. P2.

The honest-failure half: a kind that cannot be restored delivers exactly one trigger_lost_on_restart envelope and then the row is DELETED. Both halves matter — silence leaves the conversation waiting forever on something that will never fire, and a retained row re-announces the same loss on every subsequent recovery. P1.

The point of persisting notify waits at all: after a restart a restorable row is re-armed and appears in the live wait list. Without it every wait a conversation was holding dies silently at the first process restart, and nothing ever tells the user. P1.
uncertainties: No row in this file is an inP0Prefix member, so no P0 is proposed here.

rationale: Recovery must never block on a full input channel: with a non-blocking tryNotify wired, every terminal row is attempted, and only rows whose envelope was ACCEPTED are deleted — the two rejected ones are retained for redelivery instead of being lost. Non-vacuous on the second claim too: the blocking delegate throws, so any fallback to it fails the test rather than passing quietly. P1.
A second route to the terminal verdict already held at :100 — a row whose kind is no longer registered at all. Same envelope, same deletion. P2.

A store double cancels the caller's own token mid-save and observes it; ArmAsync must throw rather than return an armed result, and the aborted arm must leave nothing in ListWaits. The recorded defect is precise — the persist step caught ALL exceptions including OperationCanceledException and merely logged, so an abandoned call was reported successful. Both assertions are needed: the throw alone would still permit a dangling live wait holding a disposed source and an unreleased gate. Catches an arm that reports success for a request the caller withdrew, leaving a wait nobody knows about firing into a cancelled conversation. P1: an important failure-handling contract on the arm path, distinct from the fire lifecycle.
requirements: in-process only; store double cancels the caller token

rationale: Cancelling an armed notify wait reports one cancellation and delivers an envelope whose payload mentions cancellation, so the model learns the wait ended rather than being left expecting events that will never come. Catches a silent cancel. P2: a third terminal path over the ceiling and budget arms already pinned, and the payload assertion is a substring match rather than a check on the envelope's structure.
uncertainties: Does not assert the wait left ListWaits, unlike the ceiling and maxFires terminal cases.

rationale: A bounded wait persists fires_so_far on a MIDDLE fire, and the comment names why the construction is the only one that discriminates: fire 1 persists unconditionally and the final fire persists anyway, so maxFires 5 with two fires is the smallest case where fire 2 is neither first, nor a multiple of ten, nor final. Without that reasoning the test would look like an arbitrary two-fire case. Catches a restart resuming a bounded wait from a stale count and re-spending its remaining budget from the beginning. P1: the durable-count contract, distinct from the in-memory budget the sibling test pins.

An unbounded notify wait delivers on both of two fires and is STILL listed as armed afterwards. Asserting the wait survives is the half that separates notify mode from block mode, which retires on its first fire, and it is the non-vacuity partner for the maxFires bound: a runtime that terminated on every fire would satisfy the budget test's teardown assertion. Catches a notify wait that silently degrades to one-shot, so a recurring trigger stops after its first event with no error. P1: the primary notify-mode behaviour.

A notify wait armed with maxFires 2 is fired three times: exactly two envelopes are delivered, none after the budget, and the wait is gone from ListWaits. The over-budget third fire is what makes it a bound rather than a counter — a runtime that delivered on every fire would pass a two-fire test. Catches an unbounded notify wait: a source that keeps firing keeps waking the loop, and each wake sends the whole history to the provider, so a single armed wait becomes an open-ended spend with no user action to stop it. Nominated P0: this is the only bound on how many times an armed wait may re-enter the loop, and it is the criticality argument for the whole Triggers component. Nominating one row for this component rather than one per class. Confirmation held pending the facts join.
requirements: in-process only; manual trigger source, no store
uncertainties: DEMOTED in the end-of-slice P0 prune. Eighteen nominations across 347 in-scope rows is 5.2%, against the lane's healthy 2.4-3.1% band; ten survive. The nomination recorded above stands as the reason this row is the strongest in its component and is NOT withdrawn as an assessment - it is simply not a surviving candidate. Demotion reason: a runaway notify wait announces itself as load and repeated turns. Triggers keeps no candidate, which is the right outcome for a component whose worst failure is noisy.

rationale: The ceiling timer alone — no manual fire — delivers exactly one timed_out envelope and tears the wait down. ContainSingle rather than a presence check is what catches a ceiling that keeps re-firing after expiry. The poll-to-a-deadline rather than a fixed sleep is a real robustness choice, not a hidden pass: the loop exits on the envelope appearing and the assertion runs regardless, so a never-delivered envelope fails after five seconds rather than passing quietly. Catches a wait that outlives its own ceiling and holds its source open forever. P1: the ceiling arm, a distinct terminal path from cancel and from maxFires.
requirements: in-process only; 50ms ceiling with a 5s polled bound

rationale: An unparseable timeout is refused at arm time with its own reason. Accepting it would arm a wait with no ceiling — the one state this runtime has no way to recover from short of a restart. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: An unregistered kind is refused with a typed reason. Input validation on the same admission path whose typed-refusal contract is held at P1 by the concurrency and timeout cases. P2.

The concurrency bound refuses the second arm with the typed max_concurrent_waits reason rather than queueing it invisibly. The bound is what stops a runaway agent arming waits without limit, and the typed reason is what the tool result tells the model. P1.

The selector overload cancels every wait matching a label — two of two here, with the armed set asserted empty afterwards. A different admission path from cancel-by-id, and the one a bulk teardown takes. P1.

Cancelling an unknown id reports zero without throwing, and cancelling an already-terminal wait reports zero rather than one. The count is what a caller reports back, so a second cancel claiming success would tell an operator it stopped something that had already finished. P1.

Cancellation resolves with the cancelled status, disposes the underlying source, AND the test then fires the source anyway to prove no second delivery occurs. That last part is the real claim: a fire arriving after a terminal transition must be a no-op, or the agent receives a result for a call it already abandoned. P1.

The single-resolution latch under a genuine race, twenty-five times: a fire and a cancel dispatched together must produce exactly one resolution. Two resolutions mean the agent receives two results for one deferred tool call, which is the shape that corrupts a turn rather than merely losing one. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 4 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The permitted half of the guard above. Every other test in this file constructs a runtime, so a constructor that always threw could not survive the file regardless. P2.

A parameter inserted before logger in the primary constructor broke every pre-existing positional (options, resolve, logger) caller, so the compat overload must still produce a runtime that arms AND fires — the test drives a real fire through it rather than just constructing. A binary-compat break of this shape compiles fine and fails at load. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: A notify wait store with no thread id is rejected at construction. The store keys its records by thread, so the alternative is a runtime that appears configured and silently persists nothing — discovered only when a restart finds no waits to restore. P1 for failing at configuration time rather than at recovery time.
uncertainties: Holds 2 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The register-window race: for the first two attempts the deferred placeholder is not yet in history and resolve throws, and the runtime must retry rather than drop the resolution. Dropping it loses the result of a real external event and leaves the tool call unanswered forever. P1.

The fire-path token bug: the built-in timer cancels the token its own fire callback carries when it disposes, so delivery must run on an uncancellable token. The fixture reproduces exactly that source and combines it with a transiently failing resolve, so a delivery that honoured the source's token would abandon the retry and lose the result. P1.

A ten-thousand-byte payload is truncated to the configured cap and SAYS SO in the payload the model receives. An untruncated fire is unbounded external text entering the conversation window, and a silent truncation is worse than a loud one because the model cannot tell it is reading a fragment. P1, and the highest exclusive-span row in this file.
uncertainties: Holds 14 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The primary lifecycle end to end: arm through the registration seam, fire, and the wait resolves once with the fired status, the source's payload carried through, and the entry removed from the armed set. Four separate claims about one transition, and the removal is what frees the concurrency slot. P1.

Regression: an earlier version fired synchronously inside ArmAsync and re-inserted the terminal wait, leaving an armed entry that could never resolve. That zombie holds a concurrency slot for the life of the process, so after enough restarts the runtime refuses to arm anything at all. P1.
uncertainties: Shares its fixture with :420; that one pins the status, this one pins the armed set.

rationale: A timer armed thirty minutes ago with a five-minute timeout elapsed while the process was down, and on restart it resolves as FIRED rather than timed out. That distinction is the whole semantic of a restored timer: the time it was waiting for did arrive. P1.
uncertainties: Shares its fixture with the zombie-wait test at :471; neither subsumes the other — this one pins the resolved STATUS, that one pins the armed set.

rationale: A source that cannot be restored resolves the wait as failed with the trigger_lost_on_restart marker rather than dropping it. The wait cannot be honoured after a restart, so the only safe outcome is to say so — a silently discarded wait leaves its tool call unanswered with nothing to look for. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: When re-arming a restored wait is REJECTED — here because the one concurrency slot is already taken by a live wait — the wait resolves failed instead of being left parked forever. The rejection path is easy to leave unhandled precisely because it only fires under load at restart, which is when it matters most. P1.
uncertainties: Holds 3 exclusive product spans, so the P1 floor applies.

rationale: The ceiling timer resolves a wait whose source never fires, exactly once. Without it a blocking wait on a source that goes quiet parks the agent forever with no diagnostic — the failure mode a timeout exists to make impossible. P1.

Args with no mode parse to Block with a null maxFires. The default is the substantive part: the two modes behave oppositely — Block parks the turn until the wait resolves, Notify acknowledges and lets the turn finish — so a wrong default silently changes whether the conversation is blocked. Asserting maxFires stays null alongside stops a default budget being invented for an unbounded wait. Catches every wait that omits mode being armed in the wrong lifecycle. P1: the default-selection contract, a distinct primary behaviour of the parser.

A notify request with maxFires 3 parses to Notify with the budget preserved. The budget is what the runtime later enforces as the only bound on how many times an armed wait may re-enter the loop, so a parser that accepted the mode but dropped the number would arm an unbounded wait from a request that asked for three. Catches the model's stated bound being silently discarded at the boundary. P1: the parser's primary positive contract.

maxFires 0 is rejected rather than parsed. Catches a zero budget being armed, which is either a wait that fires nothing or — if zero is later treated as unset — an unbounded one; the rejection removes the ambiguity at the boundary. P2: a value-range variation on the notify parse.
uncertainties: Covers 0 only; a negative maxFires is not exercised.

rationale: A numeric and a boolean mode are both rejected. Catches a JSON type mismatch throwing out of TryParse instead of returning false, which would fail the turn rather than handing the model a correctable rejection. P2: a JSON-type variation on the unknown-mode case.

An unrecognised mode string is rejected rather than falling back to a default. Catches a misspelled mode arming the opposite lifecycle from the one requested — the failure the default-mode test cannot see, because there the field is absent rather than wrong. P2: an invalid-value variation over the two parses already pinned.

An explicit JSON null mode is accepted and treated as Block, distinguishing an explicitly null field from an invalid one. This is the non-vacuity partner for the non-string rejection: a parser that rejected every non-string mode value would reject null too and fail here. Catches a model emitting an explicit null being told its wait was invalid. P2: a null-shape variation on the default-mode case.

Two timer waits are cancelled by a single kind selector, reporting two and leaving the list empty. Catches a kind selector that cancels only the first match, which would leave a model believing it had cleared its waits while some stayed armed and later woke the loop. P1: the bulk-selector arm, a distinct selection path from cancel-by-id and the one whose partial failure is invisible in the response.

A CancelWait with empty args cancels ZERO waits and leaves the armed one listed. The comment names the rule it protects — Matches requires at least one of id, label or kind — and the consequence is a blast radius: an unfiltered cancel that matched everything would let one under-specified model call tear down every armed wait in the conversation, silently abandoning work the user is waiting on. Asserting the survivor as well as the count is what makes it a no-op rather than merely a zero report. Catches a match-all default on a destructive operation. P1: an important failure-handling contract on the cancel path.

A timer wait with no mode returns Deferred, which is the regression guard the notify test is measured against: without it, a change making every wait return an acknowledgment would satisfy the notify assertion and silently stop block waits parking at all. Catches block mode being lost when notify mode was added. P2: a single-assertion guard whose value is bounding the adjacent notify case rather than pinning behaviour of its own.

A notify-mode Wait must NOT return Deferred; it returns a result whose text reports status armed and mode notify. The negative assertion is the load-bearing one: Deferred parks the tool call, so a notify wait that deferred would block the very turn it was designed to let finish, and the conversation would hang until the wait's ceiling. Reading the serialized text also proves the model is told which mode it got rather than having to infer it. Catches the two modes collapsing into one at the tool boundary. P1: the mode split at the provider seam, distinct from the runtime lifecycle the TriggerRuntime tests pin.
requirements: in-process only; real TriggerRuntime, handlers invoked directly, bounded teardown

rationale: An armed wait appears in ListWaits with its id and kind alongside the registered kinds, is then cancelled by id with a resolved status and a count of one, and the list is empty afterwards. Reading the serialized JSON rather than the runtime's own objects is the point — this is the shape the model actually sees, and a naming-policy change would silently rename every property it reads. Catches a roster the model cannot use to find or cancel its own waits. P1: the read-and-cancel-by-id contract, the provider's primary control surface.
requirements: in-process only; asserts on serialized PascalCase property names

rationale: A process parked on a timer Wait and exited; the deferral row is seeded as armed 30 minutes ago with a 1-minute timeout. On restart the reconcile pass must resolve it. The stated closure condition is the point and the assertion message says it outright: a restored timer wait must not be left hanging. This is the failure mode with no observable symptom — the host comes up clean, the thread looks healthy, and the conversation is simply frozen forever on a timer whose moment passed while the process was down. Constructing the elapsed state as PERSISTED ROWS rather than by waiting is what makes the scenario reachable at all; the alternative would be an unrunnable 30-minute test. Catches a wait that survives a restart as a permanent park. P1: important failure handling on the recovery path.
requirements: in-process only; InMemoryConversationStore seeded through MessagePersistenceConverter
uncertainties: The row asserts only that the deferral CLEARS. Whether it resolves as 'fired' or as 'timeout' — a meaningful difference to the model reading the result, since the timeout elapsed while offline — is not pinned by any assertion here.

The poll is a hand-rolled deadline loop rather than the Wait.UntilAsync helper the sibling trigger classes use, so on regression it fails at the final BeEmpty with the custom because-message rather than at the wait; the outcome is the same but the class is inconsistent with its neighbours.

rationale: A host registers an entirely new trigger kind through TriggerOptions.AdditionalRegistrations, the LLM waits on it, the host fires it out of band, and the run resumes carrying the host's own payload. This is the extension seam's only proof, and it is the claim the feature is sold on: a new kind with NO loop change. The row is stronger than the timer case in one specific way — it asserts the fired payload string reaches the resolved result, so it pins that host-supplied data survives the arm/fire/resolve round trip rather than being replaced by a generic 'fired' marker. Catches an extension point that arms but cannot deliver, or delivers an empty payload. P1: a cross-component contract between the loop and third-party trigger sources.
requirements: in-process only; ManualLoopTriggerSource fires on demand, no timers
uncertainties: The fake source captures the sink into a single field, so only one armed instance is representable. Two concurrent waits on the same host kind — a plausible real shape — cannot be expressed by this double and are covered nowhere in the class.
The registration declares Capabilities(true, false, false) and nothing asserts on capability enforcement; the row would pass on a loop that ignored the capability flags entirely.

rationale: The whole Wait primitive, end to end through the real loop: the LLM calls Wait, the run PARKS with the tool call registered as deferred and exactly one provider call made, the timer fires, the run auto-resumes on its own, and turn two receives the tool result with status 'fired' while the deferral is cleared. Every other trigger row in this lane presupposes this cycle. The parked half is asserted before the resume rather than only afterwards, which is what separates 'the wait parked and then resumed' from 'the wait never parked at all and the loop simply ran twice' — a distinction the end state cannot make. Reading the resolved payload out of the SECOND call's message list proves the result reached the model, not merely the store. Catches a Wait that never parks, never resumes, or resumes without its result. P1: the primary behavior of the trigger feature.
requirements: in-process only; Moq streaming agent, default in-memory store, built-in timer source
uncertainties: Was a Triggers P0 contender as the base park/resume cycle. Declined: the component's single candidate is already NotifyWait_Terminates_WhenMaxFiresReached, and this row costs a real 1s timer delay whereas that one does not. If the lead prefers the primary cycle over the runaway guard, this is the row to swap in.

The 1s delay is a deliberate widening of a race the comment documents in detail — at 150ms a scheduling hiccup let the timer fire before the parked assertions ran. The reasoning given (assertions and the timer callback share the same thread-pool queue, so load delays both) is sound but it is still a wall-clock margin, not a gate; the parked assertions could in principle be starved past a second under extreme load.

The loop task from `_ = loop.RunAsync(cts.Token)` is never observed, so a fault thrown on that path surfaces as a timeout rather than as its own exception. This is the pattern across the whole LmMultiTurn loop family, not specific to this row.

rationale: A Wait on an unregistered kind must FAIL FAST as an inline error result rather than parking: no deferral is created, the tool result is flagged IsError with 'unknown_kind', and the run reaches a normal completion in the same turn so the LLM can self-correct. The alternative failure is the expensive one — parking on a kind nothing will ever fire leaves the run hung until its timeout, and a model that hallucinated a trigger name would stall a conversation for as long as the timeout allows with no diagnostic. Asserting BOTH the empty deferral list and the error result is what makes this a fail-fast row rather than an error-shape row; either alone would pass on a loop that parked and also reported an error. Catches an unknown trigger kind becoming a silent hang. P1: important failure handling on the arm path.
requirements: in-process only; drives ExecuteRunAsync directly rather than the queue
uncertainties: This is the only row in the class that drives ExecuteRunAsync directly instead of SendAsync, and its enumeration is unbounded — a loop that failed to terminate the run would hang the test rather than fail it.

rationale: With the fault scoped to the TERMINAL ledger write only — Queued and InProgress succeed, Completed and Errored throw — CompleteRunAsync must not reach its publish call, and the failure must propagate out of the run loop rather than being swallowed. The comment states the invariant precisely: the ledger is the status API's source of truth, so publishing a RunCompletedMessage after the terminal write failed leaves a subscriber told the run finished while GET /status reports InProgress forever, with no later event to reconcile them. Scoping the fault by RunStatus rather than failing every ledger write is what makes the scenario reachable at all — the run has to start successfully to have a terminal write to fail. Asserting BOTH the missing publish and the propagated exception closes the obvious wrong fix, which is to catch the write failure and publish anyway. Catches an observable completion that the durable record does not support. P1: important failure handling on the run-completion path.
requirements: fixed 200ms delay; leaves a faulted run task whose fault DisposeAsync would re-throw, swallowed in the finally
uncertainties: `received` is a plain List appended from a background subscribe task and read from the test thread with no synchronisation, after a fixed 200ms sleep. The read is unsynchronised across threads, and it is also the row's absence assertion — so a publish that arrived but was not yet visible would read as the desired empty.

The 200ms delay is the only thing sequencing the run against the assertions; a slower runner reaching the assertions before CompleteRunAsync is even called would satisfy the empty-publish check for the wrong reason. The propagated-exception assertion afterwards limits but does not eliminate that, since it awaits the run task and would then observe the fault regardless of ordering.

The finally block swallows InvalidOperationException from DisposeAsync with a documented reason. That is correct for the intended fault, but it would equally hide an unrelated InvalidOperationException raised during disposal.

rationale: Once StartRunAsync folds an accepted input id into the new run's ledger InputIds, the pre-run acceptance record must be cleaned up rather than retained forever. The row establishes the record's presence BEFORE starting the loop and its absence after, so the disappearance is demonstrated rather than assumed — the standard failure of an absence assertion, which is that the thing was never there, is closed here by construction. The consequence of skipping the cleanup is not a crash but a slow one: accepted-input records accumulate for every input ever sent, and the set that is supposed to mean 'accepted but not yet folded into a run' comes to mean nothing at all, so any recovery logic reading it re-processes inputs that already ran. Catches a two-phase durability record that never completes its second phase. P1: the lifecycle half of the accepted-input contract.
requirements: fixed 150ms delay after starting the loop
uncertainties: The row asserts the record is gone but never asserts the other half of its own premise — that the id actually appears in the run ledger's InputIds. A regression that removed the acceptance record WITHOUT folding it into any run would pass, and that is the strictly worse outcome: the input is then recorded nowhere at all.

The 150ms delay is a fixed sleep; if the loop had not yet drained, the record would still be present and the row fails loudly, so this direction is safe — but it makes the row load-sensitive rather than wrong.

rationale: The ordinary accepted send: a populated SendReceipt comes back with a non-empty ReceiptId, the caller's own InputId and a QueuedAt bracketed between timestamps taken either side of the call, and the accepted-input record is readable IMMEDIATELY — synchronously as part of the call, with no loop ever started. That last part is the substantive claim, and the loop deliberately not running is what proves it: the record cannot have been written by a drain that never happened. This row is also the non-vacuity partner for the two failure rows, which assert absence; without it a send that recorded nothing at all under any condition would satisfy them both. Catches a receipt returned for work that was never durably accepted. P1: the primary behavior of TrySendAsync.
requirements: in-process only; no loop, no delay, no fault injection
uncertainties: The method name and the closing comment claim an ordering invariant — recorded BEFORE the channel write — that this row cannot observe. CallLog contains store calls only; no channel write is ever logged, so an implementation that enqueued first and recorded second would produce exactly the same log and pass. The ordering is actually evidenced by the store-failure row's zero-drain check, not here.

`accepted.Should().Contain(receipt.ReceiptId)` asserts on the RECEIPT id while the record was made under the caller's inputId 'happy-1'; the row also asserts CallLog contains 'RecordAccepted:happy-1'. The two hold together only if ReceiptId equals the supplied inputId, which the row neither states nor checks — so it silently depends on an identity relationship rather than pinning it.

rationale: Two sends fill a capacity-2 channel, a third is rejected with a null receipt, and the compensating remove must undo the REJECTED input's accepted-input record while leaving the two queued ones intact. Both directions of the rollback are asserted, and that is the whole point: a compensation that fires too little leaves a durable record for an input that will never run, so the status API reports work that is queued forever; a compensation that fires too broadly erases the records for inputs that ARE queued, so real runs become invisible to the same API. Presence-only or absence-only assertions each catch exactly one of those. Constructing the full condition takes no loop, no timer and no fault injection — a tiny channel and a drain loop deliberately not started — so this is the cheapest row in the class and the one that exercises the complete record/attempt/compensate transaction. Catches a durable accepted-input ledger drifting from what is actually queued. P1 with a P0 nomination for the send-durability component.
requirements: in-process only; InMemoryConversationStore behind a forwarding wrapper, no loop started, no delay
uncertainties: NOMINATED as the single P0 candidate for the send-durability component after reading all five rows. Criticality justification: the accepted-input ledger is what the REST status API answers from, and this is the only row that pins both halves of the compensation, so it is the one whose failure means the ledger and the queue can disagree in either direction. It is also the cheapest row here — no run loop, no fixed delay, no faulted task left behind — so it costs nothing to run first. Verified against the existing candidate list: no other row in this slice claims this component.

Contenders declined, with reasons. TrySendAsync_WhenStoreRecordFails_...NeverWritesToChannel — the strongest CONSEQUENCE in the class (an enqueue with no durable record is work the status API cannot see), but its proof rests on a fixed 150ms delay and a bare zero-count, so it is both slower and weaker as an assertion. TrySendAsync_HappyPath_... — cheapest of all, but its central 'before the channel write' claim is not actually observable in its call log (see that row's own note), so it is a poor baseline. CompleteRunAsync_WhenTerminalLedgerUpsertFails_... — a genuinely severe invariant, but it costs a 200ms delay and deliberately leaves a faulted run task the finally block has to swallow.

The rejection is produced by exhausting a capacity-2 channel with no reader. That is a faithful model of a full queue but not of the other way a real deployment reaches this path — a reader present and simply too slow — which no row covers.

rationale: When the durable accepted-input write throws, the exception must propagate to the caller (the comment maps it to an HTTP 500) and NOTHING may reach the input channel. The second half is the one that matters: a send that swallows the store failure and enqueues anyway produces a run with no durable record — it executes, consumes a provider call and mutates the conversation, while the status API that reads the ledger has no idea it exists. That is worse than a rejected send, because the caller is told it failed and the work happens anyway. The absence is checked behaviorally rather than by inspecting internals: the loop is started afterwards and asked how many inputs it drained, which means a regression is caught wherever the enqueue happened rather than only at one seam. Catches a durability failure that silently degrades into untracked work. P1: important failure handling on the accept path.
requirements: fixed 150ms delay after starting the loop
uncertainties: The zero-drain assertion is an absence with no positive control inside its own row: nothing here shows that DrainedInputCount would have moved within 150ms had something been enqueued. The fold-cleanup row supplies that evidence indirectly (its loop drains and cleans up within the same 150ms window) but on a different agent instance, so the two are coupled only by construction. A regression that made draining slower than 150ms would turn this row green.
