150ms is a fixed sleep, not a gate on any observable, so it is a load-sensitive margin rather than a wait.

rationale: A type implementing only the original IMultiTurnAgent surface still compiles, and the default TrySendAsync throws NotSupportedException (:18) without incrementing SendCount (:19) - so the optional send is never silently rerouted into the required one, which would make a legacy agent deliver a message its author wrote no path for. JoinedSubscriptionTests.LegacyAgent_DefaultOptionsForwardAndOptionalCapabilitiesThrow is the representative for this default-member compatibility contract and covers the forwarding overload plus two optional capabilities. This row adds only the no-side-effect claim on one member, a second case on an axis that P1 row already covers. P2.

A child whose canonical AgentId is literally 'primary' must not be captured by the alias: resolving 'primary' returns that child (name 'worker', :219) and the root remains reachable by its own id (:220). If the alias won, a message meant for the conversation root would land on whichever agent happened to be identified 'primary'. This is the id-precedence variation of Resolve_PrimaryAlias_PreservesTheRootsNameAndIdentity (the P1 representative), on an axis the class's canonical-over-name test already covers. P2.

A root registered as either 'conversation' or 'primary' resolves through the built-in alias to the root's own AgentId while still reporting the name it was registered under (:183-186), an unregistered synonym such as 'lead' stays NotFound rather than being guessed at (:187), and after the root is retained the alias still resolves but reports IsLive false (:189-190). The alias is what lets a descendant address the top level at all, so a break here either misdirects those messages or hides that the target has left. Representative for alias resolution in this class. P1.

A second agent asking for a name a live agent holds is admitted and granted the name suffixed with its own ordinal, reviewer-2, exactly. Production hit the old behaviour: finance-controller named two agents and the task board could only tell the model to pass the agent id instead. The mutation that must go red is binding the requested name rather than the granted one. P1: the grant itself; its resolution consequence is the component P0 below.

After two agents ask for one name, the plain name resolves to the first agent and the suffixed name to the second, and the first agent leaving does not brick either. This is the one contract of the directory whose silent failure is worst: a name that resolves to the wrong agent delivers one agent's reply to a different agent, and no caller can detect it, whereas every other directory failure surfaces as a refusal. The old latch refused both permanently, which cost both agents an address but at least failed loudly. Nominated as the component baseline the class previously lacked; no coverage capture exists for this row, so the tier rests on the contract alone.
uncertainties: No coverage capture exists for this branch's rows; the P0 stands on the contract, not on rank or prefix.

rationale: A name held by a RETIRED agent is still suffixed for a newcomer, and the plain name keeps resolving to the retired agent with IsLive false. A retained entry outlives its agent so a sender learns its target ended rather than never existed; reusing the name would turn that answer into a silent redirect to an unrelated agent. P1: the retirement arm of the grant, with the opposite temptation from the live case.

When the ordinal-suffixed name is itself already held - a model literally named an earlier agent reviewer-2 - the grant keeps going to reviewer-2-1 and the earlier agent keeps its name. The pathological variation of the grant the P1 row pins, over the same loop. P2.

An agent whose id is not an ordinal - a root's thread id - is suffixed with the id itself, reviewer-thread-xyz, since there is no number to borrow and the id is the only thing guaranteed unique. A suffix-source variation of the grant; an ugly name beats a colliding one. P2.

A child that asks for the name primary is granted primary-child, and the alias keeps resolving to the root while the child resolves under its granted name. primary is the one name every agent can rely on to reach the top of the conversation, so a child claiming it used to brick the alias for the whole hierarchy. Replaces the alias-collision latch row; the alias-resolution representative in this class is Resolve_PrimaryAlias_PreservesTheRootsNameAndIdentity. P1: the suffixing rule applied to the one name whose loss affects every agent.

agent-1 registered under the name agent-2 is granted agent-2-1; once agent-2 exists, Resolve(agent-2) is agent-2 and Resolve(agent-2-1) is agent-1. Resolution consults ids before names, so without the guard the name was honoured only until agent-2 was minted and then silently meant the newcomer (PR #764 review F-005). Mutation: dropping IsOrdinalAgentId from GrantAndBindName. P1: the routing invariant that a granted name keeps pointing at its recipient.

agent-1 asking for the name agent-1 is granted it unsuffixed and resolves to itself. The one ordinal-shaped name that is not a lie; the exclusion keeps the guard from manufacturing a collision with nobody. P2: the boundary case of the ordinal-shape rule.

After TryWithdraw on a queued agent, FindById is null, Resolve(reviewer) is NotFound, and a second registration asking for reviewer is granted reviewer and resolves to the newcomer. Retirement keeps entry and name for an agent that existed; a spawn that threw before its first turn was never announced, and keeping its reservation suffixed the caller's retry for no reason (PR #764 review F-004). Mutations: delegating to TryMarkRetained, or leaving the name binding in place. P1: the directory half of the withdrawal contract.

TryWithdraw returns false for an agent that ran and retired and for an unknown id, and the retired entry and its name are untouched. Withdrawal must not be able to turn FINISHED into never-existed for a later sender. P2: the refusal side of the withdrawal contract.

A child is spawned under a name equal to a peer's AgentId; CheckAgents on that string resolves to the peer and returns no transcript rows for it (:999-1000), and WaitForAgents reports not_waitable naming the peer rather than quietly waiting on the local child (:1004-1005). Two rules in one: a canonical identifier beats an owned child's name, and resolving an agent you do not own does not grant you wait ownership over it. Getting either wrong makes a caller block on, or read the transcript of, an agent that is not the one it addressed. P1.

The name GetAgents publishes for a spawned child is marked resolvable (:925), and that same string then drives WaitForAgents, CheckAgents - which resolves to the child's agent_id and reports it completed (:931-932) - and SendMessage, whose delivery restarts that child carrying the sent body (:946). The roster is the only place a model learns how to address anyone, so a name that lists but does not act leaves it holding an address it cannot use. P1.

From one, two and three levels down, the roster gives the root row its registered name and exactly the one alias 'primary' (:881-885); sending to that alias reaches the root's write endpoint with the caller correctly identified (:898-899); CheckAgents resolves it to the root's id (:903); and WaitForAgents answers not_waitable rather than pretending a descendant can wait on the top level (:907-908). This is how a deep sub-agent reports back to the conversation at all. P1.

Through the real tool surface: after a peer registers under a name the caller's own child already holds, the peer's granted name differs, CheckAgents on the plain name reports nothing not found, SendMessage to it is accepted, the directory resolves the plain name to the child and the granted name to the peer, every roster row is published as resolvable, and WaitForAgents by id still works. Replaces the contested-name row that pinned both agents losing the name. Previously CheckAgents reported not_found, WaitForAgents errored and SendMessage refused with ambiguous_name for a name that was a good address a moment earlier. P1: the end-to-end shape of the collision policy across every surface that resolves a name.

For both the root's own name and the primary alias, a peer asking for that name leaves the root's roster row resolvable with its one alias intact, and both names still resolve to the root in the directory. These two names are how every agent reaches the top of the conversation; a child claiming one used to leave it resolving to nothing for the whole hierarchy, and the roster had to advertise the root as unaddressable by name. Replaces the row that pinned that honest-but-broken advertisement. P1.

With no detail argument, a child row carries description, parent_name naming the root, status and is_you false, and carries NO agent_id, usage or transcript_readable; the root row carries no parent_name. The default listing is what a model reads to decide whom to contact, and ids and usage are paid for on every call by every agent that lists the roster, so they are opt-in. Asserting the absences is what makes the split a contract rather than a default. P1: the primary shape of the discovery surface.

With detail=detailed, a child row carries its agent_id, delegation_depth and transcript_readable plus a usage block whose totals, attempt count and per_model breakdown - keyed by effective model, in order, with per-model totals - match three records written to the ledger under the root thread and the child's sub-agent thread, and the root row carries its own totals under its own model. Usage is a VIEW over the one ledger the loop already keeps, keyed by execution, so the per-agent figures sum to the conversation total by construction; a view keyed wrongly would bill a child's tokens to the root. P1: the primary content of detailed mode.

With a ledger attached but nothing recorded, every detailed row carries an agent_id and no usage block at all. A zero would claim the agent spent nothing; an absent block says nothing was recorded, and only the second is true of an agent that has not run. P1: the distinguishing case that stops usage being a constant zero-filled block.
With no ledger wired, detailed mode still lists ids and omits usage without erroring. The unconfigured-host variation of the omission the sibling pins with a ledger present. P2.

An unrecognised detail value - verbose, or the empty string - is refused with text naming both valid values. A typo that quietly returned the smaller shape would have the caller conclude the ids are gone rather than that it asked wrongly. P1: the refusal that keeps the two shapes distinguishable.
The GetAgents contract carries an optional detail parameter whose description names normal, detailed and usage. Description text; the behaviour behind it is pinned by the shape rows. P2.

A SendMessage to a near-miss target is refused with text naming the registered peer by NAME and, after it, its id. The refusal a mistyped target gets is the model's main lesson in how peers are addressed, and production shows what the old one taught: 61 conversations were answered with a pointer at GetAgents for current agent_ids, a sentence that named nobody and pointed at the ordinal. P1: the correction contract on the messaging surface.

With one live peer and one retained peer, the unknown-target refusal names the live one and NOT the retired one. GetAgents lists retained agents on purpose so a sender learns its target is gone, but this sentence answers a different question - then who? - and offering a finished agent walks the model straight back into a refusal. P1: the filter that distinguishes the correction roster from the listing roster.

WaitForAgents on an unknown target returns unknown_agent whose text names the caller's own spawned child and NOT a registered peer. The two rosters are deliberately different and this is the case that tells them apart: WaitForAgents covers only agents the caller spawned, so naming a peer it may message but never wait on would answer the refusal with a target that earns the same refusal again. P1.

Through the Agent tool with a template whose factory throws, the spawn named doomed leaves Resolve(doomed) NotFound and only the root in the directory snapshot; a healthy retry under the same name is granted doomed unsuffixed and is live. The end-to-end form of withdrawal on the failed-spawn path (PR #764 review F-004). Mutation: the catch calling RetireAgent instead of WithdrawAgent. P1: a caller's retry after a provider failure must not come back under a different name.

A WorkflowController entry registered with executionId ctl-thread-1 and a ledger row filed under that thread shows agent_id wfctl-wf-1 and a usage block of 33 tokens under model-ctl in the detailed roster. The controller's directory id and its thread share nothing, so without the declared join the roster showed a controller that had spent nothing while the ledger held its rows (PR #764 review F-007). Mutation: UsageByAgentIndex.TryGet ignoring entry.ExecutionId. P1: the usage view's correctness for the one agent kind whose id does not derive its execution.

The detailed roster row carries depth equal to structural_depth; no row of the compact roster carries depth. The pre-ADR-0019 listing published structural depth under this key, so a reader written against it still finds it in detailed (PR #764 review F-001, partial). Mutation: removing the alias. P2: a compatibility key, not a routing invariant.

With one local slot held by a blocking child and a zero-length defer queue, the Agent tool refuses the spawn named overflow with queue_full, Resolve(overflow) is NotFound afterwards, and a retry through a manager with room is granted overflow unsuffixed. The other pre-start failure beside a throwing factory: admission succeeded and the bounded queue then refused, with no receipt ever naming the agent (PR #764 review F-004 re-review). Mutation: the pre-enqueue catch calling RetireAgent instead of WithdrawAgent. P1.

Across a tool turn the default stream keeps the provider's own MessageOrderIdx for both the tool call and its result (:334-335) while the joined stream renumbers to canonical block indices (:336-337). Raw consumers index into provider-shaped blocks, so a canonical index leaking into the default stream would shift every one of their correlations by one. P1.

While a deferred tool result is being replaced, the code that runs during joined publication observes history already carrying the resolved value (:534); the default stream delivers RunCompleted (:568-569) and run completion parks on the history boundary instead of racing past it, so the joined consumer sees the resolved result (:589) with exactly one RunCompletedMessage, last (:590-591). A joined consumer that received completion before the replacement was committed would persist the pending placeholder as the final answer. P1.

SubscribeAsync(default) and SubscribeAsync(SubscribeOptions.Joined, default) both bind and return a stream on the concrete agent (:510-511) and through the IMultiTurnAgent interface (:513-514). The real claim is overload resolution - adding the options overload must not make the bare 'default' call ambiguous for existing callers - and the assertions go no further than not-null. It complements LegacyAgent_DefaultOptionsForwardAndOptionalCapabilitiesThrow (P1) rather than pinning behaviour of its own. P2.

A deferred tool call's placeholder result is published on the default stream with the provider index 2 (:191) while history records the canonical 3 (:192-197), and when the call is later resolved the replacement republished on the default stream still carries 2 (:204). Deferral resolution happens outside the original run, which is exactly where the two numbering schemes are easiest to confuse; a raw consumer that received the canonical index would attach the answer to the wrong block. Representative for this claim; the store-recovery variant is Recovered_deferred_resolution_retains_raw_index_and_canonical_history_order. P1.

A reasoning update followed by two identical finalized summaries collapses to exactly one thinking TextMessage on the joined stream (:290-296) while the default stream keeps all four provider fragments untouched (:297-298) and the encrypted signature remains in history (:299-302). Delivering the summary once per finalization would show a user the same thought three times; dropping the signature would break the provider replay that depends on it. P1.

A snapshot taken before a later append still reports two entries and holds the same checkpoint instance rather than a copy of it (:482-484), while a fresh snapshot shows all three messages in order (:485-489); a joined subscription cancelled while awaiting its next message throws OperationCanceledException (:490-494). Callers hold a snapshot across awaits, so a live view would mutate under them, and a joined subscriber that ignored cancellation would leak an enumerator per abandoned client. P1.

Two separately emitted, byte-identical finalized reasoning blocks (:269-274) both survive into the joined stream (:275). This is the guard rail on the dedup that Finalized_reasoning_summary_is_delivered_once_with_signature_preserved (the P1 representative) asks for: collapsing a summary against its own updates must not become collapsing by content, or a model that genuinely repeated itself loses a block. One assertion on an axis that P1 row covers. P2.

A subscriber that joins after a run has started replays the run assignment (:406-407) and then the canonical TextMessage rather than the raw update that produced it (:416-417), receives the message appended after it subscribed exactly once (:418-419), and sees the stream end when the agent is disposed (:421). This is the defining behaviour of a joined subscription: a duplicated or missing tail at the replay-to-live boundary makes every late-joining client render a wrong conversation, and there is no larger test that would catch it first. P0.

When the replay buffer is too small to hold the prefix, the first thing a joining subscriber receives is a StreamRecoveryMessage with reason ReplayTruncated (:455-460), and live messages continue after it (:461-463). Serving a silently truncated replay is worse than serving none: the consumer believes it holds the whole run and never resyncs. P1.

Whether or not the provider emits its own finalization, the joined stream carries exactly one assistant TextMessage with the right text (:90-95) and no update fragments of any kind (:96-98), while the default stream still carries the provider's fragments and its finalization verbatim (:99-100), history holds a single assistant text (:101), and both streams complete exactly once (:102-103). The joined/default split is the whole point of the subscription feature: leaking fragments or finalizing twice would make every joined consumer render duplicate assistant turns, and canonicalizing the default stream would break every existing raw consumer. Small critical baseline for this component. P0.

An implementation of only the original interface gets a default SubscribeAsync overload that returns its own stream (:23-24) and forwards the caller's cancellation token unchanged (:26-28), while the capabilities it never implemented - the joined subscription and GetHistorySnapshot - throw NotSupportedException instead of returning something empty (:31-32). Every existing fake and custom agent in and outside this repo is a legacy implementer; a default that swallowed the token or returned an empty history would fail silently in all of them. Representative for the default-member compatibility contract. P1.

Appending both a streaming fragment and its finalized message (:501-502) leaves the public snapshot holding a single TextMessage (:503). History is what a follow-up run replays to the provider and what persistence writes down, so a leaked update fragment resends partial text as if it were a completed turn. P1.

After RecoverAsync rehydrates a thread whose deferred tool result was persisted, resolving that call republishes with the persisted default index 2 (:257) while the history snapshot reports the canonical 3 (:258-263). Same claim as Deferred_resolution_preserves_default_result_index_after_canonical_normalization (the P1 representative), reached through recovery from a store rather than a live run. A second case crossing an axis already covered. P2.

Restoring two batches on top of an existing message produces one exact index sequence (:687-691) covering continuation within a generation, an interleaved second generation, a dropped update fragment, a message carrying no generation at all, and int.MaxValue saturation (:631-685). Restore is how a recovered conversation is rebuilt before the next turn, so a wrong order replays the conversation to the provider out of sequence. P1.

Restoring 2000 messages with distinct generation ids reads those ids fewer than ten times per message (:615) and keeps every message (:616). This is a complexity guard against a quadratic rescan of earlier rows on a long recovered conversation, not a behavioural contract - the ordering correctness it sits next to is pinned by Restore_history_preserves_per_generation_order_across_batches (P1). P2.

With a one-slot output channel a subscriber that falls behind gets what it can (:435-436), then a StreamRecoveryMessage with reason SlowConsumer (:437-442) and its stream ends (:443), while every appended message still reaches history (:444). Without this the slowest consumer applies backpressure to the agent loop itself, so one stalled UI would stall the run. P1.

Thinking text, ordinary text and a plain reasoning update surface as three separate joined TextMessages in emission order with the thinking flag preserved (:127-131) and distinct (GenerationId, MessageOrderIdx) pairs so nothing collides (:132); no reasoning message type reaches the joined stream at all (:137), and the encrypted reasoning stays in history only (:138-141). Merging a thought into the answer misattributes it to the user-visible reply, and publishing encrypted reasoning would hand consumers provider-opaque material they must not store or display. P1.

Over a tool turn the joined stream delivers exactly tool call, tool result, text, usage, then completion in that order (:369-381), and the history snapshot captured at the moment the completion message arrives already contains the tool call, its result, the assistant text and the usage (:382-385) while the default stream still carries the provider's update forms (:386-387). Consumers persist or render on RunCompleted, so history that is not ready at that instant silently loses the turn it was supposed to describe. P1.

An already-cancelled token handed to the deprecated positional overloads throws OperationCanceledException through all four routes - concrete and interface, scoped and unscoped (:173-176, :179-182). A shim that dropped the token would let a cancelled listing run to completion against the store. Second axis on the same deprecated surface whose behaviour LegacyListingOverloads_PreservePaginationAndScope (P1) covers, and it exercises only the file store. P2.

For each of the sqlite, file and in-memory stores the deprecated positional overloads still return the same page unscoped and the correct tenant-and-owner-scoped row (:90-93) whether called through the interface, a decorating store or the concrete type (:110-111), and the current options-based overloads keep working with named, defaulted and exclusion arguments (:114-122, :153-156). Scope here is a tenancy boundary, so a forwarding shim that dropped it would list another tenant's conversations to an authenticated caller. Representative for this overload surface. P1.

A spawn followed by two manager follow-ups produces exactly three provider calls (:355), and the third call's history contains exactly one copy of the original task and of each follow-up (:356-358). A warm agent backed by a conversation store can re-append what it recovered on every resumption; the duplicates inflate every later prompt, cost tokens on each turn, and present the model with a conversation in which the user repeated itself. P1.

Whether the first run succeeded or threw, a direct send into the completed loop flips it back to Running before the provider is reached (:146-148) on the same monitor generation, so the fault guard stays valid (:150-151); the follow-up run completes without error and its reply is delivered (:176-178); the provider sees the original task, the earlier reply and the follow-up as one history (:179-184); the owned provider is still alive after completion (:186) and is disposed only at manager shutdown (:188). Warm resumption is this component's baseline - if the loop or its provider died at completion, every follow-up would either restart cold or throw ObjectDisposedException. P0.

When a follow-up run is already executing at the moment the previous run's completion is classified, the spawn caller's awaited result is the new run's answer, not the stale one (:242), with both provider calls and both classifications actually observed (:243-244). Settling on the superseded completion hands the caller an answer to a question that has since been replaced, which is indistinguishable from the agent ignoring the follow-up. P1.

A sub-agent that parks on a non-question deferred tool call stays Running and its foreground spawn caller's task stays uncompleted (:309-310); resolving the deferral drives a second provider call and only then does the caller receive the resolved answer (:317-319). Settling the caller at the deferral would return an empty or partial result while the work it asked for was still outstanding, and the real answer would arrive with no one waiting for it. P1.

Two background spawns ask for reviewer: the first receipt says reviewer, the second receipt reports a DIFFERENT granted name starting with reviewer-, and TryGetAgent by plain name, by granted name and by each id resolves to the right runtime instance - asserted by reference identity, not string equality. The mutation that must go red is restoring the unconditional name-map overwrite: the old code logged a warning and silently re-pointed the name at the newcomer, so a caller mid-conversation with the first agent started addressing the second. This is the collaboration-OFF path the directory does not arbitrate, so it needs its own baseline; P0 because a name reaching the wrong runtime is a misdelivery nothing reports. No coverage capture exists for this row.
uncertainties: No coverage capture exists for this branch's rows; the P0 stands on the contract, not on rank or prefix.

rationale: A newcomer asking for the name of a FINISHED agent is granted reviewer-2, and the plain name still reaches the finished agent. A finished sub-agent stays addressable for follow-ups - the capacity refusal tells callers exactly that - so reassigning its name would send those follow-ups to a different agent. P1: the retirement arm of the grant on the manager path, mirroring the directory's.

When an earlier agent was literally named reviewer-3, the third agent asking for reviewer is granted reviewer-3-1 and all three remain individually addressable as distinct runtimes. The pathological variation of the grant loop the P0 pins. P2.

Peek by the name a spawn was given returns the payload for that agent's id. A name is an address for messaging, so an observation surface that took ids only told a model that had just messaged analyst that analyst did not exist. P1: the name arm of the observation surface the id-based Peek row pins.

Peek on an unknown target throws ArgumentException saying Unknown sub-agent rather than Unknown agent ID, because the lookup takes a name too and an id-only message sends a caller who passed a name to look in the wrong place. A single-assertion lookup boundary; replaces the id-worded row. P2.

The completion block a background child sends its parent carries name="reviewer" - the granted name - with the template under its own attribute, the completed task line follows, and the envelope's Label is the same granted name. The name attribute used to carry the template, so a parent that spawned reviewer was told general-purpose finished and had to reconcile the id itself; the block is the parent's most-read sentence about a child, and the block and the envelope label are asserted together so the two cannot name the agent differently. P1: the naming contract on the completion notification, beside the wrapped-result row that pins the body.

Collaboration-OFF path: a spawn asking for the id the spawn after next will be given is granted a suffixed name; once that id is minted, the granted name still reaches the agent it was granted to and the id reaches the agent that owns it. TryResolveAgentId consults ids before names, so the legacy map had the same shadowing hole the directory had (PR #764 review F-005). The future id is computed from the first spawn's ordinal so the fixture cannot drift from the allocator. Mutation: dropping the IsOrdinalAgentId guard in GrantLegacyName. P1.

AttributeValue maps ampersand, double quote, angle brackets, CR and LF to their entity forms, leaves a plain name alone and maps null to empty. Names are unvalidated model input and SubAgentResultParser correlates a completion by the FIRST id attribute it finds, so an unescaped name carrying quote-id-equals could re-attribute a completion to another agent (PR #764 review F-003). P1: the escaping table itself, one row per character class.

A background child spawned under the name evil-quote-id-equals-agent-9 produces a completion block in which the parser's own id regex finds the child's real id first, and the name attribute reads name=evil" id="agent-9. The end-to-end form of the escaping claim, against the regex the workflow parser uses (PR #764 review F-003). Mutation: interpolating state.Name raw in the envelope. P1: a forged id in a name must not move a completion to another agent.

A background child whose first call throws, spawned under the name evil-quote-id-equals-agent-9, produces an [Error] block in which the parser's id regex finds the real id first and the name attribute is entity-escaped. The error envelope is a separate producer from the completed one and the parser cannot tell them apart (PR #764 review F-003 re-review). Mutation: interpolating state.Name raw in the error envelope only. P1.

A background child parked on an AskUserQuestion call, spawned under the forged-id name, produces an [AwaitingAnswer] descendant-question block in which the first id attribute is the real id and the name is entity-escaped. The awaiting block's id is what the root uses to route the human's answer, so a forged id there would misroute the reply (PR #764 review F-003 re-review). Mutation: interpolating state.Name raw in the awaiting envelope only. P1.

With the descendant-question notification parked (:244-245), the child's pending AskUserQuestion is answered (:250-253, :258) and the delayed-result successor run it mints reaches the provider before the notification is released (:260). Same admission-gate barrier as ABlockedParentRelay_DoesNotHoldUpTheNextRunOfTheWarmChild (the P1 representative), reached through the delayed-result route rather than a direct message. P2.

While the parent's SendAsync is parked mid-relay and the completion has been classified (:95-96), a direct follow-up into the warm child is admitted and reaches the provider (:102, :104). The manager shares one gate between completion handling and run admission, so holding it across the relay would make a warm child's next run wait on the parent's backpressure - the exact cost warm retention exists to avoid. Representative for this barrier contract. P1.

The same barrier with the durable metadata push parked instead of the parent relay (:126-127): the follow-up run is still admitted and reaches the provider (:131, :133). A second blocking side effect on the axis ABlockedParentRelay_DoesNotHoldUpTheNextRunOfTheWarmChild (the P1 representative) already covers, differing only in which awaited peer is stalled. P2.

When the notification for the CURRENT parked question throws, the sub-agent's completion latch faults with that same exception (:421-425), its status becomes Error and the failure is logged exactly once (:426-427), and the single concurrency permit is released so the next spawn can run (:428-431); the pending question is still answerable and its later run settles a fresh latch (:446-449). Swallowing the failure would leave a caller awaiting a latch nothing will ever complete while the permit stays held, which stalls the whole manager. P1.

The mirror case: a notification failure belonging to a superseded completion is logged (:344) but must not touch the child, which stays Running with its completion latch and monitor still open (:345-348); a second spawn queues rather than stealing the permit (:370); and when the successor answers, both children settle (:373-377) with exactly one AwaitingAnswer and one Completed relay per agent (:378-391). Faulting on a stale side effect would kill a live run and release a permit that is still in use. Complements AFailedCurrentQuestionNotification_FaultsItsCompletionAndReleasesCapacity by pinning the opposite outcome for the opposite ownership, so neither is redundant. P1.

With the terminal durable push still parked, a follow-up run is admitted and publishes Running into the collaboration directory (:199-201); releasing the stale push then leaves the directory at Running (:207-213) and the sub-agent state Running (:214). Running the side effects off the admission gate is precisely what lets a newer run overtake them, so a late one that re-published 'completed' would make every other agent in the hierarchy treat a live delegate as finished and stop waiting on it. P1.

A non-terminal (pending-messages) completion leaves the owned provider undisposed (:337-340) and the sub-agent still reading as running (:341); the terminal completion - waited for on the published 'completed' status, so the branch demonstrably ran - still leaves the provider undisposed (:347-361); and manager shutdown disposes it exactly once (:366). Provider ownership following the loop rather than the run is the premise the whole warm-resumption change rests on: dispose at completion and the very next continuation throws, never dispose and every completed child leaks a provider. Small critical baseline for this component. P0.

A completed run rebuilds nothing and never touches the owned provider (:454-457); a restart whose send fails reuses the live loop, and its cleanup attempts that provider's disposal once (:465-472); the next continuation, now facing a disposed loop, rebuilds both agent and provider and retries the still-pending disposal before overwriting the slot (:478-487), leaving the resumed run live (:488). Skipping the retry loses the live provider handle the moment the slot is replaced, so it can never be released. P1.

Five spawns that fail after admission each throw (:166-167) and consume no part of the ceiling, since the full retained bound is still spawnable afterwards (:171-175). Admission is taken before the spawn can fail, so a pre-start exit that forgot the slot would shrink the ceiling silently until no spawn succeeds at all. A leak-regression pin on a failure path of the accounting that SequentialSpawnsPastTheRetainedBound (P0) and WarmResumingAnAlreadyAdmittedSubAgent (P1) establish. P2.

Twelve spawns released simultaneously against a ceiling of four admit exactly four and refuse the rest (:214-217), leaving exactly four agents registered (:218). A check-then-take admission passes every sequential test and still lets concurrent callers all read 'room left' and all take it, which is the one failure mode the sequential bound test can never see. P1.

Every child completes before the next is requested, so the concurrency gate is free each time and refuses nothing (:76-82); the spawn past the retained bound is nevertheless refused with CapacityExhausted (:89-90), the refusal names the actual ceiling so the calling model can act on it (:91-96), and no admitted child is evicted to make room (:98). Retention after completion has no natural end, so without this bound a parent that spawns sequentially accumulates live loops and providers without limit - the whole reason the ceiling exists. Small critical baseline for this component. P0.

Three follow-ups to one already-admitted child all succeed against a ceiling of two (:132-136) and create no additional agents (:139), while a genuinely new identity past the ceiling is still refused (:142-144). Admission counts distinct identities, not runs: charging per resume would exhaust the ceiling with a single busy agent and make warm resumption strictly worse than a cold spawn. P1.

Array-of-IMessage round trip preserving per-element concrete types. A combination of contracts already covered singly above; only an array-context converter loss would be caught here alone. Measured (coverage-facts, greedy rank 1): this single declaration reaches 85.1% of the project's product spans on its own and holds 6 spans no other declaration touches, so it - not the single-type round trip - is the serializer's maximum-coverage front. Promoted from P2 on that basis.

The single P0 for this serializer: it is the only row that drives BOTH the write and read halves of the polymorphic envelope in one path, so it gives the most product coverage of the component per test. Catches a missing or renamed polymorphic type registration that write-only assertions cannot see. Revised after the sweep: the claim above - that this row gives the most product coverage of the component per test - is measured false. It adds nothing new over the multi-type case and holds no exclusive spans. The round-trip assertion is still worth keeping; the coverage argument for P0 is not.

Pins the wire bytes of the base message type: $type=text plus lowercase role/text property names. Coverage-informed: it drives the same TextMessage WRITE path the P0 round-trip already executes, so it is not the P0 for this serializer; it stays P1 rather than P2 because the byte-level discriminator and naming-policy claim is one the round-trip assertion cannot detect.
A second concrete variant's discriminator (text_update). Distinct supported streaming message type beyond the pinned baseline, so P1 rather than P0 per the one-baseline-per-wire-contract rule.

Round-trips a tool-call message including the nested ToolCall collection, so it detects a nested-converter regression the flat text variant cannot. Distinct supported behavior, not the minimal baseline.

Baseline of the connection registry: after Add, ConnectionCount is 1 and GetConnection returns the exact socket instance stored. A registry that drops or mis-keys connections breaks all socket delivery. TASK-1 AUDIT: demoted to P1. Outside the project's 80% greedy P0 prefix and carrying no named exception - the contract argued here is a distinct primary behaviour, a distinguishing/non-vacuity partner of another row, or a component/class baseline, and the rubric's outside-prefix exception applies only where a component would otherwise have no P0 pinning its essential contract. Kept at P1 so it still runs in the primary-contract tier.
Argument guard: null id throws ArgumentNullException instead of registering a null key. A defensive boundary extending the add contract; no caller behavior is asserted here.
Second argument guard on the same add path. Variation of the null-id boundary above.

Enumeration returns every registered id (two distinct connections), which is what broadcast paths iterate. Detects a registry that keeps only the last connection; a distinct behavior, not a variation.

The distinguishing negative for lookup: an implementation returning a shared or default socket for any id would still satisfy the single-connection Add test. Asserts miss yields null rather than throwing or aliasing.
Removal returns true and actually clears both the count and the lookup. A remove that reports success without evicting leaks sockets; distinct primary behavior beyond the add/lookup baseline.
Boundary on the remove result for an absent id. Extends the remove contract already represented by the positive case; only the false return value is new.

The helper's fundamental contract: a permanently failing recursive delete in Dispose must not throw, and the retry budget is bounded at 5 attempts. Regression here turns passing browser E2E runs red with IOException from teardown. TASK-1 AUDIT: demoted to P1. The subject is the suite's own test-host teardown helper; a regression turns browser E2E runs red from teardown, which is loud, and no shipped product contract is pinned.
Call-count boundary on the happy path (exactly one invocation). Extends the retry contract represented by the transient-failure row; a redundant extra attempt would be wasteful, not incorrect.

Asserts the retry actually re-invokes the delete until it succeeds (exactly 3 calls). Without it a swallow-only implementation would satisfy the never-throw contract while never cleaning up; distinct behavior, not a variation.
Second tolerated-exception variation (DirectoryNotFoundException) on the swallow path already pinned by the P0 row. Adds one exception type to the tolerated set.

Bounds the swallow to filesystem-contention exceptions: an InvalidOperationException from a real cleanup bug still propagates. Important failure handling that keeps the never-throw contract from becoming a blanket catch.

Non-vacuity anchor for the whole class: every other row substitutes the delete callback, so without this the default parameter could delete nothing and all still pass. Coverage-informed: the helper keeps ONE P0 (the never-throw contract), and this row's unique contribution is the default-parameter binding rather than a second critical branch, so P1.

The probe's catch is unfiltered, so its Reason string reaches skip messages and CI logs; this asserts the reason carries the exception category but not the injected secret-bearing message. Important failure handling with a disclosure consequence, beyond the minimal probe baseline.

The probe creates a real gateway session; its essential resource contract is that the DELETE runs under its own token. The stub cancels the caller token as the DELETE arrives and asserts the request token is not cancelled, so a caller-linked teardown would leak container-backed sessions. Also asserts the temp workspace leaf is emptied. TASK-1 AUDIT: demoted to P1. The subject is the suite's own prerequisites probe rather than a shipped component; the leaked-session consequence is real but belongs to test infrastructure.

Pins the Unix branch of the shape pre-check, which takes host flavour as an argument so it is exercised off-platform. Guards the named regression where a drive-letter-only rule rejected every legitimate path on a Linux agent.
Pins the Windows branch of the same argument-driven shape rule: drive-qualified accepted, relative and container-rooted rejected. Distinct branch contract rather than a variation of the Unix row.
Normalization variation of the accept baseline: a \\?\-prefixed report of the same directory still verifies. Extends an already represented contract.

Positive half of the verifier's minimal distinguishing pair: an existing directory reported identically to the expected workspace verifies. If this regressed the sandbox clone gate would skip unconditionally and the suite would silently stop testing anything. Kept in P0 only as the falsifier for the reject row - a P0 holding the rejection alone would pass on a verifier that refuses everything. TASK-1 AUDIT: demoted to P1. Held only as the falsifier half of a pair; a pair does not license two P0s, and the reject row carries the defect. Retained at P1 so the positive control still runs ahead of broader regression.
Existence boundary: a shape-legal path that is absent on this host does not verify. Extends the reject side already represented by the mount-point and mismatch rows.

Separates existence from identity: two real temp directories, reported != expected, must not verify. Without it a verifier degraded to a mere Directory.Exists check would pass everything else in the class.
Null and whitespace input boundary on the same reject path. Defensive variation; the shape theory already covers the empty string.

The distinguishing negative the verifier exists for: a Docker-backed gateway reporting the container mount /workspace must not be treated as host-verifiable. These two rows are counted as ONE P0 unit, not two independent P0s: neither is falsifiable without the other, and every remaining reject case in the class is a variation on this same path and sits at P1/P2. P0-OUTSIDE-PREFIX EXCEPTION (no-coverage-capture project, tiered structurally): it is the only row pinning that a Docker-backed gateway reporting the container mount /workspace is not host-verifiable, so a regression makes the sandbox clone gate skip unconditionally and the browser suite silently stops testing anything while staying green.

Full client-server-client journey: real AskUserQuestionToolProvider parks the run, QuestionRich renders, the browser submits over the live WebSocket, and the scripted plan drains to zero remaining turns. Whole-application offline journey, not an isolated contract.

Reload journey: after a deep-link reload the deferred placeholder rehydrates as still-pending (resolved count 0) and the answer still round-trips over the reconnected subscribe-only socket. Spans persistence, REST history and WebSocket resume.
Same end-to-end journey with the Skip affordance: resolved view reads Skipped and the parked run resumes with the scripted follow-up text. Operational journey across browser, host and agent loop.

Mid-stream stop journey: cancels an in-flight 2000-char scripted stream from the UI and asserts the control row returns to idle and accepts a new turn. Whole-application interactive journey through browser, socket and agent loop.

Real-layout journey: runs twelve tool-call turns plus a long text turn, then asserts the document cannot scroll (measured and probed) while .message-list does, and that Clear stays inside a 1280px viewport. Requires a real rendering engine, so it is a full-application check rather than a component contract.

A factory that throws before the commit line publishes nothing and clears nothing. The transactional half: a publish that happened before construction succeeded would leave the sink advertising a binding for a conversation that has no agent. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

A staged binding is published exactly once on a successful commit, with the thread id and the binding value both checked and nothing cleared. P0 baseline for the egress credential provider's validity state machine. A rejected mint throws and marks the entry invalid; a second acquisition throws again with the endpoint call count still at 1, proving it short-circuits rather than re-presenting a rejected credential; then ApplyUpdateAsync with credentialChanged clears the flag and the retried mint returns the new token with the count at 2. The call-count oracle is what makes it the baseline - without the short-circuit a provider re-presents a rejected credential on every request, which is how an upstream account gets locked out - and the recovery half also requires the ordinary mint path to work, so a broken mint cannot pass it. Prefix member at greedy rank 31 with 117 new spans and 10 exclusive.

The third kind: custom headers are returned in order, verbatim, IncludeExpiry is false, and the token endpoint is never called. The zero-call assertion is the contract - a provider that minted a token for a header-only entry would send the user's credentials to an endpoint they never configured. Greedy rank 225 with 5 exclusive spans.
