The read deny applied to the run-state poll. A route variation: the decision, the principal and the asserted status are all the ones the P0 already drives; what it adds is that this particular endpoint was not left off the scoped list. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.

A work-shape existence oracle (#389): the write path short-circuited a null-metadata thread to unknown_thread before the authorizer, so a missing thread cost zero grant look-ups and a forbidden one cost the authorizer's equalising lookup. Byte-identical bodies do not close that. Counted through a CountingResourceGrantStore, with a greater-than-zero premise guard so the equality cannot be satisfied by both sides being zero. Distinct invariant from the body-equality P0, on the write path.

The sharing round trip in one test: the owner shares, the visibility flips to Shared, the named grantee reads, and a third party with no grant is still refused. Chosen as a P0 because it is the only test here that drives the grant-store allow branch end to end - grant write, visibility transition, grant-based allow - and it carries its own control case, so the allow cannot be a blanket one. Failure means either sharing does not work at all or a grant to one person opens the conversation to everyone. TASK-1 AUDIT: demoted to P1. Outside the project's 80% greedy P0 prefix and carrying no named exception - the contract argued here is a distinct primary behaviour, a distinguishing/non-vacuity partner of another row, or a component/class baseline, and the rubric's outside-prefix exception applies only where a component would otherwise have no P0 pinning its essential contract. Kept at P1 so it still runs in the primary-contract tier.

A deny variation on the revoke route, with the grant-survives assertion that keeps it from passing against an implementation that revoked and then reported a refusal. The decision and the principal are the ones the P0 cross-tenant read already drives. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.

The other half of #376: releasing the owner's agent for an authorized caller must not become an eviction primitive for an unauthorized one. Without the final pool assertion the test passes with the release moved above the authorization check, turning a 404 into a remote eviction any tenant member can trigger by id alone. Distinct ordering invariant from the grantee-handoff case.

Establishes that same-tenant is not the boundary - the owner is. A distinct policy branch from the cross-tenant refusal: here the tenant conjunct passes and the owner/grant conjunct is the only thing refusing, so a policy that checked tenant alone would pass the P0 and fail here.

The distinguishing positive for the app-only refusal above: without it, deleting the OwnerAppId comparison and refusing every first message satisfies that test. Retained at the same tier as the negative it discriminates because the pair is one contract; alone it asserts only a 202 on a happy path.

No principal must become a filter matching nothing, not an absent filter - the tempting spelling reads as 'unscoped' one layer down and hands the whole deployment to a caller who presented nothing. Asserts the empty listing rather than a status, and accepts a 401 as the alternative safe answer. Important failure handling on a distinct input (null principal) the other listing tests never supply.

Input validation on the share request: an unrecognised role is a 400 and never silently defaulted to the weaker one, with the grant store asserted empty. A boundary case on an input the grant tests otherwise supply correctly. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.

A row the startup repair has not reached belongs to no tenant and must be refused to everyone including a tenant admin. Reading 'unowned' as 'anyone's' is the fail-open reading, and this is the only test driving null identity columns through the policy - a distinct input class from every stamped row above.

A viewer grant does not confer write, and this is the case where 403 is correct rather than 404 - the grantee already knows the conversation exists, so hiding it is theatre and the reason code is what tells them their grant is the wrong one. Distinct branch (role-to-action mapping) and the only place the 403-versus-404 choice is pinned by role.

P0 baseline for the context endpoint's precedence rule. Drives a real MultiTurnAgentLoop through one generation in a pool, then asserts the reported observation is reference-identical to loop.LatestContextObservation and that freshness is Fresh. The identity assertion is what makes it the baseline: a regression that answered from the durable projection instead of the pooled loop would still return a well-formed row with plausible numbers, and only BeSameAs separates the live observation from a durable copy of it. Prefix member at greedy rank 4 with 940 new spans and 189 exclusive.

Seeds a root, a persisted sub-agent descendant, a usage ledger and two context observations, then pins the whole durable-state shape: agent ordering and parent linkage, measured versus estimated provenance, the utilization ratio against window minus reserve, Stale freshness when no pooled loop vouches, per-agent input tokens, and the root totals with their completeness flags. Rich and highly discriminating, but outside the P0 prefix at greedy rank 98 with 25 exclusive spans, and the component already has a prefix-nominated P0 pinning the precedence rule, so it holds at P1 on the exclusive-span floor rather than being reached for.

Asserts an unknown thread gets a 404 whose body is equivalent to UnknownThreadRefusal.Body - the existence-hiding refusal, so an unauthorized caller cannot distinguish a thread that does not exist from one they may not see. Pinned by body equivalence rather than by status alone, which is the half that actually carries the hiding property. Greedy rank 593 with 2 exclusive spans, so it sits on the floor at P1.

The escape the whole gate is built around: the SPA calls the same routes with plain browser fetch and no markers, so a marker-less same-origin request must pass even with the secret configured, or enabling the guard breaks the UI. Regression for issue #153 blocker 1.
evidence: configured secret with no X-S2S-Auth and no X-Sbx-App-Id, asserts next was called
requirements: a marker-less same-origin request is admitted even when the S2S secret is configured

rationale: The keyless development path: with no secret configured the filter passes every request through unmodified. Defines the disabled state of the gate. Front member with exclusive spans (floor).
evidence: asserts next was called and no result was set
requirements: with no S2S secret configured the filter admits the request unchanged

rationale: Non-vacuity for the armed gate: a matching secret is admitted, so the refusal rows are not satisfied by a filter that rejects every S2S request.
requirements: a request presenting the configured S2S secret is admitted

rationale: This is the arming half of a marker-gated auth boundary, and the half that fails green. The filter must NOT gate marker-less browser traffic, so the only thing separating an authenticated service caller from an unauthenticated one is that a request forwarding X-Sbx-App-Id is recognised as a service request and required to present X-S2S-Auth. If that recognition regresses, the browser pass-through swallows every service call: unauthenticated callers reach the conversation API carrying a forwarded credential and no test that asserts the allow-cases can fail. InboundS2SAuthAttribute is small, is the boundary itself, and has no other P0. Coverage caveat: addsNothingNew records shared filter spans, but allow and wrong-secret cases do not assert that the app-id marker arms authentication when the header is absent, so overlap is not assertion redundancy.
evidence: configured secret, X-Sbx-App-Id present, X-S2S-Auth absent; asserts next was NOT called and a 401 UnauthorizedObjectResult was set
the paired allow-case (marker-less browser request) is asserted in the same file, so the gate cannot be satisfied by refusing everything
requirements: a request carrying a credential-forwarding marker but no S2S auth header is refused with 401 and the action is not executed
uncertainties: outside the greedy prefix (no rank); granted on the auth boundary, which coverage cannot see
near-duplicate setup to Filter_Returns401_WhenSecretConfigured_AndHeaderMissing - they are one P0 unit and only this row carries the tier

rationale: Same refusal stated as the missing-header case, with the marker supplied to arm the guard. Front member of the prefix and one of the two rows that share the P0 unit; the tier sits on the marker-present row.
requirements: an armed S2S request with no auth header is refused with 401

rationale: Wrong-value refusal, distinct from the missing-header case: a presented but incorrect secret must be refused rather than treated as absent and passed through the browser path.
evidence: presents totally-wrong-value against the configured secret
requirements: a request presenting an incorrect S2S auth header is refused with 401

rationale: Disclosure guard on the refusal itself: the 401 body serialises to something containing neither the configured secret nor the value the caller presented, and still names a stable error code. A diagnostic echo here hands the secret to exactly the caller who failed to guess it.
evidence: serialises the UnauthorizedObjectResult value and asserts it excludes both values and contains s2s_auth_failed
requirements: the 401 body contains neither the configured secret nor the presented value, and carries the s2s_auth_failed code

rationale: Credential passthrough: X-Sbx-App-Id and X-Sbx-App-Key are assembled into the SandboxCredential handed to the agent pool, and the forwarded key never appears in the response body. Widest row in the project's prefix (33 exclusive spans), so it carries the P1 floor. Declined for P0 because the rank reflects the whole controller-plus-pool path it drags in, and the contract it pins is a passthrough whose failure is loud - the sandbox call is unauthenticated and fails.
evidence: asserts CallerCredential equals SandboxCredential(app-a, a-key-value) and that the serialised 202 body excludes the key
requirements: the Sbx app id and key headers become the caller credential passed to the agent pool
the forwarded app key does not appear in the response body
uncertainties: prefix candidate declined at P0

rationale: Absent-context boundary of the passthrough: with no ambient HTTP request the credential is null rather than a NullReferenceException, which is the shape every other SendMessage unit test invokes.
evidence: deliberately leaves ControllerContext unwired and asserts CallerCredential is null
requirements: an invocation with no HttpContext passes a null caller credential rather than throwing

rationale: Cross-actor refusal (#153): a thread whose agent was seeded under caller A's identity answers 409 caller_credential_conflict to caller B rather than running B's message on A's credential, and the body names neither app id nor either key - the ids moved to the structured log once an ordinary editor grantee joined this path (#376).
evidence: seeds the pool under SandboxCredential(app-a, ...) then calls as app-b
asserts 409, the caller_credential_conflict code, the thread id present, and app-a/app-b/a-secret-key-value all absent from the body
requirements: a message from a different caller identity than the one that seeded the thread's agent is refused with 409
the conflict body carries neither app id nor either app key
uncertainties: considered for P0 and held: the refusal is enforced in MultiTurnAgentPool, whose own row GetOrCreateAgent_Throws_WhenSecondCallHasDifferentAppId already carries a P0 in this lane, so this controller row pins the passthrough of that refusal rather than the refusal itself. ConversationsController also already carries a P0 for the agent-owned thread route bypass.

rationale: With no secret configured the guard is disabled and even a marked request passes. P2 as the feature-off configuration of the reachability its sibling already pins. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

The SPA's plain unmarked fetch stays reachable with the secret configured. The regression a blanket guard causes - locking out the browser is the same symptom as the app being down, and only an unmarked request through the real pipeline can fail on it. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

A request carrying the caller-credential marker but no auth header is rejected, through real routing and filter discovery rather than by invoking the filter directly. That routing is the whole point: this fails if the attribute is removed from the controller or scoped to the wrong routes, which a direct-filter test cannot notice. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

A correctly signed S2S request reaches the controller. The non-vacuity partner for both rejection declarations, which a filter that rejected every marked request would otherwise pass. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

A present but wrong secret is rejected - and this request carries NO app-id marker, so it also pins that the header alone arms the guard. A filter that only checked marked requests would let a wrong-secret caller through unexamined. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

A deleted conversation whose thread id is reused must rescan rather than inherit the deleted one's cached rows - both resolve the same NoLiveManager sentinel owner, so owner-keyed invalidation alone cannot tell them apart and only an explicit Forget on Delete can. Carries two independent oracles: the second answer is empty where the first was not, and the store's ListThreads call count goes from 1 to 2. Greedy rank 73 with 40 new spans.

With collaboration off - the checked-in default - an Agent-tool child's only durable trace is the provenance stamp on its own thread metadata, and after pool eviction the endpoint must still reconstruct it from that scan. Pins the pre-#244 flat-listing contract that #244's replacement dropped, and it is the only declaration reaching the persisted-provenance route. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

A genuinely unknown thread gets 404 with the unknown_thread code and the id echoed. The counterpart that keeps the empty-list contract above from meaning every id is accepted. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

A persisted but not-live conversation that never spawned anything answers 200 with an empty list rather than 404, so the client's 3s poll does not log a failure every tick. The distinction between not-live and unknown is the contract, and it is the case the 404 declaration would otherwise swallow. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

A live agent with no sub-agent manager answers an empty list. P2 as a variation: the empty-list-not-404 contract is already pinned by the idle-thread declaration, and this changes only which of the two no-children routes is taken. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

A conversation whose live loop was evicted still surfaces its persisted workflow and delegate tabs with 200 rather than 404, which is what makes workflow tabs survive a restart. A different durable source from the provenance scan above - the WorkflowRunRegistry index - so neither covers the other. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

The component's primary behaviour: two children spawned through a real MultiTurnAgentLoop project into SubAgentSummary DTOs with agent id, name, template, task, status and the derived child thread id all asserted per child. The blocking provider is what makes the running status deterministic rather than timing-dependent. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans - by the greedy order the projection is already walked - which says nothing about the assertion, since no sibling here spawns a real child at all.
uncertainties: the EffectiveModelId and ModelSelectionSource claims are reflection existence checks on the DTO type, so they pin the property's presence and not the value the UI renders

rationale: The caller's instructions land after the mode prompt, the workspace suffix and the discovered-context block, with the host-built prefix intact. An ordering claim rather than a presence claim, pinned by index comparison: recency is what gives a headless caller's task its pull, and the previous version of this contract went wrong precisely because nobody asserted the sequence.

Delete has deliberately NO pending-question guard: it removes the agent unconditionally, proven from a verified-pending precondition to an empty pool afterwards. The asymmetry with the two switch endpoints is the contract being locked in, so a later 'consistency' fix cannot quietly make a conversation undeletable while a question is outstanding.

The capabilities document pins its schema version and two always-on flags, while message idempotency tracks whether the injected store actually supports it. The conditional flag is the contract: advertising idempotency over a store that cannot honour it makes a client safely retry a send that will duplicate the turn.
Supplying both ids is 400. The other side of the exactly-one rule already represented.
Supplying neither a run id nor an input id is 400. The exactly-one rule keeps the endpoint from silently answering about some other run than the caller meant.
An input id never accepted nor ledgered on a provisioned thread is 404 with unknown_inputId. A third distinct 404 code over the miss contract already represented.
A provisioned thread with an unknown run id is 404 with unknown_runId naming the id. The other branch of that pair.
An unprovisioned thread is 404 with unknown_thread. One branch of the pair the discriminator row pins jointly.

An accepted input with no ledger entry yet resolves to NotStarted with a null run id. The distinct input-id resolution path, and the window in which a poller must not mistake 'queued' for 'never accepted'.
A ledgered run resolves to a status response carrying the thread id, run id and InProgress status. The primary status-read path a headless caller polls.

The two 404s stay tellable apart by code, asserted in one test so they cannot converge. Retained above P2 under the coverage-informed exception clause: it re-executes spans the two single-branch 404 rows already cover, but only it forbids the collapse, and the client's existence probe reads exactly this difference - collapse them and every deep link reports its conversation missing.
uncertainties: Deliberately does NOT assert that a missing and a forbidden thread differ; those are identical on purpose so the route is not an existence oracle

rationale: A thread with no recorded usage is 404 rather than a zeroed aggregate, so a client can tell 'nothing spent' from 'nothing measured'. Absent-input boundary on the usage read.
A persisted usage projection is returned with its computed total and a per-model row. The read side of usage accounting, which is what a cost display and any budget decision are built on.
An unparameterised List returns the client's page size, pinned against a 45-row seed that exceeds it. A default-value boundary; its own comment notes any smaller seed cannot tell 30 from 50.

Reserved subagent- and workflow- thread ids never appear in the conversation list. Retained above P2 under the coverage-informed exception clause: its own comment records that it passed throughout the paging defect's life because three rows fit one page, so it pins the exclusion RULE while the P0 pins where the rule is applied.

sort=created orders by creation time, seeded so the two orderings are exact reverses. The reversal is the mechanism: a controller that accepted the parameter and ignored it would pass any seed where the orders agreed, and the case-insensitive 'CREATED' input is exercised too.

Page two continues exactly where page one stopped, with no row duplicated or skipped, asserted against the full expected sequence. A distinct offset-correctness claim the single-page P0 cannot make: an exclusion applied after paging counts rows the caller never saw, so older conversations vanish while every page still reports itself full.

Each stored visibility reaches the wire as its NAME, an absent one reads as private, and the JSON kind is asserted to be a string. The kind assertion is the point: the enum carries no string converter, so a raw enum would serialize as 0/1/2 and a client switching on 'shared' would silently never match.

With sixty agent-owned threads all newer than forty real ones, the sidebar still gets a full page containing only real conversations. P0 because the seed is what pins WHERE the exclusion happens: filtering the returned page instead of the store hands back thirty subagent rows, deletes all thirty, and renders an EMPTY sidebar over forty reachable conversations. The count and the content assertions are separately load-bearing - one forbids a short page, the other forbids refilling it with hidden rows. TASK-1 AUDIT: demoted to P1. Outside the project's 80% greedy P0 prefix and carrying no named exception - the contract argued here is a distinct primary behaviour, a distinguishing/non-vacuity partner of another row, or a component/class baseline, and the rubric's outside-prefix exception applies only where a component would otherwise have no P0 pinning its essential contract. Kept at P1 so it still runs in the primary-contract tier.

A misspelled sort, a negative offset and out-of-range limits are all refused. Important failure handling rather than a boundary: a silently ignored sort is indistinguishable from a working one, so a client would receive a plausible list in the wrong order forever with nothing to notice.

A minted thread id encodes its creation instant, asserted AFTER bumping LastUpdated to the year 2100 so the fallback path is distinguishable. The separation is the mechanism: at provisioning time the fallback and the real instant coincide, which is exactly how a bare guid id shipped unnoticed and left the created sort keyed on a mutable field.
An explicitly empty reasoning effort is accepted and persisted as empty, distinct from omitting the field. A value boundary on the reasoning-effort contract already represented.

A caller's system-prompt appendix is persisted at provision AND read back through the same ReadAppendixAsync and ComposeAsync calls the agent build makes, landing after the mode prompt. Going through the read path is the whole point: asserting only that it was STORED is what passed while nothing consumed the field and every review ran on the bare mode prompt.

A configured sub-agent model is persisted and read back through ConversationSubAgentModel.ReadAsync, the same call the agent build makes. The round trip is the claim; its comment records this knob was in the same accepted-but-unread state as the prompt appendix.

An unavailable provider is 503 naming it and no thread is minted. Distinct from the reasoning-effort rejection: this gate depends on live registry state rather than the request's own shape, and it too must not half-create a conversation.

An unsupported reasoning-effort string is 400 with its code AND no thread is minted at all. The empty-store assertion is what makes it a validation guard rather than a status check: a rejected request that still created a conversation would leave orphaned threads on every typo.

An unknown mode id is 404 naming it. A second validation input over the boundary the workspace row represents. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.

An unknown workspace id is 404 naming it. Validation boundary on the provision path. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.

Provisioning validates the workspace, provider and mode, mints a thread- id and persists provider, workspace, mode and reasoning effort together. Chosen as one of this controller's P0s because it drives the widest single path in the class - every validation plus every metadata write - and it is the precondition for every other endpoint: a conversation provisioned with a missing binding is unusable from the first turn. Revised after the sweep: the widest-single-path claim above is measured false - it adds no spans over the front and holds none exclusively. The metadata-binding assertions stand, and ConversationScopingTests.Provision_StampsTenantAndOwner already carries the create path's P0.
With no sub-agent model supplied the read-back is null rather than a blank model id, so children stay on the inherited model. Absent-input boundary on the sub-agent-model contract.

With no appendix supplied the read-back is null and the composed prompt is the mode prompt unchanged. The negative that keeps the appendix feature from altering every UI-created chat; a boundary on the contract the positive row represents.

When a migration replaced the sandbox session under a pooled agent, the turn is dispatched to the REBUILT agent, proven by two creations and a per-agent send count rather than by the 202 alone. The comment records that the shared pool helper wires no live-session resolver and would make this pass against either implementation, so the bespoke pool is what gives the assertion force.

A REFUSED send leaves the handoff ledger not-busy. The explicit non-vacuity partner of the accepted-send P0: an unconditional busy-mark at the top of the send would satisfy the P0 and refuse every later handoff for a turn that never existed.

A persisted-but-unavailable provider surfaces as 503 provider_unavailable on send. The availability guard already represented on provision and switch, reached through a third endpoint. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.
A full input queue is 503 with queue_full. The status-and-code half of the contract whose ledger half is the not-busy row.

When an active run makes the pool defer the session refresh, REST refuses with a retryable 503 carrying sandbox_session_refresh_deferred rather than accepting onto the superseded session. Distinct branch from the successful refresh: dispatching here queues the turn into a session the retirement grace is about to destroy.

An accept refused by a mid-send agent replacement is a 503 carrying agent_replaced and explicitly NOT queue_full, with nothing enqueued. The negative on the sibling code is the contract: the two 503s mean opposite things about whether retrying this same agent can ever work.

A send returns 202 with an input id and no run id, and the pool's handoff state reports busy for the turn the agent has not started. The pool assertion is what makes it a P0 rather than a status check: a fixture returning a bare 202 looks identical on the wire, and the named defect had a grantee handoff read that instant as idle and dispose the entry with the turn on it. TASK-1 AUDIT: demoted to P1. Outside the project's 80% greedy P0 prefix and carrying no named exception - the contract argued here is a distinct primary behaviour, a distinguishing/non-vacuity partner of another row, or a component/class baseline, and the rubric's outside-prefix exception applies only where a component would otherwise have no P0 pinning its essential contract. Kept at P1 so it still runs in the primary-contract tier.
Sending to an unprovisioned thread is 404 with unknown_thread rather than implicitly creating a conversation. The gate that keeps the REST surface from minting untracked threads on a typo'd id.

An agent that throws during the send lets the exception propagate rather than reporting a false 202. A failure boundary on the send path; only the exception type is asserted. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.
uncertainties: The name says durable write but the fixture throws from the agent's send, so what is pinned is propagation, not which layer failed

rationale: A real loop parked on a deferred AskUserQuestion blocks the switch with its own distinct code, and the question is still pending afterwards. A separate guard from the run-in-progress one - the test's comment records that the fake agent degrades this check to false, so only a real loop can reach it - and the post-assertions prove the blocked attempt did not partially recreate.

The same guard fires when the pending question belongs to a live direct CHILD while the primary has none of its own. Distinct descendant-walk branch: recreating the primary disposes the whole tree, so a child-only question would otherwise be silently orphaned.
uncertainties: The fixture polls the child's deferred-call registry with a 30s bound, so a regression that never parks surfaces as a timeout

rationale: A switch during an active run is 409 with the mode_switch_while_streaming code and the thread's mode unchanged. Important failure handling: recreating the agent mid-run would dispose the loop producing the stream the client is reading.

An unknown mode id is 404 naming the id. Validation boundary in front of the switch path. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.

An idle thread switches mode, the response carries the new mode id, the pool reports it, and no warning is attached. The primary mode-switch path; the null warning matters because a spurious one would train users to ignore the real armed-Wait warning.
A leftover run id on a non-running agent does not block the switch. The stale-state boundary of the run-in-progress guard already represented.

When neither a pooled agent nor the fallback chain yields a mode, the controller answers 500 and leaves the persisted provider alone rather than recreating the agent with an unknown mode. A distinct terminal branch of the fallback chain whose alternative is a conversation silently reset to no mode.

An unavailable target provider is a clean 503 naming it, with the thread's persisted provider untouched. The untouched-provider assertion is the transactional claim: a half-applied switch would leave the conversation bound to a provider that cannot serve it.

A pending deferred question blocks the provider switch with its own code and leaves the question pending. Mirrors the mode-switch guard on the second endpoint; a second endpoint over an already-represented guard. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.

A provider switch during an active run is 409 with its own code and no recreate. The same guard the mode-switch conflict row represents, applied to the second switch endpoint. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.

An idle thread switches provider, the new provider is persisted, the mode is preserved and no warning is attached. The primary provider-switch path; asserting the persisted provider rather than the response body is what proves a refresh keeps the switch. Measured (coverage-facts, greedy rank 36): 106 marginal spans inside the greedy front. No exclusive spans, so it is replaceable in principle - but not by anything currently in the project. Promoted from P1. TASK-1 AUDIT: prefix candidate DECLINED to P1. The rationale calls it the primary provider-switch path and records no exclusive spans; "Promoted from P1" on rank 36 is a rank citation, not component criticality.

With no live agent the controller recovers the mode from metadata plus the mode store and preserves it across the provider swap. The switch-after-refresh path, and the only row reaching the metadata-to-mode-store fallback chain the live-agent rows short-circuit.
A stale run id does not block a provider switch. The stale-state boundary applied to the second switch endpoint.

A GET must not conjure a conversation: the row it would create has no TenantId, and ConversationAuthorizer reads a null TenantId as conversation_not_found, so nobody - the owner included - could ever read it back. The caller still gets its board; only the write is declined.
Write-side companion: preferring the projection is worthless if the same request writes the empty live board over it on the way out. That would be silent destruction of the only surviving copy.

The read is the only writer on this path, so without the write-through the projection branch could never be reached in production and the board would vanish on restart. No response-shape test observes the write.

Precedence between the two sources: after a restart or provider swap the conversation gets a fresh EMPTY board while the persisted one still holds rows, and returning the live board merely because it exists blanks the panel. Neither single-source test can fail for this.

Every other case stubs the board; this one drives the real TaskManager through its own tools, so the projection is proven against the shape the agent actually produces rather than a hand-built mirror. Front member with exclusiveSpans=2 at greedyRank 123, so the P1 floor also applies.

The CLI-backed providers return before task registration and bring their own tracking, so 404 is what tells the client to render NOTHING rather than an empty board - absence has to stay distinguishable from 'the board is empty'.
Unknown-thread boundary of the same 404 answer. Measured marginalNewSpans=2 at greedyRank 601 with no exclusive spans.
Absence boundary with neither a live board nor a projection.
Primary read path: a pooled agent's live board is captured once and returned as the snapshot for that thread. The capture count is asserted, so a second capture per request would fail.
The second source: with no pooled agent the persisted projection answers, which is the reload and post-restart case.

Pins the JSON the client and the push frame both parse - camelCase names, schemaVersion, enum-by-name status, and the deliberate absence of the server-side IsEmpty. A rename is invisible to every test that inspects the CLR object and breaks both consumers.

The write-through is a cache warm, not the response: a store that is down, full, or racing a delete must cost the panel nothing. Front member with exclusiveSpans=4 at greedyRank 344, so the P1 floor also applies.

A thread carrying other properties but not the workspace key maps to null. Asserted against a NON-empty property bag, which is what distinguishes absent-key handling from an empty-bag short circuit, and it also rules out a mapper returning a constant. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

The persisted workspace thread property surfaces on the list summary. The picker reads this to show which workspace a conversation is bound to, so a dropped mapping silently offers to reuse the wrong one. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

Provision mints a thread, SendMessage returns Accepted with Queued true, and poll-by-inputId resolves to Completed carrying the echoed text. P2 as a variation on a represented contract: the queued sibling performs the same provision, send and poll against the same controller code and asserts a strict superset of these claims, and this declaration added no spans and holds none exclusively. It remains the uncontended reading of the same path, which is why it is P2 rather than lower.

Accepts an input on a pool whose agent never drains, disposes it to simulate a crash, then reconciles the durable ledger on a fresh pool and requires the orphaned input to resolve to Interrupted with a run id. Pins the crash-recovery half of the protocol - an accepted input that no run ever claimed must not stay pending forever - which no other declaration here reaches. Greedy rank 146 with 13 exclusive spans, so it also sits on the floor at P1.

P0 baseline for the asynchronous run protocol. Against a real MultiTurnAgentBase-derived agent it holds run 1 open on an injected gate, confirms run 1 reached InProgress before sending the second message so the two inputs cannot land in one drained batch, asserts the second input is durably accepted yet still NotStarted with a null run id, then releases the gate and requires both inputs to resolve to Completed with DIFFERENT run ids and with each response text matched to its own input. The distinct-run-id and per-input response assertions are what make it the baseline: an implementation that collapsed both inputs into one run, or that resolved poll-by-inputId to whichever run finished last, would satisfy every weaker check in this class. Prefix member at greedy rank 12 with 316 new spans.

The provider-info diagnostics payload carries all ten Codex fields with the values the environment set, asserted on the serialized JSON so the wire names are pinned and not only the object's properties. Diagnostics-only per the rubric: the endpoint reports state rather than computing it, so a regression costs an operator's view of the provider rather than changing what the provider does. Greedy rank 66 with 43 new spans, all 43 exclusive - it is the only declaration touching this controller - which measures sole ownership rather than criticality.

An existing REAL directory is idempotent success with no mkdir issued. The positive that keeps the symlink and file rejections from being a blanket refusal, and the reason a retried folder upload does not fail.
An existing regular file at the target is 409 with no mkdir. A second occupied-target type over the rule the symlink row represents.

An existing symlink at the target is 409 with no mkdir, never a silent 200 from letting mkdir -p follow it. The specific defect the endpoint was hardened against; the absence of a command is what proves the check happens before the shell call.

Empty, whitespace, dot names, separators, drive-qualified and NUL-bearing names are all 400 with no command run. The client-supplied name reaches an argv vector, so this gate plus the empty-Commands assertion is what keeps a malformed name from ever being executed.
A null request body is 400 with no command. Absent-input boundary on the same validation gate.
With no resolved session the create is 409 and no command runs. The prologue's NoSession outcome applied to one more endpoint.

A non-zero mkdir exit is 422. Failure-mapping boundary on the create path. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.
Creation under a resolved subdirectory composes the server path for both the response and the mkdir argument. A nesting combination of the create path already represented.

A new directory is created with a single 'mkdir --' under the resolved parent - not 'mkdir -p', which would follow a symlink in the chain - and '--' keeps a leading-dash name an operand. The primary create path, with the exact argv pinned because the flags ARE the safety property.

Recursion is derived from the SERVER-returned directory type, not a client flag, and the script re-verifies that type before its rm -r. Distinct branch with the largest blast radius in the component: a client-forced -r on a mistyped entry would delete a tree.

The script's dedicated 'no longer the resolved kind' exit maps to 409 entry_changed rather than the generic 422. The distinction is the whole value of the point-of-use guard: the caller must learn the object was substituted between resolve and delete, not merely that rm failed.

Deleting a file issues exactly ONE sh invocation carrying both the point-of-use kind re-check and the rm, with kind and path as positional parameters rather than interpolated script text. The single-invocation count is the anti-TOCTOU claim; two calls would reopen the window the guard exists to close.

A name packed with shell metacharacters - leading dash, quote, $(id), backtick, embedded newline - reaches the sandbox as ONE argv element byte-identical to the listed name, with the script text a separate element. P0 by the coverage-informed exception clause: it re-executes the same delete spans as the benign delete rows, but overlapping spans are not overlapping assertions - it alone catches a shell-join regression, whose consequence is arbitrary command execution inside the workspace sandbox. P0-OUTSIDE-PREFIX EXCEPTION: it is the only row asserting a name packed with shell metacharacters reaches the sandbox as ONE argv element byte-identical to the listed name, so a shell-join regression is arbitrary command execution inside the workspace container - a defect the benign delete rows re-execute the same spans for and cannot detect.
uncertainties: Pinned at the FakeFileBrowser recording seam, so it proves the controller emits a correct argv vector, not that the transport below it preserves one

rationale: A generic non-zero exit is 422. The fallback arm of the exit mapping whose distinguishing arm is the entry-changed row. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.
Deleting the empty path is 400 with no command run. Without this the guarded rm would target the workspace root itself; the empty Commands assertion is what proves nothing was issued.

A symlink is deleted with the symlink kind and no recursion. A third entry type over the server-type-derived rule already represented. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.

Downloading a directory is 400. A type boundary on the download endpoint. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.
A file exactly at the cap downloads. The inclusive edge of the boundary the over-cap row already represents.

A download returns the bytes as an attachment with a fixed octet-stream type and X-Content-Type-Options nosniff. The headers are the contract: without them a workspace-controlled file could be sniffed and executed as HTML in the user's origin.

The same NoSession outcome maps to 409 on Download rather than the 200-with-state List uses. The deliberate per-endpoint asymmetry is the contract: a read-only pane can render an empty state, an action cannot pretend to have succeeded.

A file whose LISTED size exceeds the cap is 413 with the read never attempted, asserted by a zero read count. The absence assertion is the point: a post-read rejection would still have pulled the whole payload through the gateway.

When the listed size is absent the pre-check passes and the SDK's typed IsDirectReadCapExceeded signal must map to 413 rather than an opaque 502. A distinct second line of defence the listed-size row cannot reach.

Two entries rendering to the same component make the path ambiguous and are 400 rather than silently picking the first. Distinct resolution rule from lossiness, with the same wrong-object consequence.
A 501-entry directory is truncated to 500 with MoreCount 1. A cap boundary extending the listing contract the P0 represents.

A resolution reporting that another credential owns the session is 409, not a listing. Important failure handling with a confidentiality consequence: serving the listing would show one user another user's workspace.

A multi-level path resolves component-wise through server-returned directory names and lists the child directory. The recursive descent the whole authoritative-resolution design rests on; the root-only P0 never exercises it.

A SandboxSessionUnavailableException thrown while resolving maps to 503 rather than escaping as an unmapped 500. The test's own comment names the trap: this exception is not a SandboxException, so it needs its own catch.

Metadata whose workspace property is blank yields 200 with the no_session_yet state rather than an error, so pre-workspace conversations still render a browser pane. Distinct legacy-compatibility branch.

An entry whose name did not survive transport losslessly has no non-lossy ordinal match and is 404 rather than being addressed by its approximate rendering. Distinct resolution rule: acting on a lossy name could target a different real file.
A resolver reporting NoSession also yields the no_session_yet state on List. Extends the same state already represented by the blank-workspace row, from the other side of the prologue.

A workspace id that round-tripped through the on-disk store comes back as a JsonElement and must still extract to exactly 'default', asserted on both the id handed to the resolver and the id echoed on the DTO. Pinning the extracted VALUE rather than 'not no-session' is what makes it catch a loose ToString; the named live bug made every operation report no_session_yet.

A persisted number or bool is ignored rather than ToString'd into a bogus workspace id, proven by the resolver never seeing it. The negative that gives the JsonElement extraction its meaning: without it, a blanket ToString would satisfy the positive row and silently mint workspace '42'.

The root listing returns every entry with its server type projected onto the DTO, including symlink, and MoreCount 0 when under the cap. Chosen as the endpoint family's baseline P0 because it drives the whole prologue in one path - metadata load, workspace extraction, session resolution, listing, DTO projection - and is the only success path every other endpoint's resolution prologue depends on. TASK-1 AUDIT: demoted to P1. Outside the project's 80% greedy P0 prefix and carrying no named exception - the contract argued here is a distinct primary behaviour, a distinguishing/non-vacuity partner of another row, or a component/class baseline, and the rubric's outside-prefix exception applies only where a component would otherwise have no P0 pinning its essential contract. Kept at P1 so it still runs in the primary-contract tier.

A thread with no persisted metadata is 404, not an empty listing of some default workspace. The prologue's first branch and the difference between 'no such conversation' and 'a conversation with nothing in it'.

With no listed size the pre-read gate passes and a post-read length guard rejects the cap+1 payload, with exactly one read. A distinct second gate for under-reported sizes; the read count proves the pre-check really was bypassed rather than the test passing vacuously.

A file under the byte cap but over the line cap reports too_large. A second dimension of the same size gate. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.
Bytes that are not valid UTF-8 report not_utf8 rather than a replacement-character rendering presented as the file's contents. Distinct decode branch from the size and allowlist gates.

Previewable text is returned verbatim with a line count fixed across trailing-newline, CRLF, no-newline and empty inputs. The primary preview success path plus the counting rule the UI's gutter depends on.

A non-allowlisted extension reports previewable false with reason binary and never reads the file. The allowlist decision is made from the listing alone, so an unpreviewable blob costs no gateway transfer.

An over-cap listed size reports too_large with no read. The pre-read half of the preview size gate, extending the read-avoidance contract the allowlist row represents. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.

A .jsonl under a dot-directory is excluded even though .jsonl is allowlisted, so a conversation's own transcript is not previewable through its own file browser. A distinct rule from the allowlist, deliberately constructed so the allowlist cannot be what rejects it.

A backslash is rejected as invalid_path rather than rewritten to '/', constructed so that rewriting would misresolve a literal POSIX file named 'a\b' onto the unrelated a/b entry. A wrong-object identity defect that a plain 400-status assertion could not distinguish; the error body is pinned by code.

A declared over-cap length is rejected before any read. The cheap first half of the size gate whose authoritative half is the observed-bytes row. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.

Traversal, separators, dot names, empty and a drive-relative name are all rejected as file names. The client-supplied name is untrusted input to a path composition, so this gate is what keeps an upload inside the target directory.
uncertainties: Asserts the 400 only; unlike the relative-path row it does not also assert that no write occurred

rationale: Ten malformed relative paths - traversal, absolute, doubled and dot segments, backslash, drive-qualified, embedded NUL, trailing slash - are all 400 with no command and no write. The syntactic gate in front of the resolution walk, asserted with the absence of both side effects.

A form file that declares 10 bytes but streams cap+1 is rejected 413 with no write, so a lying Content-Length cannot smuggle an over-cap body. The observed-count gate is a distinct defence from the declared-length one, and the only one an attacker cannot control.

A failed parent mkdir is 422 and no write follows. Failure-mapping boundary on the parent-creation walk. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.
An upload into a resolved subdirectory writes the exact bytes at the server-composed path. The primary upload path: the write path and payload are pinned, not just the 200.

A sandbox Conflict during the write surfaces as 409. Error-mapping boundary on the upload path. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.

A folder upload creates each missing parent with its own 'mkdir --' in order - never 'mkdir -p' - and writes at the full nested destination. The one-component-at-a-time sequence is exactly what makes the symlink containment enforceable, so the ordered command assertion is the mechanism, not a detail.
The response Name echoes the full relative path rather than the leaf, so the client can match the row it queued. A response-shape boundary on the same upload path.
A regular file occupying a parent position is 409 with no mkdir and no write. A second occupied-parent type over the containment rule the symlink-parent P0 represents.

An existing real directory parent is reused with no mkdir. The allowed-parent boundary that keeps the symlink and file rejections from being a blanket refusal of every existing parent. Raised to the P1 exclusive-span floor (rubric line 46): a front member with exclusive spans cannot sit below P1, and this row is not vacuous.

A symlink at the write TARGET itself is rejected without writing, so an existing link cannot be written through. A distinct position in the chain from the parent-symlink case: a parent-only check would pass this and still clobber the link's target.

A symlink in a folder-upload's parent chain is rejected with no mkdir and no write, so a relative path cannot escape the resolved directory THROUGH a link. P0 as the containment invariant of the whole relative-path feature: the absence assertions on Commands and Writes are what make it a containment proof rather than a status-code check, and a regression writes attacker-chosen bytes outside the workspace. P0-OUTSIDE-PREFIX EXCEPTION: it is the only row proving a symlink in a folder-upload's parent chain is refused with no mkdir and no write, so a regression writes attacker-chosen bytes outside the resolved workspace directory THROUGH a link, which no lexical path check can see.
A relative path composes onto an already-resolved target directory rather than the root. A combination of the resolved-target and relative-path features both already represented.
A single-segment relative path runs no mkdir and writes at the root. Degenerate-input boundary on the parent-creation walk.

An entry that was a directory at resolve time and is a regular file at removal time is refused, and the substituted file is still on disk with its contents intact afterwards. This is the destructive case - the stale-typed path ran a recursive remove earned by the RESOLVED kind. The race is a fixture, not a clock: the scripted listing and the real directory disagree exactly as a lost race leaves them, and the whole thing runs the controller's real script under a real shell so the script TEXT is what is under test. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

The same ordering on the DIRECTORY arm, which is the sharper variant: a link to a directory makes a bare directory test answer yes, so only a not-a-link check that runs first refuses it. Two arms of the script, two separate qualifiers - a fix applied to one leaves the other open, which is why they are pinned apart. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.
uncertainties: declared SkippableFact - skips when the machine cannot create directory symlinks or has no POSIX shell, so a green run is not proof it executed

rationale: The declared positive control on the same harness: an unsubstituted directory really is removed. Without it a script that refused everything would make all four refusal declarations green, which is precisely the vacuity this file is structured to rule out. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

The opposite substitution is refused as entry-changed specifically, not as a generic failure - the assertion names the refusal code, because a bare removal would merely fail and report a confusing delete-failed instead of the reason. The directory's child survives. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

A symlink to a file substituted under a file resolve is refused before any target-following test can bless it. The point is ordering inside the script's file arm - a bare file test FOLLOWS links and would return true - so the not-a-link check has to run first on this arm, and the link and its target both survive. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.
uncertainties: declared SkippableFact - skips when the machine cannot create file symlinks or has no POSIX shell, so a green run is not proof it executed

rationale: A cross-tenant mkdir is refused and runs no command. P2 as a variation: the same AccessAction.Write input to the shared helper that Upload and Delete already pin, with 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

P0 baseline for FileBrowserController authorization, and a P0 outside the prefix. The controller addresses a workspace by conversation id alone, so without the per-request check its routes answer another tenant's ids with that tenant's workspace, and Delete is the route the file's own doc calls the most damaging call this controller answers by id alone. Pins two contracts at once on that route: the cross-tenant refusal is byte-identical to the refusal for a thread that was never minted once the ids are equalised - anything else turns the route into an existence oracle - and AssertSandboxUntouched shows the sandbox double saw no command at all, which is what separates refused from refused after already issuing the rm. Other rows in the file call AssertSandboxUntouched, but no other row exercises it on the Delete route, so a controller that deleted first and refused afterwards passes every one of them. The prefix nominated only Owner_ReachesEveryRoute here, and that declaration asserts the owner reaches every route: it traverses the same lines without asserting the refusal, so a controller with no authorization check at all passes it. Under the rubric's both-directions overlap exception this is the component's essential baseline and it keeps P0. Scope note: the byte-identical argument earns P0 for the existence-hiding branch specifically - two refusals sharing a status code are not indistinguishable, so this warrant does not generalise to the same-status refusals elsewhere in the file.

A cross-tenant download is refused with the byte-identical body and no byte of the file is read. P2 rather than P1 because it is a variation on a represented contract: it reaches ResolveSessionAsync with exactly the same arguments as Preview (AccessAction.Read, isListing false), and it added no spans and holds none exclusively. Not unimportant - it is the route that would return raw bytes - but the authorization decision it exercises is already pinned.

Counts grant look-ups for a forbidden thread and for a never-minted one and requires them equal and non-zero. Pins a work-shape existence oracle that no body comparison can see: ResolveSessionAsync answered the null-metadata case before reaching AuthorizeAsync, so a missing thread cost zero look-ups while a forbidden one cost one, and the round-trip count distinguished them even though the bodies did not. P1 rather than P2 because the contract it pins is invisible to every other declaration in the class.

The disclosure the class exists for: a listing of another tenant's workspace returned by id alone. Distinct from the sibling routes at the authorization input rather than only at the URL - it is the only route that calls ResolveSessionAsync with isListing true, so it is the one case where the listing-specific branch of the check runs. Refusal asserted byte-identical against the never-minted thread and the sandbox asserted untouched.

A cross-tenant preview is refused and no read call is made, so the file's text never leaves the workspace. Same authorization input as Download (Read, not listing), but it holds 2 exclusive spans of its own preview-formatting path, so the floor puts it at P1.

A cross-tenant upload is refused and no write reaches the sandbox, so a stranger cannot plant a file in another tenant's workspace. Represents the AccessAction.Write input to the shared authorization helper on the content-planting side, and holds 2 exclusive spans, so it sits on the floor at P1.

Drives all six routes as the owner and asserts each succeeds, plus that exactly one write and two commands reached the sandbox. Declined as a prefix candidate at greedy rank 10 with 365 new spans: it is the non-vacuity partner for the refusal declarations - without it they would pass against a fixture that cannot reach the workspace for any caller - but it cannot itself fail on the disclosure defect, because a controller that authorized nobody and a controller that authorized everybody both let the owner through. Held at P1 on that partner role and on 4 exclusive spans.

A caller in the SAME tenant with no grant is refused as unknown. This is the case that distinguishes the owner check from the tenant conjunct: every cross-tenant declaration here is refused by either conjunct alone, so dropping the owner half would leave all of them green and only this one red. Held at P1 as the distinguishing case despite 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans - the spans it walks are shared, the discrimination is not.

A string of only separators and whitespace forwards NULL, not an empty list, so the gateway applies its default selection rather than being asked for nothing. The null-versus-empty distinction is the contract and is invisible to the parsing declaration. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

A comma-separated alias string with surrounding whitespace is split, trimmed and forwarded in order. The parsing is the controller's own work and no other declaration here can fail on it. Greedy rank 633 with 1 new span.

A gateway-unavailable exception degrades to 503 rather than 500, so the client can distinguish a temporarily offline gateway from a broken endpoint and retry. Greedy rank 177 with 10 new spans and 4 exclusive.

The success path returns the catalog by reference. P2 as the represented happy path: both alias declarations already drive the same success call and the 503 declaration covers the failure branch. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

With no provider mode set the default is test rather than a real provider. Pins that an unconfigured host does not silently select a provider that would attempt real calls. A distinct configuration branch, not a variation on the catalog shape. 0 marginal and 0 exclusive spans.

The catalog lists all seven provider ids with the configured default, and availability is asserted in BOTH directions against the environment - openai available with its key set, anthropic unavailable without one. The two-directional availability claim is the contract; a controller reporting everything available passes any single-provider check and offers the user providers that cannot answer. Greedy rank 102 with 23 new spans.

Measured (coverage-facts, greedy rank 195): 9 marginal and 3 exclusive spans - the duplicate-name rejection arm. Important failure handling, because two workspaces with one name collide on the derived directory leaf and would share files on disk. Its assertion is the weakest in the file, though: it reflects for the mere PRESENCE of an `error` property and never reads its value, so any 400 carrying any error object satisfies it - a misrouted validation failure would pass. Worth recording rather than treating the row as stronger than it is.
uncertainties: asserts-error-property-presence-not-value

rationale: Measured (coverage-facts, greedy rank 285): 5 marginal and 3 exclusive spans. The fail-closed default, and the comment states the principle exactly: a catalog advertising no capability at all is unknown, and unknown is not permission. Accepting the selection instead would persist a plugin restriction the gateway is not able to enforce, so the workspace would present as restricted while exposing everything - a silent over-grant, which is the worse direction of this decision. Asserts the code, so it is distinguishable from the unsupported-plugin 400 that the sibling test covers.

The accepted-selection positive for the create path, and the non-vacuity partner of the two rejection tests above: without it, a controller that refused every explicit plugin selection would pass both of them. Verifies through the store rather than the response, so it proves the selection was WRITTEN and not merely echoed back - the response view is built from the same object either way, so reading it would not distinguish the two.

Measured (coverage-facts, greedy rank 110): 21 marginal and 3 exclusive spans. Covers a path that had no plugin validation at all before the change - create, as opposed to update - and the second assertion is the one carrying the weight: the workspace must not exist AFTERWARDS. A controller that validated but persisted first would return the right 400 and leave a workspace on disk naming a plugin the gateway cannot supply, which is a broken row nothing would report. Checks the store directly rather than re-reading through the API.

Measured (coverage-facts, greedy rank 686): 1 marginal span. The create positive, and it pins three things nothing else does - the 201 result type, the Location header built from the new id, and the directory slug derived from the name. The slug matters beyond REST tidiness: it is the on-disk leaf the workspace's files live under, so a change in derivation silently relocates content for every workspace created afterwards.

Measured (coverage-facts, greedy rank 184): 10 marginal and 5 exclusive spans - the null-entry arm of the catalog read. A different kind of damage from a null FIELD and deliberately given a different answer: there is no workspace there to normalize, so it is reported as a corrupt catalog rather than skipped, and the reason is the one that matters - silently dropping the entry would make a truncated or half-written file look like a successful deletion, so a user would see a workspace vanish and the system would agree with them. Asserts the refusal code in the body, not just the 503.

Measured (coverage-facts, greedy rank 67): 47 marginal spans. The defect it pins is the worst-consequence one in the file and the docstring states it plainly: the store's WRITE paths normalize with ?? [] and its READ path did not, so an explicit "marketplaces": null in workspaces.json deserialized into a non-nullable member and every reader threw - one bad entry made the WHOLE catalog unreadable, so the UI could not load and no API call could repair it. That is an unrecoverable state reachable by a hand edit or a half-written file. Corrupts the real catalog on disk underneath a running store, which is how the shape actually arrives; the helper asserts the rewrite changed the file, so a stale-pattern edit cannot make the test pass by corrupting nothing. The second consumer of the same normalization, and its docstring gives the reason it is not a duplicate: a guard placed in List alone would leave the single-workspace read throwing. Measured (coverage-facts, greedy rank 272): 5 marginal spans, none exclusive. The unknown-id 404 on read - conventional MVC behaviour with a one-line assertion on the result type and no body. The distinguishing case for the unreachable-catalog test: a catalog that ANSWERS and does not offer the alias must serialize as "incompatible" with the gateway still marked available. Without the pair, an implementation emitting one string for both states stays green. The test is unusually honest about its own limits and the note is worth preserving: its Gateway.Available assertion is CORROBORATING, not distinguishing, because `available` is derived from the first workspace only and that is always the seeded default, whose empty marketplace list is compatible against any readable catalog - so it holds under any mutant that spares Compatible. The unreachable case is what pins the predicate.

rationale: The listing's baseline shape, and the only test asserting that the system-defined workspace is present and comes FIRST - ordering the SPA's picker depends on, and a property that no compatibility test can see because they all filter by compatibility string. Distinct primary behaviour; cheap; a real store on a temp directory rather than a fake.

The literal is asserted deliberately because it is the value the SPA branches on - an enum rename that did not reach the wire leaves the picker reading a state it has no case for, which fails as a blank or wrong control rather than as an error. Also asserts the gateway envelope stays unavailable, so the split does not pretend the catalog is readable; it only stops that fact being spelled as a per-workspace refusal. Half of a distinguishing pair with the reachable-catalog case, and the half that actually pins the predicate.

Additional variation, and its own docstring classifies it: a characterization test rather than a regression fixed here, since the create path already normalized with ?? []. Its stated purpose is to hold the two mutation entry points to the same behaviour so a future edit dropping the ?? on create reds this instead of shipping the defect on the sibling endpoint. That is worth keeping and is exactly a P2 job - it guards a property nothing is currently trying to change.

Distinct primary behaviour - what MODEL BINDING produces for the three payload shapes a client can send - and the file is right that it can only be asked over real HTTP: calling the action with Marketplaces = null! proves the action mishandles a null it was handed, not that a null can be handed to it. The state assertion is what makes the refused row meaningful - a 400 that had already half-applied the update would be worse than the 200 it replaced.

Measured (coverage-facts, greedy rank 51, inside the project's P0 prefix): 68 marginal spans and 9 exclusive - it is the last member of the greedy front that reaches the 80% target, so the prefix is not complete without it. Measured (coverage-facts, greedy rank 422): 3 marginal and 3 exclusive spans. Measured (coverage-facts, greedy rank 165): 12 marginal and 3 exclusive spans. rationale: Measured (coverage-facts, greedy rank 292): 5 marginal spans. A tenant-isolation bound rather than a traversal detail: adoption moves rows OUT of quarantine and is not a tenant-transfer tool, so pulling a descendant out of a real tenant on the strength of a parent link would let one operator move ANOTHER tenant's conversation by adopting its parent. The docstring is also honest about the limit this creates - it closes the way a split is created from quarantine and cannot repair a split that already spans two real tenants - and says it is written as a test rather than prose because the reader who wants that answer is the one who will not read the prose. That is the right instinct.

Input-robustness boundary: ["thread-1", null] is valid JSON and binds to a list with a null element, and both the parent lookup and the in-quarantine check are ordinal-comparer keyed, so a null key threw and the route answered an operator's typo with an unhandled 500. Real and worth keeping - a 500 also means no audit record on a route where every other refusal is a stable code in one - but the failure is loud and immediate rather than a wrong write, which puts it below the refusals that leave data in the wrong place. Also asserts the surviving id still expands correctly, so ignoring the null does not mean ignoring the request.

The stopping rule applied MID-walk rather than at the seed, and its docstring is careful about where the rule earns its keep: adopting a row already in a real tenant is refused by the source-tenant filter regardless, so what only the stopping rule prevents is continuing THROUGH such a parent - which would move a sibling the operator never named out of quarantine and into a tenant whose tree it is still not joined to, because the parent linking them stays put. A distinct traversal property from the seed-filtering case, and one that produces an orphan rather than a refusal.

That scale-gated silence is what makes it worth its own test rather than a comment. The second half is what keeps the refusal from being a trap: adopting the whole tenant needs no expansion and still works, so the operator has a way out. Seeds the cap exactly, referencing the controller's own constant rather than a literal.

The distinguishing case for the walk's bidirectionality, and it is genuinely distinguishing: a walk that climbs to an ancestor and never continues outward from it passes BOTH directional tests above and fails only here, leaving a sibling branch of the same quarantined tree behind - the same #405 split by a subtler route. Requires the shared root to be re-enqueued so its other children are picked up on the way back down, which is the specific implementation property nothing else exercises. Below P0 because the mechanism it refines is already pinned there.

The downward direction of the #405 walk: naming a root moves its whole sub-agent subtree, transitively, while the unrelated quarantined conversation stays where it is. Important failure handling and one third of a three-way distinction the Optional wrapper exists to carry: OMITTED means leave it alone, and the revision must not move. Getting it wrong is a silent data loss - an ordinary marketplace edit would wipe the workspace's plugin selection, changing what the sandbox exposes, with a 200 and no indication. The update positive, and the most thorough assertion set in the file: the marketplaces are REPLACED by value, the name and directory are untouched, UpdatedAt moves forward and CreatedAt does not. The last pair is the one nothing else covers - a store that reset CreatedAt on every write would lose the workspace's age silently, and one that left UpdatedAt alone would break any ordering or cache keyed on it. Note the mechanism: it uses a real Task.Delay(2) to force the clock forward, so the timestamp assertion depends on wall-clock resolution rather than on an injected clock.

rationale: Measured (coverage-facts, greedy rank 565): 2 marginal spans. Canonicalization is the collapsing half of the identity contract and the place collisions are made: five rows cover scheme-case and host-case folding, default-port stripping for both http and https, a trailing slash, and a doubled trailing slash. Getting this wrong in the permissive direction merges two gateways into one catalog; getting it wrong in the strict direction splits one gateway across two. Asserts the canonical string itself rather than key equality, so a failure names which normalisation broke instead of only reporting that two keys differed. One worklist id covering 5 theory rows. The strongest oracle in the file and the anchor for the whole derivation: a hard-coded SHA-256 digest of the exact spec material, with the computation recorded in the comment so the expectation is reproducible rather than captured from the implementation. Every part of the format is pinned at once - the domain-separation prefix, its version, the NUL delimiters and the field order - so a change to any of them fails here and nowhere else. That matters because the key names a directory on disk: a silently altered derivation does not error, it orphans every existing catalog and re-onboards the same gateway as a stranger.
