requirements: the conversation's effort floor and spawn-type model resolver reach the controller options

rationale: Null-input boundary of the policy application: with no conversation options the same instance is returned untouched.
requirements: applying a null conversation policy returns the controller options unchanged

rationale: Applies the inherit-all and structural-guard assertions to the enriched-catalog overload - the same two contracts as the built-in row, on a wider input.
requirements: controller templates built from an enriched catalog remain inherit-all and satisfy WorkflowManager's construction guard

rationale: Provider routing for delegates: the enriched catalog was built with the conversation's agent factory, so the controller overload must rebind every entry - discovered ones included - to the controller's provider factory, or a preferred-provider workflow run spawns delegates on the wrong provider.
evidence: asserts every template's AgentFactory returns the provider agent instance, not the conversation's
requirements: every controller template's agent factory is rebound to the controller's provider factory

rationale: Regression guard: a controller seeded only from the built-ins answered 'Unknown template' for any discovered plugin subagent_type. The controller must be seeded from the same enriched catalog the primary agent uses.
evidence: asserts a discovered marketplace template key is present alongside the built-ins
requirements: controller templates include discovered and marketplace sub-agents, not only the built-ins

rationale: The negative half of the structural guard: inherit-all controller templates WITHOUT NonInheritedToolNames are rejected at construction with a message naming the missing setting. Without it the acceptance rows would pass against a manager that asserts nothing. Front member with exclusive spans (floor).
evidence: asserts ArgumentException whose message mentions NonInheritedToolNames
requirements: controller options that do not exclude the workflow tools from inheritance are rejected at WorkflowManager construction

rationale: The composed contract for a workflow-only mode: root sub-agent delegation stays closed (no Agent tools exposed) while the launch tools are enabled, and the mode's effort and per-type model policy still reach the controller. Pins that narrowing the root does not silently strip the controller's policy.
evidence: asserts caps.SubAgents false, caps.StartWorkflowTools true, ExposedToolNames empty, and the controller's effort floor and type routing
requirements: a mode enabling only StartWorkflowAgent exposes no root sub-agent tools
that mode's effort and per-type model policy still reach the workflow controller

rationale: The sibling read the ancestor policy exists to refuse is refused identically when the target is addressed by the roster name instead of by id: the route 403s with not_an_ancestor and the tool reports the same code, and the tool's refusal text does not repeat the name that was asked for. Widening addressing is exactly where an authorization surface grows a second, softer door - a name resolved before the ancestry check, or a refusal that confirms the name exists, and one compromised prompt reads its peers. P1: the authorization contract under the new addressing form, a distinct guarantee from the positive resolution row rather than a variation of it.
requirements: in-process only; controller invoked directly, InMemoryConversationStore, WorkflowRunRegistry with no on-disk index

rationale: The name is taken from the roster the GetAgents tool actually publishes - the test reads the agent's row, checks name_resolves_to_agent and confirms the name is not simply the id - and that name then reads the transcript through both the route and the in-agent tool, while the identifier form keeps answering exactly as before. Reading the name out of the live roster rather than assuming it is what closes the addressing gap being pinned: readers are handed a name, messaging resolves names, and the transcript read used to match identifiers only, so the very identifier a reader was given came back as if the agent did not exist. P1, and the representative for name addressing; the sibling-refusal and ambiguity rows build on it.
requirements: in-process only; controller invoked directly, InMemoryConversationStore, WorkflowRunRegistry with no on-disk index

rationale: Two agents spawned asking for twin: the second's receipt reports a different granted name, the route read by twin returns exactly the first agent's transcript, the route read by the granted name returns exactly the second's, the in-agent tool reads the granted name without error, and both stay readable by identifier. Replaces the ambiguity row that pinned both refused as unknown_target. A read is never a guess - each name selects exactly one transcript - and a read that resolved the plain name to the newcomer would hand a reader a different agent's transcript than it asked for, silently. P1: the authorization surface under the suffixing policy; the representative for name addressing remains ReadTranscript_ResolvesTheNameTheRosterPublishes.
requirements: in-process only; controller invoked directly, InMemoryConversationStore, WorkflowRunRegistry with no on-disk index

rationale: A background spawn is held at the moment its completion relay has started but not returned - the parent's SendAsync is gated on a TaskCompletionSource - and the owned provider is asserted NOT disposed in that window, then disposed exactly once when the manager is torn down. The gate is what makes the window deterministic rather than a race the assertion might win by luck. Disposing at run completion would pull the provider out from under an in-flight relay, and it also destroys the warm resumption the manager now offers a finished child. P1: the provider-lifetime contract for the background completion path, distinct from the exactly-once teardown rule it ends with.
requirements: in-process only; Moq provider and parent agent, SubAgentManager
bounded: 5s wait for the relay to start

rationale: A second message to a finished named child is answered by the SAME owned provider: the reply arrives, neither provider is disposed during the continuation, the factory queue still holds its second agent so only one was ever created, and the first is disposed exactly once at manager teardown. The undisposed-queue pair is the real assertion - it rules out both a per-run provider rebuild and a disposal that would leave the continuation talking to a dead provider. This is the lifetime the warm-resumption behaviour rests on, so a regression shows up as an ObjectDisposedException or a silent provider churn on every follow-up. P1: the primary owned-provider lifetime contract for continuation.

An owned provider whose DisposeAsync throws is still left alone at run completion, attempted exactly once when the manager is torn down, and its exception does not escape - the test awaits manager.DisposeAsync with no catch, so a rethrow fails it. Exactly-once matters in both directions here: one attempt means teardown does not spin retrying a provider that will keep throwing, and a propagated exception would abandon the disposal of every agent queued behind it, leaking their providers on host shutdown. P1: the fault-tolerance contract of teardown, distinct from the happy-path exactly-once row and the representative of the throwing-disposal pair.

The same throwing-disposal rule reached through a provider that implements only IDisposable: not touched at completion, Dispose attempted once at teardown, exception swallowed rather than rethrown. The helper it uses deliberately omits IAsyncDisposable so the synchronous branch of SubAgentState.DisposeOwnedProviderAgentAsync is the one exercised, which is a genuine second branch. P2: the same contract as Spawn_ManagerTeardownAttemptsOwnedProviderDisposalWhenItThrows reached through a second interface, mirroring how the synchronous exactly-once row sits below its async representative.

A todo nudge delivered to a child that has already completed its first run is admitted, and it runs through the SAME provider instance - one provider ever created, never disposed, zero calls after disposal, its call count now two - with the last request carrying the message as a real NotifyMessage of kind TodoNudge rather than as flattened text. The wait before the assertions is an explicit non-vacuity guard: without it, the no-call-after-dispose check would pass on a delivery nobody ever executed. This is the board talking back to a finished agent, the way the nudge and digest paths do in the host, so a regression is a silently dropped reminder or an ObjectDisposedException from a provider torn down at completion. P1: the primary delivery contract for this component.
requirements: in-process only; Moq root agent and providers, SubAgentManager

rationale: The only positive path of the cfg- branch: with an authenticated session, an in-scope 443 destination and a matching allow rule, the webhook answers allow and returns exactly the enabled headers with their values verbatim, drops the Enabled:false header, and sets ExpiresAt from the provider CacheTtlSeconds. If this regresses, no appsettings-configured headers provider injects anything at all and every configured egress rule silently loses its credential. It is the critical baseline for this surface, not merely an important case, because the other nine families in the class only prove the deny directions.

An operator spelling the rule's AuthProvider as PARTNER-headers while the provider key is partner-headers must still be allowed and still receive both headers, because the controller compares match.AuthProvider to the route id with StringComparison.Ordinal. The contract it depends on is the compiler's ResolveProviderKey normalisation, whose representative is SandboxEgressPolicyCompilerTests.Rule_auth_provider_reference_resolves_to_the_configured_provider_key at P1; this row is the same claim replayed through the controller, so it is a second case crossing an axis already covered and sits at P2.

Setting Enabled=false on the provider must stop injection even though the rule and destination are otherwise valid, which is the ResolveHeadersProvider tombstone branch. The test deliberately removes the rule's AuthProvider reference so the config stays valid, isolating the disabled-provider branch rather than the dangling-reference one. This is the primary promise an operator relies on when switching a credential off without deleting configuration, so P1; it is not part of the small P0 baseline because the deny theory already proves the endpoint fails closed on the seven shapes it covers.

A cfg- id whose configured Type is webhook must be denied by this app, because the gateway calls that provider's own external endpoint and this route was never the intended resolver for it. The test builds a webhook-typed provider with an external endpoint and its own GatewayAuth and asserts the decision is deny, pinning the type discrimination in ResolveHeadersProvider. Answering allow here would let an id that was never meant to reach this app mint this app's configured headers, so it is a primary supported contract at P1 rather than a variation.

F-001 regression pin replayed through the controller: with a deny rule listing both /Admin/* and /admin/* at priority 100 in front of a catch-all authenticated allow at 200, both spellings must deny with null headers rather than one falling through and receiving the injected credential. The underlying ordinal path-dedupe contract is pinned by SandboxEgressPolicyCompilerTests.Case_distinct_path_patterns_are_all_kept_because_path_matching_is_ordinal, which is the representative at P1; this is that bug-regression claim crossed with the deny-precedence axis already covered by Denies_when_a_higher_priority_config_deny_rule_covers_the_destination, so P2.

A programmatic consumer can construct SandboxGatewayOptions in code and never run the validator, so the branch must survive malformed policy. The test hands it a rule with Ports="abc" and asserts a 200 OkObjectResult carrying decision deny with null headers, which is the always-200 allow/deny contract the try/catch around EvaluateConfiguredProvider exists to guarantee. An unhandled exception here would surface gateway-side as an opaque webhook failure rather than a decision, so this pins a primary contract of the endpoint at P1 rather than an edge case.

The whole defense-in-depth deny matrix of the cfg- branch in one family: unknown provider id, provider_id not matching the route, destination outside the provider host scope, a non-443 port, a method the rule does not allow, a path the rule does not cover, and a rule_id that is not the rule that actually matched. Each case asserts decision deny AND Headers null, so a regression cannot leak headers on a deny. If any of these gates regressed the endpoint becomes a credential-minting oracle that the gateway's own rule evaluation is the only remaining defense for, which is exactly the fundamental break P0 is for.

A deny rule at priority 100 must beat the authenticated allow at 200 for the same destination, so the webhook refuses to inject even though a matching allow rule exists. This pins that EvaluateConfiguredProvider re-runs the gateway's own first-match-wins evaluation over the configured rules instead of merely finding some allow rule that names the provider. Without it an operator's deny carve-out would still receive the credential, which is the primary supported meaning of rule priority, so P1.

Hosts other than the sample (the headless daemon) construct AuthWebhookController through the shorter overload with no SandboxGatewayOptions at all; a cfg- id arriving there must produce a clean deny rather than a null-reference. That is the gatewayOptions is null arm of the same fail-closed guard the deny theory already exercises through ResolveHeadersProvider, reached from a different construction site, so it is an edge case on a covered axis at P2 rather than a distinct contract.

With the Authorization header set to a secret that does not match the stored session secret, the route must return UnauthorizedResult and never reach the cfg- evaluation at all. This is the authentication gate in front of every configured header injection: the assertion is on the result TYPE, so a regression that turned it into a 200 deny would still fail. If this breaks, anyone who can reach the webhook route can drive the injection logic, which makes the surface fundamentally broken rather than merely weakened, so it belongs in the small P0 baseline alongside the happy path and the deny matrix.

Eight cases pinning IsWithinScope as a subset test between two PATTERNS: identical and nested wildcards and an exact host inside a wildcard validate clean, while a wildcard rule host under an exact provider host, a widening wildcard, the bare apex under a wildcard scope, and an unrelated host all produce an error naming the rule key and the Hosts field. This is the guard that stops a rule from widening a credential's blast radius past what its provider declares, and the rejection cases assert the message names partner-api and Hosts rather than merely being non-empty. It is the representative for host-scope containment at P1.

Two independent rejections: an authenticated rule on port 8443 must error naming partner-api and Ports, and one whose host sits outside the provider scope must error naming partner-api and Hosts. The Hosts half overlaps Authenticated_rule_host_must_be_a_subset_of_its_providers_scope, which is the representative for that axis, but the Ports half is the only assertion in the corpus on the HTTPS-443-only rule for a credential-bearing rule. Keeping it at P1 rather than tiering the whole family down avoids leaving a cleartext credential egress uncovered until P2.

A rule naming an exactly-spelled provider compiles to AuthProvider cfg-partner-headers, with its Paths and its explicit Priority 100 carried through. Every one of those claims is also asserted by Rule_auth_provider_reference_resolves_to_the_configured_provider_key, which additionally proves the emitted id equals the compiled provider's own Id and covers the case-varying spellings; that family is the representative at P1. Priority passthrough is separately pinned by Rules_compile_in_ascending_priority_order, so this is a second case crossing covered axes at P2.

F-001. Paths="/Admin/*,/admin/*" must compile to BOTH patterns in order, and FirstMatchingRule must then return block-admin for both /admin/secrets and /Admin/secrets rather than letting one spelling fall through to the catch-all allow behind it. Two contracts nothing else in this class covers: the Ordinal comparer on the Paths call site of ParseList, and the FirstMatchingRule matcher the auth webhook depends on. Kept at P1 rather than treated as an ordinary bug-regression pin because it is the only direct exercise of FirstMatchingRule here and the regression it pins silently opened a denied path.

ParseList is the primitive every configured host, port, method, path and scope passes through, and this family pins its whole contract at once: entries trimmed, empties dropped, case-insensitive dedupe keeping the first spelling, and ports projected to ints. It also pins the compiled defaults a rule inherits when the operator omits them - Action allow, Priority 500, AuthProvider null. If this breaks, every rule and provider in the file compiles to the wrong shape and no other family's arrange survives, which is what makes it the critical baseline for this component rather than an important parsing test.

A *.github.com allow validates clean at both priority 100 and 500, because config-only validation must not reason about managed or predefined gates - those exist only in the merged set, and a config rule named after a managed rule replaces it. This is a scope boundary asserted as an absence: a regression rejects a legal configuration at startup rather than admitting an unsafe one, and the positive shadow-detection contract it bounds is already pinned by Wildcard_allow_overlapping_a_gate_is_detected_pattern_to_pattern at P1. Edge case on a covered axis, so P2.

Enabled=false on a rule and on a provider must validate clean AND drop out of both compile paths: CompileRules and CompileProviders each come back empty. Three assertions covering the validator's early return for a tombstone plus the Where(Enabled) filters on both compile methods. This is the operator-facing promise that switching an entry off removes it from the wire policy instead of shipping a disabled entry to the gateway, which is a primary supported contract at P1.

Ten hand-built rule sets over ValidateEffectivePrecedence, the public authority for the MERGED policy: a broad allow in front of an overlapping auth gate errors naming both rules; the same pair behind the gate is clean; an auth-bearing wildcard is still a broad allow but cannot shadow itself; a bare "*" on either side overlaps everything; an empty host set on either the allow or the gate is a catch-all; disjoint hosts never conflict. This mirrors the gateway's hard 400 at create time, and it is the only direct test of this method, so P1.

One rule carrying three independent faults (loopback host, port 0, method CONNECT) must yield at least three errors rather than throwing on the first, so an operator fixes the whole file in one pass. The assertion is only a count floor, so it pins the aggregation shape and nothing about the messages themselves - those are covered by Invalid_configuration_fails_closed_naming_the_offender at P0. An operator-ergonomics guarantee whose regression costs iterations, not safety, so P2.

The mainline compile output of the whole feature: a headers provider becomes id cfg-partner-headers, wire type webhook, an endpoint pointing at THIS app's /api/auth/webhook/cfg-partner-headers route, gatewayAuth set to the per-session secret, and the configured CacheTtlSeconds carried through. Every one of those four values is what makes the injection round-trip work; if the endpoint or the secret is wrong the gateway either cannot call back or is rejected when it does, and no configured header ever reaches a request. That is the fundamental-break criterion for this component, so P0 rather than P1.

Twenty-eight configurations covering nearly every rejection branch of the validator - malformed, bare-wildcard, loopback and empty hosts; empty, non-numeric, out-of-range and zero ports; empty and unknown methods; malformed paths; unknown action; dangling auth provider; reserved rule id; unknown provider type; missing or invalid provider hosts; negative TTL; a headers provider with no enabled header; invalid and empty header names/values; a webhook provider missing its gateway secret; and non-absolute, cleartext, userinfo-bearing and fragment-bearing endpoints. Each asserts the messages are non-empty, name the offending id and field, and contain neither the secret canary nor the external secret canary. Validation is the entire reason the compiler is a trust boundary: if it stops rejecting, invalid egress policy reaches the gateway unchecked, so this is the P0 baseline for the surface.

The positive counterpart of the F-003 grammar guard: three legal keys (a hyphenated one, one mixing underscore and dot, and a single character) validate clean and compile to an endpoint whose last path segment is exactly cfg-<key> and contains no separator, query, fragment, space or percent character. The grammar contract itself is pinned by Provider_and_rule_keys_outside_the_id_grammar_fail_closed, which is the representative at P1 because it is the fail-closed direction; this row crosses the same axis from the accept side, so P2.

F-003. Eight keys carrying a separator, query, fragment, space, percent-escape, emptiness or an illegal leading character must be rejected for BOTH a provider and a rule, with the message naming the right configuration section and the fixed "id must be" reason. A configured key is emitted verbatim as a wire id and, for a headers provider, as the last path segment of this app's webhook URL, which the webhook route middleware accepts only as one non-empty segment - so without this a config validates clean and then is never routable. Primary fail-closed contract, and the representative for the id grammar, so P1.

Four reserved keys - github, github-auth, m365 and the predefined-e1 runtime prefix - must each produce an error naming that key. Configuration may not define or shadow an identity that code owns, or a partner's static headers could be served under a managed OAuth provider's id and the two credential namespaces would collide on the wire. Distinct fail-closed contract from the id-grammar guard (these keys are grammatically legal), and nothing else in the corpus covers the reserved set, so P1.

Three spellings of the same reference - partner-headers, PARTNER-headers, Partner-Headers - all validate clean and compile to AuthProvider cfg-partner-headers, and the test additionally asserts the compiled rule's AuthProvider equals the compiled provider's own Id. Configuration keys are case-insensitive but the gateway resolves auth_provider by exact match, so emitting the operator's spelling would validate clean and then deny every request. This is the representative for reference-to-key normalisation at P1; Authenticated_rule_references_the_prefixed_provider_id is the narrower single-spelling case below it.

A rule pointing at a tombstoned provider must error naming partner-api and AuthProvider. This reaches the same validator branch as the "unknown auth provider" case already covered by Invalid_configuration_fails_closed_naming_the_offender at P0, just via the !provider.Enabled half of the same condition rather than the lookup miss. It is also belt-and-braces downstream: the auth webhook's ResolveHeadersProvider independently returns null for a disabled provider and denies. Variation on a covered axis, so P2.

Validate rejects a dangling reference, but CompileRules also runs unvalidated on the auth-webhook hot path via FirstMatchingRule, so its behaviour there decides fail-open versus fail-closed. The test asserts a dangling "ghost" compiles to cfg-ghost and not null, that whitespace around it normalises to the same unresolvable id rather than a second distinct one, and that only a BLANK reference compiles to null. Dropping the reference instead would silently downgrade an authenticated rule into an anonymous allow, so this is a primary fail-open-prevention contract at P1.

Two rules declared late-then-early in the dictionary compile out as early, late - ascending by Priority, not declaration order. Every first-match-wins decision downstream, in both the gateway and the auth webhook's own re-evaluation, is built on this ordering, so reversing it silently inverts every deny carve-out and every credential gate without producing a single validation error. One assertion, but on the contract the rest of the precedence machinery presupposes, so P1.

F-002. Six configurations plant a canary inside the offending value - a bad port token, a bad method, an interior-wildcard path, a dangling provider reference, an out-of-scope host, and a shadowing wildcard host - and each asserts the joined messages name leaky-rule and the field while containing no canary. Validation messages land in startup logs, so echoing a value can persist operator-supplied material there. The P0 rejection theory only guards the two provider-side canaries; this family is the only coverage of the rule-side value echoes, so it is a distinct primary contract at P1.

The other provider kind: a webhook provider keeps its own configured endpoint, its own gateway secret, its TTL and its parsed RequiredScopes, and the test asserts explicitly that gatewayAuth is the external secret AND is not the app's per-session secret. That negative is the security claim - handing an external endpoint this app's session secret would let it impersonate the app to the gateway. Kept at P1 rather than P0 because it is the second kind crossing the CompileProviders axis whose baseline is Headers_provider_compiles_to_this_apps_webhook_with_the_session_secret.

Nine allow/deny pairs pinning shadow detection as a PATTERN-to-PATTERN comparison: identical wildcards, nesting in both directions, and both apex directions must be reported naming both rule keys, while a deny at a lower priority number, disjoint wildcards, and a narrow sub-host carve-out in front of a broad deny must produce no error at all. The nested-wildcard and apex cases are exactly the ones a pattern-vs-bare-host comparison misses, which is how a broad allow silently opens a gated host. Representative for config-level shadow detection at P1.

A *.example.com allow at 150 in front of an authenticated api.example.com rule at 200 must be rejected naming both broad and partner-api. This is one concrete instance of the wildcard-covers-exact case the nine-case theory Wildcard_allow_overlapping_a_gate_is_detected_pattern_to_pattern already covers, differing only in that the gate here is auth-provider-bearing rather than a deny and the whole thing runs through Validate with a real provider attached. Second case crossing a covered axis, so P2 with that theory as the representative.

A *.x.com allow at 50 that CARRIES an auth provider still counts as a broad allow, so sitting in front of a *.x.com deny at 100 must throw ArgumentException naming wide-auth and blocked. The claim that an auth-bearing wildcard is not exempt is already asserted directly against ValidateEffectivePrecedence by SandboxEgressPolicyCompilerTests.Effective_precedence_mirrors_the_gateways_broad_allow_rules, and the registry-level integration of the post-merge check is represented by Broad_allow_shadowing_a_managed_oauth_gate_fails_closed. Third case on the same axis, so P2.

The same *.github.com allow moved to priority 500 must build successfully, emitting both the broad rule and the managed github rule with its github-auth provider intact. It is the negative counterpart of Broad_allow_shadowing_a_managed_oauth_gate_fails_closed - identical inputs with the priority flipped - so it exists to stop the precedence check over-rejecting rather than to pin a distinct behaviour. Second case crossing an axis whose representative is that family at P1, so P2.

A configured *.github.com allow at priority 50 sits in front of the managed github gate at 100, so GitHub egress would proceed with no credential gate at all; BuildAuthProviders must throw ArgumentException whose message names both broad and github. The config-only validator cannot see managed gates, so this is the reason the post-merge ValidateEffectivePrecedence call exists at the merge point - and it converts an opaque gateway 400 at sandbox-create into an actionable startup failure. Representative for the registry-level post-merge precedence contract, so P1.

A runtime predefined egress key for api.example.com produces a predefined-e1 gate at priority 100; a configured *.example.com allow at 50 in front of it must throw naming broad and predefined-e1. The mechanism and failure mode are identical to Broad_allow_shadowing_a_managed_oauth_gate_fails_closed, which is the representative at P1 - this row varies only the SOURCE of the invisible gate (runtime registry state rather than code-owned managed rules). It also costs a real temp directory and a PredefinedKeyRegistry, so P2.

With GitHub configured and a partner-headers provider in appsettings, the merged provider list is exactly github-auth plus cfg-partner-headers - the configured entry lands under the cfg- wire prefix and never displaces or shadows the managed identity. The rules merge is key-based and DOES allow replacement, so proving the provider merge is additive is a separate claim, not a corollary. Without it a configured provider could take over a managed credential id and serve static headers where an OAuth token is expected, so P1.

A configured rule keyed github-egress must replace the managed rule of that id whole - the merged rule carries the configured host mirror.example.com and priority 120 - while the sibling managed github token-injecting rule keeps its github-auth provider untouched. That second half is what makes this a replacement rather than a wipe. It is the operator-facing promise that a built-in rule can be retargeted without a code change, and it is the representative for the key-based rule merge, so P1.

A rule keyed github with hosts *.github.com replaces the managed github gate, so after the merge no gate remains for the wildcard to shadow and the build must succeed: the merged rule carries the configured hosts with a null AuthProvider, and the managed github-auth provider entry survives because only the RULE was replaced. This bounds the same post-merge precedence check whose representative is Broad_allow_shadowing_a_managed_oauth_gate_fails_closed at P1; the regression it catches is a false rejection of a legal configuration, not an unsafe policy, so P2.

An anonymous configured rule must survive the merge unchanged and never acquire a credential: the public-docs rule keeps its hosts, GET, 443, a null AuthProvider and empty RequiredScopes both when GitHub is configured and when it is not. The two-case axis is what carries the claim - with GitHub on, the managed github-auth provider and rule appear ALONGSIDE it; with GitHub off, providers is null and public-docs is the only rule. That an anonymous rule is never handed a token is a primary supported contract, so P1.

An Enabled=false entry keyed github-egress removes the managed rule entirely while the managed github rule stays, which is the tombstone half of the same key-driven merge: removal is driven by the configured KEYS regardless of Enabled, and only enabled rules are re-added. Config_rule_named_after_a_managed_rule_replaces_it is the representative for that merge at P1; this is the second case crossing it, so P2. Note the failure direction here is restrictive - a regression leaves an extra allow rule in place rather than dropping a gate.

The load-bearing security invariant of the whole configured-headers design, asserted where it actually matters: the merged providers and network pair is JSON-serialized in full and the configured header value canary must not appear anywhere in it, while the rule still links to cfg-partner-headers. Header values are meant to stay in this app and be resolved on the webhook callback; if one ever reaches the create request it is handed to the gateway process and every deployment leaks its partner credentials. Serializing the whole payload rather than checking named fields is what makes it a baseline test instead of a shape assertion, so P0.

F-002 at the registry boundary. The ArgumentException message that BuildAuthProviders throws is what actually reaches startup logs, and the test asserts it names leaky and Ports while not containing the planted 9x-CANARY port value. The compiler theory covers the individual error STRINGS; this covers the wrapping - the exception prefix and the joined aggregate could reintroduce a value the compiler kept out. Distinct surface for the same secret-hygiene contract, so P1.

A loopback host in a configured rule must make BuildAuthProviders throw ArgumentException naming the offending rule, rather than compiling and shipping the policy. This is the only assertion that the registry runs SandboxEgressPolicyCompiler.Validate at all before merging - a programmatic consumer that builds SandboxGatewayOptions in code never runs the host startup check, so this call is the last gate before the create request. If it regressed, every compiler validation contract in the corpus would still pass while invalid policy reached the gateway unchecked, which is the fundamental break P0 exists for.

Binds the CHECKED-IN samples/LmStreaming.Sample/appsettings.json (found by walking up to LmDotnetTools.sln) and asserts the shipped policy is exactly one public-docs allow rule over ten named documentation hosts on GET/443 with no auth provider and no providers block at all. This is the only guard on what the default deployment's egress policy actually is: a host added to the shipped file without review widens default-deny egress for every deployment, and the exact host list means a silent addition fails. Primary supported contract of the shipped configuration, so P1 - it is in-process, not a deployment journey, so not P3.

With no AuthOptions, no predefined keys and default gateway options, BuildAuthProviders must return null for BOTH the providers list and the network list - not empty collections, which the create request would serialize as an explicit empty policy. Every deployment that configures nothing at all goes through this path, and emitting rules here would attach unrequested egress to a sandbox that asked for none. Primary supported default behaviour at P1; the injection-path baselines are the two P0 families in this class.
Smoke assertion: LogData destructuring an anonymous object with a nested object does not throw. Ends in Assert.True(true).
uncertainties: No assertion on the destructured payload; only absence of an exception is proven.

rationale: Asserts LoggerFactory.CreateLogger<T> returns non-null and logging through it does not throw. Regression: a null or throwing factory in the test base.
uncertainties: Despite the name, no assertion inspects the emitted log for test-context properties.

rationale: Smoke assertion only: LogTestStart/Logger.LogInformation/LogTestEnd run without throwing, then Assert.True(true). Regression it can detect is a throw during LoggingTestBase logging, nothing about log content.
uncertainties: Assert.True(true) proves nothing about test-context enrichment; the in-file comment says verification happens by inspecting the log file, which this test does not do.

rationale: Smoke assertion: Trace with zero, one and two template arguments does not throw. Regression: a format/arity crash in Trace.
uncertainties: Assert.True(true) only; nothing about trace output is verified.

rationale: Idempotence boundary: purging a never-created root and re-purging an already-purged root both return without throwing. Regression: per-test teardown failing on its second call.
Happy path: the root is gone and no "-detached" sibling is left behind. Regression: renaming out of the way without deleting would grow temp storage while still looking successful.
uncertainties: As the in-file comment states, both assertions would also pass for an implementation that never detaches; this case does not pin the rename.

rationale: The only discriminating case for the helper's reason to exist: with a descendant handle held, Purge must leave the attached root and an untouched sibling record intact and throw an IOException naming the root. Regression: an in-place recursive delete races an in-flight CreateNew writer.
requirements: platform-windows-only ([WindowsOnlyFact]; POSIX rename of a busy directory succeeds)
uncertainties: Skipped entirely off Windows, so on other platforms this contract has no coverage at all.

rationale: Same exclusion on the OpenAI wire shape, where the notification arrives as a plain string user message rather than a text block. Regression: fixing only the Anthropic content-block path.

Chain selection must ignore an instruction chain relayed inside a sub-agent completion notification and resume the parent's next step ("Wrap up", assistantCount 1) on the Anthropic wire shape. Regression (#711): the child's chain hijacks the parent's script, silently rewriting every multi-agent test-mode scenario.

The distinguishing positive: a genuine later user chain does replace the earlier one, with assistantCount reset to 0. Without it the notification-exclusion cases are compatible with an analyzer that always keeps the first chain.

Control case: a completion notification carrying plain task text also leaves the parent chain in place. Regression: over-broad notification handling that resets the plan. Variation on the P0 case, so P2.
Same resolution on the Anthropic handler, where the system prompt arrives as a top-level "system" field rather than a message. Regression: reading the system prompt from the wrong request location.
Anthropic-side variation of the tools_echo contract already pinned at P1 on the OpenAI handler. Regression: descriptions dropped only on this provider path.
Anthropic-side variation of the tools_list resolution, reading tools from the Anthropic tools array. Regression: provider-specific tool extraction returning nothing.
uncertainties: Contains-only assertions; see the OpenAI counterpart.

rationale: End-to-end: the __SYSTEM_PROMPT__ sentinel resolves to the request's actual system message in the OpenAI non-streaming response body. Regression: the sentinel leaking through literally, which the parser-level test cannot detect.

Distinguishes tools_echo from tools_list: descriptions of both tools appear, not just names, read out of the OpenAI function.description field. Regression: the two directives collapsing so description-probing tests silently lose their subject.
Names of both declared tools appear in the resolved output. Regression: an empty tool list. Weaker than the tools_echo case, which subsumes the name assertions, so P2.
uncertainties: Contains-only assertions cannot distinguish a names-only list from an echo that also emits descriptions.

rationale: Anthropic-handler variation of the filtered-params resolution, with different model and max_tokens values. Regression: resolution on only one handler.
Anthropic-handler variation of the URL resolution (/v1/messages). Regression: resolution implemented on only one handler.
End-to-end resolution of __REQUEST_HEADERS__, asserted only by the presence of "Content-Type". Regression: an empty header dump.
uncertainties: A single Contains on a header name every request carries; it cannot distinguish a full header echo from a hardcoded string.

rationale: End-to-end: the encoded field list resolves to the request's actual model and max_tokens values in the response body. Regression: the resolver ignoring the filter or reading defaults instead of the live request.
uncertainties: Contains-only assertions; does not prove unrequested fields are excluded.

rationale: End-to-end: __REQUEST_URL__ resolves to the real request path (/v1/chat/completions) rather than the literal sentinel. Regression: an unresolved placeholder reaching the caller.
Combination: three metadata directives in one instruction keep their order and individual encodings. Regression: positional mix-up when several placeholders share a step.
Sentinel mapping for request_headers_echo (__REQUEST_HEADERS__). Regression: sentinel rename. Variation over a represented mechanism.

The only placeholder that carries an argument list: fields are encoded as "__REQUEST_PARAMS__:model,max_tokens" in order. Regression: dropping the suffix silently turns a filtered echo into a full dump.
Boundary of the field-encoding rule: no fields yields the bare sentinel with no trailing colon. Regression: emitting "__REQUEST_PARAMS__:" which the resolver would read as an empty filter.
Directive-to-sentinel mapping for request_url_echo (__REQUEST_URL__), the same mechanism already pinned for system_prompt_echo. Regression: sentinel rename.
Same byte-for-byte reassembly claim applied to a compact JSON payload with no interior spaces. Regression: chunking inserting or trimming whitespace around punctuation. Variation on the P0 case.

Reassembling every delta must reproduce the original text exactly, including the space that falls on a chunk boundary. Regression: word-chunking that drops boundary whitespace corrupts the text every streaming test reads back.

The optional capture parameter is wired into the handler chain: one request recorded and deserialisable to the typed OpenAI request. Regression: an ignored capture argument. Composition of contracts already represented, so P2.

A configured status sequence takes precedence over the test-mode handler and advances per request (503 then 200). Regression: the inner handler swallowing the sequence would make retry tests over test-mode clients never see a failure.

Baseline for the non-streaming branch: application/json, object "chat.completion", the echoed model, non-empty choice content and the fixed 100/50/150 usage triple. Regression: a malformed completion envelope breaks every non-streaming test-mode consumer.
uncertainties: The usage numbers are fixed constants, so this also pins them as literals rather than computed token counts.

rationale: Anthropic-handler variation of the single-tool schema document, reading input_schema instead of parameters. Regression: schema extraction implemented on only one provider shape.

tool_schema resolves to a markdown document for exactly the named tool: headings, a parseable pretty-printed JSON schema containing the tool's own property, and explicit absence of the sibling tool. Regression: dumping all tools or emitting unparseable schema text.
An unknown tool name yields a "not found" message rather than an empty document or an exception. Regression: silent empty output would let a probe misread a typo as an absent capability.
uncertainties: Asserts only the substring "not found"; the surrounding message is unconstrained.

rationale: Parser half of the tool_schema directive: the name is encoded as "__TOOL_SCHEMA__:get_weather". Regression: dropping the name suffix. Same encoding mechanism as request_params_echo, already pinned at P1.
Boundary: no name yields the bare sentinel with no trailing colon. Regression: "__TOOL_SCHEMA__:" being read as a tool literally named empty string.

Pins the handler's provider-selection rule: the first registered provider whose CanHandle is true serves every request, so later providers are unreachable. Regression: switching to round-robin or last-wins would silently change the response of every multi-provider fixture in the repo. Cross-cutting dispatch contract, so P1.
Preset variant fixing 401 + authentication_error over the Anthropic envelope. Regression: preset status/type drift. Variation over a represented contract, so P2.

Pins the Anthropic error envelope the builder emits: status code plus {type:"error", error:{type,message}} with caller-supplied values. Regression: a reshaped or wrapper-less error body would silently make every downstream Anthropic error-handling test assert against a body the real API never sends. Fundamental wire contract of this helper, so P0 rather than P1.
requirements: in-process-http-only (HttpClient built over the mock handler, no socket)

rationale: Preset variant of the Anthropic envelope fixing 429 + rate_limit_error + a canned message. Regression: preset status/type drift. Variation over the P0 envelope contract, so P2.

Provider-parameterised auth-error builder asserted for the "openai" argument; message/type/code are the same fields already pinned by the P0 OpenAI envelope. Regression: the provider argument being ignored. Variation, so P2.
uncertainties: Only the "openai" provider argument is exercised; the anthropic/default branches of this overload are unasserted here.

rationale: Preset variant fixing 401 + invalid_request_error/invalid_api_key over the OpenAI envelope. Regression: preset drift. Variation over a represented contract, so P2.

Pins the structurally different OpenAI error envelope (error.message/type/param/code, no top-level type). Regression: emitting the Anthropic shape for OpenAI would invalidate OpenAI error tests. A second provider family is a distinct wire contract, not a variant of the first, so it earns its own P0. Demoted from P0 under the coverage-informed directive: RespondWithAnthropicError already drives the builder-plus-dispatch path, so a second provider envelope is breadth of data over one path rather than a new path. It stays P1, not P2, because the OpenAI envelope is structurally different (error.message/type/param/code, no top-level type) and the Anthropic test cannot detect an Anthropic-shaped body being emitted for OpenAI.
Preset variant fixing 429 + rate_limit_error over the OpenAI envelope. Regression: preset drift. Variation over the P0 OpenAI envelope, so P2.

Provider-less overload of the same builder: asserts the generic message text and a numeric retry_after body field. Regression: the default branch falling back to a provider shape. Variation on the header/body contract already pinned at P1, so P2.

Only test asserting the mock emits a Retry-After response *header* with the requested value alongside the provider-shaped body. Regression: dropping the header would make backoff-honouring tests unable to observe a delay hint. Header emission is a distinct contract from body shape, so P1.

Same per-request advancement as RespondWithStatusCodeSequence, exercised through the preset that hardcodes 503/429/200. Regression: the preset drifting from the documented retry pattern. A preset over an already-represented mechanism, so P2.

Asserts the handler advances one recorded status per request (503, 429, 200) and returns the success body only on the third. Regression: a non-advancing index would make every retry/backoff test pass on the first attempt. Distinct dispatch mechanism beyond the P0 envelopes, so P1.

Asserts the timeout provider honours the request CancellationToken so a 50ms client timeout cancels a 30s mock delay. Regression: ignoring the token would hang every timeout test for the full mock delay instead of failing fast. Cancellation guard protecting the principal operation, so P1 not P2.
Opposite branch of the timeout provider: the delay elapses and a 408 is returned. Regression: returning 200 or skipping the delay. Variation on the P1 cancellation contract, so P2.
uncertainties: Asserts a wall-clock lower bound (>=45ms) measured with DateTime.UtcNow; coarse timer resolution could in principle make this flaky, unverified here.

rationale: Distinct helper serialising objects into data: payloads with camel-free property names as written. Regression: a serializer policy change would silently reshape every JSON SSE fixture. Separate entry point, so P1.

Distinct helper: plain strings plus one event name, with ids auto-assigned 1..n. Regression: dropped or non-monotonic auto ids. Separate supported entry point, not a variation of the SseEvent path, so P1.
Boundary: omitting the event name emits no event: field at all. Regression: writing an empty event: line. Variation on the CreateSimpleSseStreamHandler contract, so P2.

Pins the SSE wire framing this fake emits (text/event-stream, no-cache, keep-alive, id:/event:/data: lines) including an event with neither id nor event type. Regression: malformed framing would make every SSE parser test read a stream real providers never send.
Boundary on the P0 framing: embedded newlines become one data: line each. Regression: emitting a raw newline inside one data line, which breaks SSE parsing.

Cross-component: an instruction chain posted to TestSseMessageHandler produces an OpenAI-style SSE stream whose final data line is exactly "data: [DONE]". Regression: a missing terminator would hang streaming consumers.
uncertainties: The per-line JSON loop at :246-266 catches JsonException and only logs a warning, so this test does NOT prove the non-terminal data lines are valid JSON; only NotEmpty and the [DONE] terminator are actually asserted.

rationale: Boundary asserting id and id_message stay separate: an instruction with only id yields empty IdMessage. Regression: a convenience fallback would emit the step id as user-visible text.
Combination: two sentinel directives as separate chain steps keep their own id_message. Regression: merging steps. Extends contracts already represented.
Boundary distinguishing an explicit empty messages array (kept, because reasoning is present) from the fully empty instruction dropped at P1. Regression: over-eager skipping.

Distinct message form: a literal {"text":...} yields ExplicitText with TextLength null, separate from the length-generated text_message form. Regression: collapsing the two would make scripted exact text unreproducible.
Combination of four already-represented message kinds in one instruction, asserted positionally. Regression: reordering or dropping one kind when mixed.
Variation: two tool calls in one message parse in order. Regression: keeping only the first tool call. Extends the tool_call contract already pinned at P0.

Pins the depth-aware end-tag scan: a literal inner <|instruction_end|> inside a tool argument must not terminate the outer chain, and the nested chain survives verbatim in ArgsJson. Regression: naive first-match truncation returns null and silently drops the whole scenario. Important failure handling on the principal parse path, so P1.

Empty instruction objects are dropped rather than yielded, so surviving steps shift index. Regression: emitting a no-op step would desynchronise every index-based assertion downstream. Distinct filtering rule, so P1.
Single-step variation of the reasoning-only case already covered by the P0 baseline's first step. Regression: reasoning-only instructions being skipped.
Combination of reasoning plus a text_message in one instruction, both already represented by the P0 baseline. Regression: reasoning suppressing the message list.

Broadest baseline: a 4-step chain covering reasoning-only, tool_call with and without id_message, and text_message, all indexed in order. Regression: any shift in step ordering or field mapping breaks every test-mode scenario that scripts a provider.

Introduces the directive-to-sentinel mechanism: system_prompt_echo maps to ExplicitText "__SYSTEM_PROMPT__" with TextLength and ToolCalls null. Regression: a renamed sentinel silently turns an echo probe into literal output. First representative of a distinct message family, so P1.

Parses the server_tool_use / server_tool_result message family and correlates them by tool_use_id across a 4-message chain. Regression: dropping either would make server-side-tool provider scenarios unscriptable. Distinct message family, so P1.
Third sentinel directive (__TOOLS_ECHO__), distinguished from tools_list only by which sentinel string is produced. Regression: the two directives collapsing to one sentinel.
uncertainties: The test comment describes runtime behaviour (descriptions surfaced alongside names); the assertions only check the sentinel string, not any emitted description.

rationale: Second sentinel directive (__TOOLS_LIST__) over the mechanism represented by system_prompt_echo. Regression: sentinel rename.
The distinguishing negative for the matcher: differing model returns false. Regression: an always-true matcher would pass both flexible/exact positives, so without this the positives prove nothing.
Direct-unit positive for exact mode on byte-identical JSON. Regression: exact mode rejecting identical input. Extends the matching contract already exercised through the handler, so P2.
Direct-unit restatement of the flexible-matching behaviour already pinned at P1 through the handler. Regression: extra properties defeating flexible mode.

Variation of the P0 playback path with a tools array present and a tool_use response block. Regression: a tools payload defeating flexible matching. Combination of contracts already represented, so P2.

End-to-end baseline of the record/playback middleware: a matching request is served the recorded response body with 200. Regression: broken playback silently turns every recorded-fixture test into a live-call or a failure.

Through the full handler, extra request properties (max_tokens, temperature) do not defeat matching on model+messages. Regression: over-strict matching would break recordings whenever a caller adds a parameter. Distinct supported matching mode, so P1.

Unmatched requests throw InvalidOperationException naming "No recorded interaction found" instead of returning a default response. Regression: a silent fallback would let fixtures drift from recordings undetected. Important failure handling, so P1 not P2.

Boundary: a missing store file yields an empty set rather than an IO failure, so requests fail with the same "No recorded interaction found" error already pinned at P1. Regression: throwing FileNotFoundException at Build time.
uncertainties: The name claims an empty data set is created; the assertion only shows no recorded interaction is found, not that a file is written.

rationale: Cross-feature: CaptureRequests and WithRecordPlayback compose, and the captured body deserialises to a typed Anthropic request with the expected model and first message. Regression: one middleware consuming the request stream so the other sees nothing.

Cache keys are content-derived: identical requests collide, differing content does not, and keys are 64-char uppercase hex. Regression: a key that ignores request content would let one recording serve every request. Distinguishing pair, so P1.
requirements: reflection-private-api (resolves RecordPlaybackMiddleware.GenerateCacheKey by name via BindingFlags.NonPublic)
uncertainties: Bound to the internal type name "AchieveAi.LmDotnetTools.LmTestUtils.RecordPlaybackMiddleware" and method name; a rename breaks the test for reasons unrelated to the contract.
IsValidHexString at :459 accepts only 0-9 and uppercase A-F, so it additionally pins hex casing.

rationale: Boundary: a default (Undefined) JsonElement yields the literal sentinel key "undefined-request" rather than throwing. Regression: a NullReference/InvalidOperation during key generation.

Capture and response middlewares compose: the request body is recorded once and a JSON response still reaches the caller. Regression: a capture middleware consuming the body stream so the responder or the caller sees nothing.
uncertainties: Despite the name, no assertion observes relative ordering of the middlewares; only that both had an effect.

rationale: Both matching modes asserted with a positive and a negative each on the same inputs, so an always-true or always-false matcher fails. Regression: mode selection being ignored.
The distinguishing negative for the ignore-sibling-properties rule: a differing content text must not match. Without it the P1 positive is compatible with a matcher that ignores content entirely.

Message comparison is limited to role and content deep-equality: differing sibling properties (extra_property, model) do not break a match, including structured content with a base64 image block. Regression: whole-object equality would break every recording after an unrelated field is added.

Content-shape routing: a JSON array argument selects the SSE branch (text/event-stream plus [DONE]). Regression: mis-routing would silently give streaming tests a non-streaming response. Half of the distinguishing routing pair, so P1.
uncertainties: Also pins that the array is emitted as ONE data line, not one per element; the comment at :412 states this is intended.

rationale: The other half of the routing pair: a JSON object selects application/json. Without it the array case is compatible with an always-SSE responder. Regression: routing collapsing to one branch.
uncertainties: Only the content type is asserted; the response body is never read.

rationale: Builder-side SSE contract: SSE headers, one data: line per item, terminated by "data: [DONE]". Regression: a missing terminator hangs streaming consumers. Distinct from FakeHttpMessageHandler's SSE path, so it needs its own coverage; P1 under the builder's P0 envelope baseline.
Variation contrasting with RespondWithJsonOrSSE: passing items individually yields one data: line per item. Regression: collapsing items into one line. Extends the represented SSE contract, so P2.

File-backed SSE playback: an on-disk Anthropic SSE transcript is replayed with SSE headers and its event lines intact. Regression: buffering or re-encoding a recorded stream would corrupt provider streaming fixtures. Distinct supported source (file, not in-memory), so P1.

Captured bodies round-trip into the real OpenAI ChatCompletionRequest type including Union-typed message content, role enums and the tools array. Regression: a capture that cannot be deserialised makes every request-shape assertion in the repo fall back to substring matching.

Demonstration case re-asserting tool name, description and property types already covered by ToolCapture_ShouldProvideStructuredAccessToToolData, with a single-tool payload. Regression it adds: number-typed schema properties reported correctly.
uncertainties: Written as an illustrative comparison; its assertions largely restate the P1 case above.

rationale: The Anthropic side: GetAnthropicRequest exposes tools with name, description and input-schema introspection (HasInputProperty / GetInputPropertyType), including negative answers for an absent property. Regression: introspection helpers that always answer true/null.

Reasoning plans emit thinking_delta then signature_delta then content_block_stop, asserted by index ordering rather than mere presence. Regression: an out-of-order or missing signature delta breaks Anthropic thinking-block consumers.
A plan ending in a tool call streams a tool_use block and a stop_reason of "tool_use". Regression: reporting end_turn would make agent loops stop instead of executing the tool.
uncertainties: Assertions are substring Contains over the whole SSE text, so they do not pin which block carries the stop_reason.

rationale: Empty template test body with no arrangement, action or assertion. It can detect nothing beyond the test project loading and xunit discovering a fact.
uncertainties: Leftover project template scaffold; asserts nothing. Flagged for the lead as a candidate for deletion, but this task does not modify product tests.

rationale: A pre-cancelled token exits as some OperationCanceledException rather than burning the full budget and reporting a timeout. Regression: cancellation misreported as a stalled condition. Guard on the principal operation, so P1.
An already-satisfied condition is evaluated exactly once and does not sleep the poll interval. Regression: a sleep-first loop makes the poll interval a floor on every wait, taxing the whole suite.
requirements: wall-clock-timing (asserts elapsed < 5s against a 10s poll interval)

rationale: The distinguishing positive for the P0 timeout case: a condition true only after several polls completes without throwing. Without it a Wait that always throws would still pass the timeout test. Demoted from P0 under the coverage-informed directive: the never-holds test drives the fuller span set of the same Wait.Until loop (polling plus failure-message construction). It stays P1 as that test's non-vacuity partner - a Wait.Until that always threw would satisfy the timeout test and only this positive case detects it.

The central contract: a wait whose condition never holds throws TimeoutException naming the description, the caller member and WaitTests.cs. Regression: a silent-on-timeout wait makes every caller's subsequent assertion vacuous.

The IAsyncDisposable overload delegates to the same bounded path, asserted through a disposal that blocks until released. Regression: an unbounded convenience overload. Variation on the P0 teardown contract, so P2.
Same guard on the IAsyncDisposable overload, ParamName "subject". Regression: an unguarded overload.
Argument guard: a null delegate raises ArgumentNullException with ParamName "teardown". Regression: a NullReferenceException at an unrelated site.

A teardown abandoned at the ceiling and faulting afterwards has its fault marked observed, so no UnobservedTaskException reaches the finalizer and gets misattributed to another test in a parallel run. Cross-cutting stability contract, so P1.
uncertainties: Relies on GC collecting the abandoned task within three forced collections; a non-collection would make the DoesNotContain assertion pass vacuously.

rationale: Ordinary-case half of the discriminator already pinned at P1: a non-TimeoutException fault passes through with its message intact. Regression: wrapping every disposal fault.

Discriminates a ceiling breach from the subject's own TimeoutException: the inner message survives and the ceiling wording is absent. Regression: type-only catch relabels every internally timing-out disposal as a deadline that never fired.

Baseline for the second public surface: ForTeardownAsync bounds a non-returning disposal and names the subject, member and file. Regression: an unbounded teardown hangs the whole run with no attribution.

Boundary: the default overload resolves to DefaultTeardownTimeout, read back out of the message, and the two defaults are asserted distinct. Regression: the teardown path silently inheriting the poll default.
requirements: long-running (deliberately elapses the full DefaultTeardownTimeout every run)

rationale: The same guard on the async overload's independent throw site. Regression: fixing only the sync overload leaves this one raw.

A throwing observed supplier is caught and reported inline, so the TimeoutException (with its name and call site) still reaches the caller. Regression: the supplier's exception replacing the timeout entirely.
Same append asserted on the async overload's separately written throw site, which the sync test cannot reach. Regression: a mutation dropping the append from only this overload.

The observed-state diagnostic is appended verbatim as "Last observed: <value>." on the sync overload's timeout. Regression: dropping it forces every reader to reproduce a stall to learn what the wait saw.
Boundary of the observed-state feature: without a supplier no dangling "Last observed" clause appears. Regression: an empty clause in every legacy caller's message.
Boundary on the evaluate-before-sleep rule already pinned at P1: a zero budget still evaluates once. Regression: a failure that never actually looked, indistinguishable in logs from a genuine false.
The Func<Task<bool>> overload is a separately written code path; asserts both success and a named timeout on it. Regression: an async overload that never times out or never names the wait.
A throwing condition surfaces its own exception rather than being converted into a timeout or retried silently. Regression: a swallow inside the shared helper hides the real fault from every caller.
Boundary: the diagnostic supplier is only paid for on the failure path. Regression: an expensive supplier evaluated on every successful wait.
The non-throwing overload returns false on timeout and true on success in one method, so a constant return value cannot pass. Distinct public API alongside UntilAsync, so P1.

After the fail-fast the unit does not reappear in nextExpectedAction and its spawn correlation is cleared. Non-retryability is a separate property from failing: a failure that re-surfaced would have the controller respawn the same unsupported mode forever. P1.

Demoted from P0 by the prefix rule: on the maximum-coverage front at rank 21, but outside the 8-declaration prefix (1016 spans covered, 0 exclusive). The contract it pins is unchanged and still distinct — "An observed background spawn receipt fails the task terminally, surfaces the node's onFailure route, and writes the same stable reason into all three sinks: the output _error marker, the tas" — which is why it lands at P1 and not lower; coverage is source-span granularity, not assertion granularity. Its full prior argument is retained in tierRevisions.

A non-receipt spawn result on the same entry point validates and records its payload. This is the distinguishing positive: a guard that rejected every ObserveSpawnResult would satisfy both fail-fast tests and break the only supported spawn mode. P1.

Raised to the exclusiveSpans floor: it is on the maximum-coverage front at rank 37 and holds 16 span(s) no other measured declaration reaches. Dropping it would leave those product spans with no exerciser at any tier. Its own contract — "An injected result whose agent id was never correlated is surfaced as unmatched rather than throwing or being applied" — argued P2 as an extension of a represented contract; the floor lifts it to P1 without claiming it is a distinct primary behavior.
uncertainties: The declaring class states ObserveInjectedResult is dormant in V1; the tier assumes that comment is accurate and was not verified against the production call sites.

rationale: Bracket indexing works on its own and with a property continuing after the index, at two different indices so an off-by-one would show. forEach results are arrays, so this is the shape real templates bind against. P1.
A single two-level property walk; the simplest navigation step, subsumed in practice by the array/property mixed path. P2.

Demoted from P0 by the prefix rule: on the maximum-coverage front at rank 91, but outside the 8-declaration prefix (74 spans covered, 2 exclusive). The contract it pins is unchanged and still distinct — "One assertion per root channel — inputs, state, notes and the bare step scalar — covering the whole binding surface every prompt template and condition path is written against" — which is why it lands at P1 and not lower; coverage is source-span granularity, not assertion granularity. Its full prior argument is retained in tierRevisions.
uncertainties: outputs is exercised only through the array-navigation test, not here.

rationale: Four distinct absent shapes return null: a missing leaf, an unknown root, a property read off a scalar, and the empty path. The scalar-then-property case is the one a naive walk would throw on. P1.

item, index and count are null outside a loop — and the fixture's state deliberately also holds a 'count', so this proves a bare loop-local does not silently fall through to a same-named state field. P1 for the shadowing case.
Past-the-end and negative indices return null rather than throwing; a template binding an index that a short result did not produce must render empty, not abort the run. P1.
visits.<node> resolves to the count and an unvisited node resolves to 0, not null; loop guards compare against visits, and null would make every ordered comparison false and disable the guard. P1.
A loop context exposes item (navigable into), index and count while the outer channels stay resolvable through it, so a derived context adds locals without shadowing or dropping the shared state. P1.

Demoted from P0 by the prefix rule: on the maximum-coverage front at rank 147, but outside the 8-declaration prefix (461 spans covered, 2 exclusive). The contract it pins is unchanged and still distinct — "At the step budget a normal advance throws with a message naming the budget and the escape target and the position is unchanged, while routing to onBudgetExhausted succeeds even though the c" — which is why it lands at P1 and not lower; coverage is source-span granularity, not assertion granularity. Its full prior argument is retained in tierRevisions.

With no onBudgetExhausted declared the advance proceeds and the step increments, while the projection still flags exhaustion and carries no escape key. A rail that refused unconditionally would deadlock every definition without an escape, which the escape-present test cannot detect. P1.

At the budget the projection reports budgetExhausted true and the escape target. The flag is already asserted in the no-escape case and the escape name in the refusal message, so this is the positive variation of a surface both neighbours already reach. P2.
all is true only when every child is, proven by an all-true and a one-false pair; short-circuiting to the first child would pass a single-child test but not this one. P1.
any is true when one child is and false when none are; the mirror of the all composite already pinned, with the true case deliberately in second position. P2.
not negates its child and the composites nest three deep (all containing any and not), which is what proves evaluation recurses rather than handling only a flat level. P1.

empty is true for an empty string, an empty array and an absent path but false for a populated string, with nonEmpty asserted as its complement; treating absent as non-empty would route past a gate meant to wait for data. P1.
uncertainties: The name promises an object case but the fixture has no empty object, so that arm is unexercised.

rationale: Demoted from P0 by the prefix rule: on the maximum-coverage front at rank 164, but outside the 8-declaration prefix (105 spans covered, 1 exclusive). The contract it pins is unchanged and still distinct — "Equality is numeric, not token-shaped: 5 equals 5.0, 5 does not equal 6, and Ne mirrors it" — which is why it lands at P1 and not lower; coverage is source-span granularity, not assertion granularity. Its full prior argument is retained in tierRevisions.

Raised to the exclusiveSpans floor: it is on the maximum-coverage front at rank 136 and holds 2 span(s) no other measured declaration reaches. Dropping it would leave those product spans with no exerciser at any tier. The launch description states that a started status is success, tells the model not to launch a replacement, and points at Check and Wait. Steering text against a real failure mode, but three substring checks on a description. P2.

With the only slot held by a gated run, a second launch returns workflow_capacity as an error payload rather than throwing backpressure at the caller. A workflow authored in the flat step DSL is translated, validated and started through the real handler, returning status started. The behavioural counterpart of the advertised schema: advertising the DSL is worthless if the handler only accepts the internal node form, which is the shape that used to fail. P1.

An agent step with no agent or prompt is rejected as invalid_workflow at the tool boundary rather than starting a run that can do nothing. On its own contract this is the DSL-shaped variant of the invalid-definition mapping; it is at P1 by the exclusiveSpans floor, holding 3 spans nothing else reaches, and the translation path it fails on is distinct from the node-form path.

The first launch succeeds and a second on the same id returns duplicate_workflow. Asserting the first is not an error is what stops the pair passing on a provider that refuses everything. P1, and it holds 3 exclusive spans.

A definition with no terminal maps the manager's validation exception to an invalid_workflow error payload. The exception-to-code mapping is what turns a launch failure into something the model can act on. P1, and it holds 3 exclusive spans.

A sync launch returns a non-error payload whose JSON carries status completed and the workflow id back. The primary success shape of the tool, and echoing the id is what lets the caller correlate later Check and Wait calls. P1.

The static ToolNames list equals the names the provider actually advertises. Hosts keep this family out of sub-agent inheritance by that list, so a tool advertised but missing from it leaks workflow-launch capability into every inheriting child. Equality in both directions is what makes the list trustworthy as an exclusion key. P1.

For both Check and Wait, a guessed id returns unknown_workflow whose text lists the ids that would have worked and names the agent_id namespace mistake. A bare unknown_workflow leaves the model with no move except guessing again or launching a duplicate. P1.

Past the cap the message says "showing N of M" and keeps the first ids in ordinal order. A silently truncated list is worse than none: the agent concludes its id does not exist and launches a duplicate workflow. On its own contract this extends the unknown-id message; it is at P1 on that reasoning and also holds a span no other declaration reaches.
WaitWorkflow's description contains "open-ended", the caveat that stops an agent blocking its whole turn on a long run. A single substring check on prompt text. P2.

WaitWorkflow with no arguments at all returns invalid_args rather than waiting on an empty id. On its own contract this is a required-argument boundary that would argue P2; it is at P1 by the exclusiveSpans floor, holding 2 spans no other measured declaration reaches.

A number-as-string timeout, which some models emit, and a ~57-day value both succeed against an already-terminal workflow, exercising the string and clamp paths of the timeout reader through the real handler. Rejecting "5" would make the tool unusable for those models; failing to clamp faults the wait. P1, and it holds a span no other declaration reaches.
uncertainties: The workflow is already terminal, so the clamp is exercised only on a path that returns immediately; nothing here proves the clamped value is actually used as a deadline.

rationale: A negative number, a negative number-as-string and a non-numeric string are all rejected with invalid_args rather than collapsing into an unbounded wait. Silently treating a bad timeout as "no timeout" turns a typo into a wait that never returns. P1, and it holds 6 exclusive spans.
Wait on an unknown id returns unknown_workflow. The second tool through the same mapping the Check case covers, and the Theory over both tools already pins the richer message. P2.

The class doc used to enumerate the other three writers and omit this one, which is how the hole stayed invisible. P0 as the component baseline: the single writer whose silent failure defeats the resolution contract the other rows pin, in a component that had no P0. No coverage capture exists for this row.
requirements: in-process only; the resolver is a test lambda, no directory or collaboration layer
uncertainties: No coverage capture exists for this branch's rows; the P0 stands on the contract, not on rank or prefix.
